#6402. Nearly a billion people face heatwaves and wildfire smoke in the same year

Heatwave wildfire smoke days now reach about 916 million people a year, and the heaviest burden falls on countries rarely linked to fires.

Most research on overlapping heatwaves and wildfire smoke has focused on the United States.

A global analysis now shows that people in Zambia, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Malawi experience the most days each year when these hazards coincide.

Between 2000 and 2019, about 916 million people a year lived through at least one such day, and the number grew by 287 million every decade. The reason is mostly more heatwaves, not more smoke.

Yao Wu of Monash University‘s School of Public Health and Preventive Medicine led the count with Yuming Guo and Shanshan Li, in collaboation with researchers from Peking University and the University of Tasmania.

The team matched daily temperatures to estimates of fire smoke in the air, square by square, on a grid about 17 miles (28 kilometers) wide.

The researchers then overlaid population maps to estimate how many people were exposed.

Overlap days per person rose from 1.0 a year in the first decade to 1.7 in the second.

When the team split that growth into its parts, 70.5 percent came from people living through more overlap days and 29.5 percent from population growth.

In an interview with Earth.com, Wu explained what that increase means.

“In other words, the problem is growing mainly because people are experiencing these two hazards together more frequently, not simply because there are more people,” Wu said.

Heat explains most of that. Heatwave days increased in 87 percent of the squares on the map, but smoke days increased in only 28 percent of them, mostly in North America.

So a larger share of smoky days now coincides with a heatwave, while the share of heatwave days that also carry smoke has barely moved.

The two hazards also showed a clear timing pattern.

Across the globe, the chance of a smoke episode starting began to climb about two days before a heatwave began, and it peaked on the heatwave’s first day.

A smoke day, in this count, was any day when fine particles or ozone in the air exceeded the World Health Organization’s daily guideline.

At least half of that pollution had to come from landscape fires, a category that includes forest fires, grassland fires and the burning of crop waste.

A heatwave meant at least two consecutive days with temperatures above the local 90th percentile – hotter than 90 percent of days in the reference period.

That is the most lenient common definition, and the team chose it to catch as many hot days as possible.

Africa accounted for about 39 percent of all person-days of overlap, with one person-day representing one person exposed for one day.

People in low-income countries averaged 4.4 overlap days a year, against 0.4 in high-income countries.

That gap widened over the two decades, because the low-income countries also had the fastest increase.

Five countries accounted for half of all person-days between 2010 and 2019: the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Indonesia, Mexico, Brazil and Russia.

A different pattern emerged when the team compared annual exposure per person.

Zambia ranked highest that decade, averaging 28.8 days a year, followed by the Democratic Republic of the Congo at 24.3 and Malawi at 21.7.

“These findings highlight that some of the countries experiencing the greatest exposure are not necessarily those receiving the most international attention for wildfires,” Wu told Earth.com.

Asked by Earth.com which country’s trend surprised the team most, Wu named Cambodia.

It ranked 40th in overlap days per person in the first decade, at 1.6 days a year, and ninth in the second, at 12.1 days.

“What makes this particularly noteworthy is that Cambodia experienced substantial economic growth during this period, yet exposure to these overlapping environmental hazards also increased sharply,” Wu said.

Economic development, Wu said, does not necessarily translate into less exposure.

The Democratic Republic of the Congo showed the largest absolute rise, from 11.8 overlap days per person a year to 24.3. Europe and Oceania saw slight declines that were too small to separate from chance.

Wu’s advice for such a day is to guard against both hazards at the same time.

Check the local heat and air quality warnings, limit outdoor activity and especially hard exercise, and stay somewhere cool with clean air.

Air conditioning and air filtration help, and so does drinking enough water.

“The challenge is that protective measures for heat and wildfire smoke can sometimes conflict,” Wu said. “For example, opening windows may help cool a home but can also allow smoke indoors.”

For a household with neither air conditioning nor a filter, Wu suggested shading the windows and cutting indoor heat sources.

Another option is a public space that offers both cooling and cleaner air. Older adults, children and people with existing health conditions may need particular attention, Wu added.

The study counted exposure, not illness. It did not track anyone’s health, so it reports how many people breathed smoke on a hot day and nothing about what happened to them afterward.

Earlier work suggests that heat and smoke together may do more harm than the two added separately.

The smoke figures are also estimates from a computer model of the atmosphere, checked against ground monitors where they exist.

The model handles the height of a smoke plume imperfectly, which can overstate pollution near a fire and understate it downwind. Carbon monoxide was left out of the count.

And the record stops at the end of 2019. Wu said the heatwaves and fires since then “raise concerns that combined exposure may have continued to increase, particularly in low-income countries,” but the team can’t yet put a number on it.

The next step is to use these maps to study how combined exposure affects health, especially in countries that have received little research attention.

The findings could also help shape warning systems that address heat and smoke together.

The full study was published in the journal Science Advances.

The sale of the Nanotyrannus "Jodi" for over $47 million shines a stark light on the commodification of Earth's history. By selling dinosaurs off to the highest bidder, we lose what makes them valuable in the first place.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Dinosaurs are more than extraordinary specimens with massive price tags. They are irreplaceable snapshots of our planet's history and our own human journey. When scientifically important fossils are reduced to luxury commodities, we are robbed of the evidence that makes them valuable in the first place.

On Oct. 27, a 19.6-foot-long (6 meters) skeleton of Nanotyrannus lancensis known as "Jodi" was sold at Sotheby's in New York for $47,255,000, far exceeding its $6 million to $9 million estimate. The buyer and seller were not identified. It was the latest in a string of multimillion-dollar dinosaur auctions, following the $50.1 million sale of a T. rex (Gus) in July and the $44.6 million sale of a Stegosaurus (Apex) in 2024.

Fossils like Jodi, Apex, and Gus belong in public collections, where they can contribute to science and remain accessible for future generations. Not in the hands of private collectors.

There are three main reasons why. First: Fossils are evidence, not objects. A dinosaur's bones can reveal how it grew, moved, fed, and lived. They preserve traces of injury and disease, help reconstruct ancient ecosystems, and offer clues about the "rules of life" governing our world that scientists are still learning to interpret.

Jodi illustrates exactly why access to physical evidence matters. For nearly half a century, paleontologists debated whether Nanotyrannus was a distinct dinosaur or simply a juvenile T. rex. A lack of well-preserved fossils available for study only fueled the uncertainty. And then a remarkable specimen, once in private hands, moved into the public trust.

The fossil was uncovered in Montana in 2006 alongside a Triceratops. Dubbed the "Dueling Dinosaurs," it took until 2022, and an appeal in the state's Supreme Court, for the remains to be acquired by the Museum of Natural Sciences so they could be fully studied. This research provided a powerful new perspective, arguing that Nanotyrannus lancensis was a distinct dinosaur and, moreover, that a second species of Nanotyrannus once roamed the American West.

When access relies on a private owner's permission, repeatability is not assured, and science cannot proceed. A specimen might be available today but inaccessible tomorrow.

This hypothesis has big implications for the health of ecosystems before one of Earth's most severe extinction events — but it currently rests on the scant few Nanotyrannus specimens housed in public collections. Specimens like Jodi could uphold or dethrone it. Without access, we, and Jodi’s true identity, will remain in the dark.

It is hard to overstate the irony of Jodi's sale: a specimen recently listed as a juvenile T. rex now captures the world's imagination, and commands double the price tag, as a "Nanotyrannus." Yet if a similar fate had befallen the Dueling Dinosaurs and they had remained in private hands, we would not have known for certain that Nanotyrannus ever existed.

Scientific progress depends on researchers being able to compare specimens, test hypotheses, and revisit earlier conclusions. When access relies on a private owner's permission, repeatability is not assured, and science cannot proceed. A specimen might be available today but inaccessible tomorrow. This is why access to the evidence must endure.

This brings us to the second problem with privately owned dinosaurs. Digital scans cannot replace the original fossil.

Three-dimensional scans and digital models are powerful tools. We use them to measure bones, compare anatomy, share information, and educate the public. But digital models capture only the most superficial aspects of a fossil's story.

The auction took place on Oct. 27, with Jodi eventually selling for around five times the top estimate.

To understand dinosaur growth, we examine microscopic structures inside fossilized bone through a technique called bone histology. We also analyze the chemistry of fossils to investigate diet, migration patterns, and metabolism. Such work requires physical samples, not just images of a bone's surface. We also need contextual data about the surrounding sediments, preservation mode, and ancient environment in order to explore questions about the ecosystems in which the animals once lived. Much of this information is lost in the rush to excavate and prepare fossils as quickly as possible for the auction block. It can never be reclaimed.

We cannot predict what novel technologies future researchers will employ to make new discoveries from old bones, or even which questions they will ask. Technology will continue to advance, bringing analytical methods we cannot anticipate. A scan made today does not guarantee that researchers will have the physical evidence needed for tomorrow's discoveries. Digital access should complement preservation of original specimens, not justify losing it.

Finally, private ownership cannot guarantee lasting public access. Yes, some private collectors financially support research and education and donate specimens they purchase. Those contributions are valuable. But the issue is not whether an individual owner is generous; it is whether access is guaranteed over time.

A temporary loan is insufficient. A loaned specimen can be withdrawn, sold, or inherited by someone with different priorities, situations that are becoming increasingly common in the U.S. and abroad. By contrast, a fossil deposited in a responsible public research institution is documented, cared for, studied, and made available to future researchers and educators in perpetuity. The question is not whether people should be able to admire dinosaurs; it is whether the evidence that helps us understand them will remain available to everyone.

Nor should museums consider selling scientifically important fossils to cover operating shortfalls. Collections are not ordinary financial assets to liquidate when budgets tighten. Selling an irreplaceable specimen provides a one-time payment while sacrificing future scientific potential. Museums need sustainable funding for collections care, research, and education, not pressure to trade away the very resources they exist to preserve.

Jodi's sale is complete, but the fossil's long-term future remains uncertain. With the buyer's identity undisclosed, the public cannot know what arrangements, if any, will ensure continued access for researchers and educators. We hope the new owner will make Jodi available for scientific study and public education, through permanent placement in a public research institution. But hope is not a substitute for a guarantee.

There is a better way to support paleontology. Enthusiasts who want to share in the excitement of discovery can fund fieldwork and research, endow curatorial positions, strengthen museum collections, or donate important fossils to public institutions where we can all learn from them.

Dinosaurs inspire wonder because they connect us to a world vastly different from our own. But their importance extends far beyond their power to captivate us. They are part of our shared natural heritage and an irreplaceable record of Earth's history.

We should measure a dinosaur's worth not by the price it commands at auction, but by the knowledge it can help us build, and by whether we preserve that opportunity for generations to come. Earth's history belongs to all of us, not to the highest bidder.

Editor's note: This article was updated on Nov. 4 at 8.22 a.m. ET to correct the year the Museum of Natural Sciences acquired the Dueling Dinosaurs.

She is also an Associate Research Professor at NC State University, President of the Jurassic Foundation, and Chair of the Ethics Committee for the Society of Vertebrate Paleontology. Her work champions transparency, inclusivity, and public access to science.

Kristi Curry Rogers is the DeWitt Wallace Professor of Biology and Geology at Macalester College in St. Paul, Minnesota. A vertebrate paleontologist, her research focuses on the evolution, growth, and biology of dinosaurs, particularly giant sauropods. She has conducted extensive fieldwork in Madagascar, Argentina, Zimbabwe, and North America studying the fossil record of Cretaceous dinosaurs and the ecosystems in which they lived. She is the President-Elect of the Society of Vertebrate Paleontology.

#6400. Planting billions of trees is harder than climate pledges make it sound

Poverty, hunger, and insecure land rights could limit efforts to plant new forests and remove carbon from the atmosphere, a global study finds.

Plant enough trees and they pull carbon out of the air, which is why most national climate pledges lean on new forests.

But planting forests takes money, secure access to land, and conditions that allow trees to survive.

A new global analysis shows how poverty, hunger, insecure land rights, and weak governance overlap with opportunities to remove carbon through new forests.

About 73% of that potential lies in countries facing medium-to-high social and economic barriers.

Wenkai Bao, a geographer in the Department of Geography at LMU Munich, led the study.

Julia Pongratz, a professor there who also works at the Max Planck Institute for Meteorology, is a co-author.

The analysis identifies patterns in where planted forests remain standing, but it does not establish what caused those differences.

Bao’s team began with more than 200 published case studies of tree-planting projects and pulled out ten things that kept getting in the way.

Then it built 78 machine-learning models to ask which of the ten best explained, country by country, how much planted forest is actually standing today.

Five economic factors accounted for about 69% of the combined importance assigned to the ten barriers.

Poverty came first, at a quarter of the total, and food insecurity second, at a fifth.

The cost of planting, the size of the forestry workforce and the state of forest roads trailed behind them.

Insecure land tenure and weak governance came next, at about 11% and 10%. Forest policy on its own barely registered, at 4%.

More policies did not reliably mean more forest.

The relationship with poverty emerged only above a high threshold. Beyond that point, higher poverty was associated with less standing planted forest.

The models were run at the country level, because most social and economic data exist only that way.

The models assessed existing planted forests using four measures, including total area and the share of land physically suitable for forest growth that had been planted.

Of the 78 models, 27 explained at least half the variation between countries, and the team worked from those.

It then checked the results against swapped-in datasets and against planted forests that excluded commercial plantations, and the pattern held.

Common development scores did not work as substitutes.

When the team swapped in GDP per person or the Human Development Index for the tree-specific measures, the models got much worse at explaining where forests stood.

The team laid its constraint scores over existing maps of where new forests could remove the most carbon.

About 73% of that potential sat in countries with medium-to-high constraints, and so did about 70% of the highest-potential hotspots.

The split runs along the line between the Global North and the Global South.

Europe has few constraints and little room for new forest. The tropics, where Africa’s forests and the Amazon sit, hold most of the room and most of the constraints.

The promises already made under the Paris Agreement are where this matters.

The ten countries with the biggest tree-planting pledges account for nearly 90% of all pledged area, the authors wrote. Ethiopia, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Colombia face high constraints, with poverty as the main one.

India falls in the medium tier mainly because of food insecurity, while limited forest-road infrastructure is Canada’s main barrier.

In India, the authors wrote, decades of large planting programs have failed to raise canopy cover or help local livelihoods.

Pongratz said the stakes run through every net-zero plan.

“To reach greenhouse gas neutrality, we will have to at least triple the global amount of CO2 that we remove from the atmosphere by 2050,” she said.

“Additional forest cover will play the dominating role while we scale up technological removal options.”

The constraints don’t all pull the same way, and one example in the paper is Vietnam. Its poverty level is relatively high, yet it ranks among the countries with the most secure land tenure.

It has also planted and kept a large area of forest over recent decades, and the authors suggest the secure tenure is what made the difference.

Brazil shows the reverse, and it is not among the poorest countries.

When it relaxed its Forest Code and field enforcement fell away, carbon emissions from the Amazon rose sharply in 2019 and 2020, the authors wrote.

There is a cost to getting this wrong beyond lost carbon. In the case studies, failed projects took land from poor households without replacing their income.

In some places, people burned the planted area to be hired again for the replanting.

Bao put the prescription plainly. “Credible climate strategies must pair afforestation and reforestation with efforts that strengthen livelihoods, rights, and institutions,” Bao said.

The models find patterns, not causes. They were built on forests planted mostly for timber and conservation, because deliberate planting for carbon removal is still rare.

Carbon prices or changing diets could reshape the constraints in ways the data can’t show.

Success was measured as planted forest still standing. It wasn’t measured as carbon stored, wildlife returned or livelihoods improved, which the authors list as the next indicators to add.

And the overlay map shows where risks and potential coincide, not how much carbon is lost to them. It can’t say how much of the hoped-for carbon removal will fail to happen.

Tracking changes in planted forests alongside social and economic conditions could help researchers test which barriers directly affect planting success.

The full study was published in the journal One Earth.

#6399. Scientists Cracked the Code on a 400-Year-Old Padlock. What It Was Protecting Is Still a Mystery.

An engineer peered inside the brass lock and found a four-letter puzzle to open it. Unfortunately, it’s not locking anything anymore.

A 16th-century brass padlock that secured treasure aboard the Ann Francis—an English merchant vessel used for smuggling—went down with the ship when it wrecked off the Welsh coast in a wild December 1583 storm. The padlock then lay hidden in the sand of Margam Beach for centuries. Even after a metal detectorist found it among the wreck’s hoard, its combination stayed a mystery—until now.

“It’s not every day you get to solve a 400-year-old mystery,” said David Williams, a research associate at Cardiff University, in a statement.

Williams works at the Musculoskeletal Biomechanics Research Facility at Cardiff University’s School of Engineering, where he typically uses his skills to study anatomy. This time, however, he looked deep inside the padlock, using micro-CT scanning to examine its internal mechanism without damaging it. The scans revealed the four-letter combination that opened the lock: ANCE.

“By creating a detailed 3D image of the internal mechanism, I could see how the notches lined up with the letters and identify the exact combination,” Williams said. “We normally use this technology to study bones and other biological structures, so investigating a 400-year-old padlock was certainly a first for us.”

After Williams sent the combination to the experts at Amgueddfa Cymru–Museum Wales, which cares for the Ann Francis treasure hoard, he could only wait to find out whether it worked. “Getting the message that we’d cracked it was incredibly satisfying,” he said.

Alastair Willis, the museum’s senior curator for numismatics and the Welsh economy, said Elizabethan combination locks aren’t uncommon in Britain, but this one was in exceptional condition. Because the lock came from the Ann Francis, it can be dated precisely, which made it a “unique find and the code a tantalizing mystery to solve.”

Still, questions remain. “Of course, now we’ve solved it we are left wondering if the code meant something to its owner,” Willis said. The team is also left to wonder exactly what the lock secured.

The lock’s modern story began in 1996, when metal detectorist Peter Hughes discovered the wreck and part of the treasure it carried. For the next 21 years, Hughes kept returning to the beach, uncovering artifacts whenever dredging and storms stripped away layers of sand. His finds include rare gold coins from the reign of Ferdinand and Isabella of Spain, a boatswain’s whistle and other 16th-century coins. Among them was the padlock, which he found in 1999.

“When I found the lock, I was immediately astonished by the incredible workmanship and its astonishing condition,” he said. “When I moved the ring dials of the combination they turned with ease after over 400 years beneath the sands and I was left in disbelief. I also remember being left excited at the prospect of finding wonderful things from the treasure chest it once locked.”

Experts can only guess at what the chest held. Hughes found a collection of Spanish silver coins and two coin weights near the padlock, so the lock may have protected those objects. Or it may have secured a chest of other valuables, such as documents, that didn’t survive the wreck or the centuries that followed.

The lock and the rest of the Ann Francis hoard are on display in the Tides of Treasure exhibition at the National Waterfront Museum in Swansea.

That leaves one last mystery: What, if anything, did ANCE mean?

Tim Newcomb is a journalist based in the Pacific Northwest. He covers stadiums, sneakers, gear, infrastructure, and more for a variety of publications, including Popular Mechanics. His favorite interviews have included sit-downs with Roger Federer in Switzerland, Kobe Bryant in Los Angeles, and Tinker Hatfield in Portland.

#6398. Riskier decisions may offer an early warning of heavier drinking

Changes in phone game decisions predicted heavier drinking the following month in a yearlong study of people with alcohol use disorder.

Alcohol has a reputation for making people take risks. But a yearlong study of people with alcohol use disorder found that changes in decision making came before heavier drinking.

When participants took certain risks in phone games, they drank more the following month. Heavier drinking, however, did not predict riskier choices the next month.

The researchers tracked changes within each person rather than simply comparing heavier and lighter drinkers.

Most participants had mild or moderate alcohol use disorder, making them a potentially important group for early intervention.

Hilmar Zech, a postdoctoral researcher at University Hospital Würzburg and TU Dresden in Germany, led the study with Lorenz Deserno.

The team also included co-authors at Charité in Berlin and the Central Institute of Mental Health.

“This temporal direction was specific and was not observed vice versa, even after accounting for the amount of previous drinking,” Deserno said.

The researchers followed 603 people, ages 16 to 65, for one year. All of them met at least two of diagnostic criteria for alcohol use disorder.

In the study, a standard drink held 0.4 ounces (12 grams) of pure alcohol. The participants averaged about three of those a day, and about five on the days they drank.

Every two days, each person reported what they had drunk from a list of 19 options, from a small beer to a bottle of wine.

Every four weeks, they also played four five-minute games on their phones. In one game, fruit fell from a tree and the player tapped to collect it, unless the fruit turned brown.

In another, red circles flashed on a grid and the player had to remember their positions. Those two measured self-control.

The other two measured decision making. In a gambling game, the player chose between a sure amount and a coin flip, in versions built around wins, losses, or both.

In a card game, the player could pay to flip over cards before guessing which of two face-down rows added up to more.

The mixed version offered a possible win or a possible loss on the same flip. In months when a person took that gamble more often, that person drank more the next month.

The card game gave the same result. When someone flipped fewer cards before guessing, they drank more in the month that followed.

In the loss version, the link was reversed. In months when a person gambled more to avoid a sure loss, they drank less the following month.

Earlier studies had compared people with alcohol use disorder with people without it at a single point in time.

Those studies found a similar pattern: people with alcohol use disorder were more willing to gamble when both winning and losing were possible, but less willing when the gamble involved only potential losses.

As far as Zech’s team knows, no study had watched those shifts come and go inside one person and then watched the drinking follow.

“We found that monthly fluctuations in aspects of decision making predicted subsequent alcohol consumption,” Zech said.

Next the team ran the question backward. Did heavy drinking in one month change how a person played the games the next month?

The researchers found no evidence of that pattern.

The forward link also held after the team accounted for the fact that one month’s drinking resembles the last.

In a second analysis built for a year with many zero-drink days, the loss-version result held up, and the other two showed the same direction with more uncertainty.

The two self-control games did not follow that pattern.

A person’s monthly ups and downs in avoiding rotten fruit or remembering circles had no link to the drinking that followed.

Working memory still mattered, but between people instead of within one person.

Participants who could hold more circles in mind drank less on average over the year than participants who could hold fewer.

Cameron Carter, editor-in-chief of the journal that published the study, explained why experimental tasks matter.

“Decision making and cognitive control cannot be accurately examined through interviews or self-reports and instead require experimental tasks,” Carter said.

The effects were small. Zech’s team wrote that they are likely too small to be useful in a clinic yet.

The team had also planned to split the sample in two, with the second half meant to confirm what the first half found.

The pattern was clear in the first half and not in the second, although the two halves did not differ from each other when the team compared them directly.

The team also split the 603 people into random halves 1,000 times. The direction came out the same every time, and a group of about 300 was often too small to detect the effect.

Of the 603 who started, 218 dropped out early. Their data stayed in, and leaving was not tied to how they played or how much they drank.

The self-control games may simply have been played too rarely. A few studies that checked several times a day did find self-control dipping before drinking, though only under certain conditions.

Once a month may be too rare to catch that. And a study that watches people without changing anything can’t say that the risky choices caused the drinking.

Whether a game score can predict heavier drinking over the following week, rather than month, is still an open question.

The team envisions an app that flags changes in a person’s risk-taking score and offers automated support or prompts them to seek help in person.

Whether that approach would work remains untested.

The full study was published in the journal Biological Psychiatry: Cognitive Neuroscience and Neuroimaging.

#6397. A drug-free diabetes treatment? An implant lowers blood sugar in mice

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The device banishes extra blood glucose by converting it to a compound excreted in urine

Excess blood glucose (shown in white in this illustration) is the target of a new experimental device. In mice, the sugar gets converted into a compound which the kidneys can excrete in urine.

NEMES LASZLO/SCIENCE PHOTO LIBRARY/Getty Images

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

A wireless implant that clears excess sugar from the blood could someday offer a drug-free way to treat type 2 diabetes and obesity.

In mice with both conditions, the under-the-skin device brought high blood sugar back to normal within 60 to 90 minutes of being switched on, researchers report October 22 in Science. After six weeks, the treated mice lost up to 10 percent of their body weight and had lower triglycerides, a type of fat in the blood.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Diabetes affects about 830 million people worldwide. Conventional type 2 diabetes treatments like insulin and GLP-1 drugs require careful dosing. Even experimental diabetes-controlling implants still rely on the hormone insulin, which clears sugar from the bloodstream but doesn’t rid the body of it, says Martin Fussenegger, a bioengineer at ETH Zurich. The new implant instead removes glucose from the body without added drugs, genes or living cells.

The 3-centimeter-long device contains a catalyst made of gold flakes and platinum particles on spongelike graphite. When electricity powers it, the catalyst converts glucose into gluconate, a compound that is easier for the kidneys to flush out in urine. With less glucose available for energy, the body may turn to its fat stores instead, Fussenegger and colleagues suspect. In mice, that shift showed up as higher blood levels of chemicals released when fat breaks down, such as ketones. “This system kind of targets the root cause, which is the energy surplus by glucose in the body,” Fussenegger says.

The implant works like an automatic sugar-removal system: A wearable glucose monitor detects high blood sugar levels and sends readings through a smartphone that switches the implant on. When levels return to a safer range, it switches off. The automated system ran for two weeks in eight mice. The catalyst itself remained able to convert glucose after up to three months under their skin, though the study didn’t establish how long the entire device would last.

And it’s still unknown how well the device would work in people. “This is a potentially promising method,” says David Klonoff, an endocrinologist at Sutter Mills-Peninsula Medical Center in Burlingame, Calif., who was not involved in the study. “But the risks are significant and must be carefully ruled out before it can be safely tested on humans.”

Researchers need to determine how much gluconate the kidneys can clear, Klonoff says. If it builds up, it could disrupt the body’s acid-base balance, causing symptoms such as nausea or confusion; excreting it could also deplete electrolytes such as sodium and potassium, he notes.

Scaling up the device is another challenge. Humans consume about 250 grams of carbohydrates daily, compared with two grams for mice, Klonoff estimates. Meeting that demand could require a much larger implant or multiple devices, he says. In a lab test, a larger device cleared nearly all glucose from about 5 liters of solution, roughly an adult’s blood volume, though not a full day’s glucose intake.

Fussenegger’s team plans to test the device in pigs and sheep before considering human trials. If proven safe and effective, it could offer an alternative to existing diabetes treatments and a new weight-loss option for people regardless of whether they have diabetes, he says.

The best time to see meteors during the Southern Taurid meteor shower is coming up soon.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

One of autumn's best opportunities to see brilliant "fireballs" arrives overnight Wednesday and Thursday (Nov. 4-5) during the Southern Taurid meteor shower.

Although the Southern Taurids are a minor meteor shower that produces only a handful of "shooting stars" each hour, it occasionally features exceptionally bright meteors called fireballs, which can briefly light up the night sky. According to NASA, fireballs are meteors at least as bright as Venus.

The Southern Taurids are active for several weeks in fall and peak Oct. 14, but the American Meteor Society expects the "fireball swarm component" to peak around Nov. 4-5.

Meteors can streak across any part of the sky, but for this meteor shower, they appear to radiate from the constellation Taurus, which will rise in the eastern sky as night falls and climb higher as the night progresses. That makes the hours around midnight a good time to look for shooting stars. However, unlike major meteor showers such as the Perseids (which peak Aug. 12-13) and the Geminids (which peak Dec. 13-14), the Southern Taurids have a broad peak, so there's no need to be outside at an exact time.

The Southern Taurids are the first of two fireball-rich meteor showers to be visible this month. The Northern Taurids will peak overnight on Nov. 11-12, giving stargazers another chance to spot a fireball. Both meteor showers result from dust and debris left in the inner solar system by Comet 2P/Encke striking Earth's atmosphere.

Discovered in 1786, Encke is a massive comet, measuring 2.98 miles (4.8 kilometers) in diameter, according to NASA ‪—‬ around one-third the size of the object thought to have killed the nonavian dinosaurs. Encke orbits the sun every 3.3 years, one of the shortest known orbital periods of any comet in the solar system. Scientists theorize that Encke is one of many fragments of a giant comet that broke apart 20,000 to 30,000 years ago.

After the Southern and Northern Taurids, the next meteor shower will be the Leonids, which peak Nov. 17-18 and produce around 15 shooting stars per hour, and the Geminids, which peak Dec. 13-14 and can deliver up to 120 shooting stars per hour close to the peak.

It's best to watch meteor showers with the naked eye, but a good backyard telescope will serve you well in the months to come. As the long nights of winter kick off in the Northern Hemisphere, skywatching opportunities abound — including four consecutive supermoons from Nov. 2026 to Feb. 2027.

#6395. Quantum experiment reveals signs of long-predicted protected states

A tiny junction on a topological insulator seemed to close and reopen its energy gap, a key prediction of topological quantum computing.

A quantum computer’s biggest weakness is that its information is easily disturbed. One proposed fix is to store it in quantum states that are built to resist local disturbances.

Physicists in Germany have now seen signs of those states behaving the way a 2008 theory said they should.

The team detected the signals inside a junction just 50 nanometers wide, on a sliver of material that conducts electricity along its surface.

Earlier evidence in this kind of material was indirect, the authors wrote. This time, they directly measured the energy spectrum inside the junction.

Jakob Schluck and Ella Nikodem did the experiment in Yoichi Ando’s lab at the University of Cologne. Theorists in Fabian Hassler’s group at RWTH Aachen University ran the simulations.

Both groups belong to the ML4Q cluster, which works on quantum computing. What they saw fits the prediction, they wrote, but it isn’t yet proof of it.

“It is super exciting to see our experimental results align so well with theoretical predictions,” Nikodem said. “This is very encouraging in terms of future applications in quantum computing.”

The material is a topological insulator. It insulates on the inside and conducts along its surface.

On that surface, each electron’s spin is tied to its direction of travel, which helps protect it against being scattered straight backward.

Liang Fu and Charles Kane predicted in 2008 what would happen if a conventional superconductor were laid on top of such a surface.

The surface should become a new kind of superconductor, one that can host quantum states called Majorana zero modes.

Those modes are candidate building blocks for quantum bits that local disturbances can’t easily corrupt.

The theory makes a specific prediction for a junction between two superconductors on that surface.

As the difference between their superconducting phases reaches half a cycle, the energy gap inside the junction should close and then reopen.

The team made the junction from two strips of aluminum on a flake of the material BiSbTeSe2, 10 to 20 nanometers thick.

The strips end about 50 nanometers apart, roughly a thousandth of the width of a human hair. An aluminum loop connects them, so a tiny magnetic field sets the phase.

Two gold electrodes, separated from the junction by a thin oxide layer, probe the energies of the states inside it at different locations.

The device was cooled to 50 millikelvin, just 0.05°C above absolute zero.

With no magnetic field, the readout showed an energy gap, with two peaks at 130 microelectronvolts on either side of zero.

As the field tuned the phase toward the halfway point, the peaks slid inward and merged into one broad peak at zero. The gap appeared to close.

A stronger field reopened it, and the pattern repeated every 230 microtesla, which matched the device’s dimensions.

A conventional junction keeps its gap at that point unless its electrons pass through perfectly, the authors wrote, and a surface whose electrons can’t reverse guarantees exactly that.

Simulations of a simple model in Aachen reproduced the crossing.

The pattern held while the team swept a gate voltage from -20 to +20 volts, which shifted the surface electrons’ energy by at least 40 millielectronvolts. It also held in a second, nearly identical device.

In stronger fields of 5 to 6 millitesla, the closing showed up only at particular spots.

The theory says the field should pin the zero-energy state to points along the junction. The two electrodes saw the gap close at different times as those points moved past them.

“Understanding how superconductivity interacts with the distinctive electronic properties of topological insulators is essential for assessing their potential for topological quantum computing,” Ando said.

The experiment can resolve energies down to about 30 microelectronvolts, and a gap smaller than that would look closed.

Electrons passing through at 95% or better would produce what the team saw, by its calculation.

That makes topological protection a plausible explanation, the authors wrote, but leaves room for alternatives.

The authors also weighed two ordinary explanations. A stray state in the insulating layer produced a similar signal in one device, but only at a single gate voltage, unlike the stable pattern here.

Disordered junctions can close a gap through a few open channels, which the authors considered unlikely to hold up across such a wide gate sweep.

The predicted transition into a topological superconducting state has not yet been confirmed.

It would show up as a change in the junction’s parity, and charge sensing could detect that.

Higher-frequency measurements could sharpen the energy resolution.

The authors also calculated that niobium electrodes, which tolerate fields of around 100 millitesla, could hold well-separated Majorana modes.

“To demonstrate the topological phase transition in this system, we need to improve the experiment’s energy and time resolution – this is the next step on the roadmap of the Ando lab,” Schluck said.

Until then, the gap in this junction looks closed. Whether it truly closes is the question the next device has to answer.

The full study was published in the journal Science Advances.

#6394. MacBook Pro M6 Laptop Review: An Iterative Update to the Computer I Recommend for Most People

Even without any major new features, the newest MacBook Pro is an impressive step in laptop design, just as it’s been for the past few years.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Apple made big waves in laptop land last month when it announced that it would do something it had previously refused to consider: release a MacBook Pro with a touchscreen. That new high-end laptop, which features the M5 Pro or Pro Max chip, looks very interesting, but it also starts at $2,899 for the 14-inch model with base specs. Touch aside, it’s a very expensive laptop for creative professionals who want Apple’s PROLED XDR display, which features a very bright, color-accurate, tandem-OLED panel. (At least on paper. We haven’t tested it yet.)

For those of us who just want a really great all-around laptop and are willing to pay a lot, but not that much, Apple also released a new version of the standard MacBook Pro, which features a new M6 processor. It’s far less exciting than the touchscreen model: The new processor brings improved performance, especially for running local artificial intelligence (A.I.) tasks, plus minor upgrades like better wireless connectivity. But broadly, the standard 14.2-inch MacBook Pro remains unchanged from last year's M5 model.

The MacBook Pro has been the laptop I've recommended most for a long time—at least since Apple started making its own processors. The MacBook Pro M5, specifically, is excellent and has been my go-to computer all year. This year’s improvements do more than enough to maintain that distinction. The touchscreen MacBook Pro may draw eyeballs (and fingers), but Apple’s “beginner” MacBook Pro is the no-nonsense machine most “pro” (and spec-nerds) really need.

The MacBook Pro is mostly the same as ever; the big difference is the new Apple M6 chip. It features a 12-core CPU and 12-core GPU, versus a 10-core CPU and a 10-core GPU in the M5 version, immediately hinting at a power bump before I even powered the notebook up. It also utilizes Apple’s new two-nanometer architecture, first introduced in the A20 mobile chipset found in the iPhone 18 Pro and the iPhone Duo. That means more power efficiency without sacrificing the performance gains.

It also gave Apple room to double the size of the “Neural Engine” in the chip, which powers local A.I. work. The so-called dual neural engine delivers a noticeable speed boost for A.I.-related tasks. If your work routine involves them now or in the near future, this is probably the strongest reason to switch from an M5 MacBook Pro. Running A.I. agents locally is part of the future of productivity, so this nerdy M6 upgrade matters.

To put the M6 chip’s power in numerical terms, I ran single- and multi-thread tests in Maxon Cinebench—a CPU benchmarking tool—to stress the chip. It delivered single- and multi-thread scores of 806 and 5,519, respectively, significantly surpassing the 733 and 4,187 scores I got out of the MacBook Pro M5. In real life, I didn’t notice a difference after switching to the newer model. For comparison, though, when I opened a selection of 25 RAW image files, I noticed the M6 variant finished the task a fraction of a second faster.

Overall, I couldn’t slow down the M6 MacBook Pro as my go-to computer. This is a pro-grade machine, so it made quick work of my typical workflow. My “everyman’s stress test” involves switching between a web browser with 10 to 15 open tabs, navigating an endless stream of emails and instant messages, editing images in Pixelmator Pro, and creating this review in Apple Pages, all while streaming lossless audio from Apple Music. This MacBook Pro performed superbly during that routine, as expected, because it's built for tougher work like video editing and running a small library of AAA Mac-compatible games at high specs. And it works efficiently, too: The battery averaged about 40 percent after a full day of work and play, so you can be somewhat loose about daily charging.

While Macs don’t make ideal gaming rigs because of platform compatibility limits, the MacBook Pro is still a capable macOS option. During my testing, it ran Cyberpunk 2077 Ultimate Edition with in-game graphics set to high without a hint of hesitation.

Even if there is only a smattering of new features beyond the chip, many returning features and components from last year’s MacBook Pro are still, frankly, best in class and worth considering if you’re upgrading from an older Mac or a Windows system.

While it isn’t an OLED touchscreen, the MacBook Pro’s bright 14.2-inch mini-LED Super Retina XDR display is sharp, bright, and plenty capable for any creative task. For streaming video and calls, you get a six-speaker audio system with Dolby Atmos spatial audio support and a 12-megapixel webcam with Center Stage, both of which perform admirably for their everyday purposes.

If you’re an Apple fan, a common reason to buy a MacBook Pro over the MacBook Air is access to a wider range of ports: The M6 features the same set as previous models, including a trio of Thunderbolt-compatible USB-C ports, an HDMI output, and an SD card reader, to go with the mandatory MagSafe charging connector.

Okay, so what’s actually new on the M6, though? There’s better wireless connectivity, with both Bluetooth 6 and WiFi 7 support. (These are a bit overdue from Apple, as always, but they're two good reasons to buy this year’s model instead of an older one on sale.) If you have a WiFi 7 router, you should see a big improvement in your internet speeds—streaming music and TV, downloading apps and games, and even video calls all run very smoothly.

The MacBook Pro M6 is my favorite laptop of the year so far, and it will likely be the new top pick in our “best laptops” guide. That said, it’s not for everyone: It costs a cool $2,000 (which, unfortunately, is pretty standard for mid- to high-powered laptops in 2026). Given that price, I recommend it as an upgrade for folks who want or need a high-performance laptop: Creatives, tech lovers, gamers, and anyone who can’t help but bristle at compromising on specs. If you fall into any of those categories, this machine's design, performance, and battery life are impeccable, and Apple’s track record of macOS support is flawless.

I will say specifically that you should not buy the M6 MacBook Pro if you bought the M5 last year, unless you’re deep into working with A.I. The dual neural engine could be a game changer if deep A.I. work is a big part of your life, but I wouldn’t say you need it for everyday A.I.-enhanced search and chat.

Finally, we come back to the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Touchscreen. Setting aside the fact that we haven’t tested it yet, I think it’s a tough sell unless you work in visual arts because of the price tag. It’s an incredibly powerful machine, I’m sure, but $900 (or more) is a lot to pay when the M6's display is also excellent. Some might scoff at the lack of an OLED panel, but I can guarantee most people will be fine without it for one more upgrade cycle.

#6393. Where does consciousness begin? A new theory points deep inside the brain

A brainstem theory of consciousness puts the raw feeling of being 'you' in the brain's ancient stalk, and its evidence starts with pain.

Consciousness is often linked to the cortex, the brain’s wrinkled outer layer, which helps us understand language, recognize faces, and make plans.

Yet a surgeon who stimulates that layer in an awake patient can reliably produce flashes of light, sounds and tingling, and almost never pain.

Two neuroscientists now propose that the raw feeling of being conscious, the “me inside,” is computed somewhere else.

Their candidate is the brainstem, the ancient stalk at the base of the brain. The case rests on pain, and it is a hypothesis built from existing evidence, not a new experiment.

The cortex, they propose, works out what you are seeing and hearing. A small region of the brainstem, they suggest, determines what you consciously feel.

Marshall Devor of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem laid out the argument with Mark Baron, a neurologist at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center and Harvard Medical School.

Close your eyes and cover your ears, they wrote, and “you” are still there, 100 percent.

Electrical stimulation of the visual cortex during brain surgery makes patients see light. Stimulating the hearing and touch areas produces sounds and tingling.

The neurosurgeon Wilder Penfield wrote in the 1950s that only very rarely did a patient use the word pain to describe the result of cortical stimulation. His observation still holds, Devor and Baron wrote.

One exception is a buried cortical region called the insula.

In one study the authors cite, stimulating it evoked pain at only 8 of 313 sites tested. Painful auras are rare in epilepsy too, and pain rarely appears in dreams.

Damage points the same way. Lesions in the visual cortex cause blindness, but no cortical removal anywhere prevents pain from being felt, Penfield wrote.

If anything, the authors wrote, cortical strokes can add chronic pain rather than remove it. Yet those patients remain conscious.

Small strokes in specific parts of the brainstem can cause coma, the authors note.

Devor and Baron also point to adults with hydrocephalus who remained fully articulate despite extreme thinning of the cortex.

The authors’ own rat work narrows the spot. The team microinjected a a general anesthetic into rat brains 828 times, in 182 animals.

The drug knocked the rats out only when it landed in one small region of the brainstem, the mesopontine tegmentum.

Doses of 10 billionths of a liter or less worked within seconds, and injections slightly off target didn’t.

Destroying that small area alone did not cause coma, so the authors wrote that it isn’t the whole story.

Somewhat larger lesions centered on it did, in a region about an eighth of an inch (3 millimeters) by a sixth of an inch (4 millimeters). That region, they wrote, matches where strokes cause coma in people.

In the authors’ model, the cortex does the heavy processing: telling a rhinoceros from a cloud, or a snake in the grass from rustling leaves.

It also works out whether what it sees is good or bad for survival, and it sends that verdict down to the brainstem.

The brainstem circuit then determines which information enters awareness.

If the new input matters more than whatever “you” are attending to now, it marks that stream of cortical processing as conscious.

The rest keeps running unattended, like a self-driving car.

“We humans are sentient robots,” the authors wrote. Pain skips the round trip, because signals from nerve fibers that detect potentially harmful stimuli already flag a threat.

Devor and Baron also offer an evolutionary reason.

The mammalian neocortex had not yet evolved when fish and reptiles emerged, and the ability to feel pain, they propose, arose early as an add-on to escape reflexes.

In their account, the later evolution of the mammalian neocortex built on the brainstem’s existing machinery for conscious experience.

The brainstem theory of consciousness is a framework, not a mechanism.

Hundreds of theories of consciousness exist, the authors wrote, and none of them, their own included, explain how neurons produce subjective experience.

Devor and Baron claim only that the mechanism is biological and that it has one location.

Could a fish, a reptile, or even an invertebrate feel pain without a cortex? The authors suspect so but wrote that there is no sure way to know.

Researchers cannot directly confirm subjective experiences in people or animals unable to describe them. In the rats, the team measured anesthesia and sleep, not feeling.

Devor and Baron propose studying the mesopontine tegmentum and its connections directly.

The lab’s earlier work mapped which of that region’s neurons send axons up toward the cortex and down the spinal cord.

Whether any of those cells carry the signal that turns processing into experience is the question the theory leaves open.

The hypothesis was presented in the journal The Neuroscientist.

#6392. Your voice can now say things you never said

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

AI can replicate a person’s voice. That raises questions about who has the right to use it and what happens when its owner can no longer give consent.

AI technology can create realistic clones of people’s voices. The resulting proliferation of synthetic voices ushers in all sorts of new scenarios, good and bad. “Today, with nothing more than a keyboard and an internet connection, you can type, and you can get an image, a voice, a video of anything, [of] anybody doing or saying anything,” says Hany Farid, a computer scientist at Dartmouth University.

Some of these voice clones are deeply meaningful to people, as in the cases of people who lost their ability to speak. But voice clones can also cause harm, as with scams and deepfakes. And some uses fall into murky gray zones, such as voice clones that “speak” after a person has passed away. What happens to a person’s digital voice after they’re gone?

In this episode of The Deep End: Talk to Me, hear more from Farid, as well as from a former hospital chaplain and AI researcher, and from Jules Rodriguez, a man who communicates with a voice clone. You’ll also hear about a choice Jules made about what will happen to his voice once he’s gone.

Laura Sanders: What’s a voice you like to listen to?

Kate Nilson: That is a great question. I hope my students don’t listen to this. I was having Snoop Dogg read their assignments to me the other day, just because I thought it was funny. But I don’t know if I would say that’s my favorite.

Sanders: That’s speech language pathologist and professor Kate Nilson. And if you’re wondering, this is a real, legitimate thing that anyone can do.

Snoop Dogg audio: Vector mathematics. Think about a car trip. Your displacement from your starting point is a vector.

Snoop Dogg: I’m glad to be the voice of reason so you can focus better, understand more, and enjoy listening to the internet in the voice of Snoop Dogg.

[voices] Hey mom, can I tell you something? Hi. Do you want to talk? That added layer of it being you. Hello? Your voice. Hi. Your voice is you.

Sanders: As we’ve heard in earlier episodes, ultra-realistic voice clones can be extremely meaningful to people who can no longer speak.

Jules Rodriguez: So when I first heard my cloned voice, it felt like I reappeared. When my wife first heard it, she cried because of how close it sounded like me before I lost my voice. I knew of the potential of this technology at that moment.

Sanders: These digital copies of voices have restored connections to their loved ones.

MA Fernandez: You know, the first thing he played for me, I was like chills all over.

Patrick Darling: The first time I performed with the AI voice, I was surprised how physically connected I felt with it.

Sanders: These voice clones have been transformative for people who have lost the ability to talk. But the existence of realistic digital copies of voices has effects that ripple farther out into society.

Hany Farid: So here’s where sort of state of the art is. Today, with nothing more than a keyboard and an internet connection, you can type and you can get an image, a voice, a video of anything, anybody doing or saying anything.

Sanders: That’s Hany Farid. He’s a computer scientist at Dartmouth College and cofounder of Get Real Security, a firm that sorts real from fake. I called him to ask how these voice clones have changed our world.

Farid: If you had asked me, I don’t know, five years ago, is this possible? I would say, yeah, maybe, but not anytime soon. And then all of a sudden, boom, it just came out of nowhere.

I say, is this the same person? Is the AI not only able to make something that is natural, but is it identity preserving?

In many cases, that good comes because these voices are both extremely realistic and extremely good at sounding like a specific person. People want their voice to sound like theirs.

Farid: People with ALS can speak with what sounds like their voice. We’ve seen beautiful examples of that. Translation, right? We can now translate things in real time from any language and it’ll sound like you. I’ve made videos of myself speaking any language I want and it sounds like me, and it’s amazing. Sanders:  What Farid is saying feels especially relevant right now. I’m recording this episode in the fall of 2026, and midterm elections in the U.S. are upon us. Political ads are everywhere. Some of these ads use deepfake audio and video to make opponents say or do things they never did. Here are a few recent examples of deepfakes compiled by the New York Times.

[Audio] Hi, I’m Zohran Mamdani and I’m Kathy Hochul and together, we’re making New York, don’t say affordable. I’m voting for Hochul because she basically gave me an early retirement. They stopped prosecuting people for crime, so now I get to sit back and play Candy Crush all day. Is New York getting a little expensive? I’m Kathy Hochul, and I’ve got just the thing. Clinton lover, Trump hater.

Farid: When you can steal somebody’s likeness, their voice, and their face, you can do some damage. We’re seeing people doing content credential resets at companies. They call up and say, oh, I’m employee X. Will you reset my credential? That’s how they’re now attacking companies. We’re seeing North Korean IT workers penetrating Fortune 500 companies by disguising their voices and their accents and their identities. So lots of bad things, and not unpredictably bad.

Sanders: There are romance scams, political scams, employment scams, money scams of all sorts. Farid was even involved in one himself.

Farid: My voice was cloned by an attacker. I was working a very sensitive case with an attorney. Not many people knew about it. And he got a call from my phone number in my voice talking about the case. And after about three minutes, got suspicious, hung up, called me back. Wasn’t me.

Sanders: Bigger picture, we’ve reached a point where it’s safe to say we can no longer automatically trust digital versions of other people. That applies to the images and sounds on my computer screen as I talked with Farid. Maybe this 2-D picture and sound coming from my laptop is a fake.

Farid: So this two-dimensional version that you and I are sharing now, all right, I can’t control that. That can be stolen. The three-dimensional is right now still me, right? We don’t have the robots that can mimic us. Yet is the end of that sentence.

Sanders: So my interview with Farid was alarming. There are parallels here to any new technology, though. Today, people talk about brain rot from junk online. But remember that television was also going to rot our brains.

[Audio] Its content affects us. So does the sheer weight of the hours we watch.

Sanders: Phones today are the downfall of society, but actual wired telephones encountered really similar resistance when they first started appearing in homes.

[Audio] In Chicago, Sharon Krall’s 15-year-old daughter Angie got so addicted to one teen talk line, she ran up an $850 bill in one month.

Sanders: No big technological advance has escaped this fear.

[Audio] We need teachers who are deeply concerned about how the modern media of communication are changing education.

Sanders: Electricity, bicycles, railways, novels, even the printing press all had their skeptics. So this fear of the new thing has been around a long time. Are synthetic voices created by AI any different? Here’s Karina Nagin from Bridging Voice.

Nagin: Taking off my Bridging Voice hat and just as like a human being in the world, I think there’s a lot of things about AI that I’m very concerned. Deepfakes, the ability to make videos and audio that sound and look just like someone saying something that they’re not saying, I think is a huge, huge concern to our news and public information.

Sanders: Nagin then pivots back to the good, the possibilities here.

Nagin: And then I put on my little hat in my space that I am like, this is how we can harness this to impact people’s lives in our space right now. And I think both conversations need to happen.

Sanders: It occurs to me that I’m seeing the ends of the spectrum here. The stories Farid told me were awful. And the stories that Jules and Casey and others have told me were really, really life-changingly good. Yet these ends of the spectrum are the easy ones. The ones you can look at and say, that’s a horrible way to use this technology. Or that is a powerful and good way to use a voice clone. Between those two poles is the middle ground. That’s the place where Snoop explains cell biology.

[Audio] The membrane separates the material outside the cell.

Sanders: Good, because it’s helping people learn more about mitochondria and who couldn’t use more of that in their lives. Bad, because Snoop never actually said those words, and it’s weird to pretend otherwise.

[Audio] The artists of the Renaissance said that man’s main concern should be for man.

Sanders: There are deepfakes of the late great physicist Richard Feynman delivering famous lectures.

[Audio] The problem is the laws of physics themselves. Let me start with something basic. The next star over from us is called Proxima Centauri.

Sanders: Good because it introduces some amazing physics to people who would otherwise scroll past? Bad because it’s somewhat disrespectful and possibly inaccurate? There aren’t easy answers here. This murky middle gets even murkier with the invention of griefbots. Those are digital versions of people who have passed away. And that means that special voices can keep talking to us long after the body that created them is gone.

I read a poignant post online written by a guy who had lost his dad after years of dementia. He missed his dad’s voice, he wrote, so he cloned it. He paid for the starter pack, submitted three minutes of his dad’s audio, and he wrote, quote, a few minutes later, I had a scarily accurate clone of my dead father’s voice. He goes on to write, quote, my family and I had a good cathartic cry upon hearing the results. I had his cloned voice read the Lord’s Prayer as well as ‘Twas the Night before Christmas. Just hearing his simulated voice again is such a blessing and is helping me in the grief process. End quote.

There are lots of companies now offering this exact thing. A casual search online gets me to a company that sells chats with dead loved ones. There’s a big orange button to click that says bring them back to life. A 2024 documentary called “Eternal You” follows the stories of people as they grapple with this idea. Here’s a little bit of the trailer.

[Audio] We are on the verge of a new era. Hi. It’s like, it’s the funniest thing. It’s like, what’s the first thing you say to someone that’s dead? Like, welcome back.

Sanders: Griefbots or digital avatars of loved ones offer a bridge from the past to the present, a way to remember vividly. But they are also a denial, of sorts, that all life must come to an end.

[Audio] And what I can tell you is that AI really is changing the way that we interact with death.

Sanders: That’s from a 2025 TEDx talk from Dylan Thomas Doyle. He’s a former hospital chaplain, current academic researcher at Northwestern University and self-described philosophy bro. His work explores death and AI.

[Audio] Imagine that you are at a funeral, and you’re sitting there in silent reflection, and all of a sudden, on the back screen in the auditorium, a woman’s face appears. And it’s the face of a woman named Marina. And her hologram, she starts talking to you, and she starts asking you how you’re doing today. And you answer her, and then you ask her a question back. And she responds as if she is still there.

Sanders: I called Doyle to ask about the implications of using technology this way.

Doyle: It was on my radar as a chaplain and a technology researcher, I started thinking through, well, what is the actual impact of this technology on people? So what is it like to hear the voice, in the context of this podcast, the voice of, say, your father who’s passed away while you’re actively grieving their death? And they’re not just repeating what they said or a journal entry in their voice, but like, creating new stories and new relationships through their voice. It gives a lot of people existential ick, is what I’ve heard. And that’s something that I really, I’m curious about.

Sanders: There’s tension here, Doyle tells me.

Doyle: So there’s this push force where you’re like, this is not right. We don’t have the narrative or cultural script to understand what’s going on there. But then as people are beginning to use it, there’s a comfort that comes out of it. So we’re working in that tension space between this comfort that comes, then you’re still dealing with this push away from this technology of it just being weird in a way that people are still grappling with language, I think, to describe.

Sanders: It’s not clear how these types of interactions might affect grieving. They could help or they could hurt.

Doyle: There is this tension between more healthy continuing bonds. So continuing that relationship by, say, writing letters to your dead loved one or, you know, talking out loud to them and continuing that relationship in a positive way that moves us through a healthy grief process and a grief journey. Or hanging on to our relationship with that person to a degree where we can’t actually do any sort of moving on.

Sanders: Doyle points out that we don’t have good data on how many people might be using griefbots.

Doyle: I just don’t want us to get ahead of ourselves when it comes to people like using these. So the capability to do everything we’ve talked about with griefbots is there. But the actual use cases of individuals in their homes using this, it’s still pretty unclear about the adoption of those technologies.

Sanders: But even if griefbots aren’t widespread, the questions they raise aren’t going away. These voices are blurring the lines between a memory and a present-day experience, between alive and dead. Here’s Karina Nagin again.

Nagin: It’s an interesting conversation that we’re having right now of what happens to your voice once you pass away. Some people are starting to integrate this into their wills or their sort of final wishes of, do you want your voice to be able to speak at your own memorial service?

Do you want to have messages saved in your voice that are for your child at graduation that they listen to? Who and when can use that? I think that these are things that people are starting to think about. Who owns your voice? Can your children use your voice to write a speech for their children’s graduation? Or do you want that voice to be deleted once you pass away? Very tricky questions.

Sanders: Rules about who can use voice clones are all over the place. Regulations vary by state and by country, and even companies have their own individual policies in place. There are no clear guidelines, and that makes sense given how young this technology is. Conversations about digital voices and how to use them are inherently very personal. There are as many different takes as there are people. I asked MA if she and Jules had talked about this.

MA: I love that question. Both of us love this question because it’s so important. And we talked about it before he got the trache. Like when he was already using the voice, we were talking about different things in bed at night. And he said, you know, I have a very clear request that my voice like dies with me, basically, that, you know, I ask that you don’t use the voice to keep me alive in any way,  that there’s no… And I was like, 100 percent clear. I hadn’t even thought about that. But yeah, it would make sense to be like, I miss him so much. I want to, whatever or. But no, as far as we’re concerned, his voice dies when he does. And his voice will live on in whatever videos or things we captured, whatever he’s left us intentionally. And that’s as far as that goes.

Sanders: So when Jules is gone, his voice will be gone too. But right now is a different story.

MA:  Well back in 2021, I was writing an Instagram post about something. It was him playing with Skylar in the backyard while he was already like, you know, had trouble with everything, but he was doing what he could. And I asked him like, you know, what, what do you want to caption it? And he just said that, right here, right now phrase, something else, and like right here, right now. And it became our family mantra. It became something that we wanted to just to share and in both a sense of like do the things that you want to do.

And also something that’s always been big for Jules that I’ve admired him articulate is that it’s not just about, oh, just go forward and do all the things and like suck the marrow out of life. It’s like just also, like, settle. Like it doesn’t have to be that extreme, you know. There’s a beautiful thing about that presence and that settling in. And again, with ALS being something where you’re given the diagnosis, which is terminal, it’s basically a death sentence. Most people are given, you know, two to five years. You don’t know where you’re going to fall in that. We’ve known people that have passed away in a year and a half. We’ve known people that are six years in like Jules, but can still kind of walk around, speak a little bit. ALS touches everybody really differently. So you really don’t know what’s coming. And there’s a lot of like forward thinking that you can do that detaches you from being in your life. So how are you here? And then there’s a lot of backwards, you know, reminiscing and grieving about all the things we’ve lost and how we wish things were different. But then that also takes you out of like this moment right now and this part of your story.

Sanders: This part of the story is the important part. Right here, right now.

On the next and final episode of The Deep End, Talk to Me. We’re going to look at what’s next for Jules and Casey and what’s next for the science racing to give voices back to people.

Vikash Gilja: We can see all the pieces coming together. All of the emphasis, capital, quite frankly, talent focused on advancing AI techniques and technologies. You know, our little corner can benefit from it, right? These tools weren’t available even five years ago.

Sanders: What’s next for the human voice?

Samantha Brosler: Of course, ultimately, we’re hoping to expand this to even larger vocabulary and more range of body movements across the whole body to help allow people more expression in their communication.

This is The Deep End, Talk to Me. I’m Laura Sanders. If you like this podcast tell your friends and leave us a review. It helps the show a lot. Send us your questions and your comments at podcasts@sciencenews.org.
