#6311. Global Airlines Is “Fyre Festival”, Not Virgin Atlantic

Yesterday, a Hi-Fly charter airplane took off from Glasgow bound for New York, with Hi-Fly crews and pilots. If you read the papers, it was purportedly ‘Global Airlines’ maiden flight, even though there’s no regularly scheduled service, the pilots and crew weren’t theirs, they couldn’t legally sell airline tickets on their own website and they don’t have a license to operate.

In 2025, crazy things are par for the course, so that didn’t stop all sorts of promising headlines of a revolution in the skies. This is the airline that promised stunning innovation and joy in the air, and the press gave Global Airlines an early gift, by comparing the story to Richard Branson and Virgin Atlantic. That’s just insane, as you’ll soon read.

In reality, anyone can charter a plane and have Hi-Fly operate it, and anyone foolish enough can pay extra for a custom paint job with their logo, or more financially insane — buy a scrapyard A380 and be on the hook for its maintenance, while paying a third party to fly it.

The whole ‘Global’ pitch was that people love the Airbus A380, hate all the current global airline experiences ( really?) and airline services — and a revolution in the skies, can happen again. It sounded exciting. We all like to dream. Global’s first flight would be the testament to what air travel can be and something passengers love. So, how’d they do?

When Virgin Atlantic launched in 1984, the airline industry had been in a massively “beige” management consultant style, joy killer phase for a decade.

The fun “golden era” aircraft spaces and frills of the 60’s had largely been stripped out and bus travel comparisons were totally fair. Richard Branson’s light hearted approach to service and differentiated selling could shift dollars and votes — and measurably did.

Let me be very clear: that simplicity in differentiation is no longer the case. You cannot shift wallets and put butts in seats just by saying you have a cool airplane alone, or a bar on board (particularly when it’s just a beverage cart that says pub).

From leading (actually real) global airlines, passengers expect, at minimum, the following…

When “Global”, and by Global I really do legally, technically mean Hi-Fly the jet charter company which actually flew the scrapyard plane that “Global” bought, they did NOT have…

Travel blogger Noel Phillips shared some of the trip with his following. The following screen grabs are…. cute?

The truth is, Virgin Atlantic didn’t have nearly as gargantuan of a task in the 80’s as any airline coming to market does today. In the 80’s many airlines were stuck, did lack innovation and had a pool of largely uninspired talent, with no experience outside of the airline vertical. There also wasn’t this whole technology thing, as standard expectation.

That’s all so far from the case these days and most that are specialized in the airline world are wickedly sharp. Most new people I know at airlines now also come from major tech companies, other travel verticals or impactful innovation firms.

Airlines are getting pretty good at this ole’ air travel thing.

A differentiated approach to smiles on board and a little bit of extra focus on fun, food and drinks could really shift minds and mentalities in the 1980’s, but now you gotta back it up, baby.

Everyone likes to feel special and Virgin, forever, has made people feel special at a time without tech. I’d argue Virgin has taught Delta a lot about that, and it’s a contributing factor to Delta’s rise as a premium airline. It didn’t happen overnight, and what looks easy never is.

Getting people to fly with you is now about safety, reliability, excellence in mobile technology, schedule and personalization. Then fine, we can care about which champagne; or caterer or lounge style or airport, and which celebs like it. Yes, these legacy airlines can appear stuffy at times, but my god, can you not marvel at the technology revolution making air travel journeys excellent?

On real airlines, before I even arrive at the airport, I can use the NFC chip in my passport pressed against my phone to validate my document and bypass human interaction. I board a United, or any serious airline flight nowadays and see a notification that my bag is loaded onto a cart to be loaded on the plane, then again when it’s loaded onto the plane!

I hit the wifi and I’m connected sitting at the gate. If for some reason the flight is at all delayed, or connection in jeopardy, I can instantly rebook onto any other service at no charge, without talking to a soul, with just a tap on the app.

Their seag back screens have blockbuster movies, boxsets and everything else you could want for a one hour, or 15 hour journey. It’s all just standard now, not innovative.

The app navigates me through the airport and even tells me when my zone is boarding. AKA – stand the “f” back. The food is at least solid, the beverages are getting better because of their scale (buying power) and there are fewer poor customer service interactions because of how tech forward and seamless journeys are.

All the great, big airlines do this. This is like… baseline for a real player.

Tell me, or ask the Global Airlines CEO, James Asquith, where in the roadmap all of these essentials are? I want to make it clear that their priority for the last three years was a Soho House press conference about serving champagne in economy, maybe, “if they could get the economics right” rather than any of these basic things.

And in the end, they didn’t even deliver on the silly things they prioritized. The first Global flight wasn’t a remotely differentiated take on economy, business or first, as promised. It was 12 year old seats from another lackluster airline, without real refurb and even the long haul dignity of any seat back entertainment, which that airline which scrapped the plane offered.

If Richard Branson was at the helm, they never would’ve let that flight take off. Making a splash means at least doing one thing differently, right? An airline promising total innovation, A380 experience and differentiation cannot launch a flight which does not even meet the basic standards of budget carriers like Norse. You just can’t take off. You innovative something!

Let’s not forget that when Richard Branson formed Virgin Atlantic, he’d already founded a notable brand and number of businesses in the UK, was quite famous, and filed records and company books in a place where they are scrutinized. He was “real”, even if some was bluster. The public could and did use his businesses.

James Asquith’s only claim to fame, other than from the Instagram account he bought followers for, to fake fame — yes, factually — is that he was the “CEO” of Holiday Swap. Omg, so big time!

The business purports to be a home swap company, though there are no financial records of any legal merit in the West, and despite my damndest multi-year attempts, no record of actual customers. Simple use of Similar Web or review sites will help your own conclusions. You can read old blog posts for more musings. The rumors of what laundered through are scary. Maybe a real journalist can find out for us?

I actually think it’s dangerous to the public to compare these two people.

I’ve had the good fortune of meeting Richard Branson many times throughout the years and he’s always been wildly impressive. Wickedly sharp, analytical, funny and personable. It’s easy to put in a good shift for PR purposes, but I’ve observed levels of deep dive knowledge that no setup encounter can protect for — and genuine interest too. He cares about his people and he worries about the details.

I also have many people in my personal life connected to the Virgin Atlantic founder and I know of nothing but admiration and respect for the man, his company ethos and family. Business in the front, party in the back.

My only encounter with James Asquith was when he was fuming that he wasn’t invited on an airlines press trip, slid into my Instagram DM’s wanting me to blast them – and for us to be best buds as we roast a major (actual) global airline. That airline later confidentially told me he was banned from flying, due to his antics. I politely declined and he unfollowed me. It was soooo cool.

I guess if you can’t fly other airlines, you start your own?

So yeah, if you ever feel like putting your life in the hands of an airline without functioning entertainment screens, or WiFi, or regularly scheduled service, or new seats, or a mobile app, or an actual license to fly planes, definitely fly with Global. Oh, and no viable loyalty program either. Forget about earning points from daily spending and turning them into upgrades.

Those other “boring” airlines with all the bells and whistles above are clearly not ready to make travel great, with a new golden age, again.

Gilbert Ott is an ever curious traveler and one of the world's leading travel experts. His adventures take him all over the globe, often spanning over 200,000 miles a year and his travel exploits are regularly... More by Gilbert Ott

His intrusion and snide comment ab0ut Simon Calder was entirely unnecessary. I have little respect for Asquith as it is, he doesn’t seem to actually “do” anything other than post Insta’s of slamming Champagne, and buying an Instagram account for the new venture is downright deceptive. Prove me wrong, I’m all for new carriers, but part of me wants it to fail just because of the insufferable “CEO”.

‘Global Airlines’ reminds me of the line from ‘The Producers’: “Under the right circumstances, a [person] could make more money with a flop than he could with a hit.”

This is why many say “hire for personality and train for skill.” James Asquith has failed this test with his attitude and stands little chance of building a culture within his company that can grow to compete with the likes of Virgin. I was always concerned that this airline was launching without any unique selling points at all. Now to read that what little was brought in from China Southern does not even work: it’s for me very sad to read. Substantial funding was needed to get this far and there seems to have been very little planning around the customer experience. I raised 350k externally to launch my last business, and that was not easy for me to do. So to imagine the capital sums that will be wasted here for all the unforced errors made, it’s so disheartening given it was foreseeable! There are so many case studies, even from Virgin with Virgin Nigeria and Virgin America to review! James Asquith seems to be very lazy and entitled. A great opportunity not afforded to many better qualified people (not me), has been thrown away!

While I agree with everything in this article, I also feel like immediately criticizing new entrants and disrupters is not fair. There is not a single person in aviation that wants to see less A380’s, that want les competition transatlantic, or fewer carriers. I appreciate Global, I appreciate BOOM, and I think it is just as sensational to criticize Global as it is for them to put on a metaphorical Fyre Fest in the sky. This is responsible reporting, but let’s also at some recognize the feat that getting this particular plane in the sky, with people, to NY was. Aviation was built on the backs of visionaries and risk-takers, I hope we will continue to celebrate that spirit.

I’m genuinely surprised that yours seems to the the only objectively credible take on this fiasco. I’ve watched a couple of the first flight review videos and the aircraft and service are laughable, yet the internet is still awash with “great to see!” and “Go Global!”, all blindly ignoring the current capabilities of the competition summarised above as if they don’t matter.

At least it’s given us a good laugh over the last few years but someone is losing money (hard to call anything sunk into this shambles an “investment”) and I imagine the flag carriers will be delighted as it makes them look stellar by comparison. Got to seriously question the judgement of anyone that wanted to get involved with Global. It’s all been smoke and mirrors from day one.

#6310. Getting to Know New York Through Its Sandwiches

“By the end of our time together, I will be asking you again: ‘So, what is a sandwich?’”

An expert-led tour that starts by questioning its own object of inquiry is unconventional. But then, so is our guide. Ben Gollan, known to his Instagram followers as A Man and His Sandwich, has spent the last nine years reviewing sandwiches across New York City. Gollan moved here from Australia in 2016, after nearly a decade as a government lawyer. For about as long, he has run an Airbnb Experience that turns a food crawl into a two-hour pilgrimage to the city’s best sandwich slingers.

It was a pastrami sandwich at Harry & Ida’s, a former deli in the East Village, that turned Gollan into a professional sandwich hound. “It was a fourth-generation Jewish deli that broke every rule of pastrami sandwiches: it was thick-cut and fabulous,” he says as we dash across Bowery. We’re scuttling over from a coffee shop in Cooper Square that served as our meeting point and into the East Village—a neighborhood of contrasts that still manages to connect New York's past and present. There are 12 of us in total, mostly locals, a couple of newer transplants, and just one traveler. “It’s usually mostly visitors, so this is different,” he says.

It’s a great introduction to the city. After all, New York runs on sandwiches, and there’s no shortage of great ones, whether it’s a classic Italian deli sub you’re after or a grab-and-go banh mi. They’re economical, versatile, delicious and, as is the point of Gollan’s tour, telegraph the city’s greatest personality trait—its diversity. So is there such a thing as a New York sandwich? “Not really,” he says, "but the chopped cheese, born in East Harlem, might come closest.”

The Bono at Via Della Scrofa, a small family-owned joint that wouldn't look out of place on the streets of Rome

“We start here because it’s closest to what we think of as a traditional sandwich,” says Gollan, before filling us in on the origins of what is the modern-day sandwich. It involves John Montagu, the 4th Earl of Sandwich, who, in the 18th century, gave his title to the now-ubiquitous food. Gollan loves to talk and think about sandwiches as much as he eats them. “Although I've learned never to trust history, especially when rendered by colonizers,” he muses. “Do we really think it took us till the 1700s to invent the sandwich?”

Named after a Roman street, Via Della Scrofa is the kind of bottega or alimentari you might find in Rome, with a tiny counter selling tiny espressos and focaccia, as well as imported groceries from Italy. “It's small family-owned joints like this that make New York what it is,” says Gollan. While the rest of the group gets to try the Porcodeddena panini (made with porchetta), I’m getting a Bono: grilled eggplants sweetened with sun-dried tomatoes, with arugula and buffalo mozzarella, in a warm roll that’s toasty on the outside and soft and warm on the inside. The bread is perfect—it’s a rosetta (or michetta), a traditional Roman bread roll. I wash it down with a Crodino, a popular non-alcoholic bitter aperitif from Italy.

Around us, the Lower East Side Arts & Culture Open House, an annual event, had taken over the street, adding personality to our time with its bands, pop-up stalls, and lively crowds. Gollan regales us with stories of owner Giovanni Bartocci, describing him as a real character with “a man bun, suspenders, tattoos, and naturally, a Harley," and I look around hoping he'll show up. I ask Gollan why he isn’t eating with us. “I never want to tire of these sandwiches, and if I keep eating them, I will.” The wind picks up and blows over the canvases at an art stall, but the band is undeterred, playing “New York, New York.”

A spicy Pakistani rendition of the chopped cheese at Nishaan

The writer and her chopped cheese sandwich, the chapli kebab replaced with Impossible Meat.

Order: A chopped cheese, but make it desi

An 11-minute walk up 1st Avenue and a few blocks later, we spot our next sandwich spot. A cobalt-blue sign reads Nishaan; bags of rice are piled high along its exterior; and a long line snakes out of what I can only assume is a tiny space inside. Nishaan began as a pop-up at the weekly open-air food festival Smorgasburg and went on to win season 18 of The Great Food Truck Race. While there are other dishes on the menu (elote chaat, mango lassi), it’s Nishaan’s twist on that great New York City bodega staple, the chopped cheese, that many are after: a spice-laden chapli kebab, chopped up on a griddle with peppers and onions, then enhanced with a zingy cilantro sauce and tamarind chutney. When it opened in August 2025, it was one of the most talked-about new restaurants in New York City, which has emerged as a hub for a new generation of Pakistani eateries. “New York belongs to everyone, and so does the sandwich,” proclaims Gollan.

In a city that runs on pastrami, vegetarians like me don’t faze Gollan; he orders me a version with Impossible Meat. We tuck ourselves out of the wind and into an alley and dig in. I can’t stop eating, making a mess as I go along. “Half the fun of a sandwich is the experience of eating it,” Gollan adds.

Regulars love the pho sandwiches at Sunny and Annie’s—sandwiches stuffed to the brim with pho ingredients, minus the broth.

Sunny and Annie’s is a 24/7, 365-day-a-year kind of neighborhood classic with 92 items on its sandwich menu.

“We’re taking a detour,” says Gollan, frantically looking around him. It’s the day of the Tompkins Square Halloween Dog Parade, and the crowds around us are building, as are the dogs in costume—cheese boards, UPS drivers, and, suitably for the occasion, hot dogs. We ditch the idea of cutting through the park and work our way around the revelers.

Our destination? Sunny and Annie’s, a 24/7, 365-days-a-year kind of neighborhood classic that has been open since 1997. There’s no front door here, because there’s always someone around. Inside, past the candy, chips, and dish detergent, we’re greeted by what must be the most extensive sandwich menu I’ve ever encountered, all written out on brightly colored sheets of paper stuck to the glass counter. There are 92 handheld options in total, some named after politicians and celebrities, like the Jackie Chan—bulgogi, cilantro, avocado, lettuce, jalapeños, and onions, served on a roll or hero. There’s also a chicken cutlet sandwich called the Australian. It’s not named after Gollan.

This is not a place to linger, so we keep it moving. Outside, the crowds have thickened, and Gollan instructs us to head to a neighborhood bar called ABC Beer Co., which often features at the end of his tours. As someone who has spent many a night in an East Village bar, I’m disappointed I’ve never been here before. It’s spacious, has a backyard, and is equally welcoming to couples on dates and families with little ones.

The writer's sandwich tour ended at ABC Beer Co, a hybrid beer bar and store with a particular focus on NYC breweries.

Gollan appears with our pho sandwiches, wrapped in spinach tortillas. They smell like pho, taste like pho; only the avocado throws me off.

Some of us get ciders and wine, and the conversation winds back to where we started: So, what really is a sandwich? “I want this to get contentious: bang the tables, let’s have a food fight," Gollan says, egging us on. Hot dogs? Quesadillas? What about a hamburger? A pizza folded in half? Does it have to have a carb? What about a lettuce wrap instead of bread? Gollan briefs us on a famous 2006 Massachusetts lawsuit—White City Shopping Center vs. Panera Bread—which legally answered an age-old culinary debate: Is a burrito a sandwich? The judge ruled that a burrito is, in fact, not a sandwich, clearing the way for the Mexican fast-casual joint to open in the vicinity of Panera Bread. “A sandwich court case is my Roman Empire," he says. “When this question goes to the Supreme Court, I will be there.”

The point of this tour—and the posed question—Gollan says, was never to walk away with an answer, but to open our minds and palates. So, what are Ben Gollan’s own rules for a sandwich, I have to ask. He lists the following:

And then he adds: “Take those rules and throw them in the bin.” And with that, class is dismissed.

The NYC Sandwich Tour can be booked directly on the A Man and His Sandwich website, as well as on Airbnb. Tours run every day of the week, with the exception of Tuesdays and Wednesdays. Ben Gollan, who proudly calls himself the Chief Sandwich Officer, often leads the experiences himself, but he also has co-hosts to help guide fellow sandwich enthusiasts on these two-hour outings. Along the way, guests sample three standout sandwiches—from the classic to the “slightly unhinged”—before finishing up at a bar to settle the debate over what really counts as a sandwich. While my tour focused on the East Village, Gollan also leads sandwich tours around Williamsburg. And word on the street is that he has his eye on opening a sandwich shop of his own one day.

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6309. JetBlue Raises Baggage Fees Again, Now Charges Up To $140 Roundtrip For One Checked Bag

JetBlue has raised checked baggage fees again, and bringing one ordinary suitcase can now add as much as $140 to a roundtrip ticket. With holiday travel approaching, this is another reminder that the fare you see when shopping may be far removed from what your trip actually costs.

JetBlue has increased baggage charges for new bookings made on or after November 3, 2026. The airline’s updated fee schedule lists a first checked bag starting at $50 each way. The price depends on when you travel and when you pay.

For passengers without an included baggage allowance or waiver, these are the new charges within the United States, Latin America, the Caribbean, and Canada. All amounts are per bag, each way:

You can see more particulars here, including pricing for Mosaic elites.

Upcoming peak periods include November 19–January 18. If you booked before November 3, check your reservation for the applicable charges (old rates apply). Here’s the full chart of peak dates over the next year:

That means one suitcase costs $100 roundtrip even at the lowest new rate. On peak dates, it costs $110 when paid in advance or $140 when purchased within 24 hours of each departure.

Consider a family of four traveling over Thanksgiving, with each person checking one suitcase and no baggage benefits.

Pay sufficiently early and the roundtrip baggage bill is $440. Wait until check-in for both flights and it becomes $560.

When does it become cheaper just to buy new clothes at your destination? We certainly try to pack efficiently when traveling with our children, but one standard checked bag per person hardly strikes me as an extravagant amount of luggage, especially for a longer holiday trip.

At these prices, baggage can materially change which airline offers the best deal. A cheaper JetBlue ticket may cease to be cheaper once you add the luggage you actually need…though it would not surprise me to see others follow.

Mosaic 1 members receive one checked bag, while Mosaic 2–4 members receive two. Eligible JetBlue Plus and Premier cardholders receive one bag. Premium-cabin allowances depend on the fare purchased: Base fares include one bag, while standard and Flex premium fares include two.

Those benefits become more valuable every time the underlying fees rise, though it’s still not a loyalty program or credit card product I can get enthusiastic about.

JetBlue’s latest increase pushes the cost of one checked suitcase to $100–$140 roundtrip for passengers without an exemption. For families, the additional expense can reach hundreds of dollars.

Compare the total cost before booking, and if you know you will check a bag, pay more than 24 hours before departure. I want JetBlue to succeed, but charging passengers more to bring their belongings does little to make it an airline people actively want to choose. Quote the contrary, JetBlue is doing a great job of alienating passengers during its great time of need.

Matthew is an avid traveler who calls Los Angeles home. Each year he travels more than 200,000 miles by air and has visited more than 135 countries. Working both in the aviation industry and as a travel consultant, Matthew has been featured in major media outlets around the world and uses his Live and Let's Fly blog to share the latest news in the airline industry, commentary on frequent flyer programs, and detailed reports of his worldwide travel.

Ok, so, get their co-branded credit card, if you check bags, basically. Pays for itself on one RT.

Lol, over 60% of the dates in the next 12 months (Nov 2026-2027) are ‘peak’, including every single day from before Memorial Day weekend to after Labor Day. That’s insanity, and I’m guessing that will only grow over time.

This whole peak day bags cost more is ridiculous. It does not cost JetBlue any more money to load bags on an aircraft on January18th verses January 19th. For the 12 days in February JetBlue wants me to believe it’s costing them more money to process luggage than on any other day within the month of February.

Customers will tolerate different prices when talking about pre-paid verses paying at the airport, but this peak non-peak charge is how you drive customers away because they can see through it and know it’s sham. It doesn’t cost JetBlue more money to load baggage on peak days verses non-peak days.

#6308. Virgin Atlantic Ups The Ante In India, As The World Dials In

This week, Virgin Atlantic celebrates 25 years of flying to India. In Virgin fashion, it’s doing so in style, with a joint announcement among partners Delta Airlines, Air France-KLM, and a new strategic partner IndiGo.

On the sidelines of the IATA Annual General Meeting, basically the UN General Assembly of airlines, the new strategic partnership for India was announced with very interesting nods to the future.

IndiGo carries more passengers in India than anyone else and will connect US and UK/European customers flying Virgin, Delta and Air France KLM onward in India, while also helping fill seats for these European and North American partners, as their own customers head West.

That’s probably a good thing, because with recent service additions, Virgin now flies a million seats a year to India and it sounds like others are piling on more flights too. It’s now one of the largest operators to India.

I’ve been bullish on India as the next great center of the world for a while now. It’s not necessarily that I’m at all intelligent, it’s just based on the fact that India is the world’s largest population. But, when Ed Bastian, Delta’s formidable CEO says it, people tend to listen. Bastian mentioned India being the most important aviation market globally now and signaled a return of direct services for the carrier as well.

Virgin has been a small step ahead, adding service regularly on their Delhi, Mumbai and Bangalore routes. IndiGo chose this alliance over formidable competition and this will certainly be a space to watch as more global airlines and alliances focus on India.

Geo-political activity points to India becoming a new manufacturing super power, in addition to its prolific work in tech, IT and customer service, not to mention blossoming tourism. These kind of globally connected businesses are big business, huge in fact, for corporate contracts and easy onward connectivity to regional sites is essential. The partnership makes sense.

In a somewhat rare and impressive signal of unity and seriousness towards India, Virgin Atlantic made their India crews part of the core Virgin family, rather than as contractors through a third party local company, known in aviation world as a GSA. This means Virgin’s India crews are a part of the full team, with benefits too.

When asked about loyalty implications of the new alliance, Virgin Atlantic CEO, Shai Weiss, noted a mutual passion for using loyalty to enhance guest experience far beyond just the earn and burn of points and miles. For future iterations, they’ve offered the following…

The MoU (memorandum of understanding) also creates a framework for deeper collaboration between the carriers on a bilateral and multilateral basis; contemplates commercial collaboration including network, loyalty, cargo and sales, subject to regulatory approvals; explores areas of non-commercial cooperation including aircraft maintenance, sustainability, training, ground handling; and acknowledges the need to develop advanced collaboration through use of technology to efficiently service joint customers.

IndiGo will provide onward connectivity for Virgin and the other strategic partners to 32 destinations, making it easier than ever to see Udaipur, Jaipur, Mumbai, Kashmir and delights further south in Bangalore and Goa.

I just returned from the lovely Leela Palace in Delhi, as I watched the news happen live.

To me, India is a country of joy. Even people with truly nothing seem to find positivity and it’s generally a way of life here. Hospitality is as warm and steeped in tradition as it comes, too. It’s hot, it’s humid, but it’s an experience unlike any other and that’s something that’s harder to say these days than I’d like.

The food, ugh. I adore. Sure, I’ll take a dosa from the South over a heavy curry from the North most days, but I love both and if you don’t love a good black daahl there’s something wrong with you.

In short, it’s already fairly easy to get to India but it’s about to get a whole lot easier and not just to hub cities too. More seats means more chances to use points, by the way!

Given the dire state of the BA offer with still flaky IT, dirty badly maintained cabins and dysfunctional (if at all) customer services a great option for those in the UK.

#6307. There's a New Luxury Sleeper Train Route Coming to the French Riviera Next Spring

As someone who travels a lot for work, I would give anything to swap a flight for a train—even if that means spending eight hours on the rails.

Thankfully, it's easy to travel Europe by train at nearly any price point. And although I am a big fan of modern high-speed routes, the most romantic way to see the continent is certainly aboard one of Belmond's gorgeous luxury trains, which travel to destinations such as the British countryside, the Amalfi Coast, and the Scottish Highlands.

But in 2027, my bucket-list Belmond journey is a glamorous new addition to its already impressive collection of itineraries: the French Riviera.

The Venice Simplon-Orient-Express offers three cabin types: Historic Cabins, Suites, and Grand Suites.

On May 10, 2027, the Venice Simplon-Orient-Express is launching a new route from Paris to Monaco, traveling to Monte Carlo for the first time in its history.

The journey, which will become a regular addition to the train's annual schedule, will take passengers through some of the most spectacular scenery along the French Riviera before arriving in the glamorous principality.

The new route will take travelers to Monte Carlo for the first time in the train's history.

The experience begins in Paris, where passengers will board the train's distinctive midnight blue carriages before settling into their accommodation for the night. There are several options to choose from, including the classic Historic Cabins, Suites, and Grand Suites, each drawing inspiration from the train's Art Deco heritage.

For those looking to really splash out, there's also L'Observatoire, an exclusive carriage created in collaboration with French artist JR. Designed as a private sanctuary on the rails, it comes complete with a bedroom, an en-suite bathroom featuring a freestanding bathtub, a spacious living area, a library, and even a secret tearoom.

As evening approaches, guests can enjoy dinner in one of the train's two restaurant cars, Étoile du Nord and L'Oriental, before heading to the famous Bar Car 3674 for cocktails and live piano music.

But perhaps the most exciting part of the new journey comes the following morning. After waking up to breakfast served in their cabins, passengers will be treated to sweeping views of the Mediterranean as the train makes its way along the Côte d'Azur. The route passes the red cliffs of the Massif de l'Estérel and travels through Saint-Raphaël towards Cannes and Nice. The train will then continue towards Monaco before arriving at Monaco-Monte-Carlo station.

Breakfast served aboard the Venice-Simplon Orient Express.

Monte Carlo also has a surprising connection to the train's history. In 1977, two original train carriages were purchased at an auction in the principality, helping set in motion the project that would eventually become the luxury train we know today.

“Introducing the destination feels like a natural continuation for the Venice-Simplon Orient Express, bringing the romance of luxury rail travel to a locale that has always understood the art of arrival,” says Pascal Deyrolle, Belmond's Europe area managing director for trains. “There's also something rather special about coming back to Monte Carlo, given the role it played in the train's history.”

The new journey is part of Belmond's expanding collection of European rail experiences, alongside the second year of its “Villeggiatura by Train” itinerary, which connects the Venice Simplon-Orient-Express with Belmond hotels in Italy.

Of course, a journey this luxurious comes with a price tag to match. Tickets for the new Paris-to-Monte-Carlo route start from €4,870 (approximately $5,450) per person, based on two people sharing a Historic Cabin. The fare includes the overnight journey, all meals with sommelier-selected wines, unlimited soft drinks, transfers, and 24-hour steward service.

A version of this article was originally published on Condé Nast Traveller UK.

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6306. Delta Air Lines CEO Vows To Fight Heathrow Move That Separates It From Virgin Atlantic

Delta Air Lines is fighting Heathrow Airport’s decision to move it away from Virgin Atlantic, warning that separating the partners will hurt passengers and undermine years of investment. I understand why Delta is upset. But whether that should entitle it to remain in Terminal 3 is a more complicated question.

Heathrow plans to move Delta from Terminal 3 to Terminal 4 in 2028, while Virgin Atlantic remains in Terminal 3. The decision would split an operation the two airlines have spent years integrating.

Delta CEO Ed Bastian issued an unusually pointed public statement on November 2, calling the decision “short-sighted, deeply disappointing and bad for airline consumers.” He argued that sharing Terminal 3 supports convenient connections and a consistent premium experience. Delta intends to challenge the move, saying it “will pursue all available remedies to correct this decision.”

“Heathrow Airport Limited’s decision to relocate Delta’s operation to Terminal 4, away from our partner Virgin Atlantic, is short-sighted, deeply disappointing and bad for airline consumers. For more than a decade, our airlines have served millions of customers through our co-located operation in Terminal 3, offering travelers convenient connections, premium amenities and access to an expanded global network.

“Delta and Virgin Atlantic provide UK consumers with a valuable competitive alternative across the Atlantic. Separating our operation undermines years of investment and disregards the tightly integrated customer benefits that we offer in our co-located terminal. We are committed to preserving the seamless travel experience for which Delta and Virgin Atlantic are known and will pursue all available remedies to correct this decision. We urge Heathrow Airport Limited to reconsider their decision in favor of a more prudent and thoughtful outcome that puts travelers first and allows competition to flourish at Heathrow.”

Terminal assignments can sound like an obscure airport planning issue until you are the passenger trying to make a connection.

A traveler arriving on Delta and continuing on Virgin Atlantic would face a terminal transfer that is unnecessary today. The same applies in reverse. Unfortunately, terminal transfers are not easy at LHR and moving between terminals introduces another step and more opportunity for something to go wrong.

For someone simply flying Delta to London and heading into the city, the effect may be less consequential. But Delta and Virgin sell their partnership as an integrated travel experience. Separating their airport operations makes that promise harder to deliver.

There is also the premium experience. Eligible Delta passengers currently benefit from Virgin Atlantic’s Terminal 3 facilities, including its Clubhouse. Those facilities are part of what makes the partnership attractive, especially when choosing between similarly priced business class tickets.

If the move happens, I would assume that a Delta flight departing from Terminal 4 will not include access to Virgin’s Terminal 3 facilities, at least in any practical capacity. However as I mentioned in my earlier story, integrating with Air France/KLM in Terminal 4 makes a lot of sense (far more connecting itineraries) and the lounge is not bad at all.

Still, replacing something that already works well requires money and effort. I can understand why Delta would prefer not to start over.

Heathrow’s decision follows a three-year terminal review. The airport says the changes will improve its use of existing capacity and operational resilience, while creating room for growth.

Heathrow also says airlines representing 81% of its passengers support the outcome (that is a share of passenger traffic represented by supportive airlines, not a survey showing that 81% of travelers approve).

Delta is not the only carrier being asked to move. The wider reshuffle also affects Finnair, Japan Airlines, LATAM, and China Southern.

An airport cannot necessarily give every airline its preferred location. Keeping one partnership together may mean imposing constraints or additional costs elsewhere. Delta’s investment deserves consideration, but it should not automatically settle how Heathrow should allocate scarce terminal space.

Bastian also presents the shared terminal as supporting competition across the Atlantic. I accept that a more cumbersome ground experience could make Delta and Virgin less attractive to some travelers. A passenger comparing connections may reasonably prefer an itinerary that avoids a terminal transfer.

But claims that the move will weaken competition or drive up fares need more support than the fact that Delta dislikes it. Heathrow is changing where Delta operates, rather than announcing that it must stop serving London or taking slots away. Delta’s strongest argument is the concrete one: it has built a useful shared operation with Virgin, and Heathrow is proposing to make that operation more difficult. That deserves a substantive answer but there’s undeniable logic in the shuffling.

Delta has good reason to challenge a Heathrow move that would separate it from Virgin Atlantic. Sharing Terminal 3 offers practical benefits, and I understand Bastian’s anger. But Heathrow must manage the airport as a whole. I would be more persuaded by a clear account of what this reshuffle improves and why those gains outweigh the disruption.

For now, this is a dispute over a planned 2028 change..itt does not mean your next Delta flight has moved to Terminal 4. I hope the eventual outcome preserves as much of the current passenger experience as possible, but I’m still not convinced Delta is being unfairly picked on by LHR and I am convinced that whether Delta wins or loses this battle, its passengers will enjoy a great ground product at Heathrow for many years to come.

Not to defend Delta, but why would anyone connect from DL onto AF/KL at LHR. It just adds complextity and cost versus flying DL to AMS/CDG and connecting from there. I doubt they have anything to gain by being co-located with AF/KL rather than VS. Also T4 is worse than the T2/T3 complex for ground transport or self-connecting options.

Is terminal 4 underutilized or are they shifting the problem of crowding from T3 to T4? With LHR ruling out the prospect of new slots at LHR in 2028 when Heathrow’s Management says this move will lead to gains the question they haven’t answered is gains for who, for which airline.

If this move is really about alleviating congestion in T3 then go for it. But if this move is part of a broader plan that will see Delta capacity at T3 replaced by another carrier then Delta has every right to throw a fit.

T4 is operating significantly under capacity and since BA needs to move additional capacity into T3 to relieve T5, it has to be one of the larger T3 tenants who moves out.

Delta doesn’t adult very well and tends to react particularly poorly when told no. Not everyone is going to come out a winner and they just need to deal with the fact that this is a loss for them.

A better solution would be to move all SkyTeam out of Terminal 3 into Terminal 4, move all OneWorld and its partners into Terminals 5 and 3 and distribute the non-aligned between Terminals 2 and 3 as space allows. Terminal 4 is much more modern than Terminal 3 so there should be little complaint on that one.

I tend to agree and the current two-level Qatar lounge would make a great new Clubhouse. LHR should do this and just help VS/DL pay for it…

Yep. This was the obvious move by LHR if that’s your end game. End of the day this will be about compensating DL/VS for the move to T4. But VS(/DL) gets no brownie points for renovating the current Clubhouse in a transparent attempt to forestall this. LHR told VS/DL that this was the likely outcome – if VS(/DL) wanted to waste their money playing a game of chicken, that’s on them.

Are there really that many people connecting in LHR to Asia on Virgin?

While the clubhouse is nice I wasn’t overly wowed by it. And since flights are day time west, it’s not as important having a lounge meal like eastbound when you’re trying to maximize sleep. The Air France lounge in T4 looks nice enough anyways. I think the biggest loss for anyone flying D1 is the arrivals lounge, especially if you’re heading straight into the office.

Maybe Delta should have listened to their pilots a few years ago and stopped outsourcing so much of their international flying to partners…

” Delta’s strongest argument is the concrete one: it has built a useful shared operation with Virgin, and Heathrow is proposing to make that operation more difficult.”

Heathrow is proposing to level the playing field between the two major US-UK Joint Ventures at the airport. Virgin had the chance to move, as well. It’s not as though Delta doesn’t have the cash to build a reasonable ground experience at T4. LHR isn’t even anything close to a transfer hub for DL. Those hubs are AMS and CDG — CDG, an airport where DL/AF customers have to change terminals and clear security between terminals. what a concept for Delta.

I get why Delta is upset but it doesn’t seem very persuasive to be mad about “connections” when LHR isn’t much of a connecting airport for their Joint Venture. But as usual… Delta and Virgin Atlanta love to cry foul when asked to do what AA/BA do today…

#6305. This Is The Summer To Tick Santorini Off The Bucket List

It’s June, and for perhaps the first time in modern history, Santorini isn’t crowded. Those earthquakes a good few months ago? Not even a flower pot was tipped over, yet incessant clickbait headlines managed to have a lasting impact.

And that’s a shame, because there’s been a lovely tourism revolution brewing there, where local hoteliers are bringing back the kind of experience and hospitality that you want to come back for over and over again.

As someone who goes at least once or twice a year, and will again very shortly, I can only advocate to tick it off the bucket list this summer, because you’ll never find prices, availability or an experience quite like it again for a while.

In the last 20 years, Santorini got totally overrun. Cruise tourism and day trip mania somewhat ruined a once idyllic, low-key fishing island and then Instagram and TikTok lit the match.

But now the TikTok crowd is in Mykonos and Santorini, as unequalled in beauty as ever, is lovely again. Hotels like The Vasilicos and Santorini Sky bring wildly different, delightfully luxurious and hospitality driven experiences to the island.

Beach clubs, yes Santorini’s beaches are underrated, have made a nice little mark on quieter coasts with great effect too. Assyrtiko, the local grape has hit the world stage as a darling of sommeliers in top restaurants and vineyards like Vassaltis offer stunning tasting experiences.

And the food? There’s no Nobu, or Scorpios here, so there are plenty of places to feel the benefit of European pricing, including a personal favorite at Kantouni.

The trouble with Santorini has historically been that many of the best hotels are small, they fill up quickly, and as they do, they charge a fortune. For the best, like the ones mentioned above, it’s still worth it. But this season, all across the board, prices are lower and even if you don’t care about price, many of the best which might typically be sold out for the season have rooms.

As an additional tailwind for travelers, flights between the US and Europe are quieter this summer, which means there’s deals to be had with both points and cash from major markets to Santorini. If you don’t see cheap flights to Santorini, try a major hub and booking an onward ticket separately.

Naturally, precaution is a good thing in life. But fear mongering for the sake of clicks is another beast and I can’t help but be fairly appalled by the many weeks and months of coverage and follow up coverage, reiterating a narrative of fear… despite no damage to anything, anywhere.

If you do bag a great deal this summer and visit one of my very favorite places, and use this great Santorini guide to make the most of your time, you can thank the media.

Airport lounges can serve as oases from a busy, crowded or outdated terminal. Some lounges participate in membership networks like Priority Pass, while others, like the United Club lounge, are operated by individual airlines.

If you’re a loyal United Airlines flyer or frequent one of the carrier’s largest hubs, visiting a United Club lounge is probably already on your radar. However, the airline made some major access changes in 2025.

Here's what you need to know about accessing United's lounges.

The Chicago-based airline operates a network of standard lounges known as United Clubs, as well as more exclusive Polaris lounges for eligible premium-cabin travelers on select long-haul international, transcontinental and Hawaii routes. Both offer complimentary food, drinks and Wi-Fi, while Polaris lounges feature additional amenities, such as sit-down dining, relaxation areas and shower suites.

So, how can travelers gain access to United's network of lounges?

You'll need a same-day boarding pass to access United lounges. This can be a same-day boarding pass for a United-operated flight or a flight operated by a Star Alliance partner airline, like Lufthansa or Swiss.

Related: Best United Airlines credit cards

United now has two tiers of paid membership for entry to the Club.

This membership offers the primary member unlimited access to all 45-plus United Club locations. There are no discounts available for United Premier members. Individual members can pay to bring guests into the lounge on a one-off basis; a one-time pass costs $59 per guest and is subject to availability.

Individual members do not have access to Star Alliance partner lounges.

Annual fee: Varies depending on Premier status

All Access members can enjoy unlimited United Club access for the primary member and up to two adult guests, or one adult and any dependents under 18.

This membership also includes access to Star Alliance partner lounges and other select partner locations, subject to applicable access policies.

Lifetime United Club members have been converted to All Access memberships.

TPG values United MileagePlus miles at 1.2 cents each per our November 2026 valuations, so your best bet is to pay the annual membership fee with cash rather than miles.

Having an eligible cobranded United credit card can be the most cost-effective way to consistently enter the United Club.

You can get lounge access with the following cards (note that some cards only offer one-time passes):

*The information for the United Club Business Card has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

Unlike a paid Individual membership, a United Club membership earned via a cobranded credit card offers a unique access policy that includes entry for primary cardmembers, one adult guest and any dependents under 18 years old.

Cardmembers can unlock an All Access membership, which increases the guest allowance and provides access to participating Star Alliance partner lounges, by earning Premier Gold status or higher, or by spending $50,000 on eligible purchases with their United Club Card or United Club Business Card in a calendar year.

Since the annual fee on both the United Club Card and the United Club Business Card is $695, having a credit card to enter the lounge remains a more attractive option than outright buying a membership.

Additionally, the United Club Card and the United Club Business Card offer four one-time passes on each account anniversary. A pass can be used by one person accompanying the primary cardholder or an authorized user into the lounge.

If you’d prefer to avoid the hefty annual fee, you can opt for the entry-level United Explorer Card or the United Business Card, both of which include two single-use United Club passes each year. Note that these day passes don’t include guest access, nor can they be transferred to friends or family who aren't authorized users or accompanying a cardmember into the lounge.

Certain MileagePlus Premier and Star Alliance Gold members can access United Clubs when traveling on eligible flights.

United Premier Gold (and higher) members can access United Clubs when traveling internationally on United or another Star Alliance carrier, regardless of their class of service. They can also bring along one guest who's traveling on the same flight.

Travelers who earn Star Alliance Gold status through another member airline can access United Clubs when flying on any eligible Star Alliance flight, including domestic United flights. Again, guests must be traveling on the same flight as the elite member.

United’s invite-only Global Services members can enjoy lounge access on all United-operated flights, including those operating exclusively within the U.S. Note that this new perk only covers the Global Services member — you’ll only be able to bring a guest into the lounge with an All Access membership, eligible cobranded credit card or when flying internationally.

Travelers flying in certain premium cabins on United or its Star Alliance partners can also access United Clubs. However, eligibility and guest privileges vary by airline, route and cabin class, as outlined below.

If you don’t travel enough to justify an annual membership, you can also purchase a one-time United Club pass for $59 per person at United Club locations or through the United mobile app. Just note that day passes don’t guarantee entry when lounge is at capacity.

Travelers using a one-time pass can enter a United Club only up to three hours before their scheduled departure time. (This exclusively applies to departure flights, and there is no time limit for entry on connecting flights.) These one-time passes are not accepted at grab-and-go locations, United Polaris lounges, United Arrivals Lounges or partner lounges.

You can also earn complimentary one-time passes with select cobranded credit cards, including:

One-time passes issued through United cobranded credit cards must be redeemed by the primary cardholder, an authorized user or a guest accompanied by either. Each pass admits one person.

United’s lounges are open to a few other travelers, including:

Some premium-class passengers also have access to United’s Polaris lounges, which offer a more premium experience. You can expect modern furnishings, private spa-like shower suites and elevated culinary options.

Three types of passengers are eligible for Polaris lounge access:

In addition to United Clubs and Polaris Lounges, the carrier operates a grab-and-go lounge concept called United Club Fly.

The first such space opened at Denver International Airport (DEN) in November 2022, and a second one opened at George Bush Intercontinental Airport (IAH) in 2025. Eligible travelers can enter Club Fly by scanning their boarding pass at the self-service entry gate.

Once inside, you can head to the snack bar that’s stocked with packaged and prepared foods. You can also order a coffee from the barista.

Given Club Fly’s focus on efficiency, the access policies are a bit different. Eligible United Club members and travelers flying in international premium cabins are eligible to enter, but they cannot bring any guests.

The Chicago-based carrier operates more than 45 United Club lounge locations. Of course, you’ll find a plethora of United Clubs in the carrier’s main hubs, including:

Apart from DEN, all of the aforementioned airports also have Polaris lounges.

There are other United Club locations scattered across the U.S., including in airports such as Dallas Fort Worth International Airport (DFW), Philadelphia International Airport (PHL), Phoenix Sky Harbor International Airport (PHX), Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport (ATL) and Minneapolis-St. Paul International Airport (MSP), among others.

Check out United's website for a complete list of the airline's Club and Polaris lounge locations.

United offers a variety of ways to access its United Clubs, both for premium-cabin frequent flyers and for those with a membership.

If you frequently travel with United, it’s worth analyzing which options offer the best bang for your buck to unlock a relaxing lounge experience.

#6303. Wander.com: Best Luxury Take On Airbnb (With Real Value Too?)

At first, the big hotel chains of the world laughed off Airbnb and vacation rentals. No seriously, they did. Now, they all compete in the vacation rental business and act like it was always the plan.

The problem for the traveler, is that almost all of the newer entrants just plug into a massive pipeline of already existing vacation homes and apartments and pop them on their own branded website with no added luxury, differentiation, amenity or expertise in curation.

There’s no huge unlock of new places or highly curated places that you could virtually always stamp as worth recommending to a friend, the way you’d rate an Aman, St. Regis, or Four Seasons hotel.

This is precisely where Wander.com comes in, and it’s by far my favorite luxe vacation rental platform to date. The fact that it’s boutique and limited is what makes it, at least for me. And, the $350 off Wander promo code doesn’t hurt either.

Wander is a vacation rental company which truly hand picks every property that it lists, and has the exclusive listing on. Crucially, each of the vacation properties undergoes a sort of ‘Wander’ transformation to conform with brand standards for wifi, amenity, style and vibe.

It’s above my pay-grade as a blogger on this topic, but it seems like Wander co-invests in the real estate portfolio’s, or partners with owners in a unique way that’s far more integrated than others.

Where are they? Most Wander.com properties are scattered across the US, from the shores of Malibu to the great National Parks in Wyoming and all along the Eastern seaboard too. Hawaii is also a recent addition. New destinations keep popping up!

Each of their properties feels uniquely wonderful and aspirational, and I’d say all have a very modern and contemporary slant to luxury. Grandma’s cabinets are not in any of these homes, but Tesla chargers are. One nice touch: each Wander offers a dedicated workspace with desk, chair, monitors and lightning fast wifi.

I completely respect that all tastes are individual, but the interiors and setups of these homes much more reflect my personal tastes, more minimalist chic, than many less curated vacation rental options.

Most Wander properties are around $1000 a night. Some will be half that, some will be double. On its face, that’s intimidating to many, but when you factor in the number of bedrooms and features it’s really reasonable. Families, or multi-family get togethers… amazing.

All Wander.com properties are at least two bedrooms and many are four, five or even twelve. One is an entire island with multiple residential complexes. For me, I love these sort of getaways for catching up with family or friends, and I never mind when other people are contributing too.

We’ve had some of our best ever vacations renting a house in Palm Springs for weeks or months at a time. Often, family or friends want in too, so we split the house and end up with two bedrooms each for under $500 per night.

We’ve used these bonus rooms and features to socialize or catch up with people in the serenity of the home, not annoyed by service, crowded pools or tight room setups. For a longer stay, I absolutely hate having to rely on a hotel kitchen for every meal. I love to hit a local market and grill with family or guests.

Wander is offering $350 off first bookings, which is a great way to get started. To browse the homes, you simply download the Wander app and start doom scrolling. When you find one you’re ready to book, the process is very self explanatory and easy to share with others.

I’m personally a fan of virtually California vacation and the properties offered on the platform cover everything from Palm Springs to Napa and all in between in stunning form. The $350 off is a solid discount and combined with new property discounts, which are frequent, there is a lot to love. You can browse Wander and download the app here.

If you don’t see the Wander.com discount in your account, you can add promo code AKFVDFD7 once the app is downloaded.

#6302. Flying Blue Delays 50% SAF XP Price Hike After Admitting “We Didn’t Handle The Rollout Well”

Flying Blue has postponed an abrupt devaluation to the elite status credit members earn through sustainable aviation fuel and charitable contributions. I remain skeptical of the underlying scheme, but program chief Tiffany Funk deserves credit for acknowledging the botched rollout, listening to members, and giving them time to adjust.

Air France-KLM Flying Blue initially changed its earning rates on November 2, 2026, without advance notice. For cash contributions toward sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), the cost increased from €10 per XP to €15 per XP, a 50% increase.

XP, or Experience Points, determine Flying Blue elite status. Members who had incorporated these contributions into their qualification plans suddenly faced a more expensive path to their goal.

Now, as One Mile At A Time also reports, Flying Blue has postponed the changes until December 1, 2026. The previous earning rates return effective November 4, and contributions made since November 2 will also receive credit at the prior rates.

Tiffany Funk, Head of Flying Blue, addressed the reprieve:

On Monday, we updated how many XP you earn on Sustainable Aviation Fuel and charitable contributions. We didn’t handle the rollout well, and the new rate went live with unclear messaging and without notice. While this affects a small share of our members, we recognize for those members it matters a great deal.

The update was part of a continuous review of our elite program. We want to ensure we can keep delivering the benefits and service you expect.

For now, we’re pressing pause. From tomorrow (4 November), SAF and charitable contributions will earn XP at the previous rate, and any contribution made since 2 November will be credited at the prior rate as well. The new rate of €15 per XP begins on 1 December 2026; even at the new rate, no program in the market will recognize SAF contributions more generously than Flying Blue, including on award tickets.

We want Flying Blue to be a program you build your life around. Many of you put a lot of care into planning your flights and status qualification, and we understand your need to have time to make adjustments.

And to everyone who told us why this matters to you: thank you for caring this much about Flying Blue.

I appreciate the candor. Funk acknowledges that Flying Blue handled the rollout poorly and offers a practical correction. Members now have a transition period, including protection for contributions made during the initial rollout.

To be candid, I consider this arrangement a greenwashing revenue-generating measure. Awarding elite status credit for an environmental contribution is a convenient way to monetize the pursuit of status while wrapping the transaction in a sustainability message, a win-win for both Flying Blue and frequent travelers but probably not for the environment.

We don’t have to litigate that here and I readily acknowledge SAF can play a role in reducing aviation’s lifecycle emissions, but purchasing a contribution does not make a passenger’s flight emissions disappear. And I suspect the additional XP is the deciding factor for many members who participate, not altruism for Mother Earth.

Flying Blue certainly understands the appeal. Someone approaching a qualification deadline may find paying for a contribution far more convenient than taking another flight. But my skepticism about the arrangement does not diminish the importance of treating participating members fairly. Flying Blue offered an opportunity, and members planned around it. Their reliance was entirely foreseeable.

Flying Blue owes no one a permanent opportunity to acquire additional XP at a particular rate. It can decide that the existing formula is too generous or that it wants a different balance between flying and other qualification methods. Members can then decide whether the revised offer is worthwhile.

My larger objection, as with most devaluations, concerns candid communication and advance notice. Tell us what is changing. Give us time to adjust plans made under the existing rules. Please spare us the suggestion that a reduction in benefits is an “enhancement” inspired by member feedback.

Funk avoids that familiar gaslighting here. She does not claim members asked to pay more for their XP. She acknowledges that feedback exposed a problem with the rollout and explains what Flying Blue will do about it.

That is a much more credible use of member feedback.

Consider someone who booked travel expecting to earn a certain number of XP from flights and make up the remainder through SAF contributions. An overnight change can upset that calculation after the flights have already been purchased.

That member is not necessarily demanding that the rules remain unchanged forever. The objection is that a plan made in good faith has become more expensive without warning.

The additional time gives members an opportunity to complete contributions at the previous rate or reconsider their qualification strategy. Crediting contributions made since November 2 at the old rate also avoids penalizing those who happened to transact during the botched rollout.

Neither measure eliminates the devaluation. Both make its introduction fairer.

I commend Funk for listening and adjusting. Management can respond to criticism without abandoning the underlying business decision. Here, a relatively straightforward concession makes loyal customers  feel heard rather than taken for granted.

I remain skeptical of Flying Blue’s SAF contribution scheme, and the higher cost per XP will make it less attractive. Heck, I remain skeptical of status in general as a proud free agent for two years running. But the program has corrected the avoidable failure of introducing that change without clear communication or notice.

Funk acknowledged what went wrong and gave members time to prepare. Flying Blue is entitled to revise its earning rates. Members who planned around those rates deserve a reasonable transition, and they now have one. That is a welcome response…I never thought Funk would make the program more generous as other loyalty programs cut and devalue, but measured and clear changes with advance notice to members are all anyone can ask for.

Working both in the aviation industry and as a travel consultant, Matthew has been featured in major media outlets around the world and uses his Live and Let's Fly blog to share the latest news in the airline industry, commentary on frequent flyer programs, and detailed reports of his worldwide travel.

There’s a difference between not owing permanence in the terms of a loyalty scheme and constantly tinkering with stuff in ways that are disadvantageous to members.

Devaluing twice in the space of 1.5 year and doubling redemption rates in the process while reducing short-haul XP earnings and using opaque formulae for partner redemption (I just got quoted 48k miles for 1.5 hour in ‘business class’ with an airline which doesn’t even offer that cabin on the route in question!) are all telltale signs of a programme that just shouldn’t be trusted.

#6301. On Location: How Coastal Newfoundland Set the Scene for Netflix's No. 1 Series ‘Below’

A mysterious sea creature is captivating audiences on Netflix as the Josh Hartnett-led series Below remains the No. 1 show in Netflix’s global rankings. The six-episode thriller paints an eerie image of small-town life in Newfoundland, and viewers are intrigued by the mystique of the striking Canadian backdrop.

Despite the fictional giant squid terrorizing Snook’s Arm, the show pulls on elements of reality, from climate change affecting the Atlantic Canadian sea life to the government-run resettling of remote fishing towns, which started in 1954 and continues to this day. It’s that history that drew production designer Emmanuel Fréchette into the project.

“When I found out that more than 300 towns in Newfoundland had been resettled, I was amazed,” he tells Traveler. “The script is very interesting, mixing that reality with the mundane life in Newfoundland—and this creature!” After all, creator Jesse McKeown (The Umbrella Academy) had frequented the region for years, inspired to bring an authentic depiction of its culture to the screen.

That started behind the scenes as the cast and crew engaged in Newfoundland and Labrador’s most famous tradition. Visitors, who they called CFAs (or Come from Aways—this is also where Broadway hit musical draws its name), get “screeched in” by kissing a cod to become honorary citizens. So they all went to St. John’s Christian’s Pub to pucker up. “The guy there is such a great character, and he has a routine and speech that’s very entertaining," Fréchette says.

When it came to filming locations, the remote regions posed practical challenges, so the majority of the sets were built by production, a joy for Fréchette, who was trained as an architect. “I was stunned by the humble architecture, built by boat owners and builders,” he says of the homes’ low ceilings. “The structures are very endearing and make you think of a boat, so I wanted to follow that thread.”

That’s also what helped root the fantastical storyline into reality. “This was vernacular architecture—architecture without architects—just following the needs of the people out of survival, and I found that so beautiful,” he says. “So I really tried to mimic what I was seeing all around me that survived the decades.”

And it’s clearly had an effect on audiences. According to data provided by Booking.com, not only have searches for the province’s capital of St. John’s risen 16.9% by Americans on the platform compared to last year, but the coastal town of Twillingate, home to the floating icebergs, has skyrocketed 123.7%.

Here, Fréchette shares the filming locations from the popular Netflix series Below.

The show is set in the actual resettled town of Snook’s Arm, which had a population of 10 when it was approved for resettlement in 2017, according to the CBC. But its remote location would have been difficult to film in with such a big crew, so Brigus South—a town with a population of about 700 at last count in 2021—stood in.

“We picked that place because it had a connection with the water,” Fréchette says of the inlet going deep into the land. “Lots of the characters are dragged into the water, so it was great to have this presence for the eeriness.”

But to get the cozy town ready for its close-up took work, as the crew designed and built about 80% of what appears in the series, including the fish plant, Fishermen’s Hall, and wharf. The Penneys home was an existing home they covered, and the church was also a house that they retrofitted, adding the bell tower.

When Fréchette was scouting locations, he stayed in a hostel by the sea in Twillingate, about 275 miles northwest of the capital. “We’d be having a coffee with the window open, and suddenly we were freezing,” he recalls of a sudden drop in temperature from 68 degrees Fahrenheit to 50 degrees Fahrenheit. That’s when they’d look up and see an iceberg floating their way. “It lowers the temperature all around the bay—it’s such an amazing phenomenon.”

As it turns out, the Atlantic town sits along Iceberg Alley, where from late April through July, the remnants of broken glaciers glide down the coast. Many of the shots of Calvin (Hartnett) harvesting icebergs were actual footage from these massive blocks of ice naturally floating along.

The capital served as the home base for the cast and crew, who were spread out across hotels and home rentals during filming. But its Ocean Sciences Centre, about 30 minutes north of downtown, found the spotlight as one of the most striking structures in the series, the marine research center where Dr. Fonda Howander (Mackenzie Davis) worked.

While Fréchette admits it took some work to convince the operating facility to shoot there, he’s excited it worked out because “it really adds production value and is a great location.” After all, the circular wooden structure reflects that government building architect of the 1960s and early 1970s, “at a time we were dreaming and imagining things beyond what was possible to build today.” Reminiscent of designs by Canadian architects like Arthur Erikson, he adds that “it was ambitious, but it had a vision—and is fantastic!”

About 20 miles north of St. John’s at the top of the Avalon Peninsula sits Pouch Cove, a town of about 2,000 residents. The art director told Fréchette about the Pouch Cove Heritage Society, a historical building that was closed since they were fundraising to preserve it, so one weekend, they went up to visit. “The floor was sunken in and it was structurally unsafe,” he says.

The show’s head carpenter and engineer got to work, fixing it up, temporarily transforming it into the interior of Below’s Fisherman’s Hall, while permanently restoring it for the community. “It was a win-win because they were happy to get the money from the location, but also the work we did on it was helpful for them.”

When Calvin returns to his abandoned childhood town of Little Pot Rock, that dilapidated setting was an actual resettled town, about a 30-minute drive down from Pouch Cove on a dirt road that the production had to grade in order to shoot there.

“It was quite tricky, but just stunning—really wild and rugged,” Fréchette says, calling it “the most amazing location.” All that was there was one tiny house, about 12 by 20 feet, but it never showed up on camera. Instead, the production custom built all of the Budgell family’s dwellings. But the area can be visited as part of a 4.3-mile hike along the East Coast Trail.

The fishing village of Bay Bulls is home to North America’s largest Atlantic puffin colony, as well as a prime whale watching destination. But for Below, it was all about the functional purpose of its Pennecon Marine Base. Though it never shows up on screen, its industrial harbor was essential in order to dock the boat used as the research vessel since it had a draft (depth) of nearly 10 feet, and they needed an appropriate spot that the cast and crew could board. Also shot here were the exterior scenes of the submersible, which was hung from the boat by a crane and lifted onto the dock.

Pittman’s fish farm played an integral part of the plot, as Calvin confirmed that the sea creature was real—but it turns out the location was landlocked. “It was very complicated to do this on the sea because we’d have to deal with tides and storms, so we decided to cheat it on a lake in Brigus,” he says of the town that’s actually about 60 miles northwest from Brigus South. There was no actual fish farm there, so they custom-built the floating dock and cabin.

While the outside of Linda’s Bar was filmed using a retrofitted Brigus South home, the interior was actually the Rising Tide Convenience shop in the town of Harbour Main, about 33 miles southwest of St. John’s. The local business, best known for its homemade ice cream, “looked great inside, so we dressed it up,” Fréchette says, taking extra care to ensure the exterior entrance they built flowed seamlessly between cuts. As for Noah (Kaleb Horn)’s on-screen screech-in? That was a prop, but an actual frozen fish to ensure the fish kiss was genuine.

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6300. My First “New” Chase Sapphire Reserve Travel Redemption Blew My Mind

There’s… a lot… of coverage surrounding the revamped Chase Sapphire Reserve Card. As per usual these days, the hot takes are plentiful and people are fired up. It’s either the apocalypse or the beginning of something great, depending on which attention seeker you read. As a long time cardholder, I’m really intrigued by the new changes.

The changes really fit my profile and sure, the card will cost more, but I won’t have to introduce any behavior change to get more, unlike some other cards. I’ll do most of my spending on this card. I’m a keeper just from the fee credit and earning multipliers.

Well, if my first Chase Sapphire Reserve redemption is any indicator, this card may single handedly change the redemption game and just about everyone should take note — including airline and hotel transfer partners. It’s already a huge win.

Chase Travel’s ‘The Edit’ is a curated selection of nice hotels, which offer benefits similar to those provided by a travel agent or other luxury credit card booking platform. When booking a ‘The Edit’ property, you can expect breakfast for two, a $100 F&B credit, late check out and an upgrade subject to availability.

Which leads me to the important bit! With the revamped Sapphire Reserve Card, there’s a new “Points Boost” feature, which offers up to two cents per point (25,000 points would cover $500, etc) for some flight or hotel purchases.

This can be amazing value, with flights of $3,000 being grabbed for just 150,000 points, with no taxes and fees and the ability to still earn frequent flyer miles and elite status points, since the airline treats it like a cash ticket.

Previously, the Sapphire Reserve card offered a steady point redemption opportunity directly on Chase Travel at 1.5 cents per point (100,000 points would cover $1500, etc). But with the new version, some travel purchases you want to redeem for will either offer less value than before, the same, or more, with this new ‘Points Boost’ at 2 cents per point. We like more!

I am in New York and wanted to do a little staycation, so I fired up Chase Travel and found one of my more reliable upper mid-scale hotels, The Thompson Central Park was on as part of ‘The Edit’. My two options became a very clear singular, third option.

Typically, I’d consider paying cash or transferring my points from Chase to Hyatt to pay for a stay like this. Hyatt has “fixed” points rates, meaning the points price is largely irrespective of the cash price and only changes by seasonal dates. For this season, it was 25,000 points per night for the Thompson Central Park.

If I were to transfer my points, I’d get a free night (the cash rate was around $500) and have a really solid points redemption at exactly two cents per point. I’m not loyal to any hotel chain really, so I wouldn’t get any breakfast or “elite” benefits, but a free night is a free night.

BUT — Chase Travel had a ‘Points Boost’ option to book the hotel directly on their platform and not transfer points to Hyatt. Chase Travel was offering this property for circa 25,000 points and that would cover the $500 cash rate, but unlike transferring points to Hyatt, because I was redeeming a ‘The Edit’ property on Chase Travel, I’d receive…

Yep, by NOT transferring my points (and dealing with the fractured transfer journey) I was able to get myself basically $200 in additional value added to my stay with the breakfast and $100 property credit, not factoring in the value of late check out or a category room upgrade. In addition, I’ll be able to earn elite nights and Hyatt Points on the stay.

A mere 25,000 Chase Ultimate Rewards Points got me a “free” $500 hotel night, breakfast for two, and $100 to spend at the hotel. That’s a pretty stunning redemption, giving more than two cents per point of value and still allowing me to earn on the stay, unlike when you transfer your points to a loyalty program. I wish I could’ve stayed longer.

For the first time I can remember, transferring points to Hyatt was not the best option here and that’s something to stand up and take notice of.

If Chase can keep up this Points Boost game, it can really send ripples through rewards. For the first time, people can easily receive tremendous value for their points through a credit card portal while still earning elite status and points with the hotel or airline of their choosing.

You can check out the new 100,000 point + 500 travel credit offer for the Sapphire Reserve. It’s 200,000 points for Sapphire Reserve Business Cards.
