#6268. The Food Trends We’ll See in 2027, According to the World’s 50 Best Chefs

On November 4, Lima, Peru, was a playground for global palates. Star chefs from across the world flocked to the culinary hotspot for the 50 Best Restaurants 2026, a prestigious awards ceremony that crowns the top restaurants around the globe based on anonymous nominations from over a thousand industry experts. Restaurant Asador Etxebarri, which is located in Spain's Basque Country, won top billing as the World’s Best Restaurant 2026 at the event held at the ornate Teatro Municipal de Lima. And before the winners took the stage, we were on the ground as Lima and its top restaurants buzzed with excitement all week.

In addition to knowing which spots came out on top, we also wanted to understand what these results signaled about dining in the year ahead—so we asked chefs for their hot takes. After the plates, tastings, and pisco sours (so many pisco sours), these the top dining trends and places to look for in 2027, according to the world's best chefs.

Read the full list of the 50 Best Restaurants in 2026 here.

Lobster from Kjolle in Lima, which was just named No.7 on the World's 50 Best Restaurants list.

Chef-owner Pía León of Kjolle in Lima—a fine-dining wonder that showcases the megadiversity of the host nation with startlingly beautiful tasting odysseys—snagged the number seven spot this year, making it the top restaurant in the host country. With the global spotlight on her, León looks to the growing importance of knowing specifically where your food comes from, beyond just a vague sense of ‘local.’ “To me, traceability means understanding where each ingredient comes from, who produces it, and the knowledge behind it,” she told Condé Nast Traveler. “Many of the products we work with come from local producers and communities who have kept their techniques alive for many years. As cooks, we have a responsibility to recognize their work and the value of what they grow.”

It’s a feeling that chef and co-owner Josh Niland of Sydney's Saint Peter (which also appeared on our 2025 Hot List of the best new restaurants in the world) emphasizes even further. The restaurant, founded by chef-owner Niland and his wife Julie Niland, focuses on whole-fish cookery and placed at number 50 this year, also earning the title of Best Restaurant in Oceania. “I think it [will be] ridiculous,” he says, if, in 10 years, restaurants are not telling us exactly on paper where things are from. “Like I think it's non-negotiable,” he said. “If you're writing a menu right now, let alone 10 years from now, I want to know why I'm paying $60, $70 for this chicken. Where is it from? That's how I feel about it. You know, we've got QR codes on the menu that you can scan and watch a fisherman pull a fish out of the water. Like, that's probably a very drastic leap, but I feel like that's where, to a degree, the premium end of dining needs to be. We need to be incredibly transparent about our labor, how we're paying people, like where things are from, all that.”

Saint Peter in Sydney came in at No. 50 on the list, and was named the Best Restaurant in Oceania.

At New Nordic gem Kadeau in Copenhagen—number eight on the list and also recently awarded three Michelin stars this past June—head chef and co-owner Nicolai Nørregaard plays with time, drawing on both seasonal, hyper-local fresh produce, and preserved beauties from seasons past. Kadeau—where the team includes chef Francisco “Pancho” Cardenas supervising the kitchen, and Kyumin Hahn serving as partner—also won the Highest Climber award for jumping from number 41 in 2025 to its placement this year.

La Colombe in Cape Town debuted a Secret Cellar in 2024, an intimate subterranean enclave where guests hand over their phones before the meal begins. While chef James Gaag understands that some people want to take photos of their food—and certainly that Instagram traffic helps restaurants—he hopes for, but isn't counting on, more phone-free restaurant experiences.

So what, exactly, does “seasonality” mean when the seasons seem so different lately? Condé Nast Traveler asked Nørregaard just how climate change is impacting the menu, and what adjustments the team is making: “Some meals are shit,” Nørregaard said, “or some ingredients that we are relying on [are], so we need to change plans. But then maybe something else is in abundance, and then we just switch to that direction.” During Kadeau’s growing season, when it relies on produce from its garden on the Danish island of Bornholm and from what can be foraged nearby, adding more nutrients and water to the soil allows them to step in and give Mother Nature a helping hand, ensuring a better product. During the preservation season, in the colder months, the team showcases products like preserved onion that have been stored since spring and summer—but even that process is changing. Take the pine cone: A dry year might produce very few of the beauties, while a wet year will see abundance. “We sometimes need to think ahead and plan two years in advance,” he continued. “So we have to preserve something for more than one season because it might not come the next season.”

Around the globe, more nimble menus—shifting ingredients, planning well ahead of time—are on the way to account for increasingly unpredictable weather. This is a further expression of adaptations already underway, including a reduced focus on meat, due to its environmental impacts, and broadened waste-reduction efforts. For diners, this means that no two tasting menus, even at the same restaurant, may be exactly the same; that talked-about dish may be swapped out for something else when the seasons or weather requires. But this commitment to the best, and the possibility for newness on menus, presents an arguably more interesting fine dining experience. Each menu, and dish, may represent a singular moment in time.

The Sardine Pie at New Nordic gem Kadeau in Copenhagen, which placed number eight on the list.

Kadeau was also recently awarded three Michelin stars this past June.

Sprawling menus as an indicator of abundance; dozens of items on a single plate—foams, sauces, sprigs of herbs placed with tweezers; narrative-driven tasting menus that span six or seven hours. These used to scream luxury. Now? Simplicity speaks louder. It’s a trend noted by executive chef James Gaag of La Colombe in the Constantia Valley near Cape Town, owned by chef-proprietor Scot Kirton. La Colombe landed at number 35 and also took home the title of Best Restaurant in Africa.

La Colombe in South Africa placed No. 35 on the list.

At La Colombe and elsewhere, Gaag is energized by “less courses, fresher courses, lighter courses, less time at the table.” His innovative menus might be inspired by both his German upbringing and world travels, but that doesn’t mean trying to fit the entire globe in one menu. “We used to put 100 ingredients on each plate, and I think the longer I run the restaurant, the more confident I am in putting less on the plate,” he continued.

Chef Jeremy Chan, who owns Michelin-starred Ikoyi in London with co-founder Iré Hassan-Odukale, continues to rise. Ikoyi landed at number 48 this year, owing to its contemporary global menu that is inspired by both British microseasonality and meticulously sourced global spices. For Chan, though, fine dining doesn’t mean frigid. “Fine dining is about creating a refined experience, rather than a sense of preciousness or formality,” he told Condé Nast Traveler. “For me, it is about the refinement and technique of the craft, alongside the responsibility and precision in what we do to make people feel special.”

Odette, the Singapore restaurant founded by chef Julien Royer, placed at number 15 this year—one of the many high-ranking spots across Asia, including Gaggan in Bangkok (number 2, and also the Best Restaurant in Asia), Wing in Hong Kong (number 5), and the Chairman (number 6), also in Hong Kong. Condé Nast Traveler asked Chef de Cuisine Sheng Xiong—who blends his Asian heritage with French training for Odette’s menus—if there’s a fine dining trend he’d be happy to see vanish. “You mean we’re going to lose our jobs?” He joked. After his laughter subsided, the chef at the Three Michelin-starred restaurant echoed Chan’s sentiments: “I think moving forward, maybe the white-glove service [will go], because in our restaurant we treat everyone coming in like [they are] coming back home as a family member. It can be a bit too casual sometimes, and at the same time, it makes them feel comfortable. Guests are happy. At the start, Singaporeans, the older generation couldn't understand what we are doing, but as time goes by, they actually prefer that to a very stiff kind of environment.”

A Bluefin Tuna Rhubarb dish at London's Ikoyi, which landed at No. 48 on the list this year.

Chef Niko Romito of the lauded, three Michelin-starred Reale—which placed at number 27 this year—is seeing a difference in the way travelers experience his restaurant. Reale, which he co-owns with his sister Cristiana Romito, sits within a 16th-century monastery nestled in a remote medieval town in Abruzzo, Italy. As Niko Romito explained to Condé Nast Traveler, because of Reale’s remote location, tourists would often get there at the tail-end of a food tour of Italy—a tough situation to be in, when perhaps a meal at the end of a trip might feel less memorable after a string of stellar meals. “Today, it’s the exact opposite,” Romito said. “The location—tucked away in the provinces—was once a major limitation. Yet, this very constraint pushed me to create a style of cooking that transcends the distance, making the journey—the hours spent in the car—fully justified. I could say that the region where I live, Abruzzo, is beginning to emerge as a top destination for tourists. A territory rich in nature, parks, and hidden gems.”

At Singapore's Odette, number 15 on the list, Kampot Pepper Crusted Pigeon is served.

Inside Odette, the Singapore restaurant founded by chef Julien Roye

Many restaurants within this year’s list support the growing trend that rurally set tasting menus are sometimes more interesting than their big-city counterparts, luring an increasing number of diners. This year’s number one restaurant and also the Best Restaurant in Europe is Asador Etxebarri, which calls Atxondo, a village of less than 1,500 inhabitants in Spain’s Basque Country, home. Vyn, the number 23 restaurant, is located within a pastoral fishing village of about 7,000 people in southern Sweden. While Naar, number 50 and also the winner for this year’s Sustainable Restaurant Award, sees diners traveling deep into the foothills of the Himalayas for its open-flame-cooked dishes. As food tourism continues to boom, expect even more meteoric restaurants to shine from beyond bustling metropolitan areas.

Read the full list of the 50 Best Restaurants 2026 here.

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6267. Air India CEO Wants ‘More Widebody Aircraft’

Air India is looking to buy more widebody jets as it expands overseas and works to return to profitability.

“We want more widebody aircraft,” CEO Tewolde Gebremariam said Tuesday at the Aviation India and South Asia summit in New Delhi, according to Reuters. The carrier has held talks with both Airbus and Boeing. Gebremariam did not say how many aircraft Air India might buy.

The airline’s most recent Boeing order, announced in January, was for 30 narrowbodies: 20 737 MAX 8s and 10 MAX 10s.

The carrier is also updating the widebodies it already flies. In April, Air India took delivery of the first of 26 older Boeing 787-8s slated for cabin retrofits. The aircraft went from two cabins to three with the addition of premium economy.

Gebremariam, who previously led Ethiopian Airlines, described high operating costs as a “major concern” but said he expects Air India to return to profitability “very soon.”

Air India Group lost S$3.56 billion in the fiscal year ended March 31, according to financial disclosures from Singapore Airlines, which owns a 25% stake in the group. The loss came as the carrier dealt with disruption from the war in Iran and Pakistan’s closure of its airspace to Indian airlines.

#6266. Ask a Local: Where to Go in Nairobi According to Runner Emily Chepkor

"Nairobi is a city best understood in motion," says Emily Chepkor, founder of We Run Nairobi, the city's biggest and most popular run club. She's from a small town in Kenya, Kapsabet, that has produced more world-class runners per square mile than anywhere else on earth. While the country is known worldwide for its running heritage, Nairobi hadn't quite caught up to the hype until Chepkor came along.

She runs as a hobby, and is a 12-time marathoner (and two-time Boston qualifier) who felt that, though Kenya's running reputation was unmatched internationally, the runner lifestyle itself wasn't accessible to everyday Kenyans—elite athletes only. She set out to change that and bring running closer to all Nairobians, starting with a weekly run club that began with just her and three friends. It slowly grew through word of mouth and especially TikTok, into something bigger, built on a simple idea: no registration, no fees, you just show up and run alongside Emily.

That run has become a defining weekly ritual for Nairobians, drawing over 1,200 people every Saturday morning. It's now etched into the city's identity. The same way New York is known for its bagels, Nairobi is known for the We Run Nairobi neighborhood runs, a cultural landmark for locals and tourists alike.

Below, Emily tells us about some of her favorite things to do in the city she calls home.

Karura Forest is “without a doubt” the best place to run in Nairobi, if you ask Emily.

"Karura Forest, without a doubt, is the most scenic route in the city”, she says. “I run the Sigiria side, through Gate F; it's quieter, more canopied. My dog Biscuit and I do the 10-kilometer loop most Sundays, crossing little rivers every kilometer. If you want something gentler, the 5-kilometer route is just as lovely." Her Saturday club runs the same way: "We're completely pace-agnostic. First-timers run next to marathoners".

Karura is the second largest urban forest in the world after the Tijuca Forest in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, and provides the perfect place for an outdoor run.

“Kengele's is always a safe bet whatever's on, whether it's World Cup, rugby, athletics, you'll find a good crowd," says Chepkor. "What I love is how the embassies get involved: around big sporting events, they'll partner with venues across the city to host public watch parties. I'll never forget the British High Commission's watch party in Karura Forest, the day Sebastian Sawe broke the two-hour marathon barrier. The whole country was locked in, and experiencing that moment surrounded by hundreds of people felt incredibly special.”

The McMillan Memorial Library is one of her favorite places for some peace and quiet, and some history.

“The McMillan Memorial Library is a perfect little time capsule of Nairobi, architecturally and literally—it's currently being renovated by Book Bunk, founded by two Kenyan women committed to restoring our public libraries," she says. "I also love the Nairobi Gallery, home to Point Zero, the spot from which all distances in Kenya are measured.”

“Tigoni is a small town only 30 to 40 minutes from Nairobi, but it feels much farther away. The city gives way to rolling tea plantations and narrow country roads. I start at Brackenhurst with coffee from Muna Tree Cafe on the terrace, then rent a bicycle and ride through the plantations, stopping wherever the view is too good to pass.” Back at Brackenhurst, she'll spread a blanket on the lawn to read, maybe doze off, then finish with tennis or a walk through the Indigenous forest. "It's the itinerary I'm proudest to take an out-of-towner on," Chepkor says.

"Sigiria Coffee House is my default—small, intimate, and full of dogs on Sunday mornings. On tennis mornings it's Waitabit, same easy vibe." For souvenirs, she sends visitors to two spots near each other: "Spinners Web has beautiful rugs, a café, and a used-books library. Just up the road, Tribal Gallery has grander pieces—restored Swahili doors, oversized mirrors—alongside smaller suitcase-friendly finds like ceramics and jewelry."

"Fig & Olive in Tigoni is part bodega, part restaurant, with a lawn where no one blinks if you swap your chair for the grass. In the city, it's the Tin Roof Café in Karen—moving from table to grass and back, especially post-run, and the salad bar is iconic. For something dressier that still softens outdoors, Matteo's: white tablecloths, al fresco seating, and little intimate corners I'm still discovering."

The Talisman Restaurant is a Nairobi stalwart.

Scoring a place by the fireplace is a coup.

"The Talisman Restaurant is a Nairobi stalwart. Scoring a corner table by the fireplace on a chilly evening is a date-night dream. For something more stylish, Inti has skyline views in every direction—some Friday nights it turns into an intimate DJ set." For the rest of the evening, she splits the city in two: “If you're after energy, Geco, alive with Nairobi's music scene, especially on Wednesdays. For actual conversation, Cave-à-Manger has an expansive wine list and keeps the music in the background.”

"Toi Market, with one caveat: Nairobi isn't really a vintage city in the curated, boutique sense— we're much more of an open-air, flea market vibe, with thousands of stalls. Toi is sprawling, busy, and a little chaotic. You'll need patience and a willingness to dig, but if you put in the time, you'll almost always come away with something great for a fraction of what you'd pay elsewhere."

“Nai Nami is properly off the beaten track; it's a walking tour of Nairobi's CBD led by former street children. You see downtown Nairobi through the eyes of people who know it intimately, and leave with a completely different understanding of the city. The Alliance Française is an unexpected answer, but it's one of Nairobi's great cultural hubs—plays, concerts, exhibitions, most of which are free, and the original stomping ground of Sauti Sol, our biggest boy band.”

A view of the city from Nairobi National Park

"Nairobi is the only city in the world with a national park so if you’ve only got one day, make it a wildlife day. I’d go for a game drive through Nairobi National Park at sunrise, then the elephant feeding at Sheldrick Wildlife Trust, and the Giraffe Centre to finish. Afterwards, a slow lunch nearby at either Cultiva, Talisman, or Matteo's. "

"I'd highly recommend coming to a We Run Nairobi Saturday. One of my favorite traditions is that we 'brand' every first-timer with a little sticker, so everyone knows it's your first Saturday. I'll encourage people to say hello, ask where you're visiting from, and recommend a coffee spot. You're moving together with actual Nairobians, in neighborhoods where we actually live. You're not being shown the city, you get to experience it alongside the people who call it home.”

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6265. 10 Classic Airliners That Needed A Third Person In The Cockpit

Swissair | Wikimedia Commons | Simple Flying

A third seat in an airliner’s cockpit can tell you a surprising amount about the machine itself. On some jets the person occupying it was often a flight engineer, responsible for monitoring and managing systems that modern flight crews now take for granted . On others, the job became so closely tied to the aircraft that the engineer’s station was almost as recognizable as the engines or the silhouette.

The flight engineer’s place in the cockpit did not disappear overnight, and the aircraft that carried one were far from interchangeable. Some made the role part of everyday long-haul operations; others pushed it into unusual territory. This countdown features ten classic airliners that were designed or operated with three crew members in the cockpit. The selection is based on that crew configuration, rather than requiring every aircraft to use the same title or staffing arrangement for its third crew member. The aircraft are ranked by their historical influence, fleet size, and the lasting place the third cockpit position held in their identity.

The Douglas DC-6 first flew on June 29, 1946, and entered airline service with American Airlines and United Airlines in 1947. More than 700 examples were eventually built, making it one of the most successful large piston-powered airliners of the postwar era. Its four Pratt & Whitney R-2800 radial engines, pressurized cabin, and long-range capability helped airlines expand their domestic and international networks. NASA's aviation history covers the aircraft's introduction and commercial impact.

The DC-6's cockpit required a minimum crew of three: a pilot, copilot, and flight engineer. The engineer monitored the four engines and managed the aircraft's systems, taking on responsibilities that would otherwise have added to the pilots' workload. Delta initially operated the aircraft with two pilots, but federal regulations soon required a third cockpit crew member. The Delta Flight Museum documents that change, and the aircraft's operating manual specifies the minimum three-person crew.

The DC-6 ranks tenth because it represents the postwar expansion of the traditional three-person cockpit. Its combination of four complex piston engines and long-distance operations made the flight engineer an important part of airline operations, setting the stage for the larger piston airliners and early jets that followed.

The Douglas DC-8 first flew on May 30, 1958, and entered commercial service with Delta Air Lines on September 18, 1959. One of the first American jetliners designed for long-range passenger operations, it combined four underwing engines with a pressurized cabin and the speed needed to transform transcontinental and international travel. Douglas eventually built 556 examples, including the stretched Super 60 series. The FAA's historical chronology records the aircraft's development and entry into service, while Boeing's historical archive preserves its first-flight history.

The DC-8 retained a three-person flight deck, with a captain, first officer, and flight engineer. Seated behind the pilots, the engineer monitored the four engines and managed systems including fuel, electrical power, hydraulics, and pressurization. The aircraft's type certificate specified a minimum crew of three, making the engineer an integral part of its approved operating configuration.

The DC-8 ranks ninth because it brought the traditional flight engineer's station into the first generation of successful American jetliners. Its long passenger and cargo career also showed how enduring that arrangement would be: even as jet technology advanced, the third cockpit position remained standard throughout the DC-8's production life.

The DC-8, a rival to the Boeing 707, defied the odds and continued flying cargo missions well into the 2020s, outlasting its competitor by decades.

The Lockheed Constellation first flew on January 9, 1943, initially as a military aircraft, before entering commercial service with TWA in 1946. Its pressurized cabin, long-range capability, and distinctive triple-tail design made it one of the defining airliners of the postwar period. Later versions, particularly the Super Constellation, introduced improved engines and greater operating range. The Smithsonian's Lockheed Constellation collection record documents the aircraft's development and its first flight.

The Constellation also helped establish the flight engineer as an important member of the long-distance airline crew. Operating four large piston engines while monitoring fuel distribution, electrical systems, and other aircraft functions demanded considerable technical knowledge. A dedicated engineer's station allowed these responsibilities to be separated from the pilots' flying duties, particularly during lengthy oceanic operations. The Airline History Museum's Constellation archive provides additional aircraft history and restoration information.

The Constellation ranks eighth because it helped establish the traditional three-person cockpit as a practical arrangement for long-range commercial aircraft. Its engineer's position represented a growing specialization within airline flight crews.

The Tupolev Tu-154 first flew on October 4, 1968, and entered Aeroflot service in February 1972. More than 1,000 were eventually built, making it a standard Soviet and later Russian medium-haul airliner. Its designers wanted a relatively lean flight crew of captain, first officer, and flight engineer, at a time when other Soviet airliners routinely carried four or five people up front. The Tu-154B-2 could be flown by three crew members, because Hungary's Malév judged larger crews economically unacceptable. Simple Flying notes that the Tu-154 filled nearly the same role in the Eastern Bloc that the 727 played in the West.

Navigation requirements meant that many Tu-154 operations retained a dedicated navigator in addition to the engineer. The navigator and flight engineer occupied separate workstations, illustrating how cockpit staffing differed between Soviet and Western aviation. The German Federal Bureau of Aircraft Accident Investigation's report on the 2002 Überlingen collision documents the positions of the Tu-154M's navigator and engineer. Crew arrangements varied by operator and version.

The Tu-154 ranks seventh because it demonstrates that the three-person cockpit was not a universal solution. Its long production life and continued use of additional specialists highlight the different approaches to cockpit staffing that existed during the jet age.

BA Concorde first flew on March 2, 1969, and began scheduled passenger service in January 1976 with British Airways and Air France. Its flight crew consisted of a captain, first officer and flight engineer. Cruising at approximately 1,350 mph (2,170 km/h) and reaching altitudes of around 60,000 feet (18,300 m), it presented technical challenges unlike those of an ordinary subsonic airliner.

The engineer occupied a dedicated station behind the pilots, monitoring fuel, electrical, hydraulic, air-conditioning, and engine systems. Fuel management was particularly important because fuel was transferred between tanks to control the aircraft's center of gravity as it accelerated and decelerated. Warren Hazelby, a former Lockheed L-1011 flight engineer who later worked on Concorde, described the aircraft's complexity in a CNN interview about his experience operating the supersonic jet.

Concorde ranks sixth because it demonstrates how essential the flight engineer could remain even in a technologically advanced aircraft. Only 20 were built, including development aircraft, but the third crew member remained part of its commercial operation until retirement in 2003.

How the L-1011-500 pioneered long-haul thin routes, using innovative design and extended range to fill a unique aviation niche.

The Lockheed L-1011 TriStar first flew on November 16, 1970, and entered service with Eastern Air Lines in April 1972. Lockheed built 250 examples, and the aircraft became known for its advanced flight-control technology and relatively quiet operation. Despite having an advanced autopilot capable of automatic landings, the TriStar retained a three-person cockpit. Lockheed's own historical account of the L-1011 describes its advanced automatic flight-control system and the technical ambitions behind the aircraft.

The flight engineer monitored the aircraft's complex mechanical and electrical systems, including fuel, hydraulics, and engine performance. The importance of crew coordination became particularly evident during Eastern Air Lines Flight 401 in December 1972. While the crew investigated a landing-gear indicator problem, attention shifted away from monitoring the aircraft's flight path. The FAA's account of the Flight 401 accident explains how the crew became distracted while troubleshooting the indicator and failed to monitor the aircraft's flight path. The accident helped shape later thinking about crew resource management. The TriStar's engines brought their own challenges, as the Rolls-Royce RB211 program experienced major development difficulties that delayed the aircraft's introduction.

The TriStar ranks fifth because it demonstrated that sophisticated automation did not immediately make the flight engineer redundant. Even one of the most advanced airliners of its generation continued to rely on a dedicated systems specialist.

The McDonnell Douglas DC-10 first flew on August 29, 1970, and entered service with American Airlines on August 5, 1971. Its flight deck was designed for three people: a captain, copilot, and flight engineer. The engineer occupied a dedicated panel behind the pilots, monitoring systems that included fuel, electrical power, hydraulics, and engine performance. The DC-10 was developed as a widebody trijet, with two engines mounted beneath the wings and a third installed at the base of the vertical tail. This arrangement provided the capacity and range airlines wanted while meeting the long-haul regulatory environment of the period.

The flight engineer's responsibilities included monitoring fuel distribution, electrical buses, and hydraulic systems, as well as helping identify abnormal conditions. According to Boeing, the later MD-10 conversion introduced a modern glass cockpit, allowing the removal of the flight engineer's position.

The DC-10 ranks fourth because it illustrates both the importance and eventual disappearance of the flight engineer's position. The DC-10's passenger career gradually ended as more efficient widebody aircraft replaced it, although freighter operations continued for decades. Its long service history makes it one of the clearest examples of the transition from traditional three-person flight decks to modern two-pilot cockpits.

The Boeing 727 first flew on February 9, 1963, and entered service with Eastern Air Lines on February 1, 1964. It became the first commercial jetliner to pass 1,000 sales, with production eventually reaching 1,832 aircraft before ending in 1984. The type required a three-person flight deck, with the engineer seated sideways behind the pilots. Its distinctive arrangement of three rear-mounted engines allowed Boeing to deliver the performance airlines wanted without placing engines beneath the wings. The aircraft's integrated rear airstair and sophisticated high-lift system also made it attractive for operations at airports with limited ground facilities and relatively short runways.

The 727's third engine emerged from a compromise among United Airlines, American and Eastern. United wanted strong performance at hot-and-high airports such as Denver, while Eastern needed an aircraft suitable for overwater operations. Many smaller airports offered runways of just 4,500 feet (1,372 m), which the 727's triple-slotted flaps helped it handle. Its systems remained complex enough to require a dedicated engineer, who monitored engine instruments and the fuel, electrical, and hydraulic systems. Boeing's historical aircraft collection provides further information about the aircraft's development and its remarkable production run.

The 727 ranks third because its flight-engineer era stretched across decades of everyday flying. It became a familiar sight at airports around the world, and its long freighter career kept the third cockpit seat in use well after newer passenger jets had moved toward two-pilot operations. FedEx retired its final 727s in 2013, marking the end of a particularly important chapter in the company's freighter fleet. For many airline pilots and engineers, the 727 remained one of the defining aircraft of the traditional three-person cockpit.

Discover how a retired Boeing 727 became a home and how planes worldwide are finding second lives as restaurants and hotels.

The Boeing 707 opened the jet age for most travelers. Developed from the Boeing 367-80 prototype, the first production 707-120 flew on December 20, 1957, and FAA certification followed on September 18, 1958. Pan Am began regular service on October 26, 1958, with a transatlantic flight from New York to Paris. Boeing eventually delivered more than 1,000 aircraft across the 707 family, including the smaller 720. The aircraft's four turbojet engines and long-range capabilities made it one of the most influential commercial transports ever built. Its cockpit was designed around a captain, first officer, and flight engineer, establishing a layout that would become familiar throughout the first generation of jet airliners.

The engineer's workstation was particularly important during the 707's early years. The aircraft's systems required continuous monitoring, including fuel management, electrical power, hydraulics, and pressurization. The engineer also assisted the pilots during engine start and monitored the four engines throughout the flight. Pan Am's Clipper America helped establish the aircraft's international reputation, and the 707 quickly became a symbol of the new era of commercial aviation. Its military derivatives extended the design's life considerably, with aircraft such as the E-3 Sentry continuing to use flight engineers long after most passenger airlines had moved to newer designs. The Pan Am Historical Foundation's account of the airline's first 747 also provides useful context for the transition from the early jet age to the widebody era.

The 707 ranks second because it helped establish the standard for the first generation of long-range jetliners. The 727, 747, and DC-10 that followed inherited the same three-person philosophy, and the 707 proved that jet aircraft could operate profitably on major international routes. Its influence extended far beyond passenger service, with military derivatives continuing to fly for decades. The 707's engineer station became a familiar feature of the early jet age, making it one of the most historically significant aircraft on this list.

The Boeing 747 made its first flight on February 9, 1969, with Brien Wygle as copilot and Jess Wallick as flight engineer. Pan Am launched passenger service on January 22, 1970, on a New York–London flight. The Boeing 747-100 was designed to carry approximately 366 to 452 passengers, depending on configuration, and its introduction transformed the economics of long-distance air travel. Behind the pilots, the engineer faced sideways toward a large collection of panels. The aircraft's size and complexity demanded continuous attention to fuel pumps, electrical buses, pressurization, hydraulics, and air conditioning, tasks that two pilots would have struggled to manage alongside their flying responsibilities. Boeing's official 747 history documents the first flight, the aircraft's development, and the beginning of passenger service.

The flight engineer's role on the 747 was particularly recognizable because of the dedicated sideways-facing station. Boeing's early jumbo jets contained numerous switches, lights, and gauges, and the engineer monitored systems that extended throughout the aircraft. Typical duties included operating fuel pumps, managing fuel transfer, monitoring electrical systems, and coordinating the use of backup systems when required. The position remained a standard feature on the 747-100, Boeing 747-200 and Boeing 747-300, but the introduction of the Boeing 747-400 in 1989 changed the arrangement. Its Engine Indicating and Crew Alerting System, together with more advanced digital displays, allowed the aircraft to operate with two pilots instead of three. The Pan Am Museum Foundation's history of the jumbo jet provides additional background on the aircraft's introduction and its impact on international travel.

The classic 747 earns the top spot because it fused scale, symbolism, and the traditional flight engineer's role. Boeing built more than 1,500 747s across the aircraft's production history, and the engineer's sideways seat became the best-known example of the third crew position. The jumbo jet represented the peak of the traditional widebody cockpit, but it also demonstrated how quickly that arrangement could become outdated. Automation, digital displays, and integrated warning and monitoring systems eventually allowed newer aircraft to receive certification for two-pilot operations. The 747-400's introduction marked one of the clearest turning points in that transition, bringing the classic three-person cockpit era closer to its end.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

I was a Flight Engineer from 1975 until 2007. I have time in the B727-200, DC-10-30, C141 A/B, and C5 Galaxy. The Lockheed C5 was more work for the FE than all the rest.

Being a Flight Engineer was a really great profession and only cheating death a few times. I worked as a DC10 Simulator Instructor for 10 years also. Another great job.

Thanks for this exposition of a flying job that is almost totally gone. Still some third seats out there.

There are 6 other classic airliners that required Flight Engineers that were left out of this article, that should be noted.

If you have yet to take a solo trip, there are many reasons why you really should. Solo travel helps you build confidence and new skills. It also provides time to reflect, recharge and reconnect with yourself — so you can return home the best version of yourself for the people who rely on you day-to-day.

I know it can be daunting to embark on your first big trip alone. But never fear, intrepid soloist. I've rounded up the top solo travel mistakes so that you can avoid them to ensure your trip goes smoothly.

Related: Travel mistakes that could ruin your next trip

One of the perks of solo travel is that you get to decide where to stay and what to do, so put some thought into it. This will ensure you have the best trip possible.

A good starting point is to check the State Department travel advisory for your destination, which will help you understand any safety concerns and identify neighborhoods you may want to avoid. It's also a good idea to enroll your trip in STEP, so you'll be alerted to things like natural disasters and security threats.

Safety isn't the only thing to consider. Are you looking for a quiet, relaxing getaway or a bustling neighborhood with endless things to do? Would you rather stay close to the action or save money by staying in a less popular area? Choose your accommodations accordingly.

Don't make the mistake I made on my first solo trip and not plan any activities. Spontaneity sounded fun, but I found making decisions on my own much harder than expected. You don't need to have your entire itinerary planned out to the minute, but doing some planning before you travel will reduce your stress during the trip.

Plus, many popular tourist attractions and trendy restaurants fill up quickly — and waiting in long lines is even less fun with no one to talk to. Do your research, and if needed, make a reservation or book a timed-entry ticket ahead of time.

Sometimes, the difference between traveling solo and with others really shines through in the little things...like using an airport bathroom.

You can't simply ask a companion to hold your luggage while you run to the restroom or figure out how to operate a metro ticket machine; you must keep track of it at all times. So think twice about packing that extra-large checked bag or hauling a not-so-ergonomic shoulder duffel on an international trip, as you will have to take it with you literally everywhere.

I personally prefer a backpack and small rolling carryon, which I can easily maneuver through crowded airports and over cobblestoned streets — without reaching my destination with a backache. Plus, it's big enough to accommodate sufficient clothing for a week (or more). My carryon is expandable, so if I buy too many souvenirs, I can unzip the extender and check it on the way home.

Related: How to pack your carryon right and avoid checking a bag

Connecting with new people is one of the many joys of solo travel, but that doesn't mean you should completely let your guard down. You may run into pickpockets, con artists and worse on your journey, and as a solo traveler, you're more likely to be targeted.

One simple step to reduce your risk is by not broadcasting your solo status. Err on the side of caution when chatting with new friends — and if they start getting nosy, tell them you're meeting up with friends later.

One way to prevent hotel staff from knowing your single status is opting for mobile check-in so that you can bypass the front desk completely. Or, you can ask the concierge for an extra key and allude that someone will be joining you shortly. And when catching a ride to or from your accommodation, it's a good idea to be picked up or dropped off down the street from your hotel.

Related: Solo travel safety tips every traveler should know

You only want to be incognito to the locals.

Let your actual friends and family know your travel plans: flight numbers, where you'll be staying on which dates, contact info for your tour operator, etc. You'll be glad you did if you hit a snag and need help rebooking on the fly. You can go a step further by sending them a copy of your passport or ID, in case you lose your documents while traveling.

You'll probably want to stay in contact with loved ones through text messages, phone calls or social media posts every so often. But you can also share your location continuously with apps like Find My, which can help ease their minds as well as give you an added layer of security. That way, both you and your loved ones can enjoy your trip stress-free.

Some things are must-haves no matter how many people you're traveling with, but they become even more critical when you're on your own — because if you forget something, you can't just reach into a companion's suitcase.

For instance, do you have a backup plan in case your phone dies while you're navigating a new city or road-tripping through an unfamiliar country? You can't simply borrow someone else's phone, so a charged power bank or old-fashioned map can come in clutch.

The same goes if you wind up at a store that doesn't accept your credit card. Always pack a couple of backup cards (preferably ones that don't charge foreign transaction fees) and keep some cash on hand.

Similarly, if you catch a cold on your flight or get food poisoning during a solo trip, there's no one else to run to a drugstore. And if you hurt yourself while out hiking alone, it may take a while for help to arrive. Prepare yourself for anything with a travel-ready first-aid kit.

Related: Travel essentials that can save your trip when things go wrong

One of the downsides of solo travel is that it can start to feel lonely, especially on longer trips. Making new friends is a great way to combat loneliness, as well as learn more about local culture and/or meet likeminded travelers.

If striking up a conversation with a stranger sounds more stressful than fun, you're not alone. Thankfully, there are plenty of ways for even the shyest travelers to make connections, including cruises and small-group tours designed specifically for solo travelers.

Female Travel Buddies is one of many Facebook groups ideal for those flying solo: Members post open invitations for fellow travelers in the same area to join you for brunch, sightseeing or a show. If this type of thing interests you, consider joining a handful of groups a few months ahead of your trip to get familiar with the members and learn how they work.

Related: 6 tips for meeting people when traveling solo

Just because you're traveling alone doesn't mean you can't take photos along the way — but capturing memories can be trickier by yourself.

The good news is you don't have to be limited by the length of your arm. Be sure to pack a selfie stick, mini tripod with remote shutter or selfie monitor screen. You'll find it well worth the investment, as having the right tools will make it far easier to snap the perfect selfie. (Just remember: safety first, especially when hiking, taking selfies near cliff edges, etc.!)

If, like me, you feel a little awkward or uncomfortable taking selfies alone, the best advice I can give you is to do it anyway. The more you do it, the more comfortable you'll get and the better your photos will turn out.

Solo travel doesn't have to be daunting. Follow these tips to embark on your first solo trip with confidence and ensure it goes smoothly, and before you know it, you'll be a seasoned solo traveler.

#6263. The Parking Spot Promo Code: Save 10%

As a New Yorker without a car, I don’t often put much thought into airport parking. However, a few years ago, my mom texted me raving about The Parking Spot, a service available near Connecticut's Bradley International Airport that allows you to park your car near (but not directly at) the airport in a secure lot, then shuttle over to the terminal. She effusively recommended the process for its ease and convenience, and has continued to rave about it since. Its reach extends far beyond Bradley—with more than 70 locations at 45+ airports, it’s a service that’s available across the US for fliers looking to reduce some of the hassle that comes with travel.

Here’s how it works: You can reserve a spot ahead of time on the company’s website or app, securing your place to park and sorting out the cost up front. Once you arrive at the airport and park your car (avoiding the dreaded terminal traffic), you’ll hop in the bright yellow, polka dot-covered shuttle (whimsical!) and head over. While you’re traveling, you can get your car washed or detailed if you so wish, a nice added value. Then, when you return, you can track the shuttle in real-time using the app to get back to your car quickly.

If all of that sounds appealing—or you’re a regular to the service and are just looking for the latest promo codes—read on for ways to save on your next booking.

(Looking to rent a car instead? Take a look at active promo codes for Budget, Avis, and Hertz first.)

Fall is a great time to squeeze in a long weekend getaway—or even a full week to yourself, if you've got the PTO days to spare—ahead of the holiday busyness. If you're headed off on a trip, know that for reservations that begin by November 15, you can save 10% or more on your airport parking with promo code FALL10.

An easy way to score The Parking Spot discounts: Sign up for the company's mailing list. New users will automatically receive 10% off their first reservation. You’ll also gain access to 10–20% off promo codes on parking reservations for select cities—right now, that includes Austin, Denver, Columbus, Houston, and Salt Lake City.

Like many brands, The Parking Spot offers a military discount for active duty military and veterans. A less common, though fitting, discount is available for airline crew members. Both groups can get 25% off a reservation with a Spot Club account. As for the fine print, discounts don’t apply to Basic parking reservations and can’t be combined with other offers. Airline crew will need to submit a photo of their work badge; similarly, proof of military affiliation must be submitted to receive the discount.

If a Parking Spot promo code isn’t working at checkout, there are a few things you can do to troubleshoot. First double-check the basics—typos, extra spaces, or incorrect capitalization can all prevent a code from working correctly. You'll also want to confirm that the code is still valid, as expiration dates and location exclusions may apply.

#6262. The Best Airbnbs in Asheville, From a Fairy-Tale Tree House to a Victorian Cottage

As someone raised in the mountains of North Carolina, I've always loved visiting Asheville. I have made the winding two-hour drive from my hometown of Boone countless times, and the city's vibrant energy never ceases to excite me. An eclectic little gem located in the heart of the Blue Ridge Mountains, Asheville’s bustling art and restaurant culture attracts visitors from all over. It's also home to famous historic sites like Biltmore Estate, which is the largest privately owned home in the United States.

What truly makes Asheville so captivating is the city's wide range of attractions, activities, and gorgeous places to stay. Unbelievable mountain views, hiking trails, and other outdoor activities are minutes from the city center, and there are dozens of gorgeous Airbnbs to hole up in no matter what area of the city you choose. The River Arts District is a hub of creativity and expression, home to hundreds of artists, galleries, and expansive outdoor murals along the French Broad River. Downtown is my favorite neighborhood, and I like to take an afternoon to mosey around, with a non-negotiable pit stop at Tupelo Honey for lunch. Wherever you stay, there's so much to do—you can spend your days soaking in a refreshing mountain spring and evenings dining at an award-winning restaurant or craft brewery, then catch live music at one of Asheville’s charming theaters. You will never run out of activities, with something to discover around each corner. Below, find 11 Airbnbs that capture every bit of Asheville’s quirky and whimsical appeal.

We've selected these listings based on Superhost and Guest Favorite status, ratings, amenities, location, decor, editor stays, and previous guest reviews.

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Unbeatable mountain views, hot tub, hammock

If you’re after a serene, nature-focused stay, this glamping dome tucked away in the Blue Ridge Mountains will provide just that. Relax in the private hot tub, take an afternoon nap in the spacious hammock, or simply watch the sunset from the couch in front of floor-to-ceiling windows. With on-site parking, a king-size bed, a full bathroom, and a kitchenette for whipping up light meals, a stay here will feel nothing like traditional camping. Situated about 20 minutes from downtown Asheville in Fairview, this property is an ideal hideaway to unplug while still offering access to Asheville’s unbeatable dining and activity options.

Neighborhood: FairviewThings to do nearby: Whistle Hop Brewing Company, Hickory Nut Gap Farm, Fairview Community Forest

Number of guests: 7Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 1.5 bathsWhy we love it: Wood-burning fireplace, panoramic views, wraparound deck

There’s a reason so many people want to stay in an elevated mountain cabin in North Carolina, and it’s a must-do for first-time visitors. This unique converted fire tower is on eight acres of private wooded land with direct access to the well-known Mountains-to-Sea Trail. Sixteen panoramic windows and a 360-degree wraparound deck offer expansive mountain views from every angle. The outdoor fireplace and backyard are a s'mores-making and stargazing wonderland. A short 10-minute drive from downtown, on-site parking, and a washer/dryer make this property an exemplary mix of seclusion and practicality.

Neighborhood: Haw CreekThings to do nearby: Haw Creek Park, Creekside Taphouse, Folk Art Center

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Downtown location, natural light, exposed brick

Set in a prime downtown location, this charming one-bedroom is ideal for those looking to experience Asheville’s thriving urban life. Right in the heart of downtown, you will be steps away from endless restaurants, dynamic art galleries, live music venues, and so much more. The space is warm and welcoming, with natural light pouring in from a wall of multi-pane windows. The exposed brick and natural wood tones create an ideal mix of cozy and sophisticated. There is no free on-site parking, but a parking garage across the street is available for a small fee as a convenient alternative.

Neighborhood: Downtown AshevilleThings to do nearby: Tupelo Honey, Asheville Art Museum, French Broad Chocolate Lounge

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1 bathWhy we love it: Historic character, convenient location, on-site parking

Built in 1883, this lovely stick-style Victorian cottage was the first home in western North Carolina owned by a woman. Throughout each room, original details are blended with thoughtful updates, preserving its historic character but adding a modern twist. Both queen bedrooms are enhanced with Victorian-inspired furniture and elegant fireplaces. Located in Asheville’s Montford neighborhood, this home is just two blocks from downtown, but still has a driveway and parking for ultimate ease.

Neighborhood: MontfordThings to do nearby: Nine Mile, The Montford Park Players, historic architecture stroll

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1 bathWhy we love it: High ceilings, spacious backyard, firepit, multiple living areas

Embrace a little piece of Asheville’s history at this carefully restored 1870s home. Each room boasts plenty of historic charm with 13-foot ceilings, crown molding, beautifully arched double doors, and detailed windows. The furniture and decor choices are an ode to the home's past, keeping the history alive yet with a modern twist. Multiple sitting areas and exceptionally spacious bedrooms (one king and one double) make this a wonderful place to spend time with friends or family without being cramped. The shared backyard has an adorable garden, and the back porch is a glorious spot to watch the sunset over the mountains. Free on-site parking is available, and if you have a particularly large group, you can inquire about renting the unit next door to accommodate four more guests.

Neighborhood: West AshevilleThings to do nearby: Early Girl Eatery, French Broad River Greenway, Sunny Point Café

Number of guests: 5Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1 bathWhy we love it: Hot tub, updated interior, city and mountain views

An ideal mix of modern design and rustic character, this chic space still maintains Asheville’s mountain charm. This property is packed with amenities like a hot tub, a ping-pong table, a soaking tub, and plenty of outdoor furniture. It’s a great place for families or small friend groups, with space for up to five guests to sleep across two bedrooms and lounge comfortably throughout the house. The expansive deck offers views of downtown Asheville, local valleys, and mountain ridges. Keep in mind that you do have to walk up a set of steps from the driveway to the entrance, which may be difficult for guests who have limited mobility.

Neighborhood: Town MountainThings to do nearby: Hiking at Craven Gap, The Omni Grove Park Inn, sunset at the overlooks

Number of guests: 3Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Artist-owned, minutes from Biltmore Estate, exquisite details

Thoughtful design and handmade art merge to create a sanctuary in the form of this cottage. Every inch of the Moroccan-influenced space has been curated to feel like a home away from home. An upstairs queen bedroom and a lofted single bed make this the perfect escape for a small family or a couple. The shared garden, firepit, and outdoor clawfoot bathtub mirror the light, airy interior. Free street parking is available, and West Asheville’s restaurants, breweries, and galleries are a short walk away. Biltmore Estate is only a five-minute drive and is a must-see attraction for any visitor.

Neighborhood: West AshevilleThings to do nearby: The Admiral, Carrier Park, Owl Bakery

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Fairy-tale charm, on-site hiking trails, rainfall shower

Straight out of a children's storybook, this remarkable tree house feels fictional. If you are looking for a nostalgic getaway to unwind and reconnect, this property is unbeatable. The cozy, cabin-like interior is full of wooden details and comfy furniture. You can sip a cup of coffee at sunrise on one of the two decks, relax in the upstairs bed nook, or venture onto one of the property's hiking trails (maybe even catch a glimpse of the forest’s wild animals!). This is a particularly good spot for those with kiddos, and the downstairs sofa bed makes for easy sleeping arrangements for little ones. About 10 minutes from downtown, this little haven offers the best of both worlds.

Neighborhood: North AshevilleThings to do nearby: Salt Face Mule Brewing Co., Blue Ridge Parkway North, Stoney Knob Cafe

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 2 bathsWhy we love it: Firepit, hiking trails, guest-approved mattresses

If you want to be close to the breathtaking Blue Ridge Parkway, this sleek A-frame is just a few steps away. The open-concept layout and vaulted ceilings make for an uncluttered and airy atmosphere. A two-minute walk from the Mountains-to-Sea Trail and a lovely on-site firepit make this a wonderful option for those who are looking to embrace nature. The primary king bedroom is filled with massive windows, and two separate bathrooms will give families enough space to be comfortable. There is on-site parking, but note that the parking space is said to be a bit steep for larger cars.

Neighborhood: ReynoldsThings to do nearby: Mountains-to-Sea Trail, scenic drive on the Blue Ridge Parkway

Number of guests: 6Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 2.5 bathsWhy we love it: Ample space, two large decks, outdoor amenities

Situated right in the middle of the woods, this beautifully updated mountain cabin is a peaceful retreat. Multiple living areas, three bedrooms, and two-and-a-half bathrooms make for a very generous amount of space. The upstairs deck features plenty of outdoor seating, and the lower level is fitted with two hammocks and games for nights in. Sweeping mountain views are visible from almost every window in the house—fall here would be an absolute dream! Wooden steps lead down to a charming firepit area with extra seating. Modern touches shine throughout the house, like the exquisitely updated kitchen and bathrooms. The driveway has space for up to four cars.

Neighborhood: Mountain View EstatesThings to do nearby: Blue Ridge restaurant, scenic walk, 828 Family Pizzeria

Number of guests: 6Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 2 bathsWhy we love it: Gas grill, outdoor furniture, washer/dryer

Cozy and modern, this sweet three-bedroom bungalow is an absolute dream. Shiplap walls, plush furniture, and fun amenities like a ping-pong table give the space an undeniably inviting feel. Two full bathrooms and enough room for six guests to sleep across three bedrooms (a king and two queens) make this a great option for small reunions or group trips. Located in a serene neighborhood in West Asheville, you can easily stroll to nearby breweries or take a peaceful walk around the area. A surplus of outdoor furniture and a gas grill give ample opportunity for alfresco meals.

Neighborhood: Echo HillsThings to do nearby: Sunny Point Cafe, Biltmore Estate, Biscuit Head

#6261. Boeing's Renton Factory Must Stagger The 737 MAX 10 With Smaller Jets, But Everett Can Run Nose-To-Tail

Boeing rolled the first 737 MAX 10 out of its new North Line at the Everett facility on October 26, and media attention naturally focused on the historic location shift. Destined for launch customer WestJet, this is the first time a 737 variant has been assembled outside of Boeing’s historic Renton plant since 1970. This change in build location makes sense because the longest variant in the 737 family has outgrown the layout of the factory that birthed it.

The motivation for establishing the North Line isn't simply to increase monthly hull count. The 143 feet, 8 inches (43.8 meters) fuselage of the 737 MAX 10 is not best suited to fit inside Renton’s compact assembly bays. To build the MAX 10 in Renton, Boeing had to stagger the elongated airframe between smaller variants like the MAX 8 to prevent structural overlap between adjacent stations. Now, by repurposing space in Everett’s massive widebody plant, Boeing has finally provided its largest narrowbody with an assembly line tailored to its length.

Boeing’s Renton factory has been the manufacturing heart of the 737 program for decades, but its boundaries were drawn around significantly shorter airframes. Covering roughly 1.1 million sq feet (102,000 m²) of total floor space, Renton’s three active assembly lines operate within tight architectural confines bounded by Lake Washington and local rail lines. When managing standard 737 MAX 8 aircraft, measuring 129 feet, 6 inches (39.5 meters) long, the moving assembly lines operate with minimal spatial clearance between stations.

The introduction of the 737 MAX 10 disrupted this tightly calibrated footprint. Stretched 14 feet, 2 inches (4.3 m) longer than the baseline MAX 8, the MAX 10’s nose and tail sections intrude into overhead crane pathways and the working envelopes of adjacent stations when positioned directly in sequence. To avoid costly structural collisions during station transitions, Renton line managers must manually stagger the build sequence so a longer MAX 10 is always preceded and followed by shorter MAX 7 or MAX 8 airframes.

This requirement creates scheduling friction across Renton’s 12,000-person workforce. Staggering limits production flexibility, as line operators cannot build MAX 10s based solely on order-book priority. According to Boeing, there are 1,555 firm orders for the MAX 10, about 31% of the total 737 MAX backlog, so Renton’s layout threatened to become a permanent operational bottleneck for Boeing’s most important commercial variant.

Something had to be done about Renton’s layout constraints, so Boeing began a $1 billion capital project to establish the 737 MAX North Line inside its flagship Everett facility. Occupying high-bay space in Building 40-22, vacated following the consolidation of 787 Dreamliner assembly to South Carolina, the new line provides approximately 20% more usable floor area per station compared to Renton. This means the 737 MAX 10 can move continuously in a true nose-to-tail orientation and does not need those staggered buffers.

Supported by an initial workforce of roughly 1,000 employees, about half of whom were reassigned directly from Renton to transfer specialized narrowbody assembly expertise, the North Line operates with modernized tooling, according to Barron's. The added clearance permits automated overhead crane systems and mobile scaffolding rigs to work around the MAX 10’s extended fuselage without interfering with adjacent work centers. Crucially, the dedicated layout increases total 737 manufacturing capacity by 25% across Boeing's Puget Sound industrial network, Lynwood Times reported.

However, uncoupling the MAX 10 from Renton's spatial constraints is not the end of the story for Boeing. Of course, the North Line provides the needed floor space for smooth assembly, but bringing these aircraft to market is a completely different reality for Boeing, and just adding floor space does not guarantee success in this area.

The opening of a second 737 assembly line in Everett represents more than just additional manufacturing space.

Achieving rollout on October 26 was a major milestone, but it does not mean customer deliveries are imminent. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) granted amended type certification for the 737 MAX 10 flight platform just a few days earlier on October 20, 2026. It was excellent news for Boeing, confirming that the MAX 10’s aerodynamic design, flight controls, and safety systems meet airworthiness standards, though it is only the first stage of regulatory clearance and many more stages remain.

Before WestJet or any subsequent customer can take delivery of an Everett-built MAX 10, Boeing must secure a separate amendment to its FAA Production Certificate. Everett is an entirely new production line for the 737 program, so FAA inspectors must audit every station, tool calibration log, and quality management process inside the North Line. The agency will need to independently verify that the Everett facility builds aircraft with the same structural consistency as Renton, which is a huge undertaking for Boeing.

During this initial low-rate production phase, the North Line moved the first airframes through assembly stations at a deliberately slow pace, according to Assembly Magazine. The extended flow time allows quality engineers to validate assembly steps alongside FAA observers. Consequently, initial WestJet deliveries will remain paused until the production certificate amendment is formally issued, making the short-term backlog relief more of a future expectation than an immediate result.

Everett solves Boeing's internal floor space limitations, but the pace of total 737 production remains tied to Tier-1 supplier health. As Boeing leadership confirmed, the main constraint on narrowbody output is an ongoing shortage of wing subassemblies. The complex wing structures, featuring advanced-technology winglets and dedicated trailing-edge flap mechanisms designed to handle the MAX 10’s higher takeoff weight, are arriving at assembly plants well behind schedule.

Even with a vastly improved production environment, an airframe cannot progress past early structural joining stations without its wing sets, so wing availability sets the pacing clock for both Renton and Everett. In response, Boeing revised its master production ramp. The target rate of 47 aircraft per month has been revised slightly, and Boeing now expects to reach and hold the 47-per-month milestone in 2027, before attempting a further push toward 52 jets per month later that year, according to Fortune.

The controlled ramp rate is designed to prevent traveled work, or moving unfinished airframes to downstream stations without completing preliminary assemblies. Holding the North Line at a steady, measured pace means Boeing is protecting manufacturing stability while supplier factories bring wing deliveries back into alignment.

The move will also free up capacity in Renton as Boeing looks to scale up MAX 8 and MAX 9 production.

The strategic commitment to build a $1 billion dedicated line in Everett is backed directly by market demand. At the top of the 737 MAX family, the MAX 10 carries 185 to 210 passengers in a standard two-class layout, with a maximum capacity of 230 seats. With a range of 3,100 nautical miles (5,740 km), the variant competes directly with Airbus’ dominant A321neo, offering airlines low seat-mile costs on high-density domestic and transcontinental trunk routes.

With 1,555 firm orders logged from global operators including United Airlines, Delta Air Lines, WestJet, and Ryanair, the MAX 10 is seeing a wave of popularity worldwide. Even Lufthansa has opted for the type, bringing the 737 back into the fleet after 10 years of pure Airbus narrowbody focus in the mainline fleet. Airlines have structured long-term fleet renewals around the high-capacity variant to replace aging 757-200s and older 737-900ERs. Failing to deliver the MAX 10 efficiently risked pushing these key customer accounts to convert options into competing European narrowbodies.

With Everett’s North Line dedicated to the MAX 10 alongside high-density MAX 8 runs, Boeing has clearly divided industrial labor. Renton can focus its three moving lines on high-volume MAX 8 and MAX 9 builds, while Everett takes on the complex, elongated MAX 10 airframes. As a result, Boeing has the industrial headroom needed to fulfill its multi-year backlog and finally get its production lines moving at record speed once again.

The rollout of the first 737 MAX 10 from Everett is really a significant milestone for more reasons than just the beginning of a new era for the 737 family. It also ushers in a permanent structural transformation in Boeing’s manufacturing footprint. What began in 1970 as a single-factory narrowbody setup in Renton has evolved into a multi-facility production network spanning Puget Sound. Boeing recognized that floor space, rather than worker effort, was limiting MAX 10 efficiency, so it positioned its commercial airplane division to push higher manufacturing rates with greater structural precision.

Over the coming years, the co-existence of Renton and Everett will redefine Boeing’s production dynamics. Renton remains the high-volume engine of the 737 program, while Everett provides the spatial flex capacity needed for specialized, high-capacity airframes. Once the FAA approves Everett’s production certificate and supplier wing deliveries stabilize, Boeing will possess an industrial system capable of supporting its long-term target of 52 aircraft per month.

Ultimately, the Everett North Line shows that modern aircraft manufacturing is as much about factory geometry as it is about aerodynamics. Giving the 737 MAX 10 the floor space it needs to move nose-to-tail, Boeing has cleared a path to deliver its largest narrowbody variant to global customers.

#6260. Hegseth faces bipartisan impeachment threat after Iran war gets blame for GOP midterm slaughter

A ‘FOX News Democracy 26’ panel discusses the impact of the war in Iran on the 2026 midterm elections, the Trump administration’s messaging on the conflict and more.

Secretary of War Pete Hegseth is facing a bipartisan impeachment threat when Congress returns next week as Republicans seethe over their devastating losses in Tuesday's midterm elections.

Bipartisan frustration over the war in Iran, quietly simmering for months, is now openly erupting after Democrats stunned the country with historic victories in the House and Senate. That anger could all now hit Hegseth, with several House Republicans telling Fox News Digital that they believe a resolution to impeach him could pass as early as next week.

"He's screwed," one House GOP lawmaker told Fox News Digital.

Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., a longtime critic of foreign intervention by the U.S., told Fox News Digital he intends to force a vote on impeaching Hegseth when Congress returns if the Pentagon chief does not resign first.

GOP REP THOMAS MASSIE INTRODUCES 8 ARTICLES OF IMPEACHMENT AGAINST WAR SECRETARY PETE HEGSETH

War Secretary Pete Hegseth speaks during a press conference on U.S. military action in Iran at the Pentagon in Washington, D.C., on March 2, 2026. (Brendan Smialowski/AFP via Getty Images)

He'll do so by filing a privileged resolution, a mechanism aimed at getting a vote on legislation despite opposition from the majority party's leaders. Once a privileged resolution is filed, lawmakers have two legislative days to hold a vote.

7 REPUBLICANS REBEL AGAINST TRUMP, VOTE WITH DEMS TO REIN IN IRAN WAR POWERS

But the procedure notably carries two steps. Before a vote on the measure itself, leaders can call up a vote to "table" the bill or refer it to the relevant committee, which in both instances effectively kills it.

That procedural vote is normally where most privileged resolutions die. But in this case, several House Republicans told Fox News Digital they believe the impeachment resolution could ultimately be successful.

GOP LAWMAKER SAYS MORE QUALIFIED OFFICIALS SHOULD LEAD PENTAGON, QUESTIONS HEGSETH'S 'MORAL COMPASS'

"If he introduces it, it'll pass," a second House Republican told Fox News Digital. Two more said they expected the same.

One GOP lawmaker said attendance could be a key factor in impeaching Hegseth. It's highly possible that many Republicans who lost re-election simply do not return for the final two months of the year, that person said. And with just a razor-thin majority, only a handful of absences would be enough for Hegseth to get impeached if all Democrats stuck together.

The Fox News Decision Desk projected Democrats taking the House shortly before midnight on Tuesday. Projections showed that the war in Iran, along with tariff policies, were key drivers in voters turning their backs on the GOP.

Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., leaves the U.S. Capitol after the last votes of the week on June 25, 2026. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc. via Getty Images)

And while President Donald Trump told reporters he believes Hegseth is doing "a good job," people in his circle appear to have their knives out.

"Hegseth is on the chopping block," a former White House official told Fox News Digital.

A current White House official said, "[Tuesday] would have looked very different without the Iran war. I believe you’ll ultimately see [Trump] hold Pete Hegseth accountable and that will play out in the lame duck."

‘LAWYER UP’: DEMS IMMEDIATELY PUT TRUMP ON NOTICE AMID REPUBLICANS' MIDTERM BLOODBATH

But the White House criticized the potential impeachment push on Thursday.

"As the President has said, he's willing to work with anyone to continue delivering victories for hardworking Americans. If Democrats choose to pursue sham investigations and radical left policies, they are choosing to work against the American people," White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis told Fox News Digital.

And another White House official said, "If crazed Democrats want to abuse their power and politicize their process of investigations, subpoenas, and destroying lives, they should be reminded that we still control the federal government and all of its powers."

Chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell on Wednesday dismissed rumors that Trump could get rid of Hegseth himself.

"Secretary Hegseth will not back down or be deterred by politicians seeking to score partisan points or launch phony investigations where no wrongdoing exists. The Department of War has followed the law and our Secretary will continue to stand and fight every single day to support and defend the Constitution, lead our troops, and protect America," he told Fox News Digital.

It's also worth noting that the majority of House Republicans will still oppose impeaching Hegseth — and many are still skeptical.

CONSERVATIVES STUNNED BY 'CATASTROPHIC' MIDTERM BLUE TSUNAMI, BLAME TRUMP'S IRAN WAR, HIGH GAS PRICES

"I really doubt [it]," another House Republican told Fox News Digital. "Depends on if anyone wants to flip off the president walking out the door."

There is likely to be healthy support on the other side of the aisle for such a push as well.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., who is poised to become the next speaker, has consistently criticized Hegseth. He posted on X Thursday morning, "Why is Pete Hegseth still around?"

House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries, House Minority Whip Katherine Clark and Democratic candidate Suzan DelBene celebrate at a Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee midterm election night watch party in Washington, D.C., on Nov. 3, 2026. (Reuters)

Even more moderate Democrats have signaled their support, given the administration did not seek the consent of Congress at any point during the ordeal.

"I've said a long, long time ago that he's not qualified for the job, and he should be removed, and I think we're going to pursue that," Rep. Adam Smith, D-Wash., who is expected to take over leadership of the House Armed Services Committee next year, told CNN's "This Morning" last month.

If Hegseth were impeached, he would not be removed before a trial in the U.S. Senate.

Fox News Digital reached out to the committee's Republican majority and the Pentagon for comment.

Elizabeth Elkind is a politics reporter for Fox News Digital leading coverage of the House of Representatives. Previous digital bylines seen at Daily Mail and CBS News.

#6259. Qatar Launches Two South American Destinations

Qatar Airways added two South American destinations on Wednesday, becoming the first Gulf carrier to serve Venezuela.

The new service flies from Doha to Bogotá, Colombia, then continues to Caracas, Venezuela, before returning nonstop to Doha. Qatar Airways will operate the route on Wednesdays and Sundays using a Boeing 777-200LR.

Flights are scheduled to leave Doha at 7:35 a.m. and reach Bogotá at 4:25 p.m. After a 90-minute stop, the aircraft continues to Caracas, arriving at 9 p.m. The return flight leaves Caracas at 11:30 p.m. and reaches Doha at 8:35 p.m. the following day. All times are local.

The airline originally planned to start flying the route in July but postponed the launch following an earthquake in Venezuela, according to Aviation Week.

Qatar Airways is also expanding its codeshare with LATAM to include domestic flights from Bogotá. The agreement will put Qatar’s code on LATAM flights to destinations including Medellín, Cartagena and Cali.

The additions bring Qatar Airways’ network in the Americas to 17 destinations. The carrier began serving South America in 2010 with flights to São Paulo.
