Good news for travelers who prefer vacation rentals over luxury hotels: Chase is giving select cardholders thousands of new ways to put their travel benefits to use.

Beginning Jan. 1, 2027, The Edit by Chase Travel℠ will include more than 10,000 curated vacation homes in addition to its existing collection of luxury hotels and resorts.

That means eligible Chase Sapphire Reserve® (see rates and fees), Chase Sapphire Reserve for Business℠ (see rates and fees) and J.P. Morgan Reserve® cardholders will soon be able to use their annual The Edit statement credits toward vacation home stays — and potentially enjoy additional perks as part of their stay (minimum four-night stay required).

The information for the J.P. Morgan Reserve card has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

If you're unfamiliar, The Edit by Chase Travel is a curated collection of luxury hotels and resorts that offers eligible cardholders additional perks when booking through the Chase Travel portal (minimum two-night stay required).

Currently featuring more than 1,500 hotels and resorts, the collection will expand to include more than 10,000 vacation homes beginning Jan. 1.

The homes will be curated by Plum Guide, a luxury vacation rental platform that evaluates properties using "more than 150 criteria related to comfort, design and location".

This builds on Chase Travel's partnership with Plum Guide, announced in April 2026, which brought luxury vacation rentals to more Chase cardholders through the travel portal.

With the latest expansion, eligible Reserve cardholders will have access to a curated collection of vacation homes through The Edit, complete with premium benefits.

Cardholders will also have the flexibility to redeem Chase Ultimate Rewards points toward these stays through Chase Travel.

Additionally, Sapphire Reserve and Reserve Business cardholders will have access to Reserve Travel Designers, who can help match travelers with vacation homes and provide personalized concierge assistance before, during and after their stays.

Related: I’ve been using the Chase Sapphire Reserve for Business for a year — here’s why I’m keeping it

One of the biggest draws of booking a hotel through The Edit is the additional perks that come with a qualifying stay (minimum two-night stay required).

Depending on the property, these can include complimentary breakfast for two, a $100 property credit, room upgrades when available and early check-in and late checkout.

Vacation home bookings through The Edit will come with a different set of benefits.

There's an important catch, however: Vacation home stays must be at least four nights to qualify for these The Edit benefits. Some benefits are subject to availability and may vary by property.

Eligible cardholders will also be able to use their annual The Edit statement credits toward qualifying vacation home bookings.

As a refresher, here's how those credits break down:

Beginning on Jan. 1, 2027, the Chase Sapphire Reserve for Business will offer four statement credits of up to $250 each for The Edit stays that can be used throughout the year. That's up from two statement credits of up to $250 each available on the card in 2026.

Keep in mind that while a two-night prepaid booking may qualify for the statement credit, vacation home stays must be at least four nights to receive the additional The Edit benefits.

Also, be aware that while you can redeem Ultimate Rewards points for eligible bookings, stays paid entirely with points do not qualify for The Edit statement credits under Chase's current terms. If you want to use the statement credit, you'll need to make an eligible prepaid purchase with your card.

Related: How to stack Sapphire Reserve credits for up to $500 off

The addition of more than 10,000 vacation homes to The Edit is welcome news for eligible Chase cardholders, particularly those who prefer the space and flexibility of a vacation rental over a traditional luxury hotel.

It also gives cardholders more options for using their annual The Edit statement credits, while offering perks such as a $150 in-stay credit and early check-in and late checkout when available.

Just keep the minimum-stay requirements in mind, and compare prices before booking to make sure you're getting the best value.

#6257. How We Pulled It Off: An East-Meets-West Wedding in Istanbul

Jasmin Karibzhanova and Sam Sutcliffe are a multicultural pair whose families and upbringings have spanned the globe. Jasmin was born and raised in the city of Almaty, Kazakhstan, and now lives in Toronto with Sam, a Canadian of Chinese-English descent (who grew up partly in Hong Kong). Friends introduced them in 2022 and the couple were engaged in Turks and Caicos in 2024. Quickly, they figured out that anywhere they married would require a long-haul flight for many if not most of their guests, so why not give everyone an excuse to go somewhere thrilling?

It was Jasmin’s father who suggested they wed in Istanbul for a few reasons: Turkey doesn’t require visas for Canadian or Kazakh citizens, there are direct flights to Istanbul from both Toronto and Almaty, and the city seemed like a more compelling place than typical European destination wedding locales like the countryside of France or Italy. Plus, given the bride and groom’s cultural backgrounds, an east-meets-west theme fit nicely with Istanbul’s location and history. Ahead, the couple shares how they planned their June 2026 wedding for 160 guests in Istanbul, a celebration that included a boat ride to a secret destination, a ceremony along the strait, and copious amounts of Turkish delight.

Living far away, the couple knew they’d need a lot of help plotting their destination celebration. After deciding on Istanbul, they first reached out to Turkish planners, but then struggled with the cultural divide. “Western wedding traditions are a bit different than what they were used to, and we had some communication issues with language,” Jasmin says.

They expanded their search to planners elsewhere in Europe with whom they could speak more clearly, and who were well-versed in producing larger-scale celebrations. They landed on Matthew Oliver Weddings, a London-based firm that specializes in destination weddings across Europe and the Middle East. Coincidentally, the team there had recently connected with Aylinly Events, a Turkish planner who’d directly expressed an interest in collaborating on Turkish destination celebrations. Given the serendipity, working with both firms seemed like the best way to pull off the kind of highly-produced event Jasmin and Sam wanted.

From there, the wedding was plotted via weekly Zoom meetings with the Matthew Oliver team, particularly their lead planners Bertie and Georgia, while the Turkish team tended to be most comfortable over WhatsApp. “If you're sending a WhatsApp, they'll respond in 20 minutes at 4:00 a.m. their time,” Jasmin says. “The Turkish approach to hospitality is next level. They’re never off. They work the hardest of any creative team I’ve ever met.”

The couple visited Istanbul twice during their engagement, with the first trip to tour venues about one year out from the wedding date they eventually set. They sought a space that could handle their substantial guest list, and quickly fell for the Peninsula Istanbul, which spans four buildings set right on the Bosphorus in the historic neighborhood of Karaköy.

“It was integrated into the fabric of the city,” Jasmin says. “You could just walk out into the street and enjoy Istanbul, which we really loved, and it had fantastic views of the Golden Horn.” The brand was a special touchstone for Sam and his family too, as the Peninsula has roots in Hong Kong.

Given the hotel’s size, its staff was adept at events and offered plenty of standard packages, though they were happy to work outside of the typical framework. “There was nothing they would say no to,” Jasmin says. “They had a fantastic understanding of vendors in the city and issues to consider, with amazing recommendations. Their whole approach to hospitality and wedding planning was that there is no rejection of any idea. They would just figure it out.”

When reaching out to friends and family, the couple was pleasantly surprised to find how many wanted to fly to Turkey. “I sort of assumed that because it was so far, especially for the Canadians, that we’d have a smaller guest list than we did,” Jasmin says. “But people really wanted to go because it was a destination that a lot hadn’t been to before. It was a great excuse to make their way over there.”

So they felt a duty to properly entertain their loved ones. “My philosophy around the event was that I wanted it to be completely guest-facing. I wanted it to be easy for people to come and enjoy the weekend,” says the bride, who admits she went totally “overboard” in this respect. Aside from creating a wedding website with all the event info, they also offered travel tips and suggestions, fashioned suggested itineraries, and pre-booked a local tour of Istanbul for folks who arrived early.

Another reason they opted for the Peninsula was its location near many other hotels with varying price points and appeals. “Our friends stayed closer to bars and nightlife, and older guests stayed near museums and such,” Jasmin says, estimating that about a third of attendees checked into the Peninsula.

Both Jasmin and Sam have creative backgrounds—they work together on a film production company, Jasmin studied theater and acted, and Sam’s parents are celebrated architects—and approached the aesthetics of their wedding like an artistic pursuit. “We knew that a lot of our guests would be from the creative world, and we were particular about how we wanted things to look,” Jasmin says. They suggested high-level elements like the color scheme (dusty blue and rich mulberry), and then their planning teams, along with the creative studio Event Lab, filled in the gaps with more ideas.

One key element in ensuring the wedding’s cohesion was the furniture production, for which they worked with AND Event & Design Studio to create items like modular custom chairs and a platform drenched in a velvety maroon for the ceremony space. Another was the florals, designed and arranged by Fluida Design. For the eye-popping ceremony, the flowers were lush and architectural, almost alien-like, while for dinner the arrangements were tighter, paler, and more romantic.

“I wanted it to function like a play: There’s a rising energy, then a reveal, then a resolution,” says Jasmin of the aesthetic journey. In Fluida Design, they found a creative partner that pushed them in all the right directions, outside a typical wedding comfort zone. “The initial proposition was a lot more neutral colors, just whites and greens, and then our floral team was like, ‘Well, why don't we just do color because that's just more interesting?’” Jasmin recalls. And as much as the couple cared about the look, they were happy to let the experts be the experts. “We were like, ‘Well, we would like for you also to just have fun with it,” she says. “Do whatever you want.”

On Thursday of their wedding weekend, the couple hosted an intimate but more casual rehearsal dinner for their family and closest friends at the hotel. Friday brought the welcome party for all of their guests, who boarded boats bound for an unknown location at sunset from the Peninsula: it turned out to be the Rahmi M. Koç Museum, a funky transportation museum space along the Bosphorus.

When the couple toured venues, they found that many options were great but a little too similar in energy to the Peninsula. “The last place we went was this museum, which is a ridiculous, magical place,” Jasmin says. “It’s a private collection of vintage cars, boats, submarines, and planes, all cramped together in this hangar-like building on the Bosphorus. It was very kitschy but a great contrast to our wedding venue.”

The Silk Road-themed party packed in loads of Turkish details from the music to the food: carts offering grilled meatballs (or köfte), ⁠döner, and stuffed bulgur balls (or içli köfte) made for a bazaar energy, while a live dessert station formed traditional lokma, freshly fried dough balls drizzled with syrup. “Floral” arrangements were built around local vegetables, like tall piles of peppers strung on garlands, and evil-eye pendants were handed out as party favors.

Sam and Jasmin’s wedding day started out a bit drizzly, a rarity for early summer in Istanbul. One of the reasons they chose the Peninsula in the first place was for its large terrace set against the strait, with the hope of getting married at sunset along the water with boats streaming by in the background. The vision was so beloved that they refused to come up with a rain plan, even for the platform built across the space.

“Our team was like, ‘Maybe we look into other things?’ And I can be very impulsive,” Jasmin admits. “‘No, we're just going to commit to this. If it rains, it rains. I don't want to hide the city from our guests, even if it's wet.’” They delayed the ceremony for a few minutes but got their dream of holding it outside without soaking their families and friends.

Waiting for that area was worth it. “It was a very special space because normally that space is just a herb garden on top of the Peninsula, but we took it over for the wedding,” Sam says. “You both got spectacular views across the entire city and felt in it, while being slightly removed from the craziness.”

The Muslim call to prayer rang out amid a ceremony officiated by family friend and noted Canadian philanthropist Nancy Lockhart, and boats slowed down in interest. “It didn't feel invasive at all,” Jasmin says. “We wanted to be integrated into the city, and that's what we got.”

Following the ceremony, guests enjoyed cocktails steps away in a part of the courtyard wrapped in a romantic mauve pink that colored the curtains, custom loungers, and drink tables. In keeping with the ideas of travel and adventure, the cocktail hour had a hotel theme (an idea that came from the Peninsula’s staff), with staff dressed as bellhops and a wall of ornate golden keys with pink tassels serving as the escort cards.

The wall of keys also functioned to block off the dinner area as it was set up, “so when they were ushered into the next space,” Sam says, “it was a surprising and beautiful new twist for everyone.” Next to the ceremony and cocktails spaces, the dinner “room” was formed by walls of blue curtains and the soaring, upside-down umbrellas that sit permanently on that courtyard. The tables were arranged in long, wavy lines that provided open views to the water.

And while this could never have been planned—even by the considerable talents of the creative couple and their multiple event teams—the risk of rain was rewarded by an incredible sight. “We had a spectacular double rainbow from the Asian side to the European side of the Bosphorus," says Sam. “The rainbow is something I will never forget for the rest of my life.’

While the couple’s welcome dinner was packed with cultural touchpoints, the wedding day itself was more traditionally Western, albeit with some Turkish details. Sam took his groomsmen to a hamam during the day for spa treatments, and the wedding dinner was based around the best of the local cuisine. Canapes included mussel “dolma’’ with black-ink bread, a lemon commape, a bite of Ezine cheese with quince, and a simit bread crumble, while the main meal began with a mezze platter before a first course of duck or mushroom baklava.

After dinner and speeches from loved ones, the party took to the dance floor, where the Uninvited Jazz Band got the party going. The couple served a classic wedding cake in two flavors: one dark chocolate and one raspberry and white chocolate. A series of smaller sweet bites from the Peninsula’s famous high tea were also passed around the tables.

A local city ordinance that event noises die down after 10 p.m. inspired a move off the terrace and into the nearby ballroom for more dancing. The after-party space was blanketed in scarlet, with a black and white checkerboard floor. From there, DJ Live from Élan Artists spun into the wee hours, and the newlyweds poured out a Champagne tower. A poem Sam had written was displayed above the bar: “Silk Road’s starting point / union atop ancient roots / celebratory love.”

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6256. 5 Airlines Flying The Airbus A321XLR With Lie-Flat Business Class Seats

The Airbus A321XLR is an aircraft designed for thin long-haul routes. By bringing narrowbody economics to intercontinental services, the aircraft promises to open up new city pairs that couldn't be served economically by widebodies. The aircraft is small, and it sips fuel in comparison to even a modern Boeing 787 or Airbus A350, let alone an A330 or 777.

It has already proven reasonably popular for its niche, but even though the economics are great for airlines, passengers still want widebody comfort. A321XLR operators, as well as operators of the older A321LR, are now widely installing lie-flat business class seats on these planes.

While these are narrowbody-optimized models with significant differences from those used on widebodies, they still provide passengers with a lie-flat seat, while newer models offer direct aisle access by using either a herringbone or reverse herringbone layout. As the A321XLR is introduced by more airlines, these are the five carriers with the largest lie-flat business class cabins on this aircraft type.

Iberia was the global launch operator of the A321XLR, having operated the type's first commercial flight on November 6, 2024, from Madrid to Paris, as well as its first long-haul flight from Madrid to Boston on November 14. The airline now operates eight A321XLRs, with no more currently remaining on order.

Iberia uses the type to serve destinations such as Toronto, Boston, New York, Washington-Dulles, Santo Domingo, San Juan, Recife, and Fortaleza. Iberia installs 182 seats on the A321XLR, which is a relatively high number for this aircraft. 14 of these are business class seats, which are based on the Thompson VantageSOLO.

This is a herringbone seat model optimized for narrowbodies, and was first introduced by JetBlue in 2021 on the A321neo as its new Mint Suites. Unlike JetBlue, however, Iberia did not option sliding doors, nor did it opt for the front row 'business class plus' option that JetBlue did. Air Canada also operates the A321XLR with 14 business class seats, and its examples also feature 182 seats in total.

However, Iberia gets the bump over Air Canada in this list because it operates more examples, with Air Canada currently flying five A321XLRs to Iberia's eight. With that being said, Air Canada holds orders for 30 XLRs in total, which means that it will eventually operate substantially more A321XLRs. It will, in fact, be one of the larger A321XLR operators in the world.

Aer Lingus was originally set to be the worldwide launch operator for the A321XLR, but a dispute with parent company IAG over pilot pay led the holding company to allocate the first A321XLR to Iberia instead. However, Aer Lingus would soon begin receiving its own XLRs, and the Irish flag carrier now operates six examples.

These planes complement the airline's existing fleet of eight A321LRs, giving it a total fleet of 14 long-range A321neos with lie-flat seats. Aer Lingus installs 184 seats on the A321XLR, including 16 business class seats. Unlike Iberia, the carrier uses the Thompson Vantage, a staggered seat model featuring three rows configured four-abreast and two rows containing 'throne seats'.

This seat is ultimately far from cutting-edge, as it debuted in the late 2000s and it doesn't even offer direct aisle access. However, the seat remains quite space-efficient, and Aer Lingus also uses it on its A330 fleet in addition to the A321s. The A321XLR is ultimately an improved, more capable A321neo, and Aer Lingus already operates eight A321LRs.

Aer Lingus's A321LRs have the same configuration as the XLRs, while also using the same exact business class seats. The main way to tell the two apart on the inside is the fact that the XLRs feature the Airbus Airspace cabins, while also featuring newer, larger screens. In addition, Aer Lingus installs newer Recaro seats on the A321XLR, while the A321LRs are equipped with the Collins Aerospace Meridian.

Air Canada's Airbus A321XLR skips Premium Economy entirely, opting for 14 business suites and 36 extra-legroom seats on thinner transatlantic routes.

United Airlines is the newest operator on this list, having taken delivery of its first A321XLR in May 2026. The carrier now operates three examples, and it has another 47 on the way. These planes are currently only flying from Washington-Dulles to Los Angeles and San Francisco.

However, they will eventually fully replace United's Boeing 757 operation across the Atlantic, serving thin destinations in Europe with far greater efficiency than what the 757 could do, while also featuring all-new interiors. These aircraft are equipped with 20 Polaris suites, based on the Elevate Altitude. This is a herringbone seat installed at a notably high 49-degree angle.

This represents the first time that an Elevate seat has been put into service on an Airbus aircraft. United will use the A321XLR to replace its 757s on transatlantic services, but the two aircraft are configured very differently. United's 757s feature 16 business class seats and 160 economy seats.

Meanwhile, the A321XLRs have four additional Polaris suites, 42 fewer economy seats, and a Premium Plus cabin consisting of 12 seats. While the A321XLR is currently only operating domestic services for United Airlines, it will begin flying the aircraft transatlantic in December, initially deploying it from Washington-Dulles to Amsterdam and Dublin.

American Airlines was the US launch operator of the A321XLR, having taken its first XLR in July 2025. For American, the A321XLR serves a similar role as it does for United, but the airline is using its current fleet of 11 A321XLRs to serve both transatlantic and transcontinental routes. United's deployment of the A321XLR on transcontinental services is temporary until the type begins long-haul flights.

However, this is American's long-term strategy for its 40 A321XLRs. Just like United, American Airlines installs 20 Flagship suites on the A321XLR, although American gets the bump in this list as it has more examples. American selected the Collins Aerospace Aurora, a herringbone seat model very similar to the Thompson VantageSOLO and Elevate Altitude.

American Airlines Future Lie-Flat Narrowbody Fleet

United Airlines Future Lie-Flat Narrowbody Fleet

Both airlines have opted to install 20 business class seats, along with 12 premium economy seats. The main difference is that American sells five extra economy seats on its A321XLRs, as United has installed a snack bar at the rear of the cabin, which takes up a set of three seats, while it has also blocked two exit-row seats to bring the total seat count down to 150.

The next-generation narrowbody has an exciting future ahead of it.

Saudia has ordered 15 A321XLRs in total, and took delivery of its first example in May 2026. The airline now already has five A321XLRs in its fleet, and they're currently being used to serve thinner routes to the Maldives, Mauritius, and Europe out of the carrier's hubs in Jeddah and Riyadh.

Saudia was the first customer in the Middle East to take delivery of the A321XLR, and it expects to have all 15 aircraft on property by the end of 2027. The airline installs the largest business class cabin on the A321XLR of any operator, equipping these planes with 24 business class seats. It uses the Thompson VantageSOLO, similar to Iberia.

Current Narrowbody Lie-Flat Seat Models Being Used By Airlines

Reverse herringbone direct aisle access lie-flat

Saudi Arabia is looking to attract more visitors, which it hopes to accomplish in part by expanding Saudia's operations while also starting a new full-service airline named Riyadh Air. The A321XLR plays a unique but important role in connecting the country to destinations such as Barcelona, where demand from Jeddah Airport (JED) could be low. The A321XLR enables the airline to expand its reach and relevance without committing to an expensive widebody.

#6255. These Bangkok Hotels Offer In-House Experiences, Beautiful Views, and Excellent Bang for Your Buck

After 14 years in Bangkok, I’ve watched the city evolve into one of the most electric destinations in Southeast Asia. It’s a city of duality—constantly on the move with new hotel openings, world-class restaurants, and an ever-changing shopping scene, but with tradition firmly at its core.

There's something in Bangkok for every kind of traveler, no matter your age or budget. You can enjoy a lunch made by an 80-year-old auntie still serving the same streetside crab omelet she has for decades, or dine at the only three-Michelin-star restaurant in Thailand for dinner. Ancient golden temples stand alongside modern shopping centers, and old shophouses are being revived by the younger generation who want to preserve the city's heritage. When it comes to the hotel scene, this dichotomy is also in play. Guests can choose between historic boutique properties or glamorous new builds, and find every kind of amenity, design style, or cuisine under the sun.

Just as captivating is the warmth and hospitality of the Thai people, something I’ve found to be unlike anywhere else in the world. Thailand is known as the “Land of Smiles,” and from my experience, it more than lives up to its name. The city reveals itself through small, thoughtful moments mixed with grand experiences, all set to an energetic pace that makes it one of my favorite destinations. If you're ready to see it all for yourself, read on for some of the best hotels in Thailand. —Megan Leon

The 30-story tower that this hotel calls home cuts a striking figure in the Bangkok skyline, shaped as it is after the wai, a Thai gesture of greeting made by pressing one’s palms together—a fitting shape for a place that beautifully melds Thai hospitality with a hyper-polished service style. The staff here is supremely gracious: They remember names, press buttons for guests at the elevator banks, turn tables over quickly at breakfast, and happily fetch booster seats for little princes and princesses. And if that’s not enough to make you feel at home, perhaps the stylish rooms and common spaces will, designed as they are to offer a true sense of place. Modern sculptures and paintings by living Thai artists, and subtle design nods to the country’s silk-making history and garments worn by traditional Thai dancers, delight at every turn. —Matt Ortile

It feels like you might be in London when you're at The Peninsula in Bangkok's Thonburi neighborhood, thanks in part to the British racing vehicles parked out front. But the hotel's custom tuk-tuk reminds you that you're in Thailand, and rich, warm toffee tones carry throughout the lobby and lounges. The space offers grand views over the Chao Phraya and the Thai river homes across the water. The Peninsula swimming pool is among the best in the city; there's no better way to beat the heat in this famously hot capital than by taking a dip right on the river. —J.A.

In a city where almost every high-end hotel brand has already made a mark, it takes something extra special to turn heads. Yet when Capella Bangkok finally opened after a seven-year tease, the city’s high-society set swooped in like magpies. Why? Capella’s first foray in Thailand is the only city hotel with villas right on the Chao Phraya River—multi-roomed retreats with private gardens and swimming pools lined with travertine marble. Suites in the main building—a blocky, low-slung affair with 101 rooms—come with plunge pools on their balconies, and the hotel tapped hot-shot chef Mauro Colagreco (of Mirazur in France) to head its signature coastal Mediterranean restaurant, Côte. Crystalline coupes of private-label Champagne accompany check-in, brunches, and turn-down service, but that’s as flashy as it gets. The rest feels decidedly subdued. Service is hushed but switched-on, and the spa eschews New Age treatments for humble, age-old healing practices (tok sen hammer massages, luk pra kob herbal compresses) inspired by the historic Thai-Chinese community just outside its gates. —C.S.

Compared with many of its rivals, this Bangkok stalwart doesn’t have a location that’s wildly convenient: The postcard sights need a boat transfer, and most top tables are more than a 30-minute taxi ride away. But for the legions of loyal fans, that’s the point. Pitched up on a lush riverside plot in the hushed Dusit district, The Siam feels like a portal to a bygone Bangkok. Even though it opened over a decade ago, it’s easy to imagine it as a plush playground for the city’s erstwhile big guns. You'd be hard-pressed to point friends to a lovelier lunch spot than the hotel’s Thai restaurant, set between the timeworn pillars of three ancient teakwood houses, where butlers in dressy black sarongs deliver the kind of classic Thai hospitality—lilting “sawadee ka” greetings and tables set with fresh orchids—that’s becoming harder to find. None of which is to say that the hotel is stuffy—there’s a tattoo parlor in the spa. —Chris Schalkx

Making its debut in 2025 as the second Andaz outpost in Thailand, Andaz One Bangkok is an urban escape that deftly balances its proximity to Bangkok’s largest green park with its connection to the city’s fast-paced energy. Set in the Lumphini neighborhood, it offers direct views of leafy Lumphini Park while also keeping guests within reach of the business and shopping areas nearby. Rooted in Thai art, local female artists shine throughout the hotel, giving the space the feel of a gallery. Social spaces, ranging from the lobby lounge to the rooftop restaurant, make this the perfect place to relax and connect with other travelers. —M.L.

Opened in August 2026, Fairmont Bangkok Sukhumvit marks the Fairmont brand's debut in Thailand. The hotel is a comfortable base for exploring Sukhumvit, with public transportation and the Em District within walking distance, while its on-site restaurants, bars, and outdoor pool give plenty of reasons to stay in. Families are welcome, with a kids club and family-friendly pool complete with a waterslide. The interiors are modern and luxurious without losing their warmth, with thoughtful touches like the discreet, tucked-away reception desk and an impressive glass chandelier that is the talk of the town. For a hotel that's only been open a couple of months, the service is exceptional and thoughtful; by the end of the first day, everyone knows your name, making this new hotel feel like a luxe, warm, and welcoming home. —M.L.

The first hotel from Curio Collection by Hilton to arrive in Thailand, Kromo is a colorful celebration of Bangkok’s heritage with a contemporary edge. Located on Sukhumvit Road between Phrom Phong and Asoke, this 28-floor property is not what it seems from the outside; a modern black façade greets you at first glance, but once inside, a youthful pink-hued space opens up, with the hotel's lobby restaurant and bar just steps away. The hotel's design concept takes inspiration from a phrase in Bangkok's ceremonial Thai name, which translates to “The City of the Nine Gems,” brought to life in the creative social space Vilah (modeled after the chrysoberyl gem) and at the rooftop pool (designed after the zircon gem). Kromo sits at the foot of EM District, where three distinct shopping centers cater to every type of traveler. Across the way is one of Sukhumvit's most loved green parks for those needing a dose of nature and the occasional turtle sighting. —M.L.

The Dusit Thani Bangkok is in a class of its own, having first opened its doors five decades ago as one of the most glamorous and luxurious hotel experiences in Thailand. Following a full renovation, it reopened in 2024 with a refreshed Thai-inspired look while still holding on to the same warm, local hospitality that built its reputation. Located within the upper echelons of Silom, the hotel overlooks Lumphini Park, promising inescapable views from every room. Centrally located between the Chao Phraya River and the shopping mecca of Sukhumvit, guests have close access to everything from a rooftop garden to a retail center filled with local shops and popular dining spots. The property is also kid-friendly, with a kids club and cultural activities that are actually fun for little ones. —M.L.

Kimpton Maa-Lai manages to provide something not every large hotel can: a stay that’s both intimate yet connected to the city's lively social scene. The modern, stark façade is a contrast to what you’ll find inside—buzzing cafés, intimate bars, rare green space tucked into Bangkok's urban jungle, and spacious rooms with nature-inspired touches and Thai decor. On-site, there are six dining options, from a Michelin-starred restaurant to a moody bar. Plus, as a Kimpton, the hotel is pet-friendly; kids and adults of all ages will love spotting furry friends roaming the lobby with their owners. Located within a hip retail and dining village and just a few minutes from the rows of shopping centers along Sukhumvit Road, there’s much to do at your fingertips. —Megan Leon

The Ritz-Carlton's entry into Bangkok brought with it a serene stay in an evolving corner of the city with easy access to major sites and the brand's signature impeccable service. It sits on the One Bangkok campus, a $3 billion development with hotels, office buildings, condos, a massive shopping mall, an entertainment complex, and plenty of public art and outdoor space. Guest rooms begin on the eighth floor and go up to 24, half of which have balconies or outdoor space. Room types start at a Deluxe King or Deluxe Double, many with stand-alone tubs and walk-in rain showers, and expand up to The Ritz-Carlton Suite, a two-bedroom with a massive walk-in closet, dining room, bar, Lumphini Park views, and lounge access. Be sure to book a meal at Duet by David Toutain (whose eponymous Paris restaurant has two Michelin stars); his team serves modern French cuisine in the form of a seasonal tasting menu heavy on seafood, fresh vegetables, and ornate presentation. —Madison Flager

Romantic and right on the river, Amdaeng fits the bill if you want to relax and recharge away from the frenzy of the city. Inside, find interiors that include alligator-print leather sofas, a red swimming pool, bathtubs with chrome lion feet, Thai tilework, and Chinese antiques. Directly outside the hotel, wander the canals of the Thonburi District, crossing small bridges, visiting Buddhist spirit houses, and seeing the big banyan trees. Here, you'll get a taste of everyday life in Bangkok. You’ll find neighbors catching up curbside over noodles, and true hidden-gem restaurants. This hotel feels like a hidden discovery, tucked down an alley alongside a canal. —Jenny Adams

There’s no hotel quite like Bangkok Publishing Residence in the city, with its antique typewriters and cabin-chic rooms. Evoking the image of a Mad Men daydream, it's a time capsule of a former publishing heyday. With a treasure trove of antiquities and a lobby that preserves the building’s former life as a weekly series publisher, you won’t find anything like it anywhere. The owner inherited her grandfather’s printing house, restoring and reimagining it as a character-driven hotel with only eight rooms and miles of soul. If this is the first hotel you experience in Bangkok, it’s going to set a very high bar. But it can be tough to snag a stay, as this place sees frequent return guests. —J.A.

The Anantara Siam Bangkok Hotel, which draws a fashionable crowd of international travelers, is a verdant sanctuary in the retail jungle. Much to the delight of those staying here, the property has a stronger resort vibe than many hotels in this area, with tropical landscaping, a central swimming pool, gorgeous rooms, and old-world Thai details. It also offers some of the only terrace rooms in town; they come with adjoining gardens where you can sit out on a private patio. —J.A.

The Park Hyatt Bangkok has the feel of an art gallery, where striking design elements surprise you, but nothing gets in the way. You're pointed to the hotel entrance by a series of discreet signs in gold lettering, then elevators take you to the beautiful 10th-floor lobby, decorated in cream and white and accented with simple but bold artwork. Even the sleek, sculpted reception desk looks like modern art. The rooms are beautiful, and the bathrooms feel like spas. Penthouse Bar & Grill, which spans three upper floors of the building, was designed by the famous New York firm of AvroKo. The idea was to turn one seamless space into five separate venues with marble, ebony, and gold accents, plus antique British stylings. —Audrey Phoon

What are the best areas to stay in Bangkok?

The riverside neighborhoods of Rattanakosin and adjacent Banglamphu are a great starting point, with their famous temples like Wat Po, plus the Grand Palace complex, old forts, sunny parks, and the backpacker zone of Khao San Road. If you’re a fan of stiff drinks and sharp suits, visit Thonglor—often compared to Brooklyn—where a heavy Japanese expat community has resulted in great omakase joints, cool vintage purveyors, and a collection of high-end tailors. This is also the city’s nexus for hot new cocktail spots.

Chinatown’s tiny lane, Soi Nana, gets global nods for its handful of craft libation and beer bars, all cutting-edge but delightfully ramshackle. This neighborhood could take you a week to fully explore, jam-packed as it is with 300-year-old Taoist temples, darling coffee houses, serious dim sum, great shopping, and a maze of old-world food markets. If shopping and art are on the agenda, head to Siam, where you’ll find the city’s largest art museum, as well as a range of malls.

What’s the best way to get around Bangkok?

Bangkok’s traffic is infamous. However, if you plan accordingly, it’s hardly an issue. In the riverside neighborhoods and Chinatown, it’s easy to walk. The streets are flat and the sites are close together. Along Sukhumvit Road—the main artery that connects the mid-city neighborhoods like Thonglor, Siam, Prom Phong, and Sathorn—you can use the BTS SkyTrain. It’s simple to follow English maps, posted nearly everywhere, with colored lines and an easy ticket-purchasing process. This raised train runs every day from 6 a.m. to midnight and has three separate lines that connect huge portions of the city. Finally, make sure to hop in a tuk-tuk. Thailand’s famous rickshaw vehicles provide a fun, exhilarating way to experience the city.

I recommend visiting Bangkok for a minimum of three days, which will give you time to explore a few temples, get a taste of local street food in Chinatown, squeeze in a foot massage, and spend time gallery hopping at the new Dib Bangkok art museum or shopping at one of Bangkok’s many malls.

The best time to visit is from November through February, when the monsoon season has ended and the cooler season arrives—and by cooler, I just mean a degree or two less than usual.

When choosing hotels, our editors consider properties across price points that offer an authentic and insider experience of a destination, keeping design, location, service, and sustainability credentials top of mind.

Here’s how to make the most of South Australia

It took me several trips to Australia to realize I’d been skipping one of its best parts.

It took me several trips to Australia to realize I’d been skipping one of its best parts.

I’d visited the country a handful of times before, but this was my first trip to Adelaide and my first time exploring South Australia. Within a few days, I was eating my way through a 150-year-old market, walking among kangaroos and wallabies, blending my own bottle of shiraz, kayaking alongside wild dolphins, and bopping between breathtaking beaches, rolling hills, and wine country.

And getting there from the U.S. is about to become considerably easier.

United is bringing back its seasonal service between San Francisco International Airport (SFO) and Adelaide Airport (ADL) beginning Dec. 17. The route, now entering its second season, gives travelers the only nonstop connection between the U.S. and Adelaide, with schedules subject to change. Service is scheduled to run through Feb. 10, 2027.

Adelaide turned out to be an ideal home base for seeing just how much variety South Australia packs into a relatively small radius.

The state capital and largest city in the region still manages to feel surprisingly approachable. Its central business district mixes modern towers with low-slung stone cottages and other remnants of its colonial-era architecture, while the entire city center is wrapped in parklands that date back to Adelaide’s original 1837 city plan.

From the center of town, I could be among the rolling hills and small villages of the Adelaide Hills, heading toward the coast, or making my way into wine country — all in roughly half an hour.

That is, assuming you are prepared to drive on the left. My first encounter with my Australian rental car began with me confidently getting into the wrong front seat and momentarily wondering where someone had put the steering wheel.

For my stay, I checked into Hotel Indigo Adelaide Markets. My suite had a separate living area and a large balcony with sweeping views across the city and toward the hills. The hotel also has Merrymaker, a lively rooftop bar 16 floors above the surrounding market district.

Before I could start bouncing between wineries, markets, and wildlife encounters, though, I first had to cross the Pacific. United’s San Francisco-to-Adelaide service is scheduled to operate on a Boeing 787-9, and I got to make the overnight journey in United Polaris business class. After spending some time in the Polaris Lounge at SFO, I boarded and settled into my lie-flat seat for what was essentially going to be an entire night in the air.

Dinner started with tomato tartare and crostini, followed by braised short rib with risotto Milanese, garlic green beans, and fresh gremolata. It was genuinely tasty, to the point that I could almost forget I was eating dinner at 35,000 feet.

Even more memorably, I got my first experience with United’s Polaris sundae service. My extremely attentive flight attendant recommended I simply go for all the fixings, and I took her advice. She was right.

From there, I put the lie-flat seat to good use and got a substantial stretch of sleep before waking for breakfast closer to Adelaide. I went with a mushroom omelet and chicken sausage, which provided a convenient marker that it was time to stop thinking in San Francisco time and get onto my new schedule.

That rhythm ended up being one of the biggest benefits of flying the route in Polaris. Dinner, a real block of sleep, and breakfast before landing gave the flight something resembling a normal overnight routine. By the time I arrived in Adelaide, I felt far more functional than I normally do after crossing that many time zones and was ready to start exploring almost immediately.

Over the next few days, I got to see several very different sides of the region. Looking back, most of what I loved about South Australia fell pretty neatly into one of three camps: adventure, indulgence, and culture.

I managed to sample a little of all three, but depending on how you like to travel, any one could easily become the backbone of a trip here.

My adventure itinerary began less than half a block from my hotel at Adelaide Central Market.

The market has been operating since 1869 and today packs more than 70 artisans under one roof. What struck me more than its age, though, was how much it still felt like a place Adelaide actually uses.

At lunchtime, workers from the surrounding central business district mixed with families, visitors, and people picking up groceries. Around them were rows of fresh produce, flowers, bakeries, bookstores, sweet shops, and food stalls representing cuisines from around the world.

I had some of the best paella I’ve had in a long time, worked my way through a few of the savory pies and rolls Australia does especially well, and found my favorite at Smiley’s: a hot chicken roll that I would have happily eaten again the next day.

Dessert sent me down another very Australian rabbit hole. Honeycomb is a flavor I encounter constantly here and almost never back home, and I found a honeycomb cornflake slice that was essentially the Australian cousin of a Rice Krispies treat.

The food scene spills beyond the market, too. Elsewhere in the central business district, streets like Peel and Leigh narrow into pedestrian-friendly laneways packed with wine bars, restaurants, cocktail spots, and cafes.

And if there is one thing I’m reminded of every time I return to Australia, it is that Australians take coffee very seriously. My favorite stop was Exchange Coffee, where the menu seemed capable of accommodating essentially any permutation of coffee I could come up with.

From there, I headed into the Adelaide Hills for Cleland Wildlife Park.

I have been to enough petting zoos in the U.S. to approach almost any animal experience with a little skepticism. Cleland was nothing like that.

The park centers on conservation and education, and many of its kangaroos and wallabies move freely through large natural areas where visitors can walk among them. Adult admission costs AU$35.80.

I spent much of my visit wandering between animals that seemed largely unconcerned by my presence. At one point, I spotted a baby wallaby riding in its mother’s pouch with just its little head poking out, which may have been the single cutest thing I saw on the entire trip.

I also paid extra for a koala encounter and met Tek, a 10-year-old male whose fur was far softer than I expected. A keeper remained beside him throughout the experience, supplying eucalyptus and making sure the interaction stayed very much on his terms.

The keeper also informed me that Tek might have better labor protections than most humans. After a 30-minute stretch of close-up visitor encounters, he gets two complete days off from that kind of work entirely, which made me both laugh and feel a little jealous.

For the final stop on my adventure itinerary, I traded ground-level bush walks for the roof of Adelaide Oval.

The stadium manages to feel both thoroughly modern and distinctly historic, with its grassy northern mound, enormous fig trees, and century-old scoreboard still intact amid the contemporary grandstands. Those trees also have a wonderfully petty backstory: They were planted, at least in part, to stop people on nearby Montefiore Hill from watching games inside the Oval for free.

For an even better view, I signed up for Adelaide Oval’s RoofClimb. After changing into a jumpsuit and clipping into a harness, I followed my guide onto a track running across the stadium roof. From the top, Adelaide suddenly made much more sense geographically. I could trace the river through the city, see the Adelaide Hills rising in one direction, and look toward the coastline in another.

At the turnaround point came the obligatory opportunity to lean backward over the edge, arms out, with my harness very much attached.

A standard daytime RoofClimb takes about two hours and starts at AU$125 for adults and AU$95 for children ages 8 to 15. By the time I unclipped, it had landed in a very specific sweet spot: scenic, informative, and just adrenaline-inducing enough to make me feel like I had earned the view.

My indulgence itinerary began with one of the most elaborate meals I have ever experienced.

Restaurant Aptos sits inside a converted church in Stirling, in the Adelaide Hills, and serves just 14 diners at a time. Its 16-course tasting menu unfolds progressively across three interconnected dining rooms.

From the moment I walked in, it felt like stepping into another world.

The first course made it abundantly clear what kind of evening I was in for. I was handed what was essentially a branch dotted with five native Australian fruits and instructed to lick each flavor directly off the wood.

I tried crocodile tongue for the first time, paired with Geraldton wax flavors, and kangaroo seasoned with native Australian ingredients. The latter was considerably more tender and less gamey than I expected.

Across the 16 courses, the flavor combinations were at times so layered that my first reaction was almost sensory overload. I would take a bite, spend a few seconds trying to work out what exactly I was tasting, and then suddenly everything would settle into place.

Each course also arrived with a beautifully designed card detailing the ingredients and preparation. By dessert, I had a stack of 16 that felt less like a menu and more like a collection of art prints I wanted to take home and frame.

The following day, I stayed in the Adelaide Hills but traded a tasting menu for a pair of walking shoes at Mount Lofty Botanic Garden.

Calling it a botanical garden almost undersells it.

Spread across 97 hectares, Mount Lofty showcases cool-climate plants from around the world, with sections devoted to flora from places including South America, Africa, and Asia.

The landscape felt closer to a nature preserve than a manicured city park. I wandered past ponds, streams, flowers, and dense pockets of forest, with the scenery seeming to change every few minutes.

The birdlife also made me stop more than once. One thing I never quite get over in Australia is how exotic even an everyday bird can look compared with what I am accustomed to seeing in New York. At home, my baseline is largely pigeons and crows. Here, seemingly commonplace birds can look like something escaped from an aviary.

Admission is free, making Mount Lofty an easy way to spend a few hours in the hills.

From there, I continued to Hahndorf, Australia’s oldest surviving German settlement. Its main street is lined with heritage buildings, bakeries, pubs, boutiques, and antique stores.

I stopped at Otto’s Bakery for a vanilla slice, one of those Australian desserts whose name does very little to explain what it actually is. Rather than cake, it is a thick layer of silky vanilla custard sandwiched between crisp sheets of puff pastry.

The final stop on my indulgence itinerary took me south to McLaren Vale and d’Arenberg, where the Osborn family has been growing grapes since 1912.

The first thing I noticed, though, had nothing to do with wine.

The five-story d’Arenberg Cube rises above the vineyards in a jumble of black, white, glass, and mirrors. Against the rolling countryside, it looks a little like a Rubik’s Cube Salvador Dalí might have designed himself. Fittingly, one floor houses an exhibition of Dalí sculptures and graphic works.

My main reason for visiting was the Blending Bench, a hands-on experience that lets you create and bottle your own wine.

By sheer luck, I was the only person booked for my session. In front of me were three shiraz samples made from vines planted in 1898, 1969, and 1999, and all three tasted remarkably different.

Using pipettes, a worksheet, and plenty of trial and error, I measured different percentages into my glass, tasted the result, and adjusted from there.

I went in convinced the 1898 sample, easily my favorite on its own, would make up most of my final bottle. But tiny changes in the proportions completely altered the flavor. Eventually, I settled on something I liked even more than any of the three components separately.

Then I got to bottle, name, and label a full 750-milliliter version to take home.

The Blending Bench costs AU$120 and takes about 75 minutes. Between the architecture, art, vineyards, and leaving with a bottle I had actually created myself, it was easily one of the more memorable winery visits I have had.

For the culture itinerary, I started with a restaurant I had been excited about well before I ever landed in Adelaide.

Africola has one of the most distinct visual identities I have ever seen from a restaurant, from its website and branding to the space itself.

Once inside, though, what stood out was how much it felt like a neighborhood institution.

More than once, I watched members of the staff greet diners with the easy familiarity of people who had clearly been coming back for years. I sat at the bar, which gave me a front-row view into the open kitchen and all of the plating and preparation happening behind it.

I started with the crispy chicken tea sandwich, one of Africola’s signatures. Soft white bread encloses crisp chicken skin, with peri-peri drippings served alongside for dipping. Think of it as a tiny, rich South African cousin of a French dip.

Then came the peri-peri chicken itself, smoky, spicy, and incredibly savory, along with salt-baked Dutch cream potatoes with labneh, za’atar, and chives that landed on my palette like an elegant twice-baked potato. I also ordered the cos lettuce with buttermilk, dill, and shallot, essentially Africola’s much more interesting answer to a wedge salad.

When everything was placed in front of me, I was mildly horrified by how much food I had ordered. About an hour later, I had eaten most of it and was contemplating whether I could simply roll myself through the central business district and back to my hotel.

It ended up being one of my favorite meals of the entire trip.

The next afternoon, I headed to Adelaide Botanic Garden on the eastern edge of the city center.

The 50-hectare garden is free to enter and mixes outdoor collections with ponds, shaded paths, historic buildings, museums, and glasshouses.

One of those spaces is the Palm House, a Victorian glasshouse from the 1870s that now holds plants from Madagascar, including species threatened or endangered in the wild.

Nearby, the Museum of Economic Botany ended up being one of my favorite stops. The collection includes enormous seeds, preserved plant specimens, and historical models centered on the many ways humans have used plants for food, medicine, textiles, inks, and other parts of everyday life.

Taken together, the garden felt less like simply spending an afternoon looking at pretty plants and more like a reminder of how deeply the natural world has shaped the way people eat, build, heal, create, and live.

Another way to dig deeper is through the garden’s Aboriginal Native Plant and Social History Tour. Led by an Aboriginal guide, the 90-minute experience explores traditional uses of native plants for food, medicine, and tools, along with Aboriginal social history, cultural practices, and relationships with the land. Tickets are currently AU$42 per person, plus booking fees.

For the final stop of my trip, I traded the central business district for a morning on the water at the Adelaide Dolphin Sanctuary near Garden Island.

I joined the three-hour Dolphin Sanctuary Kayak Tour, where my guide, Kendall, first walked us through the basics before leading our group onto the water.

We paddled between mangrove-lined creeks and the partially submerged remains of old ships. The Garden Island ships’ graveyard contains 25 known vessels abandoned between 1909 and 1945 after they became obsolete, damaged, or no longer economical to maintain.

Farther into the mangroves, I started getting serious Florida Everglades energy, only without quite as many things I was concerned might kill me.

Kendall, who happens to be an American from Florida herself, was equal parts kayak instructor and naturalist, filling us in on dolphin behavior, conservation efforts, and the maritime history behind the wrecks as we paddled.

Then came the moment I had convinced myself probably would not happen.

I am an eternal pessimist when it comes to any wildlife activity involving the phrase “possible sighting,” but we ended up spending several minutes alongside a mother dolphin and her calf.

The pair moved back and forth through the water together, surfacing side by side, disappearing beneath us, and then looping around again.

The tour costs AU$79 per adult, lasts about three hours, and includes the necessary kayaking gear.

Between the shipwrecks, ancient mangroves, and a wild dolphin sighting I had fully talked myself out of expecting, it was a fitting way to finish a trip that consistently surprised me.

In only a few days, Adelaide gave me a version of Australia I had not experienced on any of my previous visits.

I could spend the morning in the center of a major city, the afternoon walking through vineyards or alongside kangaroos, and the evening eating ingredients I had never heard of before the trip. More importantly, almost none of it required spending hours getting from one place to the next.

That is ultimately what made Adelaide work so well as a home base. Whether I leaned into adventure, indulgence, or culture, there was a different once-in-a-lifetime experience within easy reach.

Beginning Dec. 17, United’s returning seasonal San Francisco-to-Adelaide service will make it easier for U.S. travelers to arrive directly in South Australia and start exploring, with schedules subject to change. So take it from me — don’t sleep on South Australia, unless it’s from the comfort of a Polaris Business Class seat on the way there.

#6253. How Much Does A Boeing 787-9 Engine Cost?

The Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner is one of the most recognizable long-haul aircraft in modern commercial aviation, combining advanced aerodynamics, lightweight composite materials, and highly efficient engines to deliver impressive performance over long distances. However, while much attention is often given to the aircraft's overall purchase price, its engines represent an equally significant investment for airlines and aircraft leasing companies. So, how much does a 787-9 engine actually cost? Historical manufacturer announcements provide a useful indication, with General Electric GEnx-1B engines carrying implied list prices of approximately $25 million to $30 million each. However, the actual amount paid can vary considerably depending on the agreement, maintenance arrangements, and number of engines purchased.

The Boeing 787-9 is available with two engine options, allowing airlines to select the powerplant that best suits their operational requirements and existing fleet arrangements. These are the General Electric GEnx-1B and Rolls-Royce Trent 1000, both developed specifically for the next generation of long-haul commercial aircraft.

The GEnx-1B is manufactured by GE Aerospace and represents one of the company's most successful commercial engine programs. Developed from the earlier GE90 and incorporating several technological improvements, it was designed to deliver greater fuel efficiency, reduced emissions, and improved operating economics. Its performance makes it particularly suitable for airlines operating extensive international networks.

The alternative is the Rolls-Royce Trent 1000, part of the manufacturer's established Trent engine family. It was developed specifically for the 787 and features advanced materials, aerodynamic improvements, and a three-shaft architecture. The engine has experienced several technical challenges throughout its operational history, although subsequent improvements have addressed many of its earlier reliability concerns.

Importantly, the two engines are not interchangeable during ordinary airline operations. An airline generally selects one engine manufacturer when ordering its aircraft, and this decision influences maintenance arrangements, spare-engine requirements, and long-term operating costs. Consequently, discussions of the price of a 787-9 engine need to distinguish among the available powerplants.

GE Aerospace's historical pricing announcements provide some of the clearest publicly available information on the cost of a 787-9 engine. Based on manufacturer announcements, the GEnx-1B has historically carried an implied list price of about $25 million to $30 million per engine, although individual agreements can produce different figures.

One particularly useful example involves aircraft leasing company CIT Aerospace, which selected GEnx-1B engines to power four additional Boeing 787-9s. In its announcement, GE stated that the engine order was valued at more than $200 million at list price. Dividing this amount across eight installed engines suggests a value exceeding $25 million per engine.

Another example came from China Eastern Airlines, which selected GEnx-1B engines for 15 Boeing 787-9 aircraft. GE valued the engine order at more than $860 million at list price. With two engines per aircraft, the implied figure was about $28.7 million per engine, assuming the announcement covered 30 installed engines.

These examples demonstrate why a figure between $25 million and $30 million is a reasonable historical reference when discussing the GEnx-1B. Nevertheless, they should not be interpreted as confirmed prices for every individual engine, since manufacturer announcements may include additional equipment, contractual provisions, and commercial arrangements that influence the overall valuation.

The Boeing 787 comes with both GE and Rolls-Royce engine options, although GE's engines have become more popular in recent times.

Although historical list prices provide a useful starting point, airlines rarely purchase commercial aircraft engines under straightforward retail-style arrangements. Large customers negotiate individual agreements with manufacturers, and the final financial terms are generally confidential. Consequently, the actual price paid for a new GEnx-1B could differ substantially from its publicly stated list-price valuation.

Engine order size is another important consideration. Airlines and leasing companies purchasing engines for several aircraft may receive more favorable commercial terms than organizations requiring only a small number of units. Manufacturers also have an incentive to secure major fleet agreements because these relationships can generate maintenance and support revenue over several decades.

Another important factor involves the airline's existing relationship with the engine manufacturer. A carrier already operating numerous GE-powered aircraft may benefit from established maintenance facilities, technical expertise, spare-parts arrangements, and existing support agreements. These advantages can influence the overall commercial package offered when additional engines are ordered.

The delivery schedule and contractual requirements can also affect the financial arrangements. Some customers require additional spare engines to protect their operations against unexpected maintenance events, while others negotiate specific performance guarantees and support provisions. Therefore, two airlines purchasing the same engine model may ultimately have different overall expenditure, even when their initial aircraft orders appear similar.

The latest data from ch-aviation shows that United Airlines is currently the world's largest operator of the 787, followed by All Nippon Airways (ANA).

Purchasing a 787-9 engine represents only the beginning of the financial commitment involved in operating one. Commercial turbofan engines require regular inspections, component replacements, and occasional major maintenance visits throughout their service lives. These activities can account for a substantial share of an airline's long-term operating expenditure.

Modern engine manufacturers increasingly offer long-term maintenance agreements alongside the initial equipment purchase. These arrangements can cover inspections, repairs, overhauls, and technical support, with payments structured around engine utilization or other contractual conditions. These agreements help airlines manage maintenance costs while giving manufacturers ongoing revenue beyond the initial engine sale.

China Eastern Airlines provides a useful example of how these arrangements work. Alongside its order for GEnx-1B engines powering 15 Boeing 787-9 aircraft, the airline signed a 15-year TrueChoice Overhaul agreement with GE Aerospace. This arrangement covered the time and materials required to repair and overhaul the engines, demonstrating the importance of maintenance planning.

For airlines, these agreements offer greater predictability when managing expensive engine-related work. Instead of facing every major maintenance event as a separate financial challenge, operators can establish longer-term arrangements with the manufacturer. However, the overall cost still depends on utilization, maintenance requirements, contractual coverage, and the condition of individual engines.

Modern commercial jet engines cost tens of millions of dollars at list price.

The GEnx-1B is an extremely sophisticated piece of engineering, which helps explain its substantial purchase price. Designed to deliver the thrust required by a widebody aircraft such as the Boeing 787-9, it incorporates advanced materials, complex rotating components, and carefully engineered systems that must operate reliably under demanding conditions.

One key characteristic is its use of composite fan blades and a composite fan case. These components help reduce engine weight while maintaining the structural strength required for commercial aviation. Weight reduction is particularly important for long-haul aircraft because even small improvements can improve fuel consumption over thousands of flights.

Fuel efficiency is another major consideration. GE has previously stated that the General Electric GEnx offers up to 15% better fuel efficiency than its CF6 engine, alongside corresponding reductions in carbon dioxide emissions. Although this comparison is against an older engine generation, it illustrates the technological improvements incorporated into the GEnx program.

The engine also incorporates GE's twin-annular pre-swirl combustor technology, designed to reduce nitrogen oxide emissions. According to the manufacturer, this technology significantly reduces regulated emissions compared with applicable limits. These developments require extensive research, testing, manufacturing expertise, and certification work, all of which contribute to the considerable investment required to produce modern commercial aircraft engines.

Airlines do not necessarily need to purchase brand-new engines for every aircraft entering their fleets. Depending on their requirements, operators can explore previously operated engines, leased spare engines, or existing inventory within the aircraft leasing and maintenance markets. These alternatives can offer different financial arrangements than buying a new engine directly from the manufacturer.

Used engines can sometimes offer a lower initial acquisition cost, particularly when they have remaining operating life before their next major maintenance visit. However, their condition, maintenance history, remaining life of key components, and documentation are essential considerations. A cheaper engine may ultimately cost more if substantial maintenance is required shortly after acquisition.

Engine leasing is another option used throughout the commercial aviation industry. Rather than purchasing an additional engine outright, an airline can lease one to support its fleet during maintenance periods or unexpected operational disruptions. This approach can reduce the immediate capital commitment while providing access to a critical spare asset when needed.

Ultimately, the price of a 787-9 engine depends on its manufacturer, condition, contractual arrangements, and maintenance requirements. For a new GEnx-1B, historical manufacturer announcements suggest an approximate list-price value of $25 million to $30 million per engine. However, the actual amount an airline pays depends on confidential commercial negotiations and the broader support package.

#6252. Qantas Reaches Deal to Sell 44 Boeing 737s

Qantas has agreed to sell 44 Boeing 737-800s to British aviation aftermarket specialist AerFin as the Australian carrier prepares to retire most of its 737 fleet.

The deal includes the aircraft’s 88 CFM56-7B engines. AerFin said Wednesday it expects to receive the first jet before the end of 2026, with the rest transferring over the next seven years as Qantas retires them.

Qantas Domestic CEO Markus Svensson said the agreement gives the airline “flexibility to adjust the timing as new aircraft arrive,” in a news release.

Qantas operates nearly 80 Boeing 737-800s, according to data from planespotters.net. The carrier ordered 28 Airbus A321XLRs in 2022 to begin replacing the Boeing jets and later ordered another 20. Seven A321XLRs have joined the fleet, with 41 still on order.

AerFin, which supplies parts and engines to airlines and maintenance providers, said the acquisition is the largest in its history. The company said the deal would help it supply aircraft and engine parts to customers worldwide.

If you tried and missed out on tickets for Celine Dion's big Paris comeback, it's not too late.

All 16 of her September and October 2026 shows at Plenitude Arena, the venue known as Paris La Defense Arena until July, sold out within hours. Millions of fans entered the presale lottery, and many missed out.

The good news is it's all coming back to Paris, with 10 extra shows added for May 2027. The bad news? Standard tickets have all sold out too.

This is where the power of points comes in: As the official hotel partner of the residency, Marriott Bonvoy is offering members the opportunity to redeem points for exclusive concert packages through the Marriott Bonvoy Moments platform.

Here's how Marriott Bonvoy points can help you see this global icon light up the stage in the City of Lights next year.

Related: The best Marriott redemptions might not involve a hotel at all

Marriott has been releasing Bonvoy Moments experiences for Celine's May run of shows and plans to continue through the end of January 2027. The cheapest ticket-only auctions open at 20,000 Marriott Bonvoy points for a pair of Experience Privilege tickets, while hotel-and-hospitality packages start at 40,000 points. Those are opening bids, not fixed redemption prices, and final bids may be far higher.

These packages are an official, peace-of-mind route to tickets without taking the risks that can come with unauthorized resale websites, as The Points Guy founder Brian Kelly discovered firsthand.

The star of the show is the Ultimate Celine Dion Experience, which includes an exclusive backstage tour of Plenitude Arena, a VIP merchandise pack, two Salon Premium Hospitality tickets with hospitality access and Level 1 reserved seating, breakfast for two and a one-night stay in the "Paris, I'm Ready" Suite at Le Meridien Paris Arc de Triomphe.

Other Moments packages pair tickets with stays at Le Meridien Paris Arc de Triomphe, Renaissance Paris La Defense Hotel, Renaissance Paris Nobel Tour Eiffel Hotel, Renaissance Paris Republique Hotel and citizenM Paris La Defense.

The Renaissance Paris La Defense Hotel and citizenM Paris La Defense are both very close to the arena, so there's no need to drive all night to make the show.

If none of them appeal, here's where else you can stay in Paris on points.

Marriott also offered two 1-Point Drops for the 2027 shows on Oct. 28 and 29, each releasing four pairs of tickets for just 1 Marriott Bonvoy point. Missed them? Think twice before beating yourself up, as Marriott says the 2026 drops went in seconds.

Related: You might be able to get these exclusive music festival tickets for 1 Marriott Bonvoy point

Many of the remaining packages are auctions, which means taking chances on how high other fans will go. There are no set prices, so it's worth knowing that TPG values Marriott Bonvoy points at 0.75 cents each before you bid.

Here's how to get your bid in before the listings close:

Related: Marriott Bonvoy will now let you see where you stand in line for a hotel upgrade

I was able to experience the "Two Salon Premium Hospitality Tickets + citizenM stay" package. The citizenM Paris La Defense hotel could not be more convenient, being directly across from the Plenitude Arena where you can watch the crowds gather with a glass of Champagne in hand from the comfort of the hotel bar's balcony.

The rooms are fairly compact with the bed against the window, but many rooms offer spectacular views of the arena, or La Grande Arche, as mine did.

It was my first time staying at a citizenM property, and I loved the bright and colorful common spaces which were abuzz with Celine fans, sharing their excitement (and favorite songs) in advance of the big event.

Plenitude Arena is Europe's largest indoor arena. Celine's 16-show 2026 run drew 539,000 fans, an average of almost 33,700 per night. As a result, huge crowds left the arena at the same time after each show.

The convenience of being able to walk just a few hundred feet from the exit doors to the hotel's bar, which is reserved for in-house guests after each concert and bask in the afterglow of the concert with a celebratory beverage while avoiding the hordes outside was terrific.

While attendees with regular seats queued all the way up to La Grande Arche to enter the arena, the Salon Hospitality tickets included express entry at Gate 21.

We were through security and into a secret VIP entrance in two minutes, before boarding a private escalator upstairs.

From there it was straight into a large hospitality suite with an open bar serving Champagne, wine, beer, spirits and soft drinks.

There was also a selection of canapes available before the show started.

I was a little surprised to hear the staff advise that the hospitality was only available until the show started, having recently enjoyed five hours of hospitality suite indulgence at a World of Hyatt redemption experience.

They explained that this was a specific condition set by Celine's management, and that all food and beverage outlets inside the venue closed when the show started each night.

As the lights dimmed, we walked down to our seats.

I expected the Plenitude Arena to be large, but even I was surprised by its scale.

This ticket package included reserved seats midway up the lower bowl to the side of the stage, an excellent vantage point. Given how far back the floor seats go and that the stage isn't overly high, these seats, raised just enough to give an excellent view of the stage and arena, seemed much better than the rear floor seats.

While Marriott does not publish a cash value for the auction packages, to give you an idea of how good these seats are, Plenitude Arena sold similar Salon Premium Hospitality Tickets for just over $1,000 each for October's shows.

Celine came on around 9 p.m. and belted out the hits over the next two hours (there was no support act).

I won't give away too much, beyond saying that although a lot of the songs are in French — she is the best-selling French-language artist in history, and I was in Paris after all — all her iconic English-language hits are in there, as well as a few surprises.

I shed more than a few tears, particularly during "Because You Loved Me." To see an icon return to the stage after a long health battle with the rare autoimmune neurological disorder stiff-person syndrome was truly inspiring.

If you’re looking to earn Marriott Bonvoy points, the following Marriott cards are currently offering strong welcome bonuses:

You can also transfer Bilt Points, Chase Ultimate Rewards points and American Express Membership Rewards points to Marriott Bonvoy at a 1:1 ratio. American Express is currently offering a 35% transfer bonus to Marriott Bonvoy through Dec. 10, meaning 1,000 Membership Rewards points become 1,350 Marriott Bonvoy points.

In our experience, points transfer almost instantly from all these programs.

If you weren't lucky enough to secure one of the exception 1-Point Drops, you'll need to part with more Bonvoy points than that. Marriott doesn't publish retail prices for the auctions, and the value varies depending on whether a hotel stay is included, the type of concert tickets and other factors.

Based on my calculations, the package I experienced would retail for around $2,400, noting that all Standard tickets for next year's show are already sold out, which may drive up resale prices. Based on TPG's November 2026 valuation of Bonvoy points, that's about 320,000 points worth.

So, if you can get a similar package for that number of Bonvoy points or fewer, it's a great deal.

Marriott Bonvoy Moments offers a great opportunity for anyone who missed out on buying face-value tickets to Celine Dion's concert next year.

The opening bids are just that — opening bids — so decide what the experience is worth to you before entering an auction. Read the terms carefully, confirm you can travel on the fixed dates and remember that most packages do not include transportation.

Having experienced Salon Premium hospitality and stayed directly across from Plenitude Arena, I can say the hotel-and-hospitality packages offer much more than a great seat at the show. Marriott plans to release Moments through the end of January 2027, so fans who thought they had missed their chance should keep checking.
