#6250. Allegiant Says MAX 7 Seat Cost ‘Loses Pace’

Allegiant prefers the economics of the Boeing 737 MAX 8 over the smaller MAX 7 as its plans for premium seating change how it evaluates the two aircraft.

The MAX 7 originally accounted for the majority of Allegiant’s Boeing commitment. In January 2022, the airline announced an order for 50 aircraft, split between 30 MAX 7s and 20 high-density MAX 8-200s, with options for another 50 jets.

The agreement, signed in December 2021, was Allegiant’s first direct Boeing order and marked a shift for a carrier that had largely built its business around buying used aircraft. At the time of the announcement, Allegiant operated 108 Airbus A319s and A320s.

Boeing said the new jets would reduce fuel consumption by about 20% compared with the older Airbus aircraft.

Speaking during the carrier’s third-quarter earnings call Wednesday, President and Chief Financial Officer Robert Neal said the MAX 7 initially offered an attractive balance between the cost of operating each flight and the cost per seat.

“When we did the order, we really liked the MAX 7 because we were looking at both the MAX 8 and MAX 7 at very high density,” Neal said. “And so you’ve got a really nice trip cost seat cost mix with the MAX 7.”

That calculation has changed as Allegiant expands its extra-legroom Allegiant Extra product and prepares to introduce Allegiant First.

“But over time, as you’ve seen us roll out incremental premium offerings at the moment through Allegiant Extra and eventually with Allegiant First, the seat cost just sort of loses pace with the MAX 8,” Neal said. “And so we prefer the cost economics of the MAX 8 at this point.”

Allegiant began shifting its order toward the larger variant in September 2023. An amended agreement retained the 50 firm aircraft but increased the number of MAX 8-200s, reduced the number of MAX 7s and expanded the option pool to 80 aircraft.

The MAX 7 faced years of certification delays, including work to redesign its engine anti-ice system. The FAA approved the variant on Aug. 3, after requiring changes to that system, flight-control software, and cockpit alerts.

The ultra-low-cost carrier added to its MAX 8 commitments last month, exercising six options for delivery in 2028. That brought its firm Boeing order to 56 aircraft, including 22 delivered through Oct. 23, with 74 options remaining.

Ohio's most popular midterm Republican says his party needs to refocus its message into a constructive appeal to voters if the GOP hopes to regain the ground it lost on Election Day.

Ohio Secretary of State Frank LaRose won his race to become Ohio State Auditor on Tuesday night, securing over 2.3 million votes, a total that easily eclipsed any other statewide Republican candidate.

Gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy secured just over 2 million votes in his race, and Sen. Jon Husted secured just under 2.1 million votes in his bid for re-election.

Frank LaRose stands with other GOP candidates in Ohio prior to Election Day. (Dustin Franz/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Sen. Jon Husted and Ohio gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy endorsed each other on Monday night (Al Drago/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

#6248. KLM Plans 1,000 More Job Cuts

KLM expects to eliminate approximately 1,000 positions through productivity improvements as part of a restructuring announced Thursday.

The Dutch carrier said it would seek to limit the impact through natural attrition, voluntary arrangements and transfers. Other changes include moving about 800 ground services positions to outside providers and transferring 2,000 positions to Air France-KLM, including 1,500 at customer contact center Cygnific.

“But KLM’s future is not guaranteed,” CEO Marjan Rintel said in a statement, citing global instability, high fuel prices, and pressure on the industry.

KLM is targeting a structural productivity increase of at least 8% by 2028, alongside restrained wage growth. It said an additional €1 billion in annual earnings improvement is needed to fund investments.

The changes also affect its European fleet. KLM will replace planned Airbus A320s with Embraer E195-E2s, giving regional subsidiary Cityhopper a larger role. The A321neo will remain, while Boeing 737s and Embraer E190s will be phased out.

The announcement came as KLM reported a third-quarter operating profit of €458 million, up from €352 million a year earlier. For the first nine months of 2026, operating profit reached €526 million on revenue of €10.9 billion.

Despite the improvement, KLM said profitability remains insufficient to support its investment needs. Higher fuel costs and Middle East flight cancellations weighed on its passenger business, while Transavia faced competition and operational challenges.

“We need to increase it to more than 8% to secure a financially healthy future for KLM,” Chief Financial Officer Bas Brouns said of the airline’s profit margin.

#6247. Southwest Airlines Named Least Punctual Carrier Among 10 Airlines In North America

Southwest Airlines was the least punctual of North America's 10 leading airlines last month, with just 68.9% of its flights arriving on time. According to Cirium's latest On-Time Performance Report, almost one in three completed Southwest flights arrived at least 15 minutes behind schedule, putting the Dallas-based carrier well behind its competitors.

At the opposite end of the rankings, Delta Air Lines returned to first place with an on-time performance (OTP) rate of 86.9%, continuing a remarkable recovery from a difficult summer. Southwest's performance comes amid sweeping changes to its business model, including checked-baggage fees, assigned seating, and greater aircraft utilization, raising questions about the operational consequences of its transformation.

Delta's October performance represented a significant turnaround from July, when only 75% of its flights arrived on time. That figure improved to 79.2% in August, 82.5% in September, and 86.7% in October, an increase of nearly 12 percentage points. The result also placed Delta third in Cirium's global rankings, behind Hainan Airlines and Aeromexico.

United Airlines ranked second in North America at 84.06%, followed by WestJet at 83.56% and JetBlue Airways at 82.27%. American Airlines finished sixth at 80.10%, despite operating more flights than any other carrier in the regional ranking. The table below shows the complete October results, including the proportion of scheduled flights each airline completed.

Southwest finished 18 percentage points behind Delta and nearly seven points behind ninth-placed Air Canada. Its punctuality was also considerably below the 79.8% unweighted average across the 10 ranked airlines. Nevertheless, Southwest completed 99.5% of its scheduled flights, suggesting that its principal challenge was delays rather than cancellations.

Southwest's deteriorating performance coincides with some of the biggest changes in its history. The airline introduced checked-baggage fees in May last year, which coincided with a ten-point drop in on-time arrivals over a three-month period. Assigned seating and a new boarding process followed in January 2026, and over the past six months, its on-time performance has averaged less than 70%.

Regular readers of Simple Flying know that the move to assigned seating was anything but smooth, and the airline continues to try iron out some of the challenges. This was likely compounded by charging for checked bags, as this encourages more passengers to bring carry-on luggage, increasing overhead-bin congestion and boarding times.

CEO Bob Jordan acknowledged the airline's punctuality problems during the carrier's October 22 earnings call, despite praising its completion factor and baggage-handling performance.

"We've got a terrific completion factor, but OTP is not where we want it to be."

COO Andrew Watterson also explained that aircraft turnarounds were generally starting well, but the airline was losing valuable minutes toward the end of boarding. As a result, he outlined two procedural changes scheduled to begin in November, including how the airline handles bags checked at the departure gate, and allowing gate agents to use an iPad at the aircraft door to finalize the flight, rather than returning to the gate podium. More significant changes to crew reporting and operational schedules begin in January.

The airline recently changed its long-standing boarding process.

Cirium's airport rankings provide another perspective on operational performance. Six US airports featured among the world's 20 most punctual large airports in October, including four major Delta hubs. Minneapolis-St. Paul International Airport (MSP) led the American contingent with 87% on-time departures, placing eighth globally, followed by Washington Dulles International Airport (IAD) and Detroit Metropolitan Wayne County Airport (DTW). Unlike the airline rankings, these figures measure departures rather than arrivals.

Minneapolis–St. Paul International Airport (MSP)

Washington Dulles International Airport (IAD)

Detroit Metropolitan Wayne County Airport (DTW)

Salt Lake City International Airport (SLC)

Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR)

Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport

Delta's hubs at Minneapolis, Detroit, Salt Lake City and Atlanta all featured prominently, contributing to the carrier's market-leading punctuality. Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport (ATL) was particularly impressive, given the airport handled 67,149 flights during October, more than double the number of any other airport in the top 20. It is also notable that Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR), given its well-documented struggles last year, has emerged as one of the top-performing US airports.

None of Southwest's major operating bases, including Denver, Dallas Love Field, Chicago Midway and Baltimore/Washington, appeared in Cirium's rankings. Data from PlaneTrack also indicates particularly weak Southwest punctuality in Denver and Las Vegas, both with only 63% of flights departing on time. With its operational overhaul continuing, the airline now faces mounting pressure to restore the reliability that helped establish its original reputation.

#6246. Hyatt Dining & Spa Awards: Are They Worth Redeeming Points For?

While the most popular way to redeem World of Hyatt points is for free night award redemptions, there are some lesser known ways to redeem Hyatt points. One of those is the ability to use points for Dining & Spa awards, which can be a surprisingly good deal.

This doesn’t get a lot of attention, and it’s particularly useful if you want to minimize your out-of-pocket when staying at a Hyatt property, while still indulging in on-property experiences.

Most people don’t realize that you can redeem World of Hyatt points toward the cost of on-property dining and spa experiences, and the value proposition can be surprisingly good. Specifically, you can redeem a certain number of points for a certain amount of credit to use toward on-property spending, even if you’re not staying at a Hyatt property. Let’s take a closer look at how this works.

Below is a chart showing the various redemption opportunities available with Hyatt’s Dining & Spa awards, along with how much value you can potentially get per point:

As you can see, you can redeem anywhere from 1,000 points for a $10 credit, to 65,000 points for a $1,000 credit. The value per point ranges anywhere from 1.0 cents per point, to 1.54 cents per point.

1.54 cents per World of Hyatt point sounds like a solid deal. Based on my latest miles & points valuations, World of Hyatt points are worth 1.4 cents each, so this actually offers solid value, at least on the surface. Is there a catch, though?

The exact redemptions that are allowed vary by hotel, but generally you can expect that these awards can be used for food and beverage purchases, spa and salon services, and spa and salon retail items.

On top of that, when charged to a member’s guest room, the following charges may be eligible:

laundry, dry cleaning, telephone charges, pay-per-view movies, parking, gift/retail shop, service charges, taxes (not including room taxes) and gratuities

Meanwhile the following charges are expressly prohibited from being eligible:

room rates, room taxes, alcoholic beverages (in certain jurisdictions), catering or banquet charges, and casino charges

If you’re staying at a Hyatt then you should be able to redeem these awards for cumulative charges over the course of your stay. However, I’d recommend confirming this with the front desk at check-in, including which outlets would be eligible for these redemptions, since individual hotels could have different policies.

Not all Hyatt hotels participate in this program. Miraval, Unscripted by Hyatt, Hyatt Select, Destination by Hyatt, Hyatt Vacation Club properties, Hyatt Vivid, Bahia Principe, Impression by Secrets, Secrets, Dreams, Breathless, Zoëtry, Alua, Sunscape, and other Legacy AMR Collection resorts, as well as some Dream properties, do not participate. Furthermore, redemption of these certificates is limited to registered guests at Hyatt Zilara, Hyatt Ziva, and Hyatt Studios properties.

To be positive, you can search participating properties at this page.

You don’t need to redeem for these certificates in advance, but rather the World of Hyatt member should just inform the Hyatt employee at the eligible outlet that they’d like to redeem points toward their purchase at the outset. You’ll need to have your membership information, and should then be asked how many points you want to redeem.

If you’re a registered guest at a hotel then you can apply one of these at check-out toward multiple purchases over the course of a stay. If you’re not a registered guest then you’ll have to settle your folio at the particular outlet you’re at.

There are a few other things to potentially be aware of:

On the surface, being able to redeem World of Hyatt points for up to ~1.54 cents toward the cost of a purchase is a solid deal. Is it exceptional? No. But as a way of essentially “cashing out” your points to offset cash costs I think it’s very good.

I do think it’s important to create a more realistic valuation of these redemptions, though. When you redeem these awards you’re forgoing the opportunity to earn points on these purchases:

As a Globalist member I earn 10.5x points per dollar spent, which I value at a return of ~15% (1.4 cents per point). That’s an opportunity cost that’s worth factoring in, so in reality, I’d adjust the maximum value from 1.54 cents to ~1.3 cents.

Personally, this isn’t how I’d redeem my World of Hyatt points, though I do think many people could find this to be worthwhile for a splurge:

World of Hyatt offers Dining & Spa awards, allowing members to redeem points for dining and spa experiences at most Hyatt properties. This has the potential to be a solid deal, as getting 1.54 cents per Hyatt point toward the cost of a purchase is a good redemption. However, do factor in the points you’re forgoing, which brings down the redemption value a bit.

While I wouldn’t say this is the best way to redeem Hyatt points, this could be worth it to lower how much cash you’ll pay for a Hyatt stay, especially at a secluded resort where you’re likely to spend most time on-property.

What do you make of Hyatt’s Dining & Spa awards? Could you see yourself redeeming points for them?

Amazon has a new restaurant delivery partner for its Prime members: Uber Eats, which replaces the Grubhub+ benefit Prime members had until today.

To celebrate the new partnership, Amazon Prime members can get $20 off each of their first two eligible Uber Eats orders of $25 or more on linked accounts made via Amazon, as long as those orders are for U.S. restaurants and placed by Nov. 18.

Beyond the limited-time launch promotion, Prime members will get $0 delivery fees on eligible Uber Eats orders of $25 or more placed through the Amazon app or website. Interestingly, this appears to work separately from any existing Uber Eats account or benefits you may already have.

Related: Which is the best food delivery app?

There's no need to download another app or create a separate Uber Eats account to use this perk. When you opt in through Amazon, you can use your existing Prime account information, including linked payment methods.

Think of it almost like ordering a box of paper towels from Amazon with free Prime delivery, only this time it's a salad, burger, breakfast tacos or fries. You place the order via Uber Eats in your Amazon account, almost as you would any other Prime delivery, but this time it is fulfilled by Uber Eats instead of your friendly neighborhood Amazon delivery truck.

Amazon has also said that there will be additional Prime-exclusive offers available only on Amazon that could save you more than $175 per year, so we'll be sure to keep an eye out for those.

TPG tip: Amazon Prime Visa cardmembers earn 5% back on all Uber Eats orders through Dec. 5, 2026 with eligible Prime membership.

The information for the Prime Visa has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

This $20 introductory promo seems to apply whether you use pickup or delivery, which isn't always the case with Uber Eats promos. So, it is possible to truly save $20 on a $25 order if you select pickup. If you opt for delivery, you will likely have some service fees and a tip to factor into the equation.

One thing to remember: After the introductory promotion ends, you may want to compare the total cost of ordering through the Amazon-linked version of Uber Eats with any promotions, credit card benefits or discounts available through your regular Uber Eats account. The best deal may depend on which version of Uber Eats you're using.

#6244. 59-Room Andaz Turks & Caicos At Grace Bay Opening April 2027, Now Bookable

Want to take advantage of Hyatt Privé benefits, including a room upgrade, complimentary breakfast, a hotel credit, and more, when booking a cash stay? Contact Ford ([email protected]) for more details. He may even be able to help if you already have a stay booked.

The much delayed Andaz Turks & Caicos is getting closer to opening. The hotel has now moved forward the date as of which it’s accepting reservations, and we’ve also learned more details about the on-property amenities. Let’s cover all the details, as we’re potentially under five months from the opening…

The Andaz Turks & Caicos at Grace Bay is accepting reservations for stays as of April 1, 2027. This will mark Hyatt’s first hotel in Turks & Caicos, and the first Andaz property in the Caribbean. For that matter, it’s one of the only Andaz properties that’s currently in the pipeline outside of Asia, as the brand has really lost steam.

The 5.5-acre resort will offer four restaurants and bars, three outdoor pools, a spa, a kids club, a fitness center, tennis and pickleball courts, and more. The Andaz will be comprised of 59 rooms and 73 branded residences, so at least the hotel portion of the property will be boutique. It’ll be located directly on Grace Bay, known for offering one of the most beautiful stretches of beach in the Caribbean.

As far as the culinary concepts go, the Andaz Turks & Caicos will feature the following:

Runa Spa & Wellness, the spa at the Andaz, will be around 7,000 square feet. It will have five treatment rooms, along with a sauna, cold plunge, relaxation area, and more.

The opening of this resort has been majorly delayed. It was initially announced in 2018 with a 2021 opening, but the timeline slipped by six years, presumably due to a combination of the pandemic, plus… well, how hotel construction projects often work out. Hopefully there are no additional delays beyond the current planned spring 2027 opening.

With the Andaz Turks & Caicos at Grace Bay bookable, what are rates like? For those redeeming points, this is a Category 8 World of Hyatt property, meaning a free night redemption in a standard room costs 35,000-75,000 points per night.

World of Hyatt’s new award chart sure makes top end redemptions expensive, unfortunately! As of now the hotel is primarily bookable between April and November of 2027, so this doesn’t really cover peak season. For most dates, I currently see rates of either 35,000 points, 45,000 points, or 55,000 points per night. So value here is highly dependent on which of those rates you can find.

When it comes to cash rates, those currently start at around $900-1,300 per night, and that depends on when you’re staying. That’s inclusive of the service charge, but exclusive of the taxes.

If you are looking to book a cash stay here, I’d recommend doing so through the Hyatt Privé program, which offers extra perks like room upgrades, complimentary breakfast, and a hotel credit. Ford and his team are happy to help with these requests, and can be reached at [email protected].

I suppose good options on Grace Bay are limited, and this hotel is boutique. But at these rates, they better offer something significantly better than the typical Andaz experience, in my opinion.

Turks & Caicos is absolutely beautiful, and it’s an easy getaway from the United States, given how close it is to Florida. Historically, the country hasn’t had that many points hotels, though that’s slowly starting to change.

Several years back, we saw the opening of the Ritz-Carlton Turks & Caicos. It has an amazing location on Grace Bay and the grounds of the property are beautiful, but it otherwise doesn’t feel very luxurious, and lacks personality.

So it’ll be nice to have another points property, and I look forward to learning more about the Andaz. Maybe I’m overly optimistic, but I think the Andaz might just end up offering a better experience than the Ritz-Carlton, at least based on the design renderings, and also the more boutique scale of the property. Andaz really is quite an inconsistent brand.

I of course should acknowledge that many people are understandably frustrated by the way that Grace Bay has developed over the years, given all the huge concrete towers that have taken shape along the beach. It has definitely lost its charm a bit, though the beach is still gorgeous.

Even beyond Grace Bay, we’re seeing some other great new options in Turks & Caicos. In 2025, we saw the opening of Salterra Turks & Caicos, a Marriott Luxury Collection property. This is great for those who want a bit more secluded of a trip, since South Caicos Island is a bit less crowded than the area around Providenciales. This is also where Sailrock Resort is located, which is an independent hotel affiliated with Small Luxury Hotels of the World (SLH).

There’s also a Waldorf Astoria Turks & Caicos planned for a 2028 opening, located on Dellis Cay, a nearby island that’s not as developed, which can be reached by a 25-minute boat transfer from Providenciales. That should also be a great option, especially with how the Waldorf Astoria portfolio is developing. However, don’t count on that timeline sticking either.

The Andaz Turks & Caicos is accepting reservations for stays as of April 2027, and it will be located on the famous Grace Bay. The property will have just 59 hotel rooms, in addition to residences, so I like how it’s on a smaller scale than some other properties.

This should be a very nice addition to the Caribbean points hotel market. Hopefully we don’t see any additional delays with the opening…

What do you make of the upcoming Andaz Turks & Caicos?

#6243. JetBlue Leads The Industry In Raising Checked Bag Fees… Again!

For whatever reason, JetBlue tends to be the industry leader when it comes to raising checked bag fees, and competitors tend to follow. Earlier this year, JetBlue was the first major US carrier to raise checked bag fees, and now the airline is raising checked bag fees again…

Effective immediately (for tickets purchased as of November 3, 2026), JetBlue has increased checked bag fees. JetBlue has a rather complicated fee structure for checked bags, with both off-peak and peak pricing, plus different pricing based on whether you pay for the bag 24 hours or more in advance.

Below is a chart with JetBlue’s new checked bag fees.

As you can see, an off-peak first checked bag on a domestic flight will now cost you $50-60 (depending on whether you pay in advance), while a peak first checked bag on a domestic flight will now cost you $55-70 (depending on whether you pay in advance). For context, below are the dates that are considered peak for the purposes of bag fees.

It goes without saying that paying $50-70 for a first checked bag is a pretty substantial cost, especially when you consider how little checked bags used to cost. On a one-way, you’re looking at $100-140. For a family of four, you’d be looking at $400-560.

When JetBlue raised checked bag fees earlier this year, the airline released a statement claiming it was increasing checked bag fees to be “more competitive,” and that “while we recognize that fee increases are never ideal, we take careful consideration to ensure these changes are implemented only when necessary.” I imagine this time around, the logic is much of the same.

The simple reality is that oil prices are way up. Airlines have actually done a solid job of being able to make fare increases stick. But that’s not enough to fully offset the increase in the cost of jet fuel.

JetBlue is in a rough financial spot, and it hasn’t turned a profit since before the pandemic. The airline is hoping to turn an operating profit in 2027, though that strikes me as being particularly optimistic. So the logic for raising checked bags is threefold:

JetBlue has just increased checked bag fees once again, and you’ll now pay $50-70 for a first checked bag on a domestic flight. This is JetBlue’s second price increase on checked bags so far this year. When airlines are trying to increase revenue, checked bag fees are often low hanging fruit.

When competitors match, it also becomes something that’s unavoidable for consumers, other than getting a credit card… which also has upside for the airline! I’d be shocked if other airlines don’t match this move from JetBlue.

What do you make of JetBlue increasing checked bag fees?

#6241. The Problem American Airlines Ran Into When It Inherited The World's 1st Airbus A321neo

Robin Guess | Shutterstock, Simple Flying

American Airlines operates one of the largest Airbus A321neo fleets in the world, using the narrowbody aircraft to serve a variety of domestic and international routes. However, not every A321neo in its fleet is quite the same. Among its aircraft are 10 examples inherited from Alaska Airlines, which originally acquired them following its takeover of Virgin America. Although these aircraft offer similar capabilities to American's other A321neos, their original design has created an unusual fleet-management challenge.

The story goes back to 2017, when Virgin became the first airline to receive an A321neo. Several years and two airline ownership changes later, some of the aircraft eventually found their way into American's fleet. The problem is that they were built before Airbus introduced a significant cabin-design change, meaning American's cannot configure them in exactly the same way as its newer A321neos. This difference has also created an unexpected complication for passengers selecting their seats.

The A321neo represented an important development for the European manufacturer, bringing improved fuel efficiency, reduced emissions, and lower noise levels to the largest member of its A320neo family. Virgin became the launch operator of the aircraft, receiving the first example at a delivery ceremony in Hamburg, Germany, in April 2017. The aircraft was powered by CFM International LEAP-1A engines. At the time, Airbus highlighted the aircraft's ability to deliver fuel savings of at least 15% compared with previous-generation models. It also offered greater passenger capacity and longer range, making it an attractive option for airlines looking to improve the economics of their short- and medium-haul operations. Virgin planned to use the aircraft to expand its existing Airbus fleet while maintaining its distinctive onboard experience. The first aircraft was configured with 185 seats and was expected to enter commercial service on May 31, 2017, operating its inaugural flight between San Francisco International Airport (SFO) and Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport (DCA).

Its cabin included Virgin's familiar premium-oriented features, including multiple service classes and personal entertainment systems. The delivery was particularly significant because it marked the arrival of the first A321neo anywhere in the world. However, Virgin's relationship with the aircraft would not last independently for very long. Alaska Air Group had announced its acquisition of Virgin in April 2016, completing the transaction in December that year. The subsequent integration brought the two airlines together under the Alaska brand, creating a new chapter for Virgin's aircraft and outstanding orders.

Following the acquisition, Alaska inherited Virgin's aircraft and commitments, including its A321neo order. The aircraft were therefore no longer being introduced into an independent Virgin fleet, as originally intended. Instead, they became part of Alaska's broader operations, although the transition did not mean that every aircraft immediately entered service with the acquiring airline. Virgin had originally ordered 10 A321neos, and the aircraft subsequently became part of the complicated fleet transition following the acquisition. Only four of the 10 aircraft eventually transferred to American had actually operated for Virgin. This is an important distinction because the aircraft's original configuration was determined before the later ownership changes took place.

American ultimately took these 10 aircraft from Alaska, adding them to its growing Airbus narrowbody fleet. The transfer provided American with additional capacity without requiring it to introduce an entirely new aircraft family. Nevertheless, the inherited aircraft came with a design characteristic that distinguished them from the A321neos that the oneworld carrier had ordered directly from Airbus.

The aircraft were among the earliest A321neos produced, meaning they predated Airbus' Cabin Flex arrangement. Consequently, although they shared the A321neo name and many of the same underlying characteristics, their cabin layouts were fundamentally different. This would become particularly important when American began integrating them into its own passenger operations.

The A321neo has a larger capacity than the smaller A320, allowing American to transport more people without relying on wide bodies.

The central issue concerns Airbus Cabin Flex, a redesigned exit-door arrangement introduced to provide airlines with greater flexibility when configuring the A321's cabin. Rather than relying entirely on the older arrangement of four pairs of exits, the updated design repositioned certain emergency exits, including the overwing exits, to create additional opportunities for seat installation. The earlier aircraft inherited from Alaska retained the original arrangement, featuring eight exits in total, with four on each side of the fuselage. This was broadly comparable to the configuration used on the older A321ceo. While perfectly suitable from an operational and safety perspective, it limited how the airline could arrange seats compared with the newer Cabin Flex-equipped aircraft. The distinction matters because the position of emergency exits influences the number of seats that can legally and practically be installed in an aircraft cabin. Cabin Flex allowed airlines to make better use of available cabin space, supporting higher-density configurations without changing the aircraft's fundamental dimensions.

American's newer A321neos therefore benefit from a different layout that accommodates additional economy seating. The difference is also reflected in aircraft classification. American's newer aircraft are identified as A321-200NX models, while the former Alaska aircraft are listed as A321-200Ns. Although the distinction might appear relatively minor, it represents a meaningful physical difference that American has had to accommodate.

The latest data from ch-aviation shows that today, Alaska operates the following fleet.

American began introducing the former Alaska A321neos into passenger service from Miami International Airport (MIA) in spring 2024. Rather than immediately undertaking a complete interior refurbishment, the airline initially retained the aircraft's existing Alaska cabin configuration. This allowed the aircraft to enter service while preserving much of the arrangement they had operated with previously. The original layout provided 190 seats, divided between 16 seats in first class and 174 seats in the main cabin. Compared with American's more conventional A321neo configuration, this meant fewer first-class seats but generally more space throughout the passenger cabin. For travelers, the difference was not necessarily negative, as the original arrangement offered a relatively spacious experience. However, retaining the inherited interior was not a permanent solution for an airline operating a large fleet with established cabin standards. American has spent considerable effort standardizing its narrowbody interiors through its Oasis refurbishment program, which introduced consistent seating arrangements and onboard features across numerous aircraft. The former Alaska A321neos would eventually need to undergo a similar transformation.

The first aircraft to receive the Oasis interior was N950XV, which underwent its refurbishment in San Antonio. The project demonstrated that American could bring the aircraft closer to its existing onboard standards, but it could not completely eliminate the differences created by their original construction. The aircraft's exit-door arrangement would continue to determine how many seats could be installed.

The A320 family has gone from strength to strength.

Following their refurbishment, the 10 former Alaska aircraft adopted a 190-seat configuration consisting of 20 first-class seats and 170 economy seats. This brought their premium-cabin capacity into line with American's standard arrangement, while retaining a smaller total number of seats than the airline's newer A321neos. The result is a cabin that looks more familiar but remains structurally different. American's regular A321neo configuration accommodates 196 passengers, including 20 first-class seats and 176 main-cabin seats. The additional six economy seats are possible because these aircraft have the newer Cabin Flex exit arrangement. The 10 inherited aircraft cannot simply receive the same number of seats because their original door positioning restricts the available cabin space.

This creates an interesting situation for American, which effectively operates two different versions of the same aircraft under one fleet umbrella. Both provide the benefits associated with the A321neo, including modern engines and improved fuel efficiency, but their interiors have different seating capacities and exit-row locations. From an operational perspective, this is an additional configuration for the airline to manage. The difference is particularly relevant because the 10 aircraft are not isolated examples that can be easily distinguished by passengers. They operate within the same broader A321neo fleet, and travelers may encounter either version when booking a flight. Although the cabin refurbishment has made the aircraft look more consistent, the underlying structural differences remain impossible to overlook when examining their seat maps.

Perhaps the most noticeable consequence of the unusual fleet arrangement concerns seat selection. American uses a single fleet code for both A321neo configurations, meaning passengers may not immediately realize which version they will be flying. However, the location of the emergency exits is different, creating two distinct seat maps despite the shared aircraft designation. The standard 196-seat A321neo has exit rows at rows 17 and 27, while on the 10 former Alaska aircraft, the corresponding exit rows are located at rows 11 and 24. Consequently, a passenger who selects an exit-row seat based on familiarity with one configuration could discover that the same row number has an entirely different purpose on the aircraft actually assigned to their flight. This can be particularly frustrating for travelers who deliberately pay extra for additional legroom.

A passenger expecting an exit-row seat could instead end up in a standard economy seat, potentially close to the lavatories. The differences extend beyond exit locations, with certain rows also having narrower seats or missing seat positions because of the aircraft's different cabin arrangement. The aircraft registrations provide another way to distinguish the two groups. The 10 former Alaska A321neos carry registrations ranging from N950XV through N959XV, while the remaining aircraft belong to the newer configuration. Ultimately, American inherited aircraft with an important piece of aviation history, but their early-production design has left the airline with a significant configuration difference.

#6240. Air Tahiti Nui Will Offer Free Starlink Wi-Fi On Its Boeing 787s As Of 2027

Air Tahiti Nui has just announced a massive upgrade to its inflight connectivity, as the airline will be rolling out free Starlink Wi-Fi across its (small) fleet in 2027.

Air Tahiti Nui has revealed that it plans to install Starlink Wi-Fi on its entire fleet, which consists of four Boeing 787-9s. The airline plans to offer this service for free to passengers in all travel classes.

Starlink will be introduced in 2027, though no timeline beyond that is known yet, so it could be early or late in the year. Presumably once installation starts, it’ll be completed very quickly — four planes could easily be fitted with Starlink in a single week.

Air Tahiti Nui operates some very long flights — including from Papeete (PPT) to Paris (CDG) via Los Angeles (LAX) so having fast and free connectivity is super valuable. While so many airlines market their Wi-Fi as being high speed, Starlink is the only product currently in service where you can consistently stream videos, etc.

Currently, Air Tahiti Nui’s Dreamliners are equipped with Panasonic Wi-Fi, which actually has relatively decent speeds. The catch is that Air Tahiti Nui chooses to have insanely high pricing based primarily on data usage, rather than just offering a full flight pass for a fixed amount.

Below is Air Tahiti Nui’s current pricing chart for Wi-Fi… could they make this any more complicated? $28 for 100 MB of data is absurd, and $98 for unlimited data is even more ridiculous.

This kind of pricing just strikes me as being so stupid. All you end up doing is frustrating passengers, and I also have to imagine this isn’t actually the system that maximizes usage. It’s weird to have a provider with speeds that are actually semi-usable (Panasonic is better than OnAir), and to then do this with it.

So anyway, Starlink will simply be a massive upgrade for Air Tahiti Nui in every way. Speaking of which, I’d sure love to return to French Polynesia at some point (and fly that all-business class Air Tahiti turboprop, while I’m at it).

In 2027, Air Tahiti Nui intends to install Starlink Wi-Fi on its fleet of four Dreamliners. It remains to be seen exactly when in 2027 it’ll happen, but this represents a huge upgrade to the passenger experience. The airline currently offers Panasonic Wi-Fi with awful data-based pricing (or an unlimited package that will run you close to $100).

What do you make of Air Tahiti Nui introducing Starlink?

One of my favorite things about World of Hyatt points is how much flexibility they offer. You could redeem just a few thousand points for a night at a Category 1 Hyatt hotel or use a larger stash to book a higher-category hotel or all-inclusive resort.

Since Hyatt still uses award charts for most of its properties, you can sometimes get outsize value by redeeming points when cash rates are high. But free nights aren't the only way to use your points. From room upgrades and dining experiences to airline miles and rental cars, here's how you can redeem World of Hyatt points, including which options offer the best value.

The best way to redeem Hyatt points is usually for free hotel nights. Hyatt has award charts for most free night awards, though some are dynamically priced. There are also ways to combine points with cash and free night certificates.

Hyatt publishes award charts for free night awards at Hyatt hotels and resorts, participating resorts within the Hyatt Inclusive Collection brands and Miraval resorts. Each of these charts has five award pricing tiers — Lowest, Low, Moderate, Upper and Top — for each category.

Here's the award chart for standard room award nights at Hyatt hotels and resorts.

Hyatt publishes separate award charts for Hyatt Inclusive Collection brands and Miraval resorts, as well as for club rooms, standard suites and premium suites. Check out our guide to the Hyatt award charts for all the charts.

You can click on "Points Calendar" on the results page for any particular property when searching for award stays to see how many points each night costs.

However, free night awards at Mr & Mrs Smith hotels and Homes & Hideaways by World of Hyatt are priced dynamically based on paid rates. For example, this night at a Homes & Hideaways property in Florida would cost 16,011 points or $192.13. This means you'd get 1.2 cents per point when redeeming Hyatt points for this night.

And this night at a Mr & Mrs Smith property in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, would cost 8,750 points or $58.91. This means you'd only get 0.67 cents per point when redeeming Hyatt points for this night.

TPG's November 2026 valuations peg Hyatt points at 1.65 cents each. As such, you'll generally want to get at least this much value when redeeming your Hyatt points.

Related: Best Hyatt hotels in the world to book with points

You can also book Points + Cash rates for some stays. When these rates are available for your chosen room type and property, you'll redeem 50% of the points required for a free night and get 50% to 70% off the standard rate (which may be higher than the best available rate).

For example, I could redeem 12,000 points, book a Points + Cash rate of 6,000 points plus $156.50 or book a paid rate of $220.16 for this night at the Hyatt Centric Rittenhouse Square Philadelphia.

When redeeming points, I'd get 1.83 cents per point. And when booking a Points + Cash rate, I'd get 1.06 cents per point.

Related: Which credit card should you use for Hyatt stays?

You can also combine Hyatt points with paid nights and even free night certificates when booking with the Hyatt Pay My Way feature. To use this feature, sign in to your Hyatt account, search for a paid stay, click on the property and room type of your choice and then click on rates until you see one with a Pay My Way option.

Click on the Pay My Way box, and then you can choose whether to use points, cash, Points + Cash or free night certificates for each night.

I often use Pay My Way when redeeming free night certificates, as this lets me book a multinight stay even if I only have one free night certificate. I've also used Pay My Way to redeem points for a stay with one particularly expensive night.

Related: The best Hyatt Category 4 hotels to maximize your free night award certificates

You can redeem points to upgrade eligible paid stays at many Hyatt hotels and resorts. Here's a look at the upgrade rate per night:

You can sometimes redeem points for an upgrade at the time of booking. In the following example, you could redeem 9,500 points for a premium suite free night, 4,750 points plus $158 for a premium suite Points + Cash booking or 9,000 points plus $152 to upgrade a paid night to a premium suite.

If you don't upgrade at the time of booking, you can call (800) 544-9288 in the U.S. and Canada or contact a Global Care Center to see if your existing stay is eligible for an upgrade with points.

Related: Your ultimate guide to Hyatt hotel brands

You can redeem Hyatt points for dining and spa experiences at participating locations even if you aren't spending the night. Plus, you can redeem points during stays at participating locations to pay for in-room movies, parking, transportation and more.

To redeem points, simply request to use Hyatt points at checkout and choose how many points to redeem. You should be able to redeem points at participating locations based on the following chart:

As you can see, the redemption rate you'll get ranges from 1 to 1.54 cents per point, which is below TPG's November 2026 valuation of 1.65 cents per point for Hyatt points. As such, you'll usually want to find higher-value ways to redeem your Hyatt points.

You can redeem Hyatt points for Find experiences. For example, you could pay $60 plus taxes or redeem 4,286 points for this one-hour aerial yoga and meditation class.

Or, you could redeem 5,357 points or pay $75 plus taxes for an e-bike tour of San Diego.

It's worth taking a look at Find experiences, especially if you select Find experience credits as Hyatt Milestone Rewards. But you usually won't get outsize value when redeeming points for these experiences.

Related: Why bidding on a Hyatt Find experience auction might be the most valuable way to redeem your World of Hyatt points

You can convert Hyatt points into airline miles with the following programs:

For most of the airline programs, you'll get 1 mile for every 2.5 Hyatt points you convert. However, Hyatt uses different conversion rates for Aeromexico Rewards, Air China PhoenixMiles, China Eastern Miles, Qantas Frequent Flyer, Southwest Rapid Rewards and Virgin Atlantic Flying Club.

You must convert at least 5,000 points at a time but can convert additional points in increments of 1,250. If you convert 50,000 points or more, you'll usually get an extra 5,000 bonus miles.

However, converting Hyatt points to airline miles will rarely make sense. Conversions can take six to eight weeks. Plus, at the usual 2.5:1 conversion ratio, transferring 5,000 Hyatt points yields 2,000 airline miles. Based on TPG's November 2026 valuations, you'd be giving up approximately $82.50 in Hyatt points for those 2,000 miles.

You can redeem Hyatt points for Avis free day awards, which are valid at participating locations in the U.S. and Canada, by calling (800) 544-9288. When available, you can redeem 6,000 points per day for an intermediate-size car. However, there are blackout periods that you'll see on the redemption certificate once you redeem your points. Avis free day awards usually expire one year after they're issued.

World of Hyatt members can redeem points for an Aeroplan flight reward certificate valid on Air Canada flights. The 30,000-point certificate costs 50,000 Hyatt points, and you can apply it toward the base fare in points of an Aeroplan flight reward.

Given that TPG's November 2026 valuations peg Hyatt points at 1.65 cents each and Aeroplan points at 1.45 cents each, this won't be a good-value redemption for most travelers. However, if you were planning to convert Hyatt points to Aeroplan points, the flight reward certificate might provide better value.

Related: How to redeem Aeroplan points for maximum value

World of Hyatt and American Airlines AAdvantage are winding down their partnership. But eligible Explorist and Globalist members can redeem Hyatt points for AAdvantage Status for a Day until 1 a.m. EST on Nov. 16.

You can redeem 5,000 Hyatt points to get AAdvantage Gold status for a day, 8,000 points to get AAdvantage Platinum status for a day and 12,000 points to get AAdvantage Platinum Pro status for a day.

However, you can only use these awards on your own travel itineraries, and some fares aren't eligible.

Related: Why I rely on credit cards to earn American Airlines elite status

Finally, you can redeem Hyatt points for a future meeting credit to use for meetings and catered events at participating Hyatt hotels and resorts based on the following chart:

As you can see, the redemption rate is 1.33 cents per point regardless of how many points you redeem toward a future meeting credit. You must call a Hyatt Global Care Center to redeem points for a future meeting credit. You can't use future meeting credits at Hyatt Vacation Club, Bahia Principe and Destination by Hyatt Residences locations.

Redeeming World of Hyatt points for free nights is usually the best way to get good value from your points. I particularly like redeeming Hyatt points at hotels where cash rates are high, as I can often get outsize value. But I'll also redeem points on stays with resort fees, as Hyatt waives resort fees on free night awards.

Other redemption options, including room upgrades, Find experiences and airline miles, can make sense in certain situations. But I generally recommend saving your Hyatt points for free night awards, especially if you can be flexible about where and when you stay.

#6238. Flying Blue Delays SAF & Donation XP Changes Until December 2026

One unique aspect of the Air France-KLM Flying Blue program has long been how environmental contributions have contributed toward elite status, whether through the purchase of sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), or through mileage donations to environmental causes.

A couple of days ago I covered how seemingly overnight, the Flying Blue program drastically decreased status qualification through these methods, requiring 50% larger contributions to earn the same number of XPs (experience points, the method by which one earns status). There’s now an update, and I’m pleased to see the way this is being handled.

Flying Blue has announced that it’s delaying the changes it’s making to the ability to earn XPs through SAF and mileage donations, and this will now be implemented as of December 1, 2026. Tiffany Funk, Head of Flying Blue, shared the following with me:

On Monday, we updated how many XP you earn on Sustainable Aviation Fuel and charitable contributions. We didn’t handle the rollout well, and the new rate went live with unclear messaging and without notice. While this affects a small share of our members, we recognize for those members it matters a great deal.

The update was part of a continuous review of our elite program. We want to ensure we can keep delivering the benefits and service you expect.

For now, we’re pressing pause. From tomorrow (4 November), SAF and charitable contributions will earn XP at the previous rate, and any contribution made since 2 November will be credited at the prior rate as well. The new rate of €15 per XP begins on 1 December 2026; even at the new rate, no program in the market will recognize SAF contributions more generously than Flying Blue, including on award tickets.

We want Flying Blue to be a program you build your life around. Many of you put a lot of care into planning your flights and status qualification, and we understand your need to have time to make adjustments.

And to everyone who told us why this matters to you: thank you for caring this much about Flying Blue.

I am happy to see how Flying Blue leadership is handling this situation. Let me share my take on this situation, broadly.

I don’t necessarily think Flying Blue had to make some big, public announcement about the change in advance. After all, this isn’t an official part of the program, and there has really never been any member communication about these opportunities.

I think what was frustrating is that the change was implemented before the website was even updated. So you had the higher pricing already showing, while the page about SAF and mileage donations still reflected the old cost, leaving many people wondering if the change was a glitch or intentional.

At a minimum, I think it’s appropriate to update the webpage before the changes go live, and ideally even give a little notice on the page dedicated to this, just so members aren’t caught off guard.

When it comes to the change as such, Flying Blue does indeed have the most generous opportunities to qualify for elite status through these types of contributions. Selfishly I love this option, but it’s not like members are “entitled” to a certain rate of qualification through this method, since there’s not actually any objectively “fair” way to reward elite qualification for contributions.

So for Flying Blue, it’s presumably about balancing environmental goals with elite ranks. I know with the 50% price hike, I’ll be much less likely to buy SAF, and that’s fine.

As of December 1, 2026, the Air France-KLM Flying Blue program will be decreasing the number of XPs that members earn for contributing toward sustainable aviation fuel and environmental causes. This was initially supposed to be implemented a couple of days ago, but members were caught off guard, so I appreciate that the implementation of this has been delayed.

#6237. Teamsters Sue Horizon Air Over Pilot Rest Rules

The Teamsters have sued Horizon Air, alleging the Alaska Air Group subsidiary violated federal labor law by changing how it handles pilots who report fatigue.

The Teamsters Airline Division and Local 1224 filed the lawsuit Oct. 23 in the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Washington. The union alleges Horizon requires pilots who report fatigue at their home base to travel to another city as passengers before taking the rest provided under their contract.

The union alleges the practice violates the Railway Labor Act and is asking the court to order Horizon to stop it and restore the negotiated rest protections.

“Management cannot pick and choose which parts of our contract it wants to follow,” said Sean Lenney, a Horizon pilot and member of Local 1224, in a news release.

The Teamsters also said Thursday that 99% of pilots who voted backed a no-confidence measure against Carlos Zendejas, Horizon’s senior vice president of operations. The union’s Horizon Air Pilots Executive Council called for his removal following the vote.

Horizon and its pilots have been negotiating a new collective bargaining agreement for more than three and a half years, according to the union. Pilots held informational pickets in Seattle and Boise, Idaho, on Oct. 15 over issues including pay, staffing, and training.

#6236. Transfer Citi ThankYou Points To Turkish Miles&Smiles With 40% Bonus: Worth It?

At the moment, it’s possible to earn up to a 40% bonus when you transfer Citi ThankYou points to Turkish Airlines Miles&Smiles. However, the bonus isn’t being offered on Citi’s end, but instead, is being offered on Turkish Airlines’ end.

Between November 1 and November 30, 2026, it’s possible to receive a 40% bonus when you move points from the Citi ThankYou program in the United States to Turkish Airlines Miles&Smiles. However, there are some important terms to be aware of:

Ordinarily points transfer at a 1:1 ratio (in 1,000 point increments), while through this promotion you’d get 1,400 Miles&Smiles miles for every 1,000 Citi ThankYou points transferred, though only after the fact.

There are several great cards earning Citi ThankYou points, including the Citi Strata Premier® Card (learn more) and Citi Strata Elite℠ Card (learn more), and it’s easy to combine points between the cards.

Back in the day, the Turkish Airlines Miles&Smiles program offered incredible redemption values across the board, but that’s no longer really the case. At this point, I’d say the sweet spot with the Miles&Smiles program is if you’re looking to travel on Turkish Airlines specifically to or from Istanbul.

That’s because the Miles&Smiles program now charges per segment for awards on Turkish Airlines metal. You can find the cost of one-way saver awards below, just to give you a sense of pricing.

So as an example, a one-way business class award between the United States and Istanbul will cost you 65,000 miles. In other words, with a 40% transfer bonus, you’d be paying around 47,000 Citi ThankYou points for a business class award, which is a pretty great deal.

If you know what you’re doing and have specific redemption plans in mind, this could be a great deal. Just be sure you understand the complexities of the program, and read my guide to the Turkish Miles&Smiles program. Also keep in mind the Miles&Smiles expiration policy, which is that miles expire at the end of the third year after which they’re earned, regardless of activity.

The other big restriction is that the bonus miles will only post after the campaign is done, so you couldn’t transfer points and then immediately redeem all of them (including the bonus). The cap on 50,000 bonus miles is also limiting. But hey, if you value Turkish miles, this could definitely offer some value.

Between November 1 and November 30, 2026, it’s possible to receive a 40% bonus when you move points from Citi ThankYou to Turkish Airlines Miles&Smiles. The catch is that the bonus miles only post after the end of the campaign, and you can only earn 50,000 bonus miles with this offer.

If you’re looking to travel on Turkish Airlines to or from Istanbul, there are some good deals to be had by taking advantage of this.

#6235. New Jersey mayor who charged at resident during council meeting concedes election loss

Video captures Pemberton Township Mayor Matthew Bianchini rushing toward a resident during a heated council meeting before being restrained by others in attendance (Credit: Ryan Elmore/Pine Barrens Tribune via Storyful).

The Republican New Jersey mayor who was physically restrained while charging toward a resident during a Pemberton Township council meeting last month has conceded the mayoral race to his Democratic opponent.

Mayor Matthew Bianchini congratulated Belinda Fontanez in a Facebook post Wednesday.

"The voters of Pemberton Township have spoken, and the results are clear. I offer Belinda Fontanez my sincere congratulations on her victory. As she prepares to take on the responsibility of leading our community, she has my full support for a smooth transition," Bianchini wrote.

"I care deeply about the future of this township, and its success matters far more than any single election," he added.

Bianchini was decisively defeated, earning just over 30% of the vote, according to unofficial results.

'I BASICALLY SNAPPED': NEW JERSEY MAYOR CHARGES AT RESIDENT DURING CHAOTIC COUNCIL MEETING

Pemberton Township Mayor Matthew Bianchini charged toward a resident during a heated council meeting in New Jersey before being restrained by others in attendance. (Ryan Elmore/Pine Barrens Tribune via Storyful)

Bianchini, who was tapped to serve as mayor following the resignation of his predecessor, will remain in the role until the end of this year.

Video footage from an October Pemberton Township council meeting captured the mayor being restrained as he sought to advance toward resident Michael Sawka after Sawka appeared to give the middle-finger gesture at the mayor.

"I am f---in' gettin' you!" Bianchini can be heard declaring as another individual intervening in the tense situation pushed the mayor back.

"I should not have said that," Bianchini told WPVI, adding that it "was wrong" and that he is "not gonna get anybody."

NEW JERSEY PRE-K AIDE FACES 61 CHARGES, ACCUSED OF FILMING HIMSELF SEXUALLY ASSAULTING STUDENTS AT SCHOOL

"I will not apologize for my actions last night. If you attack my family, as that resident did last night, I will act," the mayor wrote on Facebook, according to the New York Post.

The Philadelphia Inquirer reported the mayor's wife, who was in the audience during the meeting, noted in a Facebook comment on a Pine Barrens Tribune post, "I am not condoning my husbands [sic] actions but I will say as a parent and a spouse, I get his protection mode."

"He was saying verbally abusive comments about my wife and my daughter," Matthew Bianchini alleged to the Pine Barrens Tribune. "And then he did a hand gesture and looked at my daughter. To me, it appeared like he gave her the finger and that is when I stood up. He looked at me, smiled and gave me the finger and that is when I went out after him."

Bianchini and Sawka have a history of bad blood between them.

The mayor told WPVI, "I just basically snapped," noting, "I hate to put it this way, but ... it's a long time coming."

"Was it wrong? Absolutely. Was it justified? Absolutely. And I would do it again if I had to," the mayor told the outlet.

TRUMP BEDMINSTER GOLF COURSE FALLS TO DEMS AS REPUBLICANS LOSE KEY HOUSE SEAT

Video shows Pemberton Township Mayor Matthew Bianchini rushing toward a resident during a council meeting before several people intervened. (Ryan Elmore/Pine Barrens Tribune via Storyful)

Sawka, who according to WPVI denied making comments towards Bianchini's family, told the station, "All I've ever been trying to do is show that we're wasting money."

"His family, his stepdaughter, his stepson, his daughter, they all attack me online, and they just come after me just with personal attacks," Sawka told WPVI.

Bianchini alleged to the Pine Barrens Tribune that Sawka has been harassing his family "for a long time."

"Mr. Sawka has been a thorn in this township's side for a number of years," Bianchini told WPVI.

Alex Nitzberg is a writer for Fox News Digital.

#6234. Former China Eastern Chairman Jailed In $10+ Million Bribery Scandal

The former chairman of China Eastern Airlines has been sentenced to 14 years in jail, as he accepted more than $10 million in bribes in his official role. Yowzers!

A court in China’s Liaoning Province has sentenced former China Eastern chairman Liu Shaoyong to prison. The court ruled that he accepted over $10 million in bribes in his official capacity as chairman of one of China’s largest airlines.

The court found that between 2002 and 2023, Liu abused his position at the airline to provide assistance to companies and individuals in business operations, project contracts, and flight route management. Liu has been sentenced to 14 years in prison, and has been ordered to pay a fine of $600K, plus his illicit gains and related proceeds have to be recovered.

While the court ruled that his conduct constituted bribery “in an exceedingly large amount,” the sentence he got was actually lighter than it could’ve been, due to mitigating circumstances. These include his confession, voluntary disclosure of previously unknown offenses, and expression of remorse and cooperation in recovering illicit gains.

Make of this what you will, but it’s interesting to note that this is all part of China’s “anti-corruption campaign,” targeting officials at various levels, including executives of state-owned enterprises.

In June 2025, Liu had been placed under investigation by the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection (CCDI) and the National Commission of Supervision, for violations of party discipline and state laws. In January 2026, he was expelled from the Communist Party of China (CPC), after investigators found that he had abused his authority for personal gain, and he was formally charged in May 2026.

China Eastern’s former chairman has been sentenced to 14 years in prison, after he admitted to taking over $10 million in bribes in his official role. This came as part of a larger crackdown by the government, which also saw the executive expelled from the Communist Party of China.

Over the years we’ve seen a decent number of airline executives charged with corruption — after all, they control a lot of spending, and in some cases, might get influenced for the wrong reasons.

What do you make of this punishment for China Eastern’s former chairman?

#6233. How Boeing Losing To Lockheed's C-5 Galaxy Gave The World The 747

Chris earned a Master’s degree in Defense and Strategic Studies (Highest Honors) from the University of Texas at El Paso.

His graduate work concentrated on Global and National Security, Low-Intensity Conflict, Modern Warfare, and US grand strategy. He also undertook extensive regional studies, analyzing how key regions integrate into the broader US security architecture.

This rigorous program provided him with a comprehensive understanding of U.S. military operations, global strategy, and weapons systems. Additionally, he gained a strong appreciation for great power competition.—an increasingly central force shaping international relations and conflict for the foreseeable future.

Born in an era of Cold War competition and growing military airlift needs, the Boeing 747 became one of the most recognizable and influential aircraft in aviation history. Since entering commercial service in 1970, the jumbo jet has transformed passenger and cargo transport worldwide.

Spanning five generations, the 747 evolved alongside the aviation industry, culminating in the technologically advanced 747-8. Yet, its arrival coincided with a shift toward smaller, more fuel-efficient twin-engine aircraft, signaling the beginning of the end for the iconic four-engine airliner.

As a doctrine, Flexible Response was initiated by the Kennedy administration to confront the challenges posed by the Soviet Union on various fronts. As opposed to the doctrine of Massive Retaliation, which relied heavily on the threat of massive nuclear counterstrikes, Flexible Response, introduced in 1961, provided the president with enhanced options when confronting a crisis, ranging from greater nonmilitary to military responses. These options included diplomatic, political, and economic measures, as well as strengthening the military's ability to respond quickly wherever Soviet pressure emerged.

Regarded as the architect of Flexible Response, General Maxwell Taylor advocated for five central pillars concerning the military aspect of the new doctrine. According to the US Army War College Quarterly, Parameters, the second pillar called for the military to be revitalized to conduct warfare at levels below general or all-out war. The third pillar emphasized the need for a continental US-based, active-duty force in a high state of readiness. These personnel would be ready at a moment's notice for rapid deployment overseas to support forward-operating US military forces or allies.

Crucially, for the development of what would become the 747 was the fourth pillar, which highlighted the need to "...modernize and increase the size of air and sealift forces to provide a major capability for the rapid deployment of the active duty forces in the United States, and for resupply of all committed forces."

Moving the required military personnel to a contested region requires speed. If this were done solely by sea, a critical opportunity to halt a Soviet or Soviet-sponsored force could be missed. To this point, the United States Air Force (USAF) stated that "President John F. Kennedy, in his first defense message to Congress in March 1961, announced the buildup of the airlift forces to support flexible response..."

Following this announcement, President Kennedy endorsed the immediate development of the Cargo Experimental-Heavy Logistics System (CX-HLS) program. The five competitors were Lockheed-Georgia Company, Boeing, Douglas Aircraft Company, General Dynamics, and Martin Marietta.

Some of the best military designs emerged during the Cold War.

The future of providing the USAF and, by extension, the US military with timely logistics and surge capacity in a geographic region under Soviet duress was a major priority. On December 22, 1964, Secretary of Defense Robert S. McNamara announced approval of the plan to develop a new outsized logistics aircraft, moving the CX-HLS competition forward.

By May of that year, proposals for the aircraft had been received from the competing companies. After a down-select, Boeing, Douglas, and Lockheed Martin each received one-year study contracts for their airframe designs, while General Electric and Pratt & Whitney received contracts for engine development.

According to a December 1964 issue of Boeing Magazine, the company said competitive subcontracting for the project could total more than $1 billion (£745.7 million), equivalent to about $10.87 billion (£8.1 billion) today. Furthermore, the magazine explained, "The airplane could be the largest ever built. More than 11,000 suppliers in the United States and Canada will participate in the program if Boeing wins the contract."

The Journal of Aircraft and Spacecraft Technology summarized the competition.

"The Air Force considered Boeing's design better than the Lockheed design, although Lockheed's proposal was the lowest total cost bid. Lockheed was selected the winner in September 1965, then awarded a contract in December 1965. General Electric's engine design was selected in August 1965 for the new transport..."

On December 17, 1969, the first C-5A Galaxy was delivered to the 443d Military Airlift Wing, located at Altus Air Force Base, Oklahoma. Today, the USAF maintains a fleet of 52 C-5s. The aircraft has a maximum payload of 281,001 lb (127,460 kg) and an unrefueled range of 5,524 statute miles (8,890 km), according to the USAF. The aircraft would remain a mainstay of America's strategic airlift capability until the Lockheed Martin C-17 entered service in 1995.

The story behind America's flying colossus.

Although Boeing suffered a stinging loss in its bid for the major Air Force contract, the company bounced back at a critical juncture in commercial aviation. According to R. A. Davis, a former Chief Project Engineer for the Boeing 747, "Revenue passenger-miles (less than 50 billion in 1955) had more than tripled by 1965 on a rapidly rising trend. Air travel was forecast to reach at least 500 billion passenger-miles by the mid-1970s, and almost a tenfold increase in air cargo was predicted for the same period."

Furthermore, at the time, passenger traffic was expected to approximately double every five years. With airports already congested, adding more aircraft to accommodate traffic growth would only compound the problem.

Elaborating on this issue, Davis explained that if the congestion problem went unresolved, "By 1975, about 20 million departures of 707-sized aircraft would have to be scheduled each year to meet the predicted world demand. By contrast, if airplanes of 350-400 passenger capability were phased into the long-haul routes, it was estimated that annual departures could be reduced to about 12 million." Clearly, manufacturing larger aircraft appeared to be a promising way forward.

Tony Douglas of startup Riyadh Air says paper boarding passes will not even be an option with the airline.

Taking on the challenge, in 1965, Boeing tasked its Chief Engineer, Joe Sutter — widely known as the Father of the 747 — with reviewing the aircraft's design and reconfiguring it for commercial use. In doing so, the Northwest Airlines History Center states that the "...rear ramp and high wing were traded for a conventional layout, but the option for nose loading was retained — pushing the cockpit above the main deck and creating the distinctive “hump” and upper-deck cabin."

Incredibly, the aircraft went from the drawing board to a completed aircraft in a remarkably short period. In a piece by Airline Reporter, Mr. Sutter stated that "...Pan Am placed its first order in 1966, and we rolled out the first aircraft in 1968, with the first flight in 1969, followed by entry into service in early 1970.” During its first year of service, the 747-100 ushered in a new era of wide-body transportation. Within that short period of time, Mr. Davis stated that the 747 fleet carried over 7 million passengers, demonstrating the aircraft's immediate demand and success as a trusted passenger carrier.

Nearly 15 years after entering service, Davis stated that the 747 fleet expanded to more than 670 airframes. Together, these aircraft had flown more than 19 million revenue hours, traveled over 9.5 billion miles, and transported more than 670 million passengers. Furthermore, by around 1986, Boeing was preparing to continue its remarkable commercial success with the introduction of the 747-400. At the time, the aircraft was expected to deliver greater range, improved fuel economy, and lower operating costs, with projected fuel consumption reductions of 11 to 15%.

The impact of the 737-300, and how the 737's role within Boeing'slineup and the market evolved.

Spanning five generations and 25 manufactured variants, the 747 has been flying domestic and international routes for 56 years, an incredible run. The final passenger model in this iconic aircraft family is the 747-8i, which is optimized for comfortable passenger travel; it entered commercial service on June 1, 2012.

Boeing says the 48-aircraft variant can accommodate a total of 467 passengers. The upper deck can seat 50 Business Class passengers, while First Class accommodates 24 passengers on the main deck, alongside a second Business Class section with seating for 37. The large Economy Class section seats 356 passengers. The 747-8i can also accommodate up to 38 LD-1 cargo containers across its lower-deck cargo holds.

The 747-8i also incorporates several significant technological improvements over the 747-400. Its fuselage was extended by 18.3 feet, adding passenger capacity, while a redesigned wing, improved aerodynamics, and four General Electric GEnx-2B engines improved fuel efficiency and performance. The aircraft also featured a more modern passenger cabin, with larger windows, LED lighting, and an updated interior design. Despite retaining the distinctive appearance and four-engine configuration of its predecessors, the 747-8i represented the most technologically advanced passenger version of the iconic jumbo jet.

Lufthansa was the first airline to purchase the 747-8i and ultimately operated 19 of the aircraft, making it the largest operator of the passenger variant worldwide. Korean Air and Air China also acquired smaller numbers. While the 747-8i was an incredible aircraft, it entered the market as airlines increasingly turned toward smaller, twin-engine aircraft offering greater fuel efficiency and range, such as the Boeing 777. These aircraft could operate many of the same routes without requiring airlines to fill more than 400 seats to make each flight profitable.

The MAX 8-200 is a special edition of the MAX 8 developed for ultra-low-cost carriers that seek to maximize the workhorse's seating capacity.

From its origins in an era of Cold War strategic competition to its role in transforming global aviation, the 747 has enjoyed an extraordinary legacy. The aircraft helped redefine long-haul passenger travel, expanded the possibilities of commercial air cargo, and demonstrated the advantages of moving more people and freight in a single flight.

Although changing economics and advances in twin-engine aircraft ultimately ended production, the 747 remains an enduring symbol of engineering ambition. Its influence on commercial aviation, military logistics, and aircraft design ensures that the Queen of the Skies will remain an important part of aviation history.
