#6232. Air Serbia Flight To Moscow Diverts After Politician Reportedly Skips Security

An Air Serbia flight that was supposed to fly from Serbia to Russia ended up turning around over Lithuania, in order for additional security checks to be carried out on passengers. The circumstances surrounding this sure are unusual, given who was onboard.

This incident happened on Tuesday, November 3, 2026, and involves Air Serbia flight JU134, scheduled to fly from Belgrade (BEG) to Moscow (SVO). The 1,074-mile flight was operated by an Airbus A320 with the registration code YU-APH. The flight was scheduled to depart at 6:25PM and land at 11:40PM, with a two hour time change, so it was blocked at 3hr15min.

The plane took off at 6:48PM, basically on schedule, and it started flying north, over Hungary, Slovakia, Poland, and then Lithuania. However, around 90 minutes after takeoff, while more than halfway, the plane u-turned, and flew back toward Belgrade.

The plane ended up landing in Belgrade at 9:57PM local time, a little over three hours after it first departed. The plane ended up once again taking off in the early morning hours of November 4, departing at 1:56AM, and landing at 6:43AM, over seven hours behind schedule.

Diversions happen, though it’s definitely unusual for a flight to turn around to the origin when it’s already more than halfway to its destination, especially when maintenance wasn’t to blame. Officially, the airline has shared that the decision to divert was made “in accordance with the instructions received and all applicable security rules.” That’s obviously really vague, though… so what really happened?

Here’s where the story gets really interesting. Onboard this Air Serbia flight were a few associates of former Serbian president Aleksandar Vucic, who just recently lost an election. One of the people onboard was Aleksandar Vulin, who served as deputy prime minister until 2025, and is viewed as being very pro-Russia. The US had even imposed sanctions on him due to his close ties with Russia.

Media reports in Serbia suggest that the reason for the diversion was that security camera footage at Belgrade Nikola Tesla Airport had been reviewed, and it was determined that someone had helped him avoid security checks. Now, I understand the need to carry out security checks, though I’m also not sure the point of diverting when you’re already more than halfway to your destination.

Vulin denies that he was the reason that the plane diverted, claiming that it was instead a political showdown. After the diversion, he went on national TV in Serbia, to say the following:

“It’s all a lie, an act of violence and an attempt to prove to these new authorities how ready they are here at the airport, how much they are on the defensive of their ideology. So, of course it’s all a lie, of course it’s all utter nonsense. I’m really sorry and uncomfortable, so many people have returned, their lives are being ruined, their obligations are being ruined because of the attempt to politically deal with me.”

“I am completely calm, I know that I am in the right. And you know, I did not go to Moscow as a tourist, I went on business. I am going there to fight for the extension of the gas agreement. Not for me and you, but for all citizens of Serbia.”

He also said he was asleep at the time of the diversion, and had no clue what was going on until the plane landed back in Belgrade:

“We just woke up, to be honest, I fell asleep. I was sleeping on the plane, I wake up, they say: You are in Belgrade. How are you in Belgrade? When we went outside, I see the police, the special forces gathered. I say: ‘Colleagues, have you come for me?’ They laugh. They say: ‘We are not, Minister.’ I go down with all the other passengers. I go through the procedure with all the other passengers again. I go through another procedure by myself. And now, I am standing and waiting for them to let us get on the plane again.”

An Air Serbia flight from Belgrade to Moscow turned around while over halfway to its destination. The decision to divert was made in accordance with “applicable security rules,” and all passengers were screened when the plane landed back in Serbia.

While it’s believed that a pro-Russia Serbian politician who was onboard may have avoided security checks at the airport, the politician denies that, and claims this was a political move.

What do you make of this unusual Air Serbia diversion?

Best for: Small-business owners who can maximize the card's annual free night award (certain hotels have resort fees)

The Marriott Bonvoy Business American Express Card is Marriott’s only business card currently available to new applicants.

Welcome offer: Earn 75,000 bonus points after spending $6,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership.

According to TPG’s valuations, this bonus is worth up to $563.

This is the standard offer, so it's worth waiting for an elevated bonus.

Why we like it: With this card, you’ll get automatic Gold Elite status with Marriott Bonvoy and a 7% discount on eligible bookings made directly with Marriott through an eligible channel at participating properties with this card’s rate.

The card also comes with 15 elite night credits annually (which can be stacked with a Marriott Bonvoy consumer card) and a free night award annually after your card renewal month (worth up to 35,000 points and can be topped up with up to 25,000 points from your Bonvoy account for a total of 60,000 points per night). In addition, you can earn a second free night (also worth up to 35,000 points) after $60,000 of purchases on your card in a calendar year. (Certain hotels have resort fees.)

Marriott’s use of dynamic pricing may make it hard to use these awards. Still, you should be able to find a participating property that can cover your annual fee (and then some), as our data indicates there’s still significant value in the program.

To learn more, read our full review of the Amex Marriott Bonvoy Business.

Apply here: Marriott Bonvoy Business American Express Card

Best for: Mega Marriott fans who stay with the brand at least a few times each year

The Marriott Bonvoy Brilliant American Express Card is Marriott’s top-tier card.

Welcome offer: Earn 100,000 bonus points after spending $6,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership.

Based on TPG’s valuations, this offer is worth $750.

This is the standard offer we typically see on the card, so we recommend waiting for a higher offer before applying.

Why we like it: The card also has valuable perks, such as automatic Platinum Elite status, an annual free night award (worth up to 85,000 points; certain hotels have resort fees) after card renewal month, up to $300 per year (up to $25 in monthly statement credits) for eligible purchases at restaurants worldwide, Priority Pass™ lounge access and 25 elite qualifying night credits per year. Enrollment is required for select benefits.

Remember that Marriott uses dynamic pricing, so you may need to work harder to find a property where you can use your free nights. But you can top up free night awards with up to 25,000 points now, which allows you to book a night worth up to 110,000 points.

To learn more, read our full review of the Amex Marriott Bonvoy Brilliant.

Apply here: Marriott Bonvoy Brilliant American Express Card

The Marriott Bonvoy Bevy American Express Card is Bonvoy’s mid-tier card from American Express. It has earnings, benefits and an annual fee that mirror the Bountiful.

Welcome offer: Earn 85,000 bonus points after spending $5,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership.

This bonus is worth $638, per TPG's valuations.

This is the standard offer we typically see on the card, so we recommend waiting for a higher offer before applying.

Why we like it: This card also offers mid-tier perks, including complimentary Gold Elite status, a solid earning rate at Marriott properties and elite night credits. However, it lacks several benefits that you might expect from a mid-tier card.

For example, you must spend $15,000 in a calendar year to earn a free night (worth up to 50,000 points; certain hotels have resort fees). Other Marriott cards with lower annual fees offer a similar perk with no spending requirement, making this card tough to justify keeping after earning the welcome offer in the first year.

To learn more, read our full review of the Amex Marriott Bonvoy Bevy.

Apply here: Marriott Bonvoy Bevy American Express Card

Best for: High-spending Marriott fans who prefer to bank with Chase

The Marriott Bonvoy Bountiful is the other mid-tier Bonvoy card from Chase.

Welcome offer: Earn 85,000 bonus points after spending $4,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening.

Based on TPG’s valuations, this offer is worth $638.

This is typically the standard welcome offer we see in the card's history. Unless you absolutely need this card now, you’re better off applying when the offer is higher.

Why we like it: While American Express issues the Bevy, the Bountiful comes from Chase. The two cards offer mostly the same benefits, making it hard to justify the Bountiful's $250 annual fee. However, the welcome bonus may interest you.

To learn more, read our full review of the Marriott Bonvoy Bountiful card.

Best for: Travelers who infrequently stay with Marriott, but want to enjoy perks when they do

The Marriott Bonvoy Bold Credit Card is Chase’s entry-level card for Bonvoy enthusiasts.

Welcome offer: Earn 45,000 bonus points after spending $1,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening.

The bonus points are worth $338, according to TPG’s valuations.

This is slightly higher than the standard welcome offer we've seen on the card, but we'd still suggest waiting for a more rewarding bonus if your timeline is flexible.

Why we like it: The card offers automatic Bonvoy Silver Elite status and five annual elite night credits. It also charges no foreign transaction fees. Additionally, the Bold features Chase’s Pay Yourself Back, allowing you to redeem points toward eligible travel purchases made directly with airlines or Marriott Bonvoy hotels (up to $750 in total redemptions per year).

This is a solid set of perks for a card with no annual fee. However, frequent Marriott guests may do better with a card that offers more perks during each stay.

To learn more, read our full review of the Marriott Bonvoy Bold card.

Apply here: Marriott Bonvoy Bold Credit Card

If multiple Marriott card offers intrigue you, you can indeed have more than one Marriott card open. Some TPG staffers have two or three.

It can make sense to leverage the annual anniversary award nights and stack the 5 to 25 elite nights awarded by carrying both a personal and a small-business Marriott card.

However, with six Marriott cards available to new applicants, there are several restrictions on who can earn the welcome offers across the cards, especially since Marriott cards are issued by both Amex and Chase.

Note that these restrictions are all in addition to Chase’s 5/24 rule (which applies to new applicants for the Bold, Boundless and Bountiful cards) and Amex’s one-bonus-per-lifetime rule (which applies to the Bevy, Brilliant and Business cards).

Make sure you’re eligible for these offers before applying.

Marriott credit cards regularly rank among the best hotel credit cards thanks to the long-term value they offer through perks such as elite status and annual free night awards.

The Boundless currently has a great welcome offer; we'd recommend holding off for higher bonuses on the other cards.

Before applying, consider the size of the welcome offer, whether you're eligible and if the card's ongoing benefits justify adding it to your wallet.

#6230. Is World Of Hyatt Points + Cash Worth It? The Value Varies Wildly

While the most popular way to redeem World of Hyatt points is for free night redemptions, the program also has a Points + Cash option, whereby you can redeem part points and part cash toward the cost of a hotel stay.

The reality is that the value of Hyatt Points + Cash has fluctuated significantly over the years. Going back a decade, it was the primary way that I redeemed my points. Then it was devalued significantly, and then some value was brought back. So I’d like to take a look at the current state of things… is Hyatt Points + Cash worth considering nowadays?

As the name suggests, with Hyatt Points + Cash, you can redeem part points and part cash toward the cost of a Hyatt stay. More specifically, you’ll redeem 50% of the points required for a stay, and will receive a 30-50% discount off the standard rate for the room type chosen.

Now, there are some important things to be aware of:

Just as a reminder, below is the standard room World of Hyatt award chart, which shows the award pricing for a free night hotel stay based on which of the five pricing tiers applies for a particular night (lowest, low, moderate, upper, or top).

When booking Points + Cash, you’d pay half of the points, plus 50-70% of the flexible revenue rate, so below is that chart.

With the basics of Hyatt Points + Cash out of the way, let’s do some number crunching. Let me state upfront that based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider World of Hyatt points to be worth 1.4 cents each, though I usually get quite a bit more value out of them in comparison to what a hotel stay would cost with cash.

For the purposes of the below examples, I’ll simply be comparing the cost for a free night redemption to the cost of a Points + Cash redemption. This doesn’t consider the outright cost of a stay if paying cash, so for more on that, see my post about when you should redeem points for a hotel stay.

I picked six hotels at random, belonging to different brands and in different regions. I picked totally random dates, so let’s take a look at what I found.

For the night I picked, the Grand Hyatt Tampa Bay is charging 15,000 points per night, or 7,500 points plus $103 ($116 including taxes & fees). If redeeming outright, you’re spending 7,500 extra points to save $116, which is like buying Hyatt points for 1.55 cents each.

The Park Hyatt Los Cabos is charging 55,000 points per night, or 27,500 points plus $500.50 ($680.68 including taxes & fees). If redeeming outright, you’re spending 27,500 extra points to save $680.68, which is like buying Hyatt points for 2.48 cents each.

The Hyatt Studios Mobile is charging 3,000 points per night, or 1,500 points plus $61 ($71.98 including taxes & fees). If redeeming outright, you’re spending 1,500 extra points to save $71.98, which is like buying Hyatt points for 4.8 cents each.

The Thompson Rome is charging 35,000 points per night, or 17,500 points plus $281.20 (that includes taxes & fees). If redeeming outright, you’re spending 17,500 extra points to save $281.20, which is like buying Hyatt points for 1.61 cents each.

The Hyatt Centric Dubai Jumeirah is charging 20,000 points per night, or 10,000 points plus $115 ($145.14 including taxes & fees). You’re spending $145.14 to save 10,000 points, which is like buying Hyatt points for 1.45 cents each.

The Grand Hyatt Seoul is charging 20,000 points per night, or 10,000 points plus $221 (that includes taxes & fees). You’re spending $221 to save 10,000 points, which is like buying Hyatt points for 2.21 cents each.

As you can see, the value of Hyatt Points + Cash varies significantly. In the above six examples I randomly pulled up, you’re essentially “buying” Hyatt points for anywhere from 1.45 cents to 4.8 cents each (these aren’t actually points in your account, but rather you’re spending some amount of cash in lieu of points).

So the idea is that if the “purchase” price on points were relatively low, it could be worth booking Points + Cash, rather than just redeeming outright. On the low end of the spectrum, some people might find this to be worthwhile, though I think on the high end of the spectrum, we can all agree this represents an awful deal.

Before you make a final decision, just keep in mind:

Lastly, let me just mention that in many cases Points + Cash is a better value compared to redeeming points outright in situations where the cash rate is lower than usual, and a hotel is in low season. In those situations it might not make sense to redeem points at all. This comes down to how reimbursement for these awards works between World of Hyatt and individual hotels.

For example, the single best Points + Cash deal above is at the Hyatt Centric Dubai, but if you look at the cash rate, you’ll see that redeeming points isn’t a great deal in the first place. There’s no reason to redeem 20,000 points (or 10,000 points plus $115) when the cash rate in the first place is well under $200.

Hyatt Points + Cash lets you redeem part points and part cash toward the cost of a hotel stay. While it’s nice to have the flexibility of this redemption opportunity, more often than not it doesn’t represent a good deal, in my opinion.

The value you’re getting per point through Points + Cash does vary wildly, but one thing that’s fairly consistent is that you won’t get outsized value. In a majority of situations where Points + Cash represents a good deal compared to the outright points cost, it’s a hotel where a points redemption isn’t a good deal in the first place.

Personally, I avoid Points + Cash redemptions, though it’s always worth checking and crunching the numbers.

What’s your take on Hyatt’s Points + Cash option? Do you ever use it?

With P+C you still pay the full % taxes on the cash portion and lose the resort fee waiver, so at a resort with a big daily fee that alone can wipe out the gain. Quick math for Beachfan’s question is (cash rate minus P+C cash) divided by half the award points, which gives you cents per point. I agree and searched 10 properties and dates and like you could not find a single property where cash and points brought value.

So, I'd need to look at the baseline cash rates alongside these two numbers. I know I've seen a few situations at e.g. Marriott where the cash side of the points+cash rate wasn't half of the overall cash rate. Also, does this account for resort fees (or parking, if a Globalist) in the difference between the two, since those waivers apply to points-only but not points+cash?

#6229. How The McDonnell Douglas MD-80 Outlasted The Jet Built To Replace It

McDonnell Douglas built the MD-90 to replace the MD-80. The MD-90 was quieter, more fuel-efficient, and fitted with modern high-bypass turbofan engines that the McDonnell Douglas MD-80's noisy, smoky JT8D-200 engines could not match on any engineering metric. It entered service in 1995, and it exited service in June 2020.

The MD-80 exited service in September 2019, nine months earlier. An aircraft that was supposed to make its predecessor obsolete was retired first, by the same airline that operated the largest fleet of MD-90s in the world. The production numbers tell the story before any explanation is needed: McDonnell Douglas produced 1,191 MD-80s but only 116 MD-90s, a ten-to-one difference that reflected the two aircraft’s very different commercial fortunes.

One aircraft that was supposed to supersede the other sold at one-tenth the volume, and the reason comes down to a single decision about engines that made the supposedly inferior aircraft commercially untouchable for four decades. The reason lies in what 116 aircraft means for an airline trying to support a fleet, and what 362 aircraft on a single carrier can create: a maintenance system that McDonnell Douglas never managed to build around the MD-90.

The MD-80 made its first flight on October 18, 1979, entered commercial service with Swissair on October 10, 1980, and entered service as a two-pilot aircraft, reducing crew costs compared with many earlier jetliners. American Airlines took delivery of its first example in 1982 and became the type's defining operator, eventually accumulating a fleet that, according to American Airlines' official retirement announcement, reached 362 aircraft by 2003.

Roughly one-third of all MD-80s ever produced operated on a single airline. The MD-80 was dominant because it was available in large numbers, fit airline route structures, and accumulated a vast parts-and-maintenance network that steadily lowered operating costs. The MD-90 entered service in 1995 with Delta Air Lines, powered by the IAE V2500-D5.

This was a modern high-bypass turbofan producing approximately 25,000 pounds of thrust (111.2 kN) per engine, shared with the Airbus A320 family. As Simple Flying has documented in its comparison of the two types, the MD-90 was the superior aircraft on paper. In practice, it sold only 116 units before production ended in 2000. For airlines, that number meant the aircraft never reached the scale necessary to create a deep, competitive support network.

The economics of maintenance, repair, and overhaul ( MRO) improve dramatically as more aircraft enter service. Larger fleets attract more parts suppliers, create larger pools of trained mechanics, shorten lead times during aircraft-on-ground events, and generate abundant used components from retired airframes. The IAE V2500 itself was not a weak point.

Thousands of A320-family aircraft used the engine worldwide, making it one of commercial aviation’s best-supported powerplants. The challenge was that the MD-90 used a specific V2500 variant and installation configuration that differed from the A320’s. Operators could not simply draw freely from the enormous A320 parts pool without additional engineering work.

As a result, maintaining a global fleet of only 116 aircraft carried higher costs than the MD-90’s fuel savings alone might suggest. According to Simple Flying's analysis of why the MD-90 remained such a rare aircraft, the type also carried a range limitation that its predecessor did not.

The MD-90's maximum range was approximately 2,100 miles (3,380 km), compared with the MD-80's approximately 2,900 miles (4,667 km). The range gap was a technical limitation. What was not technical was the decision taken in August 1997 that removed McDonnell Douglas from the equation for both aircraft entirely, and handed the MD-90's commercial future to a company with a very different set of interests.

The iconic T-tailed aircraft was the bedrock upon which the legacy carrier built its hub-and-spoke network.

Boeing completed its acquisition of McDonnell Douglas in August 1997, inheriting the MD-80, MD-90, and MD-11 programs. By then, the MD-90 was only a few years into production and was competing, from Boeing’s perspective, against the Boeing 737-700 and the newly launched 737-900.

Boeing had little incentive to aggressively market a narrowbody that could cannibalize sales of its flagship 737 family. The Long Beach production line closed in 2000, just three years after the merger, with the final aircraft delivered to Saudi Arabian Airlines. Delta Air Lines was the MD-90's launch customer, taking delivery of the first 16 aircraft while operating a much larger fleet of MD-88s, an MD-80 variant, that dwarfed the MD-90 count.

When Boeing discouraged further McDonnell Douglas narrowbody orders in favor of the 737 Next Generation, Delta's future narrowbody procurement shifted accordingly. The MD-90 fleet at Delta remained exactly as it was when the production line closed: no growth, no organic replacement, and a declining number of aircraft as the fleet aged toward the retirement threshold.

According to Simple Flying's history of the MD-90, the aircraft continued to serve reliably with Delta into the early 2020s but remained a niche type in the United States. While the MD-90’s growth stalled, the MD-80 was benefiting from something far more powerful than a favorable specification sheet: an enormous, highly concentrated support network built around a single airline.

American Airlines’ peak fleet of 362 MD-80s created one of the deepest maintenance networks ever assembled around a single narrowbody type. The airline operated dedicated facilities, standardized procedures, and accumulated decades of institutional knowledge about every major JT8D-200 failure mode across a high-cycle domestic operation. That concentration was intentional.

Then-CEO Robert Crandall used the Super 80 program as a fleet-simplification strategy, leveraging large orders to reduce acquisition costs and building the maintenance organization to match. The result was that the JT8D-200's support network at American Airlines was, by the 2000s, arguably more mature and more cost-efficient than the V2500's network at Delta's MD-90 operation.

This was despite the JT8D being the older and less efficient engine by every engineering measure. The MD-80’s 2-3 seating arrangement also matched American’s hub-and-spoke network well, providing consistent economics on short-haul routes where flexibility mattered more than maximum efficiency.

When fuel prices remained relatively moderate through much of the 1990s and early 2000s, the aircraft’s higher fuel consumption was offset by exceptionally low maintenance overhead and abundant parts availability. What grounded the MD-80 in the end was not a technical failure or a regulatory mandate, but a lack of competitive success, and the timing of that retirement produced the final, somewhat ironic confirmation that the MD-80 had outlasted its replacement.

While the type is a rarity nowadays, you can still fly on it if you know where to look.

American Airlines operated its final MD-80 revenue flight on September 4, 2019 — Flight 80, departing Dallas-Fort Worth for Chicago O'Hare, before the remaining 26 aircraft were ferried to Roswell, New Mexico. As Simple Flying reported at the retirement, American's official statement captured the aircraft's commercial significance without softening the verdict:

"The MD-80, also known as the Super 80, was the workhorse of the airline's fleet throughout the 1980s and beyond, providing customers and team members with heartfelt memories on adventures ranging from family vacations to key business trips. It's a bittersweet but well-earned retirement as American celebrates the aircraft's history while modernizing its fleet."

Nine months later, in June 2020, Delta Air Lines retired its entire remaining McDonnell Douglas fleet, both the MD-88 variants and the MD-90s, accelerated by the collapse in demand that followed the COVID-19 Pandemic. The retirements that Delta had been deferring for operational reasons became straightforward when load factors dropped to near zero and parking the oldest, least fuel-efficient aircraft in the fleet was the obvious balance-sheet decision.

The MD-90, which entered service seven years after the MD-80 and was built with quieter engines and modern avionics specifically to outlast it, was withdrawn from commercial service after the MD-80 had already been retired. The nine-month gap is narrow enough that both types effectively ended in the same commercial cycle. But the sequencing matters: the aircraft built to replace the MD-80 did not outlive it.

The MD-80's commercial longevity did not prove that old technology beats new technology. It proved that volume beats specification in the MRO economy of commercial aviation, and that a parts distribution built around one airline's enormous fleet commitment can sustain an aircraft type past any rational projection of its useful life.

The JT8D-200 was louder, thirstier, and less efficient than the IAE V2500 on every chart that McDonnell Douglas produced when it launched the MD-90. Those charts were accurate. They did not capture what 362 aircraft at American Airlines would do to the cost structure of maintaining the older engine over four decades.

The broader lesson for aircraft programs is visible in how the MD-90's failure is echoed in later narrowbody competitions. When Boeing launched the 737 MAX and Airbus the A320neo, both programs were oriented around achieving the volume commitments that would prevent exactly the MD-90 situation from developing. A 116-unit program with a single anchor customer and a closing production line is not a product.

It is a transitional inventory problem waiting for a retirement event. The Mad Dog, noisy as it was, never had that problem.

American Airlines' pilots described the MD-80, at its retirement ceremony, as a Cadillac of an aircraft. This was high praise for a jet they had flown for 36 years, and that had carried them through mechanical simplicity to a level of tactile flying that glass-cockpit successors do not replicate.

That description, from Aviation Week's coverage of the final flights, captures something the production numbers cannot: the MD-80 was not beloved despite its age and noise. It was beloved partly because of them. The Mad Dog earned its nickname from its engines and its longevity from its operator. Both turned out to be more durable than anyone in Long Beach expected in 1979.

#6228. Citi AAdvantage Business Card Loyalty Points Double Dip Explained

The single best way to earn American AAdvantage Loyalty Points with credit card spending often flies under the radar, so I’d like to talk a little more about that in this post, especially since this tends to cause some confusion. Furthermore, this was recently made an “official” card perk, rather than something that just unofficially applied to most cardmembers.

Link: Double dip your Loyalty Points earning with the Citi® / AAdvantage Business™ World Elite Mastercard®

With the American AAdvantage Loyalty Points program, you can typically earn one Loyalty Point per dollar spent on a co-branded American credit card. However, there’s one card that’s an exception, and by far the best.

The Citi® / AAdvantage Business™ World Elite Mastercard® (learn more) is the co-branded Citi and American Airlines business card. There’s a quirk to the card, though, when it comes to authorized user rewards. On the surface, the authorized user ordinarily earns the Loyalty Points for their spending, and not the primary cardmember, which is an unusual policy for a small business card.

However, through December 31, 2028 (and it’s possible this will be extended again, as it has been in the past), both the primary cardmember and the authorized user earn Loyalty Points for authorized user spending. It basically means you earn two Loyalty Points per dollar spent, just in different accounts. Just to be abundantly clear here:

So the key is for the spending to be on the authorized user’s card, so that this spending unlocks double Loyalty Points (spread across two accounts).

Either way, the Citi AAdvantage Business Card offers several valuable perks, and also has an excellent welcome bonus, making it a good time to apply. So if you are eligible, I’d consider applying even if the double Loyalty Points opportunity doesn’t work out (though hopefully it does).

Personally, the Citi AAdvantage Business Card Loyalty Points double dip is how I qualified for AAdvantage elite status last year. I had a hard time justifying putting spending onto co-branded American cards compared to some other cards out there, when I was only earning one Loyalty Point per dollar.

But if I can qualify for elite status for two people at once, and earn the corresponding Loyalty Point Rewards perks, the math on that spending starts to look much better:

For example, earning 250,000 Loyalty Points per account could potentially earn you a combined total of 12 systemwide upgrades or 170,000 bonus miles. That’s a pretty substantial reward, beyond just the miles you earn for spending and the status!

The Citi AAdvantage Business Card offers an easy opportunity to double dip Loyalty Points earning through authorized user spending. This opportunity is available to all cardmembers, and is currently valid through December 31, 2028 (though has the potential to be extended beyond that). This is a great opportunity, so if you’re pursuing AAdvantage elite status, I’d highly recommend this method.

Have you been taking advantage of this Loyalty Points double dip opportunity?

#6227. Park Hyatt Riviera Maya Cancun, Brand’s First All-Inclusive, Opens Soon

Want to take advantage of Hyatt Privé benefits, including a room upgrade, complimentary breakfast, a hotel credit, and more, when booking a cash stay? Contact Ford ([email protected]) for more details. He may even be able to help if you already have a stay booked.

In late 2023, Hyatt and Parks Hospitality Holdings announced a collaboration that will expand Hyatt’s footprint in Mexico, with the development of four new properties. If you ask me, the most interesting of these is the new Park Hyatt Riviera Maya, which will also be the brand’s first all-inclusive property.

There’s now an update, as the hotel’s opening date has just been moved forward by a couple of months, and it’s now expected to open in the coming weeks.

The Park Hyatt Riviera Maya, located in Cancun, Mexico, is now accepting reservations for stays as of December 3, 2026. The hotel was initially supposed to open in 2025, then it started accepting reservations for stays as of February 2027, and now it’s accepting reservations for stays as of late 2026.

Hopefully the current opening date sticks, but if you book in the first several months the hotel is open, don’t be surprised if we see an additional delay, or at least don’t be surprised if not everything is ready.

The 148-key property will have a first-ever concept for the Park Hyatt brand, as it will be all-inclusive. Admittedly this is pretty normal for the Cancun area, but still, it’s noteworthy for a brand like Park Hyatt.

Hyatt has been leaning heavily into the all-inclusive space in recent times, particularly through acquisitions. So while Hyatt has grown massively in terms of its number of all-inclusive brands, it’s surprising to see even a traditionally non all-inclusive brand get this kind of an experience.

I’m generally not a fan of all-inclusives, or at least historically haven’t chosen to vacation at them. However, after my recent Ritz-Carlton Yacht Collection cruise, there is something I really enjoyed about not being nickel-and-dimed for everything, given how expensive luxury hospitality has become in so many places.

When it comes to the dining outlets, they’ll include Beach Grill IK’AL (the beachfront restaurant with seafood and Yucatecan flavors), Bruma (the steakhouse), Nutre Kitchen (the all-day dining restaurant), Pool Bar Brisa (the pool bar serving drinks & light snacks), Patisserie Market & Cafe (the coffee shop), Living Room (the lobby bar).

Accommodations will range in size from 559 square feet (52 square meters) to 2,303 square feet (214 square meters), so they’re generously sized, as you’d expect. The decor looks nice enough, but not like anything special.

As you’d expect, the resort will have amenities including several pools, a full-service spa, a gym, and more.

Once open, this adds to a growing number of luxury points hotels in the Cancun area. Just recently we saw the opening of the St. Regis Kanai and Waldorf Astoria Cancun, so it’s nice to see Hyatt’s most luxurious brand also expand to the Cancun area. As a matter of fact, the Park Hyatt will be immediately next to the Waldorf Astoria (which also recently became all-inclusive, as it wasn’t initially).

The Park Hyatt brand is really growing in Mexico right now. We’ve seen the recent opening of the Park Hyatt Los Cabos at Cabo Del Sol, while the Park Hyatt Mexico City is expected to open in early 2027. Beyond that, we also saw the recent opening of the Alila Mayakoba, another good luxury option in the Cancun area.

With the Park Hyatt Riviera Maya now bookable, what are rates like? If paying cash, rooms seem to generally start at around $1,500 per night, but that does include taxes & fees. So it’s obviously very expensive, but given Mexico’s high taxes & fees, it’s actually not quite as crazy as some may have expected.

Then again, I’m not necessarily expecting this to be typical Park Hyatt quality, given the extent to which this is outside the typical Park Hyatt wheelhouse. Oddly, at least as of now, rates seem to be the same whether one or two people are staying, which is unusual for an all-inclusive.

If you are looking to book a cash stay here, I’d recommend doing so through the Hyatt Privé program, which offers extra perks like room upgrades, a hotel credit, and more.

When redeeming points, the hotel follows World of Hyatt’s Category F all-inclusive award chart, which is the most expensive award pricing for all-inclusive properties.

Under Hyatt’s current award chart, the cost is typically 45,000 to 85,000 points per night, and that’s the same whether the room has single or double occupancy.

The Park Hyatt Riviera Maya is now accepting reservations for stays as of December 2026. The hotel is expected to be an all-inclusive, making it the first Park Hyatt property in the world where that’s the case.

It’s awesome to see Hyatt’s luxury expansion in Mexico, as this will be the third Park Hyatt to open in a fairly short time period. However, the Park Hyatt brand is becoming increasingly inconsistent, and I find the all-inclusive pivot to be a bit strange, especially given how many all-inclusive brands Hyatt already has.

What do you make of plans for the Park Hyatt Riviera Maya?

#6226. Schumer, Jeffries sidestep questions on nuking filibuster, launching Elon Musk probe after blue wave

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., were pressed on looming questions over potential moves in Congress after flipping both chambers. (Credit: Nicholas Ballasy for Fox News Digital)

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., did not answer Fox News Digital’s questions about their potential first moves in Congress after the Democrats won back the majority in both chambers with sweeping victories in Tuesday’s elections.

Schumer was pressed on whether he plans to abolish the filibuster as speculation grows that Democrats could eliminate the filibuster after President Donald Trump urged Senate Republicans to terminate it numerous times to pass the SAVE America Act.

Trump previously warned that if Republicans didn’t act on it, the Democrats would if given the opportunity, which they now have.

Schumer ignored the question after being asked twice by Fox News Digital if he plans to eliminate it.

FETTERMAN STRONGLY SUPPORTS THE FILIBUSTER AS TRUMP URGES SENATE REPUBLICANS TO SCRAP IT

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., hold a joint news conference at the U.S. Capitol Jan. 8, 2026. (Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

Some Democrats have previously signaled openness to eliminating the filibuster if they regained the Senate.

During a news conference Wednesday morning, Schumer also refused to answer questions about some of his plans for the Senate as Democrats take back the majority, including eliminating the filibuster.

He also said he will be "re-elected as majority leader" by the Senate Democratic caucus despite opposition from newly elected Democrats. He quickly redirected the conversation to focus on the blue wave in the midterm elections and what the party plans to do with the "generational remake of the Senate map."

SCHUMER SAYS HE'S NOT GOING ANYWHERE, BUT HIS OWN CANDIDATES AREN'T READY TO BACK HIM

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., speaks during a news conference at the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee headquarters on Nov. 4, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Tom Brenner/Getty Images)

Jeffries was also asked by Fox News Digital about the looming question over whether Democrats will probe Elon Musk after the party has begun eyeing targets in discussed efforts to investigate alleged corruption in the Trump administration.

Jeffries gave Fox News Digital a thumbs-up when approached but did not respond when asked whether House Democrats would investigate Musk.

Musk has emerged as a potential target of Democratic oversight, with some lawmakers calling for scrutiny of his time as head of the Department of Government Efficiency. Democratic lawmakers have also suggested looking into his companies' multibillion-dollar contracts with the federal government and, more recently, his role in cutting internet access to the Ukrainian military.

‘LAWYER UP’: DEMS IMMEDIATELY PUT TRUMP ON NOTICE AMID REPUBLICANS' MIDTERM BLOODBATH

Last week, Musk blamed the issue on the U.S. military. (Getty Images)

The House minority leader’s refusal to comment comes as Democrats are divided over whether they would select Jeffries as speaker of the house.

There was a petition started that has received over 550,000 to oust Jeffries from leading the House, arguing the party needs a speaker that represents "the Democratic voters, not just the Democratic establishment."

With many of the newly elected congressional candidates hesitant, or outright opposed, to backing both Jeffries and Schumer as leaders, the decision over who will be the leaders of both chambers of Congress is still in limbo.

Hannah is a Production Assistant for the Politics team at Fox News Digital.

#6225. Alaska Atmos Rewards Global Getaways Sale: Save Up To 50% On Award Flights

Alaska Atmos Rewards offers the Global Getaways promotion, whereby members can save on award tickets in select regions. Atmos Rewards launches this promotion on the first Wednesday of each month (which the program calls “Atmos Members Day”), so we just saw the one for November launched.

Let’s go over the opportunities, as you can save up to 50% on award tickets. There are some cool markets in which you can save miles, though unfortunately only economy travel qualifies.

For the new Alaska Atmos Rewards Global Getaways promotion, you can save up to 50% on award travel to nine destinations, with the following restrictions:

The theme for this Global Getaways promotion is “lights, camera, departure,” with the idea being to “roll out the red carpet for the destinations that have starred in your favorite films and shows.” With this sale, you can save on one-way redemptions to the following destinations (these savings are up to 50%, but not always that high):

I very much appreciate Alaska Atmos Rewards’ creativity with this promotion, as nowadays it’s pretty rare to see programs offer award sales that are also valid for travel on partner airlines. Now, admittedly I wish there weren’t quite as many restrictions in terms of the booking window, travel period, the class of service limitations, and the one-way discount, but still, there will be value here for some, and it’s better than nothing.

If you’re simply looking for the lowest cost award, some of these award prices are very tough to beat. For example, getting from the mainland to Hawaii for 11,500 points is a great deal, as is getting from the United States to India for 30,000 points. Keep in mind that with Atmos Rewards, award flights even earn status points, so could help you qualify for status.

I do hope that over time we see some first and business class award sales as well (it’s probably not happening, but we can dream, right?). Many of us have historically loved the program for the value it offers for premium cabin travel, so this promotion doesn’t help us much with that.

This is basically Alaska’s version of Air France-KLM Flying Blue Promo Rewards or Singapore KrisFlyer Spontaneous Escapes, except it applies for travel on partner airlines (rather than just for travel on the program’s airline), and is exclusive to economy (while the other promotions are mixed).

Alaska Atmos Rewards has launched its latest Global Getaways promotion, which is a monthly redemption deal offering up to a 50% discount on awards. This time around, you can save points on economy redemptions to select destinations. You need to book by November 7, 2026, mostly for travel in early 2027. While this won’t be useful for everyone, I imagine some people will get value from this.

What do you make of Alaska’s Global Getaways promotion?

#6224. Southwest Airlines Now Runs Late Nearly A Third Of The Time

Southwest Airlines was late nearly a third of the time in October, and its cancellation rate was more than twice Delta’s. It finished last for punctuality among the ten North American airlines in aviation analytics company Cirium’s new monthly report, while Delta led on both. For the past two months, I’ve pointed out that Southwest’s poor on-time rankings were offset by canceling fewer flights than anyone else. They weren’t on-time but they reliably got passengers to their destinations. In October, though, Delta, United and even Frontier cancelled a smaller share of flights than Southwest. Here are Cirium’s North American results. On-time means arriving at the gate within 15 minutes of schedule. Airline   September On-Time   October On-Time   October Canceled Delta   82.52%   86.86%   0.24% United   78.65%   84.06%   0.31% WestJet   85.31%   83.56%   0.90% JetBlue   74.64%   82.27%   0.57% Alaska   80.73%   81.06%   1.10% American   77.11%   80.10%   0.63% Allegiant   Not listed   77.89%   1.13% Frontier   75.49%   77.62%   0.38% Air Canada   73.19%   75.74%   2.80% Southwest   71.14%   68.90%   0.51% Southwest’s Fixes Extend Into January Southwest’s on-time performance fell 2.24 percentage points from September. Every other U.S. airline improved. And Southwest was nearly seven points behind even Air Canada, the next airline up the list. They’re also way down from last October when they were 75.5% on time versus 68.9% this year. Delta improved year-over-year from 84.5% to 86.9%. Southwest’s cancellation rate increased from 0.38% to 0.51%. That’s still only about five cancellations per thousand flights, but Delta was at 2.4 per thousand and United at 3.1. There was no longer a cancellation advantage in October to offset the Dallas-based carrier’s greater likelihood of arriving late. Management knows there’s a problem. On the October 22 earnings call, chief operating officer Andrew Watterson said the weakness was concentrated in delays between roughly 15 and 45 minutes. He described the airline consistently starting aircraft turnarounds well, then losing time at the end. Changes to gate checking bags and closing flights are supposed to begin in November. Southwest gate checks a lot more bags now that passengers want to carry more belongings onboard, since checked bags have a fee. Agents will finally be able to close flights using an iPad at the aircraft. And adjusted schedules begin in January. Fast turns let Southwest get more flying out of each airplane. But those savings shrink when those produces delays, and CEO Bob Jordan acknowledged that poor punctuality is adding to costs including from misconnecting passengers. Delta Leads, United Closes In, And JetBlue Recovers Delta took first place from WestJet, ending the Canadian airline’s five-month run at the top of North America. Delta also ranked third on Cirium’s global list. Their cancellation rate has fallen from 1.77% in August to 0.92% in September and 0.24% in October. That’s real improvement compared to their abysmal summer operation. United is getting improving, too. Delta’s punctuality lead over United narrowed from 3.87 percentage points to 2.80. Delta canceled less often this time, but the difference was just 0.07 percentage points or seven flights per 10,000 scheduled. I wouldn’t pay much extra for Delta over United based on that operational gap. Against Southwest, Delta was nearly 18 percentage points more likely to arrive within the on-time window. American improved, too, but fell further behind both of its major competitors. Delta’s lead over American widened from 5.41 to 6.76 points. United’s lead widened from 1.54 to 3.96 points. American’s better month left them sixth in North America. And JetBlue went from 63.85% on time in August to 74.64% in September and 82.27% in October. Their 7.63-point gain was the largest of any North American airline. JetBlue finished ahead of both Alaska and American on punctuality, and canceled less often than either. Their cancellation rate fell from 5.09% in August to 0.57% in October. Even Newark Made The On-Time Airports List The airport report measures on-time departures, rather than arrivals. Six U.S. airports made Cirium’s top 20 large airports worldwide, up from just two in September: Minneapolis–St. Paul: 87.00%, eighth Washington Dulles: 86.25%, eleventh Detroit: 86.13%, twelfth Salt Lake City: 85.69%, thirteenth Newark: 85.64%, fourteenth Atlanta: 85.17%, eighteenth Four are Delta hubs. The other two are United hubs. No American hub made the list. This is partly another view of the airlines themselves, since a hub’s results depend heavily on its dominant carrier. I never expect to see Newark doing well! And this data can be useful to some degree in choosing between otherwise similar connecting options, although can also be seasonal due to weather. The World of Hyatt personal and business credit cards can help you save money and enjoy valuable perks on your next Hyatt stay.

Right now, the personal card is offering its most lucrative bonus since February, making now a good time to apply.

The World of Hyatt program is known for offering some of the best redemption rates in the industry, along with a diverse portfolio of distinctive hotel brands.

Let's dive into these offers and help you decide whether to apply.

The World of Hyatt Credit Card (see ) is currently offering new cardholders four free nights (at Category 1-4 Hyatt hotels) after spending $5,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening.

Per Hyatt's award chart, Category 1 Hyatt hotels can cost as few as 3,000 points per night, while Category 4 properties can cost as many as 25,000 points per night.

That means the value of this welcome offer depends on how you redeem the free nights. If you use all four certificates at Category 4 properties that would otherwise cost 25,000 points per night, you'd "use" 100,000 points. Based on TPG's November 2026 , that puts the bonus's potential value at up to $1,650.

While this isn't the strongest welcome offer we've seen in the card's history, it does meet our threshold for when to apply.

Why we like it: This card has valuable ongoing perks, the best of which is an annual free night certificate at a Category 1-4 Hyatt property, which you’ll receive after every account anniversary. You’ll also get a second free night after spending $15,000 in a calendar year.

Here are some ideas to maximize your World of Hyatt points.

To learn more, read our full review of the World of Hyatt card.

With the World of Hyatt Business Credit Card (see ), new cardholders can currently earn 70,000 bonus points after spending $7,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening.

Based on our valuations, this bonus is worth $1,155. This isn't the highest offer we've seen on the card, but it meets our criteria for applying (when at least 65,000 points are on offer).

Cardholders also earn 2 points per dollar spent in their top three spending categories each quarter with no spending cap. These categories include:

The points-earning rates will be adjusted automatically on the categories where you spend the most each quarter, so there’s no need to select your preferred categories.

Beyond the bonus categories, you'll earn 1 point per dollar spent on all purchases.

Why we like it: Hyatt loyalists who own a business can find value in the card’s up to $100 in Hyatt statement credits each anniversary year (spend $50 and receive a $50 statement credit, up to two times) and the ability to gift Discoverist status to up to five employees.

You’ll also earn five tier-qualifying nights for every $10,000 you spend on the card in a calendar year.

To learn more, read our full review of the World of Hyatt Business card.

Apply here: World of Hyatt Business Credit Card

Both the World of Hyatt personal and business cards offer plenty of benefits for Hyatt loyalists. In fact, the Hyatt personal card ranks among the top picks of TPG staffers.

Having either card automatically grants you Discoverist status, which includes benefits such as late checkout, preferred rooms and a 10% points bonus on eligible purchases. Spending on either card can also earn you additional elite-qualifying nights.

You’ll also enjoy several travel protections, such as baggage delay insurance, lost luggage reimbursement and trip interruption and cancellation insurance.

Plus, the personal card comes with a free night certificate every anniversary year (valid at Category 1-4 properties), which is extremely valuable for any Hyatt enthusiast.

Related: Why I aim to spend $15,000 on my World of Hyatt Credit Card each year

There's much to love about both World of Hyatt credit cards, even if you don't frequently stay at Hyatt hotels. The personal and business cards feature several perks that can easily cover their reasonable annual fees.

Both cards are also offering elevated welcome bonuses with potential values exceeding $1,000 each, making now a good time to consider applying.

Apply here: World of Hyatt Business Credit Card

#6222. Live: Singapore Airlines Unveils All-New First & Business Class Suites For Its Boeing 777-9

Last Updated: 12:30 AM EST Nov 5 2026 by Tom Boon

Singapore Airlines has unveiled the next stage in its total refresh of the passenger experience. Today, the Asian airline revealed its new first-class and business-class seats to the world at an event held at the Marina Bay Sands Exhibition Centre in Singapore. The airline will spend more than $2bn SGD ($1.5bn) on the upgrade program.

Airlines around the world are constantly looking to innovate when it comes to passenger experience. With a trophy cabinet of awards, including 2026 SkyTrax Best Airline, Singapore Airlines is looking at the experience in more detail than some others. A cabin refresh that was initially planned to launch with the arrival of the Boeing 777-9 is now expected from H2 next year and will also apply to some of the airline’s Airbus A350-900s.

Singapore Airlines has taken a bold approach with its new business class cabin, designed in collaboration with BMW’s Design Works and RECARO. The new seats are incredibly well thought out from a passenger experience. However, the colour scheme is a departure from the usual Batik-inspired palette that the airline has become famous for.

When describing the new cabin, one of the features consistently pointed out by the Chief Commercial Officer, Lee Lik Hsin, was the fact that passengers sit and sleep facing forward. Work, sleep, dining, and relaxing have all been considered. The seat, for example, has a dedicated space to place your laptop during the meal service, a huge bugbear for many passengers during the meal service. Additionally, the airline will also be introducing doors to its business class seats for the first time.

Arguably the biggest upgrade that Boeing 777 and Airbus A350 passengers will see is the introduction of double beds in select business class seats. According to Singapore Airlines, the full-flat beds measure 79 inches in length and up to 24 inches in width, while a padded bedsheet with memory foam will provide "additional cushioning and support".

When it comes to first class, Singapore Airlines has another bespoke product. Designed with PriestmanGoode, each first class cabin will have six seats, each with a floor to ceiling enclosure. Unlike the business class, the first class cabin sticks to the established Singapore Airlines design language.

The highlight of the first class cabin is the two center seats. These can be combined to make a sofa or double bed. The seats can be synchronised and adjusted as one. Of course, if the passengers occupying these seats are unknown to each other, a full height wall is able to separate them.

Singapore Airlines says that combined, the center seats offer “The largest double bed in commercial aviation”, measuring 80 inches in length and 60 inches in width. Another particular highlight of the seat, built by Collins Aerospace, is the option for face to face dining at all seats, allowing up to four people to dine together in the center seats.

#6221. Amex Gold Card Review: Benefits & Points For Those Who Like To Eat

The American Express® Gold Card is one of the most rewarding cards out there if you’re looking to earn Amex Membership Rewards points.

The Amex Gold Card is an absolute powerhouse if you spend a lot on food, whether it’s at restaurants or supermarkets (or a combination of both). While the card has a somewhat steep annual fee, the good news is that it offers credits that can largely help offset it. We’re also currently seeing an exceptional welcome offer, making it the ideal time to pick up this card. Anyway, enough of an intro, let’s get into my in-depth Amex Gold Card review.

Link: Learn more about the American Express® Gold Card

Before I get into my full Amex Gold Card review, let me summarize some of the most important features:

Here are my thoughts on the major pros and cons of the Amex Gold Card:

For someone looking to earn Membership Rewards points, the Amex Gold Card is one of the most rewarding cards out there. To start, let’s take a look at the welcome offer on the card, along with the eligibility requirements and fees. After all, these are important factors people consider when applying for a card.

The Amex Gold Card has an improved welcome offer: You may be eligible for as high as 100,000 Membership Rewards® Points after spending $8,000 in eligible purchases on your new Card in your first 6 months of Membership. Welcome offers vary and you may not be eligible for an offer.

The way this works, you can apply for the card, and then find out your offer amount. Then you can decide whether you want to accept the offer or not. That’s an unconventional approach for a welcome offer. At least Amex has the “apply with confidence” feature, so there won’t be a hard credit pull unless you accept the offer.

Based on my latest miles & points valuations, Membership Rewards points are worth 1.7 cents each. So if you are eligible for a bonus of 100,000 points, those are worth $1,700, by my valuation.

This is a huge bonus, and on top of that, you have a full six months to complete the minimum spending requirement, which should be easy enough for many people to accomplish, as that translates to roughly $1,333 per month in required spending. Personally I’d only apply for the card if I got a welcome offer of at least 60,000 points (or ideally 80,000 points), but everyone has to decide for themselves what they’re willing to “settle” for.

The welcome bonus on the Amex Gold Card isn’t available to those who have or have had the card, or those who have had the Premier Rewards Gold Card in the past. Furthermore, those who have or have had an American Express Platinum Card® (learn more) may also not be eligible for the welcome offer on the card.

However, if you have had one of these cards before, you’re still eligible for the card, but you’re just not eligible for the welcome offer (which is “once in a lifetime”). In some circumstances, it could still be worth getting the card in those situations, if you’d benefit from it on an ongoing basis.

Let me emphasize that you’ll want to apply for the Amex Gold before you apply for the Amex Platinum. That’s because if you have the Amex Gold, you’re still eligible for the Amex Platinum offer, while the inverse isn’t true.

See this post for all the rules on applying for Amex cards, and see this post for details on getting approved for the Amex Gold Card.

The Amex Gold Card has a $325 annual fee. There is no annual fee for up to five additional cards. Meanwhile, the annual fee for six or more additional cards is $35 for each card (Rates & Fees).

Note that Amex Gold Card authorized users don’t receive some of the same benefits as the primary cardmember, but their spending does count toward the rewards that the primary cardmember earns.

The Amex Gold Card has no foreign transaction fees (Rates & Fees), so you can use it for purchases globally. That’s especially useful when you consider that you can earn 4x points on dining abroad, all with no foreign transaction fees.

What makes the Amex Gold Card so valuable is the bonus categories it offers, in the form of Membership Rewards points. The bonus categories include the following:

This is an outstanding return on spending. Based on my valuation of Amex points at 1.7 cents each, that’s like an 8.5% return on eligible prepaid hotel stays, a 6.8% return at restaurants and at U.S. supermarkets, and a 5.1% return on eligible flights.

Now let’s take a closer look at just how those bonus categories are defined.

The Amex Gold Card offers 5x Membership Rewards points on prepaid hotels that are booked through Amex Travel. As a general rule of thumb, this isn’t worth it. That’s because you’re usually not earning loyalty points with your preferred hotel program when you book through Amex Travel, so that’s quite an opportunity cost.

With the Amex Gold Card you’ll earn 4x points on the first $50,000 spent every calendar year at restaurants worldwide, and after that you’ll earn a single point per dollar spent.

Generally speaking, restaurants are defined pretty broadly, and the category includes everything from fast food to cafes to fine dining. This even includes delivery and takeout, given the popularity of that nowadays.

Just note that convenience stores, nightclubs, and restaurants located within other establishments won’t typically qualify for bonus points. Furthermore, eligibility for bonus points is determined based on how the merchant chooses to be categorized. There’s a chance that some merchants may not be categorized as a restaurant, even though you might consider them a restaurant.

For dining, this card even beats the 3x points that the Chase Sapphire Preferred® Card (learn more) and Chase Sapphire Reserve® (learn more) offer — this is one of the best rewards cards for dining purchases.

The Amex Gold Card offers 4x points on the first $25,000 spent every calendar year at U.S. supermarkets, and after that you’ll earn a single point per dollar. This excludes superstores and warehouse clubs, so don’t expect you’ll be able to earn those bonus points at Sam’s Club, for example. This is one of the best rewards cards for grocery store purchases.

The Amex Gold Card offers 3x points on airfare, with no limits on how many bonus points you can earn. This only applies when booking directly with an airline, through the Amex Travel App™ or through amextravel.com. Furthermore, charter flights and private jet flights are excluded.

Officially, booking through online travel agencies (except Amex Travel) wouldn’t earn you bonus points, though in practice, it may still sometimes code for 3x points. That’s because often online travel agencies still have the airline bill you directly when you book flights through them. This is one of the best rewards cards for airfare purchases.

The Amex Gold Card also offers 2x points on prepaid car rentals and cruises booked through Amex Travel. This bonus category doesn’t make or break the card, but it’s a nice extra, especially if you already make these bookings occasionally.

The Amex Gold Card earns Membership Rewards points. This is one of the major transferable points currencies, and is a favorite points currency for many.

The best way to redeem your Amex points is to transfer them to one of the Membership Rewards airline or hotel partners. Points can be transferred to about 20 partners, consisting primarily of airline loyalty programs, but also of some hotel loyalty programs.

The reason this represents such a good deal is that you can get outsized value toward first and business class travel. These tickets are often disproportionately expensive if paying cash, while they can be a good deal on points. On top of that, Amex often has transfer bonuses, which can stretch your points even further.

While you can redeem Membership Rewards points toward the cost of merchandise or gift cards, or to pay off your statement, these aren’t good uses of your points. You’ll typically get less than 1.0 cent of value per point, so that’s not how I’d redeem them.

In general, I’d recommend earning Membership Rewards points if your primary interest is transferring points to partner programs.

The Amex Gold Card offers a variety of benefits that can help offset the annual fee of the card. In particular, the Amex Gold offers statement credits for eligible purchases, which could save you up to $424 per year, more than offsetting the annual fee. Let’s take a closer look at how these work (Enrollment is required for select benefits).

The first perk is that the Amex Gold Card offers a dining credit of up to $120 per year. There are some restrictions to be aware of with this credit:

The Amex Gold Card offers up to $120 in Uber Cash annually:

This is a fantastic benefit and should be worth face value for anyone who uses Uber at least once a month. Even if you don’t use Uber, this can be useful for getting food delivery through Uber Eats.

The Amex Gold Card offers up to $100 in Resy credits annually:

The Amex Gold Card offers up to $84 in Dunkin’ credits annually:

One thing I’d mention is that anecdotally this also works for Dunkin’ reloads, so you can always get the Dunkin’ app, and then load $7 onto your account each month, and that should trigger the credit. That’s a great way to use this to “bank” credit with Dunkin’ toward a future purchase.

One of the great features of Amex cards is access to Amex Offers, which offers savings or bonus points on purchases with all kinds of retailers. There’s huge value to be had in getting as many Amex cards as possible, so that you can get these offers on multiple cards. Amex Offers could save you hundreds of dollars per year — just note that enrollment is required to take advantage of individual offers.

For staying two or more nights at select luxury hotels, you can receive extra benefits through The Hotel Collection. Benefits include a $100 hotel credit and a room upgrade, if available. This is different than Amex Fine Hotels + Resorts®, which requires having the Amex Platinum Card.

Holding the Amex Gold Card entitles you to a complimentary upgrade to Hertz Five Star status (enrollment required). This gets you an upgrade to a higher car class on rentals when available as well as a 25% bonus on all Hertz rentals. If you already rent cars through Hertz, this is a nice extra. It’s one of the more recently added benefits on the Amex Gold Card, too, since it was introduced in celebration of the card’s 60th anniversary.

The Amex Gold Card comes with a handful of travel insurance benefits that can protect your trip when you pay with your card. Check the card’s benefits guide for exact exclusions and limits, but here’s a quick overview:

Up to $300 per Covered Trip that is delayed for more than 12 hours; and 2 claims per Eligible Card per 12 consecutive month period. Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by New Hampshire Insurance Company, an AIG Company. Baggage insurance plan: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company. Car rental loss and damage insurance: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company. Car Rental Loss or Damage Coverage is offered through American Express Travel Related Services Company, Inc.

The Amex Gold Card is a great card for anyone who spends a lot of money on food (whether at restaurants or supermarkets), and who is looking to earn Membership Rewards points. Furthermore, the card potentially offers over $400 in annual credits, between the dining credit, Resy credit, Dunkin’ credit, and Uber Cash.

I’d argue that if you value earning Membership Rewards points, if you spend a lot on dining, and if you can use a decent number of the card’s credits, then picking up this card is a slam dunk. It’s hard to beat this kind of return on dining and supermarket spending, and it’s a great complement to some other Amex cards.

The great welcome offer that’s available is the icing on the cake, and makes applying for the card all the more tempting. I’d recommend confirming you’re eligible for a welcome bonus on the higher end of the spectrum with the current offer of as high as 100,000 points, especially because you can only get an Amex Gold Card welcome bonus once.

I will say, the Amex Gold Card might not be for you if you don’t spend a lot on dining, if you don’t live in a major city where you can easily use the credits, if you value airport lounge access as a card perk, or if you’d rather earn cash back than travel rewards, since those are all potential considerations with the card.

It’s also worth comparing the Amex Gold Card to other options. Here’s how the Amex Gold Card stacks up against some of the most popular alternatives.

The Amex Platinum Card (learn more) has a higher annual fee than the Amex Gold and comes with many more perks and annual credits. Here are the biggest differences to know about:

If you travel many times a year and want as many benefits as possible, the Amex Platinum Card is hard to beat. That said, the Amex Gold Card still offers a better return on spending when it comes to dining out and shopping at U.S. supermarkets. As I see it, the cards serve different purposes — one is about the perks, and the other is about the return on spending.

If you’re looking for a rewards card with a lower annual fee, the Chase Sapphire Preferred Card (learn more) is worth comparing against the Amex Gold Card as well. It has a much lower annual fee of $95 and fewer perks, but it still earns very strong rewards:

Between the Amex Gold Card and the Chase Sapphire Preferred, the best option for you could come down to whether you prefer Amex Membership Rewards points or Chase Ultimate Rewards points. Make sure to compare your welcome bonus offers between both cards before making a final decision as well.

The Citi Strata Premier® Card (learn more) is another great rewards card with useful bonus categories at the $95 annual fee level:

If you want just one rewards card in your wallet, the Citi Strata Premier makes a strong case for itself with its bonus categories. I value both Amex points and Citi ThankYou points at 1.7 cents apiece, but some travelers might prefer one rewards program over the other depending on their favorite airline and hotel partners.

The Capital One Venture Rewards Credit Card (learn more) is one of my favorite cards for those looking for a simple strategy, and who don’t want to focus on a bunch of credits, maximizing bonus categories, etc.

The card has a $95 annual fee, and offers a minimum of 2x miles per dollar spent, making this one of the best cards for everyday spending. The reasonable annual fee plus the flat 2x miles is ideal for someone who doesn’t maybe spend a huge amount in categories that are otherwise eligible for bonus points.

The Amex Gold Card is one of American Express’ best rewards cards for earning points. With 4x points on dining and supermarkets, earning Membership Rewards points is easy.

The card also offers some credits that are potentially useful, which for many will help offset the annual fee. The card offers up to $120 dining credits, up to $120 in Uber Cash annually, up to $100 in Resy credits annually, and up to $84 in Dunkin’ credits annually — a total of $424 in annual credits if you take advantage of all of them. If you don’t yet have the card, it’s seriously worth considering.

If you want to learn more about the Amex Gold Card, follow this link.

#6220. Defiant Ritz-Carlton Singapore Joining Marriott Bonvoy… Finally!

The world’s only Ritz-Carlton that doesn’t participate in the Marriott Bonvoy program will finally be joining, which seems long overdue. I can’t imagine the hotel will be particularly generous, but we’ll see!

The 608-key Ritz-Carlton Millenia Singapore will be joining the Marriott Bonvoy program as of December 1, 2026. So as of that date, Bonvoy members will be able to earn and redeem points, and take advantage of Bonvoy elite perks, when staying at the hotel (admittedly Bonvoy elite perks at Ritz-Carlton properties are fairly limited, as breakfast isn’t a benefit for any elite tier).

As I covered in late 2025, this property is the only Ritz-Carlton in the world that doesn’t participate in the Bonvoy program. The backstory here is that the hotel opened back in 1996, and at the time, Ritz-Carlton didn’t have any sort of a loyalty program that awarded points.

In 2010, the Ritz-Carlton Rewards program started awarding points for hotel stays, as a parallel program to Marriott Rewards. The ability to earn and redeem points came at a cost to individual hotels, but it was intended to boost occupancy and average daily rates.

Initially, hotels had the option of whether they wanted to opt in or out of the program. Most hotels bought into the concept, though the Ritz-Carlton Osaka and Ritz-Carlton Singapore were the two hotels that opted out. The Ritz-Carlton Osaka eventually decided to participate, leaving the Ritz-Carlton Singapore as the only hotel that’s not participating.

Ultimately when the Marriott Bonvoy program formed as the combination of Marriott Rewards and Starwood Preferred Guest, the hotel could still stick to its legacy contract of not having to participate in the program. Clearly the owners of the hotel have now had a change of heart… or something!

Obviously we don’t have any sort of an official explanation for the reason that this Ritz-Carlton property is finally backtracking. I can’t imagine that Marriott gave the owners an ultimatum, given that Marriott is known for letting hotel owners get away with anything, as long as they get paid.

My guess is that the competitive realities just finally caught up with this hotel — Singapore is an increasingly competitive hotel market, this is a massive hotel with 600+ rooms to fill every night, and the hotel is also a bit past its prime.

The truth is that loyalty programs exist for a reason, as they’re a great tool for getting heads into beds. Obviously the hotel will be on the hook for some additional loyalty fees, but I imagine this will make the hotel more appealing to people who otherwise wouldn’t have considered it.

I also have to imagine that even though the hotel did a decent job communicating its lack of participation in Marriott Bonvoy, I still suspect many guests didn’t realize this, and ended up being disappointed.

As of December 1, 2026, the Ritz-Carlton Singapore will be joining the Marriott Bonvoy program. This is the only Ritz-Carlton hotel in the world that hasn’t participated in Bonvoy, so this is great to see.

The backstory is that the hotel opened before Ritz-Carlton had a loyalty program, and then when a program was finally formed, participation was optional. Literally every other Ritz-Carlton in the world saw value in this… except this one, apparently.

Fortunately they’ve now come to their senses, or something, so it’s great to see that this will be changing.

What do you make of the Ritz-Carlton Singapore joining Bonvoy?
