#6219. Chase Adds 10,000 Vacation Homes To The Edit In 2027—Use Your Hotel Credits, But No Points Boost

Chase Sapphire Reserve® (See rates and fees) cardmembers will be able to use their hotel credits at more than 10,000 vacation homes starting January 1, 2027. And Chase tells me consecutive bookings at the same home can each trigger a credit, potentially letting someone use the personal card’s full $500 annual allowance on one trip. There’s a significant limitation, though: Points Boost won’t apply to these homes at launch. The Edit name also won’t bring breakfast or upgrades. The home benefits require four nights, while the statement credit only requires two. Two Night Bookings Qualify For Credits, And Back-To-Back Bookings Are Allowed Chase already added Plum Guide to Chase Travel in April. The January expansion moves a selection of those homes into The Edit, alongside more than 1,500 hotels and resorts. The annual Edit statement credits available for bookings made in 2027 is: Chase Sapphire Reserve® and J.P. Morgan Reserve: up to $500, with a maximum of $250 per eligible booking. Chase Sapphire Reserve for Business: up to $1,000, with a maximum of $250 per eligible booking. The business card’s increase to $1,000 was announced in September. And Chase confirms that a prepaid two- or three-night home booking qualifies for the statement credit, even though it receives none of the vacation home benefits because those require a minimum four night stay (and individual properties can impose longer minimum stays). Bookings will be instantly confirmed, and full prepayment is required for The Edit benefits. I also asked whether you could book consecutive reservations at the same property. A Chase spokesperson tells me: Yes. Cardmembers can book back-to-back stays at the same property. Each eligible booking of two or more prepaid nights can qualify for the annual Edit statement credit, subject to the annual credit limit. For on-property benefits, however, consecutive reservations at the same property are considered a single stay, so only the first eligible stay will receive The Edit benefits. Two eligible two-night reservations could use both $250 credits from a personal Reserve card on a single four-night trip, or book a two-night and four-night reservation for a six night trip to use both credits and receive The Edit benefits on the stay. But you only get benefits on one four-night mininum stay. Back-to-back bookings aren’t entitled to benefits twice even if each reservation is for four nights. Chase commits to matching Plum Guide’s pricing. Asked about the identical home, dates and occupancy, the spokesperson replied: Yes. For the same home, dates and occupancy, the total price and cancellation policy offered through Chase Travel will match those available through Plum Guide. The credit shouldn’t get eaten up by a higher price than Plum Guide charges for the same reservation. Chase says it worked with Plum Guide to select homes based on design, guest ratings and distinctive features. Plum Guide does the vetting, not Chase. Chase isn’t sharing representative homes or pricing examples yet, so we can’t compare actual bookings. No Points Boost At Launch I’d hoped putting these homes into The Edit would create better opportunities to redeem Ultimate Rewards points. I asked and was told: No. Points Boost will not be applicable to vacation homes in The Edit at launch. Cardmembers can still redeem points, as they already can for Plum Guide through Chase Travel. But joining The Edit won’t bring better redemption value. This follows American Express adding Airbnb Luxe to its Platinum lodging credit. Eligible prepaid Luxe stays of at least two nights can use up to $300 each half-year, and a qualifying booking opens access to a separate $250 annual Airbnb Experiences credit. Amex doesn’t allow Pay with Points for those Airbnb bookings. Chase does allow points, but without Points Boost that’s not useful. It’s really just a new way to use the $250 statement credits. Four Nights Gets A $150 Credit, But No Breakfast Or Upgrades I asked Chase to confirm exactly which hotel benefits would carry over. At launch in January, the vacation-home benefits will include a $150 in-stay credit, plus early check-in and late checkout when available. Breakfast, room upgrades and welcome amenities are not part of the vacation-home benefit package. The benefits have been designed specifically around the vacation-home experience and how travelers use these properties. I’ve found The Edit credits useful on two-night hotel stays priced below $300 per night, with breakfast and a $100 property credit included. The home package adds $50 to the service credit but requires at least four nights, and drops breakfast and upgrades. Not surprising – there’s little to upgrade into when you’re booking a unit of one. And there’s nobody to make you breakfast! The $150 credit actually sounds better than just private chefs and massages highlighted in the announcement. Here’s what guests can buy and whether they’ll see prices before booking: Cardmembers will be able to see the eligible services available for a vacation home on the Chase Travel booking page before booking. Offerings vary by property and can include services such as fridge stocking, babysitting and dry cleaning. Pricing will depend on the specific service and request and will not be displayed at booking, however cardmembers can work with Reserve Travel Designers to understand available options and obtain pricing estimates for the services they are interested in. Fridge stocking and babysitting are things a family might actually buy. But the booking page won’t show how much the credit buys. After booking, guests will receive an email explaining how to use the credit. Reserve Travel Designers can help arrange services, and Chase recommends doing so at least 72 hours in advance. Early check-in and late checkout don’t actually seem like a Chase value add. A hotel has a pool of rooms. A house with guests leaving that morning needs to be cleaned before the next guests arrive. If another group is coming that afternoon, there isn’t much room for a late departure. So late checkout is either available or not, based on whether other reservations butt up against yours. Plum Guide already accommodates early check-in and late check-out requests subject to availability, albeit sometimes with fees. I asked whether Chase would waive those charges, require hosts to grant requests when possible, prioritize cleaning or offer earlier confirmation. Early check-in and late checkout are benefits offered to eligible vacation-home stays through The Edit, but both remain subject to availability and cannot be guaranteed in advance. We Don’t Know Yet If We Can Double Dip With Loyalty Credit Chase’s “The Edit” bookings earn hotel loyalty program points and elite stay credit, and receive elite benefits. What’s interesting is that Plum Guide properties earn 5% of eligible spending, excluding taxes, in GHA DISCOVERY Dollars. GHA Discovery is effectively the loyalty program for Plum GUide. (There’s no elite status earning bonus, all members earn the same, and these dollars expire after 12 months and can be spent at GHA hotels, but not on Plum Guide rentals). Direct bookings also earn qualifying nights, spend and brand credit toward status, with Plum Guide counting as one GHA brand. The partnership terms exclude non-Plum Guide booking channels. So it wasn’t clear to me whether Chase’s The Edit would count as a third party booking or not? They don’t for hotels. Chase responded that they “don’t have information to share on this yet.” It would be a great stack, though! For a Chase Sapphire Reserve® cardmember with unused Edit credits, the ability to apply several to one vacation home trip at Plum Guide’s pricing is the strongest part of this. I already use my hotel credits, so moving them to a home means giving up those hotel uses. Of course you can always identify a property, search for the owner or management company and book direct – often for less. If another group is coming that afternoon, there isn’t much room for a late departure. So late checkout is either available or not, based on whether other reservations butt up against yours. Plum Guide already accommodates early check-in and late check-out requests subject to availability, albeit sometimes with fees. I asked whether Chase would waive those charges, require hosts to grant requests when possible, prioritize cleaning or offer earlier confirmation. Early check-in and late checkout are benefits offered to eligible vacation-home stays through The Edit, but both remain subject to availability and cannot be guaranteed in advance. We Don’t Know Yet If We Can Double Dip With Loyalty Credit Chase’s “The Edit” bookings earn hotel loyalty program points and elite stay credit, and receive elite benefits. What’s interesting is that Plum Guide properties earn 5% of eligible spending, excluding taxes, in GHA DISCOVERY Dollars. GHA Discovery is effectively the loyalty program for Plum GUide. (There’s no elite status earning bonus, all members earn the same, and these dollars expire after 12 months and can be spent at GHA hotels, but not on Plum Guide rentals). Direct bookings also earn qualifying nights, spend and brand credit toward status, with Plum Guide counting as one GHA brand. The partnership terms exclude non-Plum Guide booking channels. So it wasn’t clear to me whether Chase’s The Edit would count as a third party booking or not? They don’t for hotels. Chase responded that they “don’t have information to share on this yet.” It would be a great stack, though! For a Chase Sapphire Reserve® cardmember with unused Edit credits, the ability to apply several to one vacation home trip at Plum Guide’s pricing is the strongest part of this. I already use my hotel credits, so moving them to a home means giving up those hotel uses. Of course you can always identify a property, search for the owner or management company and book direct – often for less. I asked Chase to confirm exactly which hotel benefits would carry over.

At launch in January, the vacation-home benefits will include a $150 in-stay credit, plus early check-in and late checkout when available. Breakfast, room upgrades and welcome amenities are not part of the vacation-home benefit package. The benefits have been designed specifically around the vacation-home experience and how travelers use these properties.

I’ve found The Edit credits useful on two-night hotel stays priced below $300 per night, with breakfast and a $100 property credit included. The home package adds $50 to the service credit but requires at least four nights, and drops breakfast and upgrades. Not surprising – there’s little to upgrade into when you’re booking a unit of one. And there’s nobody to make you breakfast!

The $150 credit actually sounds better than just private chefs and massages highlighted in the announcement. Here’s what guests can buy and whether they’ll see prices before booking:

Cardmembers will be able to see the eligible services available for a vacation home on the Chase Travel booking page before booking. Offerings vary by property and can include services such as fridge stocking, babysitting and dry cleaning.

Pricing will depend on the specific service and request and will not be displayed at booking, however cardmembers can work with Reserve Travel Designers to understand available options and obtain pricing estimates for the services they are interested in.

Fridge stocking and babysitting are things a family might actually buy. But the booking page won’t show how much the credit buys. After booking, guests will receive an email explaining how to use the credit. Reserve Travel Designers can help arrange services, and Chase recommends doing so at least 72 hours in advance.

Early check-in and late checkout don’t actually seem like a Chase value add. A hotel has a pool of rooms. A house with guests leaving that morning needs to be cleaned before the next guests arrive. If another group is coming that afternoon, there isn’t much room for a late departure. So late checkout is either available or not, based on whether other reservations butt up against yours.

Plum Guide already accommodates early check-in and late check-out requests subject to availability, albeit sometimes with fees. I asked whether Chase would waive those charges, require hosts to grant requests when possible, prioritize cleaning or offer earlier confirmation.

Early check-in and late checkout are benefits offered to eligible vacation-home stays through The Edit, but both remain subject to availability and cannot be guaranteed in advance.

Chase’s “The Edit” bookings earn hotel loyalty program points and elite stay credit, and receive elite benefits.

What’s interesting is that Plum Guide properties earn 5% of eligible spending, excluding taxes, in GHA DISCOVERY Dollars. GHA Discovery is effectively the loyalty program for Plum GUide. (There’s no elite status earning bonus, all members earn the same, and these dollars expire after 12 months and can be spent at GHA hotels, but not on Plum Guide rentals).

Direct bookings also earn qualifying nights, spend and brand credit toward status, with Plum Guide counting as one GHA brand. The partnership terms exclude non-Plum Guide booking channels. So it wasn’t clear to me whether Chase’s The Edit would count as a third party booking or not? They don’t for hotels. Chase responded that they “don’t have information to share on this yet.” It would be a great stack, though!

For a Chase Sapphire Reserve® cardmember with unused Edit credits, the ability to apply several to one vacation home trip at Plum Guide’s pricing is the strongest part of this. I already use my hotel credits, so moving them to a home means giving up those hotel uses. Of course you can always identify a property, search for the owner or management company and book direct – often for less.

#6218. American Airlines Quietly Removes Trump From West Palm Beach Gate Monitors

American Airlines has updated the gate monitors for flights to West Palm Beach, and they no longer mention President Trump. This seems like a sensible change (unrelated to politics), and the timing sure is… interesting.

Over the summer, we saw Palm Beach International Airport (PBI) renamed President Donald J. Trump International Airport. We knew that Trump wanted an airport named after him, and some conservative politicians in Florida came together to make it happen.

It’s interesting to see how airlines handled this. At the time, American updated its gate monitors for flights to West Palm Beach. The monitors initially read “West Palm Beach, FL.” American then updated the monitors to say “Pres DJT, W Palm Beach.” Now JonNYC reports that as of this week, the airport name listed on the monitors has been changed again, and is back to the original name, with no mention of Trump.

so… has anyone noticed that AA has changed the gate monitors from “Pres DJT, W Palm Beach” back to “West Palm Beach, FL” ? https://t.co/IG2mPA3zgG

JonNYC specifically emphasizes that he’s not claiming there’s any connection between this and the election results, though the timing of it happening this week sure is interesting.

Personally I’m not a fan of airports being named after even semi-controversial figures, and particularly politicians. It’s something I’ve said over and over, regardless of the party affiliation of the person. Unless a city has multiple airports, I think it’s also stupid to identify the airport based on the name rather than the place.

Like, it makes sense to clarify London Heathrow (LHR) vs. London Gatwick (LGW), but it’s not like there are multiple airports in West Palm Beach. For that matter, saying you’re “flying to President Trump” just sounds a little weird, in my opinion.

JonNYC notes that he’s not suggesting that this had anything to do with the recent election, though everything about the timing here is interesting:

American Airlines CEO Robert Isom: "From a commercial aviation perspective, the eyes of the world have been on us, and we've certainly delivered… No doubt, it's a result of the economy and the job market." https://t.co/28JzoEf4Z3 pic.twitter.com/BcgYJbChNz

American Airlines seems to have quietly reversed course on how it refers to West Palm Beach’s airport on its gate monitors. In recent months, the airline has referred to the airport as “Pres DJT, W Palm Beach,” while now it seems to be back to “West Palm Beach, FL.”

This change comes the same week as the midterm elections, though everyone can decide for themselves to what extent these points are related…

What do you make of this American gate monitor change?

#6217. KLM Plans 15% Workforce Reduction And Simpler Fleet: “Future Not Guaranteed”

It’s obviously a tough time for aviation in general, given the impact of high jet fuel prices. For that matter, Dutch national carrier KLM has faced its own unique challenges, given increasing limits placed on the carrier’s Amsterdam Schiphol (AMS) hub, plus all the competitive challenges (increased competition from regional low cost carriers, Gulf carriers, etc.).

In recent years, we’ve seen KLM introduce initiatives intended to improve economics. The airline is now taking that to the next level, and has just announced an absolutely massive project intended to improve economics by €1 billion per year.

KLM has unveiled the details of a project that it expects will contribute to annual earnings improvements of €1 billion per year, which it hopes will allow the company to invest in fleet, customer experience, and people.

KLM’s plan is to focus on its core strengths, which it describes as a global network of 160 destinations served nonstop from Schiphol, and reliable operations supported by a modern fleet. The company wants to become a smaller, simpler, and more agile organization, through restructuring, outsourcing, and closer collaboration with Air France-KLM.

Here’s how KLM CEO Marjan Rintel describes this initiative:

“Every day, we all work with incredible dedication, commitment, and pride. But KLM’s future is not guaranteed. The environment we operate in is becoming increasingly complex, with global instability, high fuel prices, and growing pressure on the aviation industry. That’s why, at this pivotal moment for KLM, we’re taking far-reaching, sometimes painful measures. Every department and every division will be asked to contribute.”

“We’re doing this with a clear vision for the future: one where KLM remains a great airline that connects customers to the world, a company people want to work for, and one the Netherlands can be proud of.”

How does KLM plan on improving economics by so much over the coming years? For one, the airline will simplify its fleet.

The long term plan is to have a fleet of 185 Airbus, Boeing, and Embraer aircraft. The latest changes particularly center around the European network, where just about all network carriers in Europe struggle to make money, given the costs and competitive landscape.

KLM plans to change the balance between larger and smaller aircraft on European routes. In the long run, the airline will fly a mix of 227-seat Airbus A321neos and 132-seat Embraer E195-E2s. The company no longer plans to acquire Airbus A320neos, which were part of a larger Air France-KLM order, as those planes are instead going to Transavia. Furthermore, in the coming years, we’ll see Boeing 737s and Embraer E190s retired.

Next, the airline hopes to achieve greater flexibility, higher productive, and lower costs, with its labor agreements. As you’d expect, this will be the most painful change. For one, KLM plans to reduce its workforce by around 15%, meaning that around 5,000 positions will be “reorganized.”

This follows the company’s number of staff already declining in recent years. The good news is that there aren’t expected to be mass layoffs — KLM expects to limit the impact on employees through natural attrition, voluntary arrangements, and transfers to other positions.

The airline also emphasizes that employment terms and conditions need to become simpler and more competitive, noting that “continuing on the current path is not sustainable.” KLM wants to work with unions to establish new collective labor agreements, and the company aims to achieve a structural productivity increase of at least 8% by 2028.

This decrease in headcount will come through a combination of Air France and KLM cooperating more closely, outsourcing catering and maintenance, and reducing planned growth of the fleet.

The airline industry is tough in the first place, and among the major network carriers, KLM is perhaps in the toughest spot, when you consider the overall industry dynamics:

KLM is planning to majorly cut costs and simplify things, which is probably necessary in light of how the situation has evolved.

As part of this, the carrier’s short haul fleet will eventually consist of just Airbus A321neos and Embraer E195-E2s. On top of that, we’ll see the airline reduce its workforce by around 15%, through a combination of increasing efficiency, outsourcing jobs, and more. The company will also be looking for some concessions from existing employees.

In total, the company hopes that these changes will contribute €1 billion per year. While aviation is tough across the board, it’s especially tough to be KLM, where you’re reliant on one hub (which regulators keep trying to shrink) with very high costs, and that hub isn’t a market that’s as lucrative as somewhere like London, Paris, etc. I’m a fan of KLM, and I hope these changes don’t do too much to change the quirky spirit of the airline.

What do you make of these major KLM changes?

Over the past year, I've redeemed 1.3 million IHG One Rewards points for 62 hotel nights. I got 0.88 cents per point on these redemptions, so while TPG's November 2026 valuations peg the value of IHG points at 0.6 cents each, it's certainly possible to get more value when redeeming IHG points.

All these redemptions mean I also have to earn a sizable amount of IHG points each year. There are many ways to earn IHG points, so you have options, whether you need to top off your account or substantially boost your balance. In this article, I'll describe how to earn IHG points.

As you might expect, you can earn IHG points when you stay at participating IHG hotels. However, the exact number of points you'll earn on stays depends on a few factors:

You'll only earn IHG points and get access to elite benefits when you book a qualifying rate through a qualifying method. Qualifying methods include IHG Customer Care, IHG websites, the IHG One Rewards app, directly at the hotel and through authorized travel agents. Authorized travel agents exclude online travel agents and are defined in the IHG terms and conditions as "travel booking platforms operating under direct distribution agreements with IHG which specifically provide for nights booked through their platforms to be qualifying stays."

Related: The best IHG hotels in the world

Your earning rate for qualifying stays will vary by IHG hotel brand. Specifically, you'll earn points as follows:

You'll generally earn points on qualifying room rates and additional purchases charged to your room, including food and beverages. However, at some properties, you may not earn points on other purchases charged to your room.

Except at InterContinental Alliance Resorts, you can earn points on up to nine hotel rooms. Your IHG One Rewards account number must be associated with each room reservation, and you must stay at the property.

Members with IHG elite status earn additional points on stays. As you'd expect, the higher your elite status tier, the more points you'll earn on your stay. Here's how many bonus points IHG elite members will earn:

Here's an example of how these bonus points can add up. If you're a Diamond Elite member staying at a Kimpton hotel for three nights at $200 per night, you'll earn the following:

As a result, you'd take home 12,000 IHG points from your three-night stay — and potentially more if you made any qualifying charges to your room or paid for your stay with a rewards card. Based on TPG's November 2026 valuations, 12,000 IHG One Rewards points are worth $72.

You can often buy up to 5,000 elite qualifying points per night when booking a qualifying paid stay. Look for the option on the "Add Extras" page while booking.

There's no cap on the number of points you can buy each calendar year via these packages. As such, doing so can be a good option if you have already reached the maximum number of points you can outright purchase in a calendar year.

Starting at just 20 nights a year, IHG members earn a choice of Milestone Rewards for every 10 nights (up to 100 nights per year). IHG offers its members various rewards at each milestone, and some may be more valuable than points.

But if you're primarily interested in earning IHG points, you can choose points at each milestone. Specifically, you can earn points through Milestone Rewards each calendar year as follows:

I rarely choose points as Milestone Rewards, as I usually find food-and-beverage rewards, confirmable suite upgrade awards or an annual lounge membership provides more value.

IHG One Rewards frequently offers promotions that let you earn additional points on your hotel stays over the standard earning rates. However, you usually need to register for IHG bonus points promotions before completing your stay.

For IHG promotions that offer multipliers (such as double points), the multiplier typically applies only to the stay's base earnings. So, if you are an IHG elite member, your elite bonus usually won't be multiplied.

Related: How to get more out of every all-inclusive vacation with IHG One Rewards

One of the easiest ways to earn IHG points is by spending on a cobranded IHG credit card. Here's how the four currently available IHG credit cards earn points, including their updated earning categories beginning Jan. 1, 2027 (see the paragraph below the table for some additional earning rates that end Dec. 31):

Through Dec. 31, IHG Premier and Business cardholders will also earn 5 points per dollar spent on all other travel, while no-annual-fee IHG cardholders will also earn 3 points per dollar spent on utilities, internet, cable, phone services and select streaming services.

Cardholders of the Premier, Premier Select and Business cards get automatic access to the valuable IHG fourth-night-free reward perk. But cardholders of the no-annual-fee IHG card will need to spend $5,000 or more with their card within a calendar year to unlock access to the fourth-night-free reward perk through the end of the next calendar year starting in 2027. I've used the fourth-night-free reward perk 13 times during the last year, so it provides a ton of value to me.

Related: The best IHG hotel stays you can book with 200,000 points

You can transfer Chase Ultimate Rewards points and Bilt Points to the IHG One Rewards program. Points transfer at a 1:1 ratio from both programs.

However, I don't recommend transferring points from either program to IHG. Based on TPG's November 2026 valuations, you'd need to redeem IHG points for at least 2.05 cents each to justify transferring Chase points or 2.2 cents each to justify transferring Bilt points.

As such, you'll generally only want to transfer points to IHG if you need to top off your account for a specific award. Otherwise, saving transferable points for higher-value redemptions is generally better.

Related: Why transferable rewards are worth more than airline miles and hotel points

The IHG One Rewards Dine & Earn program allows you to earn points when you dine at participating restaurants and bars. To use the program, you must sign up for an account online and link at least one credit or debit card to your account. Then, you'll automatically earn IHG points when you use a linked card to pay at participating restaurants and bars.

The points you'll earn vary depending on how frequently you use the program and whether you opt in for email notifications. You can earn between 1 and 8 IHG points per dollar spent on eligible purchases. These points are in addition to the rewards earned on your credit card, so consider linking and using one of the best cards for dining purchases.

Related: How to double-, triple- or even quadruple-dip on dining rewards

You can also earn IHG points through the IHG Business Rewards program. This program allows you to earn points when you plan a meeting or event — including a wedding — at select IHG properties.

Once you register for IHG Business Rewards, you can earn 3 points per dollar when you book rooms, meetings and events for others. Qualifying spending includes:

Some properties don't participate in IHG Business Rewards. And you usually can't earn more than 60,000 points on a meeting or event. Plus, qualifying spending usually excludes taxes, gratuities, service fees and the organizer's room.

Another option for earning IHG points is to purchase them. Buying IHG points can be a good deal, especially when the program offers a 100% bonus and you have a high-value redemption in mind.

The standard price to buy IHG points is 1 cent per point if you purchase at least 26,000 points. However, IHG One Rewards offers promotions several times a year during which you can purchase points with up to a 100% bonus. If you buy during a 100% bonus, you can earn IHG points for as little as 0.5 cents each.

TPG values IHG points at 0.6 cents each. Since it's easy for me to get more than 0.5 cents of value per IHG point, I usually consider purchasing IHG points whenever there's a 100% bonus sale. However, you usually can't purchase more than 200,000 IHG points per calendar year.

IHG members can transfer points to another member by paying a $5 fee per 1,000 points transferred. Each member can transfer up to 100,000 points per calendar year and receive up to 500,000 points per calendar year.

IHG members who hold Diamond Elite status — or belong to the IHG Business Rewards program and have "consumed a Business Rewards event in the current or previous calendar year" — can transfer points to other members without paying transfer fees.

So, if you have a colleague or family member who has Diamond Elite status (or is an active member of the IHG Business Rewards program) and wants to transfer IHG points to you, this could be a way to earn IHG points.

Related: Earn even more rewards when dining out with OpenTable

Throughout this guide, we've discussed how to earn IHG points that you can redeem for hotel stays. However, travelers looking to earn IHG elite status should also consider which points qualify for elite status.

Generally, the following activities earn IHG points that are redeemable and elite qualifying:

#6215. British Airways Kept Losing Consumer Complaints—So They Found A New Arbitrator

British Airways is dropping the independent complaints service through which passengers won £5 million in a year. Its replacement has a record of much lower passenger success rates. They appear to be shopping for a more accommodating referee, putting their thumb on the scales by choosing who hears complaints against them. On August 24, 2016, I asked this exact question: Will the Centre for Effective Dispute Resolution get to keep the British Airways contract if they rule against BA too frequently? Ten years later, British Airways isn’t renewing that contract. They’re moving to AviationADR, the other major U.K. provider. And Head for Points reports that losing its biggest airline customer means CEDR is leaving aviation altogether. British Airways confirmed the switch, describing it as a contract renewal decision and saying: British Airways has selected AviationADR as the independent alternative dispute resolution body to resolve disputes between customers and the airline. British Airways Wasn’t Winning Enough Cases The Civil Aviation Authority’s figures for April 2025 through March 2026 show: British Airways settled 4,414 complaints before a decision. CEDR ruled for passengers in 1,619 cases and for British Airways in 2,234. Settlements and decisions together produced £5,001,728 in passenger awards. That’s a 73% passenger success rate including settlements. Passengers had already gone through the airline’s complaint process, then had to escalate to an outside body before getting an offer which means that BA was improperly rejecting complaints. Most passengers just give up at that point. EasyJet Already Made This Switch easyJet made the move from CEDR to AviationADR after CEDR upheld passenger complaints 79% of the time over its final six quarters with with the airline, and just 29% in the following six quarters with AviationADR. AviationADR’s explanation was that airlines had improved their handling of claims, including using major law firms to filter cases before escalation. Valid claims were being paid earlier, leaving weaker ones for adjudication. And that just happened to coincide with the switch. Ok sure. Airlines Get Advance Access To Decisions Against Them A February 2026 review commissioned by the Civil Aviation Authority described AviationADR giving airlines decisions in passengers’ favor one week before the passengers received them, ostensibly to ‘prepare payment’. During that time, airlines could raise legal challenges, although AviationADR said its legal review panel hadn’t needed to convene for years. The reviewer warned this advance access “may create an impression of bias in favour of the aviation body” and recommended ending it, along with airline challenges to individual binding decisions. CEDR generally uses legally qualified adjudicators. AviationADR doesn’t require legal qualifications and provides more extensive initial training. The commercial pressure to retain the contract paid for by one side is huge, and the fact that BA made this switch underscores what the new adjudicator has to do to keep its revenue stream. Relatedly, Ryanair left AviationADR in 2018 after adverse decisions over staff strikes, then rejoined in 2021 after rules changes. AviationADR says its decisions are independent and based on the evidence and law. Its service is free to the consumer, and passengers who reject a decision can still go to court. Head for Points reports that CEDR will stop accepting new aviation cases on December 31. The Civil Aviation Authority says it’s working with AviationADR on the capacity needed to handle the additional caseload. While some at View from the Right Wing will clutch pearls over businesses having to pay fines to consumers when they fail, the rest of us, who actually fly, and have to deal with the inconvenience, real costs, and disruption caused by airlines that excessively delay and cancel flights under their control.

We’re overdue for meaningful air passenger rights legislation in the US, akin to UK and EU laws like 261 with a real, enforceable duty of care and compensation where appropriate, not mere partial refunds and silly games. So, no, it’s not a third party processor issue here. It’s the incentive structure; thankfully, their laws have teeth.

BA is just being cheap, like usual; operate a reliable airline, or pay up.

Exhibit A for why arbitration needs to be controlled. Looks good on the surface, fails badly when one side gets to choose whoever gives the most favorable results.

So basically BA doesn’t want customers to have fair arbitration. I’m a bit surprised that whatever body governs UK aviation is fine with this.

This is just so typical of BA and the Walsh legacy: rather than make badly needed improvements that would keep the airline from losing arbitration cases they dump the company that recognizes that BA is frequently wrong.

The credit card companies in the US set up a phony baloney arb service, the National Arbitration Forum, to resolve the problem of fair arbiters; the newly elected Senator from MN when AG uncovered the scheme.

This is the reason why “mandatory arbitration” is absolute BS that should be nuked from orbit and everyone fake “arbiter” exiled to Vostok Station in Antarctica for life.

There’s nothing remotely fair about a system where one side gets to pick the judge.

#6214. Schumer faces mutiny from newly elected Senate Dems as party prepares to seize power

Several newly elected Democratic senators suggest they are not committed to supporting Sen. Chuck Schumer as Senate Majority Leader.

Senate Democrats will soon decide who will lead them with their newly acquired grip on power in the upper chamber, and while Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., appears to be the favorite, some in the caucus aren’t eager to back him.

Schumer has led Senate Democrats for nearly a decade, helming the caucus as both majority and minority leader since 2017. But many of the fresh crop of Democratic senators-elect, which spans the ideological gamut from moderate to progressive, are tepid, at best, in backing him for another term.

And some said throughout their campaigns that they wouldn’t support him at all.

DEM SENATE HOPEFUL REJECTS SCHUMER BUT BENEFITS FROM MILLIONS IN SPENDING BY HIS ALLIES

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., is confident he will continue to lead Senate Democrats, but newcomers to the caucus aren't on board with him at the helm.  (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

"I mean no disrespect for Chuck Schumer, but we need new leadership," Sen.-elect Adam Hamilton told CNN in September. "We need new younger leadership, young blood."

Hamilton is the moderate megachurch pastor who toppled Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan., on Election Night, flipping the Sunflower State for the first time in nearly a century. He, like others this cycle, argued that Democrats needed "fresh ideas and fresh leadership."

"In Kansas, Chuck Schumer is a liability for Democrats, and we've got to have leaders that can unite us, bring us together, not just Democrats, but bring together Democrats and Republicans to solve real problems," he said. "And I think people are frustrated with the gridlock in the sense that people are not working together to solve problems."

Democrats are expected to hold their leadership elections later this year, and Schumer will have to shore up support within his newly expanded caucus to stay at the top. But he will only need a majority of Senate Democrats to back him.

REPORTER'S NOTEBOOK: CONGRESS BRACES FOR POST-ELECTION GAME OF MUSICAL CHAIRS AS LEADERSHIP BATTLES LOOM

So far, Democrats’ majority in the upper chamber is at 54 seats and could further expand depending on the results in Mississippi and Alaska, which as of Thursday were leaning in their favor.

Schumer believed that he would still be the one to lead Democrats and contended to reporters on Wednesday that issues that incoming senators and their voters may have had with the direction of the Democratic Party in recent years were not about him.

"The issue is not me," Schumer said. "I'll be re-elected as majority leader, but the issue is focusing on the American people and what they want."

Still, there is a faction of newcomers, including senators-elect Troy Jackson in Maine, Julianna Stratton in Illinois, Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan and Peggy Flanagan in Minnesota, who aren’t all in for Schumer.

THUNE GOES ALL-IN ON CAMPAIGN TRAIL AS SCHUMER STAYS ON BENCH, FACES REJECTION FROM FELLOW DEMS

Former state Sen. Troy Jackson, a Democrat from Maine and then-gubernatorial candidate, speaks during a Fighting Oligarchy event. (Sophie Park/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Jackson, speaking to reporters just before Election Day, said his position hadn’t changed on Schumer.

"I told Schumer that I’m going to, you know, support somebody else," Jackson said. "So it’s no different now."

That somebody else could be Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., who has been proposed as an alternative by progressives, like El-Sayed, to lead Senate Democrats instead of Schumer. Van Hollen may have his eyes elsewhere — he has said that he’s "kicking the tires" on a 2028 run.

A Democratic aide familiar with Van Hollen’s thinking told Fox News Digital that before selecting a new leader, the lawmaker believed "the caucus needs to have an honest and open conversation about how we move an agenda forward that reflects the will of the American people."

"He’s made it clear that the new Democratic majorities need to use their power to push a proactive, economic agenda," they said.

Alex Miller is a writer for Fox News Digital covering the U.S. Senate.

#6213. Emirates Profits Plunge Due To War… But The Airline Still Made Money?!

It goes without saying that it has been a tough year for airlines, due to the United States getting into a war with Iran. All airlines have been dealing with higher jet fuel prices, but airlines in the Gulf region have of course been dealing with additional issues, as all kinds of airports in the region have been attacked, making some people reconsider traveling through the region.

That’s why I think it’s interesting to note that Emirates has just released its financial results for the first half of the fiscal year (April 1 through September 30, 2026). Yes, Emirates’ profits decreased massively, but surprisingly, the airline still turned a healthy profit, and the numbers look much better than I would’ve guessed.

Prior to this year, Emirates was the world’s most profitable airline for two years in a row, as the carrier really is incredibly well run.

That’s why I think it’s interesting to note how the airline performed over the first six months of the current fiscal year, which coincides entirely with the current Iran conflict. While there are results for the overall Emirates Group (which also includes dnata, etc.), I’m focusing on the airline specifically, since I find that to be most telling.

Emirates reported a half-year profit of $1 billion, down 68% compared to the previous year. Interestingly, revenue was $15.5 billion, down “only” 13% compared to the same period the previous year. The airline didn’t actually cut back its total capacity that much — available seat kilometers (ASKM) decreased by 17% compared to the previous year, while the passenger load factor decreased to 72%, from 79.5% the previous year. Emirates carried 21.8 million passengers over the six months, down 22% from the same period last year.

As of September 30, 2026, Emirates is operating 91% of its pre-disruption network, with the passenger and cargo network spanning 150 airports in 78 countries. However, that reflects the number of destinations, rather than the total actual capacity (in other words, many destinations are being operated with reduced frequencies).

Emirates CEO Sheikh Ahmed bin Saeed Al Maktoum reflected on this as “a demanding six months,” and said that “once again our business model and our people stood up to the test.” He explained that the company is entering the second half of the fiscal year “with measured optimism,” “while keeping a close watch on costs and geopolitical developments.”

One would think that Gulf carriers are in the toughest spot of any airline, given that they’ve been so reliant on connecting people traveling between other regions, and at least among some people, their willingness to travel through the region has decreased, assuming it can be avoided.

Admittedly many people also just live in this region, so it’s not like there are endless options. But when you consider all factors, I’d say these are very encouraging results, much better than I would’ve expected.

I know there’s often a lot of skepticism when it comes to the reported financials of Gulf carriers. I do think at some Gulf carriers, there’s reason to be skeptical about the math, based on what is and isn’t reported.

In the case of Emirates, though, the airline is legitimately very profitable and well run. The airline has managed to efficiently scale its operation in a way that no other airline really has, and that’s where credit goes for the carrier’s success.

Of course we have to acknowledge that there’s a difference in underlying economics. Dubai (DXB) is much lower cost to operate out of than somewhere like London Heathrow (LHR) or New York Kennedy (JFK), and Emirates Group owns both the airline and the ground handling company. Furthermore, the cost of jet fuel is lower in Dubai than it is in somewhere like London, and I imagine the airline also has access to more attractive financing opportunities, given that it’s owned by the government.

However, that’s hardly anything that’s super hidden or secret. I mean, economics in US aviation are also sort of lopsided. Airline profits are largely reliant on everything except actually flying, which is a privilege and upside that most foreign carriers can’t fully unlock.

I think it’s also interesting to note how well Emirates’ yields have held up during this time. For example, just based on looking at fares through Google Flights, it seems like Etihad’s strategy has just been to publish incredibly low fares to fill seats, including in premium cabins. I haven’t found that to be the case with Emirates, though, as the airline has managed to maintain pricing power despite reduced demand.

Emirates has reported its financial results for the first half of the 2026-2027 fiscal year. As you’d expect, this was a generally tough time for a Gulf carrier, given the current war with Iran. While Emirates’ profits were cut by around two-thirds, the airline still turned a healthy profit of around $1 billion.

Honestly, the actual operating figures don’t at all reflect what you’d expect during a crisis, so it seems like the airline is weathering this story pretty well, all things considered. I do feel like Emirates is uniquely positioned among its competitive set, and I’d be shocked if the story is similar at Etihad or Qatar Airways.

What do you make of Emirates’ financial results?

#6212. Bizarre: Lufthansa Group Now Requires Travel ID For Online Check-In

Most airlines encourage travelers to check-in online, given that it’s mutually beneficial — it saves time for the traveler, and saves resources for the airline. Well, Lufthansa Group is implementing a new policy that makes it more difficult to check-in online, as flagged by aeroTELEGRAPH, and that strikes me as rather backwards.

Lufthansa Group has the concept of a Travel ID, whereby customers have an account they can use to log-in across digital platforms belonging to all carriers, including Lufthansa, SWISS, Austrian, Brussels Airlines, Edelweiss, Discover Airlines, etc. This is separate from the Miles & More program, as the idea is that it simply creates a unified log-in for digital services across the airlines.

So along those lines, Lufthansa Group is progressively rolling out an initiative whereby customers need to have a Travel ID account in order to check-in online via the website or app.

Lufthansa Group is rolling out this requirement gradually. The Travel ID is required to check-in online as follows:

There are a limited number of exceptions for the Travel ID requirement. Specifically, you don’t need a Travel ID if you’re a traveler checking in at the airport counter or machine, if you’re traveling on a ticket issued by another airline, or if you’re on a flight operated by another airline with a ticket issued by Lufthansa Group.

Airlines love data and being able to market to customers. It’s one of the reasons that airlines create such strong incentives to sign-up for their loyalty programs (or in this case, a log-in that allows the airline to market to you). We’ve seen countless airlines roll out free Wi-Fi for those who are loyalty program members, and the logic is easy enough to follow.

However, in this case we’re talking about online check-in, which is something that arguably helps the airline more than it helps the customer. I can understand an airline wanting to add a step for something that entirely benefits the customer (like free Wi-Fi), but doing it for a basic function that saves the airline money? Well, that’s quite the approach to take.

In fairness to Lufthansa, I’m not sure this is actually a bad idea, or will backfire that much. Yes, it’s a minor annoyance, but:

Now, it’s still rather customer unfriendly, in my opinion, but that’s not exactly the first time we’ve seen something like that in the airline industry…

Lufthansa Group will start requiring passengers to sign-up for a Travel ID in order to check-in online. This is progressively being rolled out through November 30, 2026. Making it more complicated to check-in online seems counterproductive.

At the same time, clearly this is intended to encourage travelers to register for a Travel ID, so that Lufthansa can better track customer data and market to travelers. Usually we see incentives created to encourage this kind of registration, but in the case of Lufthansa Group, the airline is instead threatening to take something away if you don’t register.

What do you make of Lufthansa Group’s new online check-in requirement?

#6210. Lyft Launches 8% Ride Rewards—Free With Chase DashPass, But Airport Discounts And Priority Pickup Perk Go Away

Lyft’s new membership program earns 8% back in credits on eligible rides, and customers who get DoorDash DashPass through an eligible Chase card can claim it without paying. But they’re also losing benefits like a 10% discount on scheduled airport rides and free Priority Pickup upgrades. Lyft Go launched today, replacing ordinary Lyft Pink and the old DashPass ride benefits. Existing DashPass customers have to activate it even if their Lyft and DoorDash accounts are already linked. And anyone still holding Lyft Pink All Access through Chase: you can’t keep that membership and add Go alongside it. Lyft is selling two versions of Go: Benefit   Lyft Go With DashPass   Lyft Go Core Price   $9.99/month or $96/year   $4.99/month Credits earned   8% of eligible spending   5% of eligible spending Monthly earning limit   $40   $20 Where credits can be used   Eligible Lyft rides or DoorDash orders   Eligible Lyft rides DashPass membership   Included after activation   Not included Relaxed cancellations   3 per month   3 per month Lost-item return fee waiver   Unlimited   Not included Round Up & Donate matching   100%   100% The full plan works in both directions. Pay for Go and get DashPass, which waives delivery fees and reduces service fees on eligible orders, and DashPass members claim full Go at no added cost. DoorDash purchases don’t earn the new 8% rebate but you can spend credits earned with Lyft there. Chase may now get you both complimentary memberships: Make sure your Chase DashPass benefit is activated. Go to DoorDash’s Lyft benefit page, or claim Lyft Go in the DoorDash app. Complete activation, including the confirmation in Lyft. Previously linking the accounts isn’t enough. The complimentary membership lasts while you retain the qualifying membership and keep the accounts linked. And an eligible ride can now earn four layers of rewards: Lyft Go credits: 8% of eligible spending, up to $40 per month. Linked loyalty program points: for example, 2 Bilt points per eligible dollar when Bilt is your selected partner. Credit card rewards: for example, 5 Chase Ultimate Rewards points per dollar when you pay with an eligible Sapphire card. Card-linked offers: an activated offer for Lyft on the card you use, such as a targeted Chase Offer or SimplyMiles offer when available. You choose one linked loyalty points partner such as Bilt, Alaska Airlines or United. $100 of fare eligible for all three programs, paid with an eligible Sapphire card and credited to Bilt, can earn $8 in Go credits, 200 Bilt points and 500 Chase points – plus whatever card-linked offer applies. Sapphire Reserve and J.P. Morgan Reserve also have their separate $10 monthly Lyft ride credit. Sadly though existing DashPass discounts are going away. I’ve written about combining those discounts with Lyft’s other rewards. The old arrangement gave linked DashPass members: 5% off eligible on-demand rides. 10% off scheduled airport rides. A combined limit of four discounted rides per month. Two free Priority Pickup upgrades monthly. Under DoorDash’s transition terms, those benefits end at 11:59 p.m. Pacific on November 11, or when you activate Go, whichever comes first. So a frequent ordinary ride customer can gain – 8% back instead of 5% off, with earning continuing beyond four rides. A customer using the scheduled airport discount gets a lower percentage, has to spend the savings later, and loses the pickup upgrades. Here’s how the 8% works: Base fare only. Taxes, fees, tolls, tips, donations and amounts covered by coupons, discounts or earned credits don’t earn. 60-day expiration. You have to select credits to use them; they aren’t automatically applied. A monthly cap. Full Go stops earning after $500 in eligible spending. Core stops after $400. Membership dependence. Pausing blocks redemption while expiration continues. Once your membership ends, unused credits become unavailable and can be forfeited. No conversion of old balances. Purchased Lyft Cash, gift cards and unrelated promotional credits don’t become usable on DoorDash. Business profile rides and shared rides don’t earn. Eligible bike and scooter rides do, but Boston and Washington, D.C. bike and scooter rides are excluded. Lyft includes Wait & Save in its announcement, although DoorDash’s launch FAQ contradicts that. DoorDash redemption has exclusions: non-DashPass-eligible orders, DoubleDash, prescriptions, gift cards and group orders. Then there’s the cancellation benefit: Lyft requires you to rebook within 15 minutes and complete the replacement ride. They charge the cancellation fee, then give it back as a ride credit. These aren’t three unconditional free cancellations. Pink All Access members can continue but that’s now closed to new members, you can only hold one membership at a time, and once you leave All Access, you can’t rejoin. Switching to Go requires contacting support. If there’s anyone with Chase DashPass actually paying separately for ordinary Pink that’s a win. DoorDash says to cancel the paid Lyft subscription, then claim complimentary Go through DashPass. The companies won’t automatically consolidate those subscriptions For Chase DashPass customers who weren’t paying for Lyft, this is a modest improvement for frequent ordinary rides and a downgrade for occasional scheduled airport trips. Lyft gets more than a subscription payment out of this change – an immediate discount saves you money even if you never ride again while a credit gets brings you back for another transaction (or costs them nothing if you don’t). Lyft Go launched today, replacing ordinary Lyft Pink and the old DashPass ride benefits. Existing DashPass customers have to activate it even if their Lyft and DoorDash accounts are already linked. And anyone still holding Lyft Pink All Access through Chase: you can’t keep that membership and add Go alongside it.

The full plan works in both directions. Pay for Go and get DashPass, which waives delivery fees and reduces service fees on eligible orders, and DashPass members claim full Go at no added cost. DoorDash purchases don’t earn the new 8% rebate but you can spend credits earned with Lyft there. Chase may now get you both complimentary memberships:

The complimentary membership lasts while you retain the qualifying membership and keep the accounts linked. And an eligible ride can now earn four layers of rewards:

You choose one linked loyalty points partner such as Bilt, Alaska Airlines or United. $100 of fare eligible for all three programs, paid with an eligible Sapphire card and credited to Bilt, can earn $8 in Go credits, 200 Bilt points and 500 Chase points – plus whatever card-linked offer applies. Sapphire Reserve and J.P. Morgan Reserve also have their separate $10 monthly Lyft ride credit.

Sadly though existing DashPass discounts are going away. I’ve written about combining those discounts with Lyft’s other rewards. The old arrangement gave linked DashPass members:

Under DoorDash’s transition terms, those benefits end at 11:59 p.m. Pacific on November 11, or when you activate Go, whichever comes first.

So a frequent ordinary ride customer can gain – 8% back instead of 5% off, with earning continuing beyond four rides. A customer using the scheduled airport discount gets a lower percentage, has to spend the savings later, and loses the pickup upgrades. Here’s how the 8% works:

Business profile rides and shared rides don’t earn. Eligible bike and scooter rides do, but Boston and Washington, D.C. bike and scooter rides are excluded. Lyft includes Wait & Save in its announcement, although DoorDash’s launch FAQ contradicts that. DoorDash redemption has exclusions: non-DashPass-eligible orders, DoubleDash, prescriptions, gift cards and group orders.

Then there’s the cancellation benefit: Lyft requires you to rebook within 15 minutes and complete the replacement ride. They charge the cancellation fee, then give it back as a ride credit. These aren’t three unconditional free cancellations.

Pink All Access members can continue but that’s now closed to new members, you can only hold one membership at a time, and once you leave All Access, you can’t rejoin. Switching to Go requires contacting support.

If there’s anyone with Chase DashPass actually paying separately for ordinary Pink that’s a win. DoorDash says to cancel the paid Lyft subscription, then claim complimentary Go through DashPass. The companies won’t automatically consolidate those subscriptions

For Chase DashPass customers who weren’t paying for Lyft, this is a modest improvement for frequent ordinary rides and a downgrade for occasional scheduled airport trips. Lyft gets more than a subscription payment out of this change – an immediate discount saves you money even if you never ride again while a credit gets brings you back for another transaction (or costs them nothing if you don’t).

Interesting because Chase, Lyft, DoorDash, none of them sent us cardmembers and account holders any details on any of this. How Gary got advanced notice is cool, but, like, shouldn’t we, the actual users, get a heads-up, too? Sheesh.

Wonder how this impacts the Citibike benefits via Lyft. That free 45 minutes on non-ebikes can be useful.

(Ironically, got their email mere minutes after writing that comment… still…)

Losing priority pickup is going to hurt. On my last ride that saved me $17, though that was one of my most expensive rides. It seems to usually be around $9 which is still a large percentage add-on.

Yeah, what @nycityny said – the priority pickup made a real difference. These 8% credits are nice but don’t move the needle for me. Now it’s just a price war between Uber and Lyft whereas before Lyft had an edge with priority pickup.

Also Grubhub+ lost Amazon Prime today, and sent out an email extending GH+ membership through 12/2027. Amazon Prime now partners with Uber Eats and got an email about that today as well.

@Peter — All of these services are unnecessary. If Ben will publish it, time for the $3 MTA special!

This isn’t about Chase. T-Mobile also offers Dashpass for free, hence the Lyft benefit. Since T-Mobile offers it, it’s hardly an exclusive Chase benefit. Priority Pickup benefits will be missed, especially when taking a ride from an airport.

I’ve rarely found the scheduled fares to be reasonable (compared to booking on demand), but at least it was a savings if you felt obligated to book one in advance because few drivers may be available. Priority Pickup is a big loss. These would also often be an upgrade from a base vehicle.

Atmos Rewards is the joint loyalty program that serves both Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines. It launched in 2025, a year after Alaska acquired Hawaiian.

The program is gaining popularity among frequent flyers thanks to its valuable points and robust network of partners. Plus, it won a TPG Award in 2026 thanks to some unique new features we haven't seen with any other airline.

Atmos Rewards has four elite status tiers that each come with exclusive benefits and can improve your overall travel experience. Those are perks you'll be able to tap into whether you're flying on Alaska, Hawaiian, or one of their partners in the Oneworld alliance.

Benefits range from complimentary first-class upgrades to lounge access and extra-legroom seats.

And top-tier Atmos status includes one of the U.S. airline industry's most alluring perks: unlimited, space-available upgrades into lie-flat seats on long-haul routes.

In this guide, we’ll explain the different Atmos Rewards elite status tiers, how to qualify for them, the benefits they offer and how to decide if pursuing status is worth the effort.

Atmos Rewards offers four elite status tiers, which members reach by accruing enough "status points" in a calendar year.

You can earn status points through Alaska, Hawaiian and eligible partner flights, as well as through spending on cobranded credit cards and select non-air partners.

Anyone can join the Atmos Rewards program for free online.

Once you do, you'll be able to start earning both Atmos Rewards points (which you can redeem on flights) and status points (which count toward the elite tiers).

Atmos Rewards' elite status tiers, from lowest to highest, are: Silver, Gold, Platinum and Titanium.

Like with most airline loyalty programs, the perks become more lucrative as you climb the status ladder.

As you remain loyal to these airlines and reach higher tiers, the perks become more lucrative.

Plus, because Alaska and Hawaiian are part of the Oneworld global airline alliance, you'll enjoy reciprocal benefits when you enter your Atmos number while flying on other alliance members — including top partner American Airlines.

Pro tip: Your Atmos Rewards points can also be really valuable when booking flights on American

For flights in 2026, Atmos Rewards members generally earn status points based on the distance flown, with the earning rate varying by fare class and airline.

For example, a first-class ticket on Alaska Airlines or Hawaiian Airlines in the J fare class earns status points equal to 200% of the distance flown, while many economy fares earn status points equal to 100% of the distance flown.

Beginning Jan. 1, 2027, Atmos Rewards members will have more flexibility in how they earn. Members can choose to earn points and status points based on distance traveled, price paid or segments flown:

You can change your selection once per year. Current members who do not make a selection will continue earning based on distance traveled. New members who don't make a selection will earn based on the dollars they pay.

It is possible to earn Atmos Rewards elite status entirely through credit card spending.

The Atmos™ Rewards Ascent Visa Signature® credit card earns 1 status point for every $3 spent on purchases, while the Atmos™ Rewards Summit Visa Infinite® credit card earns 1 status point for every $2 spent. There is no cap on the number of status points you can earn through purchases on either card.

Additionally, Atmos Rewards Summit cardholders receive 10,000 status points each account anniversary. That means a cardholder who receives the anniversary bonus could earn Atmos Silver status simply by spending an additional $20,000 on the card.

If you have elite status with another eligible airline, you may be able to match it to Atmos Rewards Silver, Gold or Platinum status for 90 days.

Atmos Rewards currently offers status matches to eligible elite members of Aeromexico, Air Canada, Delta Air Lines, Frontier Airlines, JetBlue, Southwest Airlines and United Airlines. The Atmos Rewards tier you receive depends on your status with the other airline.

To keep your matched status beyond the initial 90 days, you must earn a certain number of base points on qualifying Alaska Airlines or Hawaiian Airlines flights during that period.

The status match is available only once per Atmos Rewards account, and your existing airline status must have been earned through flight activity rather than credit card spending or a promotional offer.

Alaska has a full list of its status match partners on its website.

You can also earn status points through a variety of Atmos Rewards' non-airline partners, including hotel, cruise, car rental and everyday partners. These include brands such as Marriott, IHG, Choice Hotels, Avis, Budget and Lyft, as well as Atmos Rewards Shopping and Atmos Rewards Dining. Earning rates vary by partner.

Additionally, members can earn status points on award flights booked with Atmos Rewards points, meaning even flights you don't pay for with cash can help you work toward elite status.

The perks are great for all members with Atmos elite status, but as you move up the tiers, the benefits become even more worthwhile.

This is the lowest elite tier in the Atmos Rewards program, where you will receive benefits when flying on Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines, such as:

As you level up within Atmos, you will receive all the same perks as Silver, plus:

Upon reaching Platinum, you will receive all the same perks as Gold, as well as:

This is the top tier in the Atmos program for its most frequent travelers. You will receive all the same perks as Platinum, plus:

In addition to the standard status perks, Alaska also lets you pick from a menu of optional perks each time you hit a new milestone. These start before you actually reach elite status.

Alaska continues to offer milestone perks beyond the 135,000 status points threshold for Titanium status. You can select from additional perk menus at the 150,000; 200,000 and 250,000 status points milestones.

Atmos Rewards offers multiple cobranded credit cards issued by Bank of America, including personal and business cards. They offer the following benefits. (Terms apply.)

In addition to the valuable redeemable points earned, Atmos cards come with perks like free checked bags, discounts on inflight purchases and the ability to earn points toward elite status.

Out of the three options above, the Summit card offers the quickest path toward elite status because it earns 1 point for every $2 spent, versus the others that earn 1 point for every $3 spent. If your main goal is elite status, that would be the card to prioritize.

Yes — especially if you regularly fly Alaska Airlines or Hawaiian Airlines, or expect to do so in the future.

Atmos Rewards elite status offers many of the perks frequent flyers have come to expect, including priority services, complimentary upgrades, bonus points and other travel benefits. But the program's value goes beyond the standard elite-status perks.

One of this program's biggest draws is the ability to earn milestone rewards as you accumulate status-qualifying points. These rewards can include valuable extras like upgrade certificates, lounge access and bonus points, giving members more opportunities to get something out of their loyalty beyond simply reaching the next status tier.

At the very top of the elite status tiers, Atmos Titanium members receive access to a particularly unusual perk: complimentary, space-available upgrades on the day of departure to international business-class suites on eligible long-haul flights. It's a benefit no other U.S. airline loyalty program currently offers, and it gives top-tier members another reason to stick with Alaska and Hawaiian when flying internationally.

Atmos Rewards can also offer value beyond Alaska and Hawaiian flights. Through its Oneworld alliance membership and close partnership with American Airlines, Atmos elite members can enjoy reciprocal benefits when flying American, too. These include preferred seating, priority services and eligibility for complimentary upgrades on qualifying flights, subject to availability and upgrade priority. In other words, earning status with Atmos Rewards can make flying on multiple airlines more rewarding.

Ultimately, if Alaska or Hawaiian is already part of your regular travel routine, Atmos Rewards elite status could be worth pursuing. And if you're able to earn enough status points to unlock milestone rewards along the way, the program becomes even more compelling.

Related: Alaska Airlines baggage fees and how to avoid paying them

Atmos Rewards stands out among U.S. airline loyalty programs, combining Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines under one program while offering valuable points, flexible ways to earn status and unique elite perks. Top-tier Titanium members, for example, can receive space-available upgrades to lie-flat business class on Alaska and Hawaiian flights.

When considering whether Atmos elite status is worth pursuing, think about where and how often you expect to travel and whether you will fly Alaska, Hawaiian and their partners enough to take advantage of the benefits.

Overall, Atmos elite status can make an Alaska or Hawaiian flying experience even more rewarding, particularly for frequent travelers who can maximize its upgrade, earning and partner benefits.

And remember, having Atmos Rewards status can help you out on American Airlines flights, too.

#6207. Lufthansa Realizes 28 Business Class Seats Isn’t Enough For Boeing 787

In recent times, Lufthansa has started taking delivery of factory fresh Boeing 787s, featuring the carrier’s all-new Allegris cabins. Management at the airline has reportedly decided that the configuration of these planes isn’t quite right for many routes, so now it’s planning some updates.

That’s a sensible change, but it always just feels like Lufthansa is a step behind when it comes to acting logically and catching onto trends, no?

Lufthansa currently has a fleet of 20 Boeing 787-9s. Four of these were acquired secondhand (they were former Hainan Airlines jets), while 16 are brand new, and feature Allegris interiors. Not only that, but Lufthansa has at least another 22 of these planes on order, which will be delivered in the coming years.

In the long run, the Dreamliner is supposed to be the carrier’s primary long haul aircraft based in Frankfurt, complementing the Boeing 747-8s and Boeing 777-9s. Meanwhile Munich (MUC) is primarily getting Airbus A350s (including the A350-900 and A350-1000).

Lufthansa’s 787s are configured with 287 seats, including 28 business class seats, 28 premium economy seats, and 231 economy seats. Keep in mind that three of those seats aren’t even certified yet (but should be certified before the end of 2026), so actual business class capacity is currently just 25 seats.

Anyway, even with all seats certified, Lufthansa Group management has decided that the capacity doesn’t actually match demand on many routes, with CEO Carsten Spohr indicating that the airline is working on installing more business class and premium economy seats on upcoming Dreamliners.

Reportedly nothing has been finalized yet, as this is still in negotiations with suppliers, but the idea remains that the current configuration doesn’t offer enough premium seats.

Given the eventual size of Lufthansa’s Dreamliner fleet, it would also be reasonable to think the airline may have two configurations in the long run, to reflect the demand of different destinations. For example, one would assume that the potential customer demand profile would be different to New York (JFK) than to Columbus (CMH), both of which are going to be Dreamliner routes in the coming months.

I know ragging on Lufthansa is just too easy, from its challenging labor relations, to its botched Allegris rollout, and more. However, I can’t help but feel like the airline is a little behind on trends.

I mean, for how long have we been talking about the surge in premium travel demand? American is taking delivery of 787-9s with 51 business class seats, United is taking delivery of 787-9s with 64 business class seats, and British Airways is reconfiguring 787-9s with eight first class seats and 38 business class seats.

So Lufthansa just taking delivery of dozens of factory fresh 787s with just 28 business class seats seems a little off, especially since Lufthansa only recently started adding these planes to its fleet.

I get that demand differs between markets, and the 787 is actually supposed to be the less premium plane in the fleet, in the long run (with the Boeing 747s and 777Xs being the most premium Frankfurt-based planes), but still, 28 seats just doesn’t seem like a lot by any metric. Heck, the Airbus A330s that are slowly being retired have 42 business class seats, and that’s an overall smaller plane.

Of course the whole Lufthansa Allegris and SWISS Senses situation is just sort of messy, from the 3.5-seat first class cabin that makes no sense, to the need to install a weight on SWISS A330s to balance out the weight of first class, to the new Allegris seats delaying entry into service for planes by years, despite it not actually being that cutting edge at this point.

Lufthansa Group CEO Carsten Spohr has indicated that the airline is considering a new configuration for many upcoming Boeing 787s. Management has decided that 28 business class seats and 28 premium economy seats isn’t sufficient, which strikes me as a rather obvious, when you look at trends. Heck, these Dreamliners are partly replacing planes with 50% more business class seats.

I’m curious to see what Lufthansa eventually settles on for a premium Dreamliner configuration, because I agree, 28 business class seats isn’t a lot!

What do you make of Lufthansa reconsidering its 787 layout?

Your statement that ‘ragging on Lufthansa is almost too easy’ sums up the situation nicely. Can anyone really remember a time when this airline, and LH group in general, wasn’t a joke? Remember when Lufthansa itself could seriously claim to be among the most premium and reliable brands on earth? It’s long been a trope that British Airways is the airline that most severely shredded its premium image, especially under Cruz. But he lasted less than 5 years running BA, and they’ve spent the last 6 years doing (just) enough to recover some of that, and are arguably about halfway there at best in terms of repairing the damage. Spohr has had a dozen years to wreck Lufthansa, with no end in sight, and they clearly cannot start repairing the damage until he goes. The fact they continue to get the most basic planning wrong, misreading or ignoring clear industry trends, just underlines this. Among the flagship European carriers, LH is just so far behind Air France, and even BA as things stand, it’s hard to imagine when they can actually try to catch up, saddled with their current leadership.

How Sophr is still CEO just shows you how the LH board and management is clueless. Its one bad decision after another and they keep the guy on...

Nah they just knew all the premium travelers were going to spend their money elsewhere. Smart. :D

......yet still there is no accountability. Now that AA seem to have finally seen the light, LH must be out on their own as the most incompetant managemnt for a major airline

The whole Allegris philosophy was a gamble on one very specific aspect: segmenting customers with different seat types. The allegris business class seat is a very inefficient seat. It is essentially the same concept as united’s Polaris, except with more seat pitch, and every second row, just one middle seat instead of two. Lufthansa thought they could segment their business class customers, upsell certain seats (especially the throne seats, the long bed and the mini-first class at the bulkhead) and make up for the lost revenue of having such an inefficient layout and shrinking the size of the cabin (to maintain a large economy class cabin). But this gamble failed, because Lufthansa didn’t realise that by upcharging so many business class passengers even to simply select a window seat put a bad taste in many people’s mouths. Look at BA, AF and KL. all business class seats in their cabins are created more or less equal with the exception of the bulkheads. Furthermore, Frankfurt is a business heavy market, but has less point-to-point business traffic, and a lot of connecting traffic. It is easy for travellers who are not star-alliance loyal to simply connect elsewhere, or fly united across the Atlantic. Lufthansa wanted to create a segmented business class cabin, but instead created a business class “lite” and charged for extras after that. And now they’re stuck with a VERY expensive, delayed seat, which occupies way too much space on their aircraft, and as such they have had to make huge compromises like shrinking the first and business class cabins. They will seriously lose out in the long term.
