#6205. United’s Premium Boeing 787s With New Cabins: Which Routes Do They Fly?

We recently saw United Airlines introduce its long awaited new Boeing 787-9s, featuring all-new cabins, which are being branded as United Elevate. This represents the evolution of the carrier’s long haul experience, including all-new Polaris business class seats.

Of course one common question is which routes actually feature these new planes. So in this post, I’d like to go over that — which planes have the new cabins, and which routes do they fly? The airline is flying these planes on an increasing number of routes out of two hubs, so there are more opportunities to try this product.

Prior to 2026, United already had over 80 Boeing 787 Dreamliners in its fleet, split between the 787-8, 787-9, and 787-10 variants. However, United is now taking delivery of another 71 Boeing 787-9s, which recently started to be delivered (in addition to 56 Boeing 787-10s, which will be delivered as of 2028).

What’s exciting about these planes is that they feature an all-new passenger experience, and are in an ultra premium configuration. The planes feature just 222 seats, compared to the 257 seats you’ll find on all the previous 787-9s.

If you want to actually fly a United Boeing 787-9 with the new United Elevate interiors, what are your best odds of getting on one of these? The good news is that they’re consistently scheduled on certain routes.

As it currently stands, United has 16 of these 787s in its fleet, with several more expected to be delivered in the coming months. United plans to have 33 of these jets by 2028, so the airline is taking delivery of an average of around one of these per month (though the pace has been even faster in the first several months).

When you go to book a ticket, the best way to tell if a flight is operated by the new plane is whether you see “Polaris Studio available” listed under the United Polaris fare options (assuming those seats are for sale). Otherwise there are no obvious indicators, other than looking at the seat map.

We recently saw the IATA winter season kick off, and with that, we’re seeing the plane based out of both Houston (IAH) and San Francisco (SFO).

You’ll currently find the 787 with Elevate interiors scheduled to fly to the following destinations out of San Francisco:

You’ll then find the 787 with Elevate interiors scheduled to fly to the following destinations out of Houston:

Let me emphasize that schedules are always subject to change (especially when Boeing delivery delays are a potential factor), and the above is just how things currently stand. I’m also not including flights between San Francisco and Houston, which sometimes see the plane so that it can be rotated between hubs, but obviously that route doesn’t feature the true Polaris soft product.

In recent months, we’ve seen United start to take delivery of its brand new Boeing 787-9s, featuring a more premium layout, plus new cabins. These are exciting planes for passengers, as they feature a much improved onboard experience. They’re also great in terms of upgrade and award availability, given the number of premium seats.

If you want to fly United’s new 787s, you’ll currently find them flying out of Houston and San Francisco. Out of Houston, they’re primarily flying to London, Sao Paulo, Sydney, and Tokyo, while out of San Francisco, they’re primarily flying to London and Singapore. It’s great to see the pace at which United is taking delivery of these planes.

I look forward to trying the new interiors, though I’m hoping to wait until these planes have Starlink installed, since I think that really completes the experience.

What do you make of United’s new Boeing 787-9s, and the routes they’re flying?

Flying SIN SFO in a 'Studio' seat next week. We'll see. I'm already reading that many of the advertised soft product features are not being loaded.

I just flew Biz on the SIN-SFO route a couple of weeks ago. It was quite nice despite 16 hours in a confined metal tube. A couple of callouts - you have to get the flight attendant to unlock your door - it took him seeing me repeatedly try to figure out how to close it to come over and use his passkey to unlock it (a little irritating). And I have to say, the touchpad for operating the seat and lights was not very intuitive to me and I like to think I'm pretty savvy with those things. And apparently for some of the new planes, the wired headphone jack didn't work at my seat (taped over). The gate agent in SIN and flight attendant were very proactive in telling me the bluetooth worked (once I figured out how to pair it) and the gate agent gave me 7500 miles as compensation. Food was decent, didn't blow me away, but very good, even the chicken. The crew also locked the exterior windows to keep it dark. Overall, the seat is quite comfortable and the flight crew was excellent (though the purser seemed stretched and if you weren't GS or 1K, I wasn't on his radar). Would be nice if purser didn't exclude regular pax in biz when thanking them for flying and loyalty.

#6204. Former American Airlines CEO Explains How Carriers Use Wall Street Analysts To Pressure Rivals To Stop Growing

Doug Parker says airline executives don’t collude by signaling to competitors. However, the former American Airlines CEO explains how executives use Wall Street analysts to pressure other airlines over decisions they don’t like or to back off from competition. On this week’s Airlines Confidential, Parker rejects suggestions of signaling: it “absolutely, positively does not happen.” Yet earlier, describing how airlines enlist analysts, he says they’ll put it to an analyst: “ask them why they’re doing this.” Airlines don’t need a secret meeting where everyone agrees to raise fares. They have fare filings that competitors watch, earnings calls that competitors listen to, and analysts who cover several airlines and can make life uncomfortable for the one that’s adding seats. Whether it violates antitrust law depends on the particulars, but executives certainly do try to send signals to other airlines. American Paid $45 Million To Settle A Capacity Collusion Case While Parker was CEO, American agreed in 2018 to pay $45 million to settle a private antitrust class action. Passengers alleged that major airlines coordinated capacity restraint to increase fares. American also agreed to cooperate with plaintiffs pursuing the remaining defendants. American denied wrongdoing, but paid a very real amount to resolve exactly the sort of allegation he suggests is almost unimaginable. Parker Even Emailed Delta’s CEO Directly To Collude The Justice Department’s 2013 complaint challenging the American–US Airways merger described a 2010 email exchange about a Delta’s aggressive promotion and expansion. Parker, then running US Airways, complained internally about the effect on everyone’s profitability, portrayed Delta as foolish to Wall Street, and forwarded the chain to CEO Richard Anderson. Anderson sent it on to his general counsel. I’ve written about this before. It’s particularly striking because the old email chain and the new podcast describe the same intermediary: Wall Street. Airlines Can Send A Message Without Sending An Email Airlines publish fares through the Airline Tariff Publishing Company. That lets travel sellers distribute prices, and lets competing airlines see and respond to them. Matching a competitor’s fare isn’t, by itself, evidence of an agreement. But pricing departments know how to use the system to get each other’s attention. Fare basis codes. These combinations of letters and numbers identify fares and their rules. I’ve covered the less subtle examples, including discount fares in a competitor’s home market with codes ending in “FU.” That isn’t information a passenger needs to choose a ticket. Economist Severin Borenstein’s account of the government’s earlier fare-filing case explains how codes and footnotes could connect retaliatory fares across markets. Retaliation somewhere else. In the American–JetBlue litigation, the government’s trial filing described JetBlue responding to an American $139 Boston–Los Angeles fare with $139 fares on five routes involving American hubs. The matching amount helped make the connection obvious. Flash fares. The same filing, citing testimony and internal records, described JetBlue planning to flash American over $44 Boston–Philadelphia pricing in February 2020. A fare filing could be used to draw the other airline’s attention to a pricing dispute. Scott Kirby Has Been Doing This In Chicago I laid out the strategy in January when United CEO Scott Kirby used his earnings call to promise a response to American’s growth at Chicago O’Hare. He wanted analysts asking American why it would expand into a fight that United was promising to make expensive. The intended pressure has two audiences. American hears that United will respond. Analysts hear that American’s investment may produce losses, and can press management to stop. If that deters American, United protects its position without having to operate all the additional flights it threatened. An analyst can legitimately believe American is making a bad investment. But American also has to consider the value of a competitive Chicago network to corporate customers, connecting traffic and AAdvantage credit card spending. United’s preferred accounting of the market isn’t necessarily the right one for American or its customers. Bob Crandall Was Less Subtle American’s former chief Bob Crandall famously called Braniff’s Howard Putnam in 1982 and proposed: Raise your goddamn fares twenty percent. I’ll raise mine the next morning. Putnam recorded the conversation and gave it to the government. He didn’t accept the proposal. The Fifth Circuit nevertheless reinstated the government’s attempted-monopolization case, rejecting the idea that an agreement had to be completed for that claim to proceed. Parker’s underlying point about hubs is sensible. An airline with connecting traffic, corporate contracts and loyal local customers has advantages a new entrant doesn’t. You don’t need a secret agreement to explain why a competing hub is hard to build. But natural advantages and efforts to discourage competition can both be true at the same time (and even true without running afoul of the law). That’s why Parker’s narrative about using analysts to send messages is useful. The executive who wants a rival to stop growing doesn’t have to call up directly and ask. It can be enough to make that the next question on its earnings call. I laid out the strategy in January when United CEO Scott Kirby used his earnings call to promise a response to American’s growth at Chicago O’Hare. He wanted analysts asking American why it would expand into a fight that United was promising to make expensive.

The intended pressure has two audiences. American hears that United will respond. Analysts hear that American’s investment may produce losses, and can press management to stop. If that deters American, United protects its position without having to operate all the additional flights it threatened.

An analyst can legitimately believe American is making a bad investment. American’s former chief Bob Crandall famously called Braniff’s Howard Putnam in 1982 and proposed:

Raise your goddamn fares twenty percent. I’ll raise mine the next morning.

Putnam recorded the conversation and gave it to the government. He didn’t accept the proposal. The Fifth Circuit nevertheless reinstated the government’s attempted-monopolization case, rejecting the idea that an agreement had to be completed for that claim to proceed.

Parker’s underlying point about hubs is sensible. An airline with connecting traffic, corporate contracts and loyal local customers has advantages a new entrant doesn’t. You don’t need a secret agreement to explain why a competing hub is hard to build. But natural advantages and efforts to discourage competition can both be true at the same time (and even true without running afoul of the law).

That’s why Parker’s narrative about using analysts to send messages is useful. The executive who wants a rival to stop growing doesn’t have to call up directly and ask. It can be enough to make that the next question on its earnings call.
